The kit now treats "fewer than two archives found" as COULD NOT LOOK rather
than NOTHING WRONG — it says so and exits 0, and still fails wherever the
estate is actually present. Verified both ways before this push: the ratchet
still refuses a regression here, and a copy of this archive on its own in a
temporary directory reports "not run" and exits 0.

commits.subject: The harmonisation ratchet was one looser than the truth
commits.body:
check:pages was set to the count before this afternoon's exemptions landed,
which left it a page slacker than reality — and a ratchet with slack in it
lets exactly one page slip back before anybody notices, which is the whole
thing it exists to prevent.
Tightened to today's actual count.

commits.subject: The errands and the shot list, both drawn by the kit, both still sorted this archive's way
commits.body:
Two pages moved to shared components and neither lost its argument.
ERRANDS. The panel is the kit's now; the grouping is not. This archive sorts
by whether anybody has replied — answered, out and waiting, waiting on a
person, closed — which is a different question from Defranceski's (what
would the answer buy) and D'Arcy's (where has the request got to). The Rule
ornament stays too, so each group keeps its own heading.
One real fault found on the way. An unknown status fell through to
`LABEL.blocked`, which quietly relabelled a state nobody had defined as
"Blocked" — a known answer standing in for an unknown one. Unknown statuses
are counted and named now.
PHOTOGRAPH THESE. The panel is the kit's Shotlist. The numbered priority
stays, because this archive ranks by what the picture would settle rather
than by how much effort the trip is worth, and `what_to_capture` stays its
own line rather than folding into the prose — that line is the difference
between a useful trip and a wasted one.
Also wires check:pages at 6, the estate's harmonisation ratchet.

commits.subject: A third son of Justa Pastora, found because the index date was impossible
commits.body:
Hilario Barros Llerena, christened at Canelones and indexed "19 April
1726" - the first year of the collection, and the same artefact that put
his cousin Carlos Ambrosio Florencio in 1726 earlier the same day. This
archive now knows to read that as a flag rather than a date.
The plate gives the year: "El dia DIEZ Y NUEVE DE ABRIL del ano de mil
ochocientos t[reinta y cinco], yo Don FRANCISCO LARROBLA, Cura y Vicario
de esta Parroquia de los Canelones, bautice solemnemente a un parvulo ...
por nombre HILARIO, hijo legitimo de MAN[uel Zeferino Barros] natural de
PERNAMBUCO, y de JUSTA LLERENA ... padrinos PEDRO ANTONIO LLERENA y
VICENTA VEGA."
So Justa Pastora has three sons by Manuel Zeferino Barros at roughly
two-year intervals - 1831, 1833, 1835 - and at every font but the first
the godparents are her own brothers and sisters. At the first it was the
President of the Republic. And Pedro Antonio Lerena with Vicenta Vega
have now been found standing at two different nephews' fonts seventeen
years apart, in 1835 at Canelones and 1852 at the Aguada.
His birth date is left unresolved and the column carries only the year.
The index says 16 March 1835; the act's own phrase appears to end "del
mismo", which would put it in April. Read at four times magnification and
still not settled - and 16 March has now turned up as an indexed birth
for three children of this family, two of them confirmed on their plates
and this one not.

commits.subject: Three rules back from the other archives, each better than what I had
commits.body:
A negative must carry proof that the instrument reached the place - the
entry before the gap and the entry after it, numbering continuous across
the page break. That is a null carrying its own evidence, where a control
query only borrows evidence from something run nearby.
A positive proves the service answered FOR THAT COLLECTION. Where access
is per-collection, a hit in an open one vouches for nothing in a
restricted one.
And a service honest in one place while fabricating in another, at the
same moment, is worse than one that always lies: a consistent liar is
caught once and distrusted for ever.
Plus the thing that hid this longest, and it is worth more than the
rules. The plate host served images perfectly all afternoon, in the same
browser, while the search fabricated. A day of successful image reads is
not evidence that the search is healthy. The host you are watching is not
the one that is lying.

commits.subject: The account was never signed out, and one tab would have told me
commits.body:
Correcting this archive's own correction. It published that the
FamilySearch account had expired and that David would have to sign in.
That was wrong and it asked a person for something the machine could
settle.
A sibling archive on this machine ran the record search and the full-text
search in the same minutes and got 3,652 and 3,967 with the account name
in the nav bar. Each Claude session's in-app browser is a separate
browser with its own cookies. One context lost its auth and recovered by
itself: in a fresh tab the Gonzalez control returned 479,662 and the
query that had returned ten that morning returned ten again.
The symptom was real and the full-text redirect did correctly diagnose a
lost session for that browser. The remedy was the error. Before asking a
person to fix something, open a second tab.
All three held-over nulls were then re-run against that live control and
all three are still zero: Luis x Carolina, Carlos Ambrosio x Luisa, Juan
Arturo x Isidora. Row 70 is closed properly - the same query shape
returns FOUR for Luis with Justiniana, among them "Alberto Otario",
christening 7 October 1850, which is Alberto Octavio's own act. So the
shape reaches this exact father, and for Carolina it returns nothing.
Also in this commit, a worse error and an older one. The register's
Sancho row was given a note this afternoon calling the 1833 FRANCISCO a
priest's slip, claiming every plate-read record says SANCHO, and putting
the count at "one act against five". All three are false and this
archive's own file and its own hypotheses page already said so - the 1846
La Mauricia acts were read off the image and say Francisco, the count is
six against three, and the readings split across methods rather than
along them. The note was written without reading the file.
What the day actually added there is worth more than what it got wrong:
the 1833 act has now been READ OFF THE PLATE - "Fran.co Lerenas y M.a
Fernandez" - so the one Francisco-bearing original is no longer possibly
a machine artefact, and the double-forename reading is stronger than it
was. The 1789 act is image-read too. The earliest and the most awkward
records in that question have both come off the machine, and they still
disagree.

commits.subject: It was a signed-out session, and only one of the two searches admits it
commits.body:
Correcting this afternoon's entry to the real cause. The search was not
degraded - the FamilySearch session had expired.
What makes it worth publishing is how differently the two searches behave
about it. Asked the same question in the same minute, the FULL-TEXT
search redirected to the sign-in page: honest, unmistakable, one
navigation. The RECORD search answered "0 - No Results Found", which is
the exact form this archive had been treating as proof of a real null.
The DeepZoom image host went on serving plates throughout, which is why a
whole day of reading images gave no warning at all.
So there is now a free test for a lost session, and it costs one
navigation: ask the full-text search anything. It admits a lost session;
the record search hides one behind a null that satisfies every other rule
on the method page - the stable count, the "No Results Found" line, the
long wait, and a control that passed earlier the same day.
Signing in again is David's to do; this archive does not sign in on his
behalf. Work list row 184 carries what must be re-run afterwards.

commits.subject: The search returned nothing all afternoon and said "No Results Found"
commits.body:
The sixteenth false zero, and it passed every guard this archive had.
"Historical Record Search Results (0)" with "No Results Found" printed
beneath it - the positive assertion of emptiness this archive treats as
the mark of a real null. Stable across two reads twelve seconds apart.
Still zero after ninety seconds. And a control on the same query shape
had passed earlier the same day.
The search was returning zero for everything. Two facts prove it and
neither is a matter of judgement: surname GONZALEZ in Uruguay returned 0,
and the same URL that returned ten records that morning - Avelino Lerena
with Ambrosia Traibel, the ten acts read all day - returned 0 that
afternoon.
What it nearly cost is the point. Alberto Octavio Lerena, whose baptism
act this archive has read off the plate, returned nothing when searched
by name. The obvious reading was a real mechanism: that the parent-pair
query reaches only the keyed index and cannot see acts held in full text
alone. That theory explains the evidence, has consequences for every
parent-pair null here, and is false. It was one step from being written
up. It was built entirely on an outage.
So the rule gains two words. A control must be RECENT - the service was
healthy in the morning and lying by the afternoon - and its answer must
be ARITHMETICALLY IMPOSSIBLE TO BE ZERO. A control that merely ought to
return something fails silently beside the query it was meant to guard.
One class of zero survives untouched: a zero that was turned into a
result by deleting a parameter. Villademoros 0->7 and Hermenegilda 0->3
both stand, because a positive result proves the service was answering.
Only the zeros that stayed zero are in doubt, and row 70's null is
flagged as one of them. Work list row 184 lists what must be re-run.

commits.subject: The sweep's result belongs on the page, not just in the tool
commits.body:
/method/ said "forty-nine rows still rest on a transcript nobody has
checked". That number was stale within the hour and is the exact kind of
claim this archive has a rule about, so the section now carries what the
sweep actually cost: four spelling claims that were the machine's, five
wrong surnames, one wrong parish, one crossed citation, a birthplace that
changed the family's shape, and about twenty-five people who were
standing on the acts and had never been entered.
And the thing worth saying beside all that: the sweep CONFIRMED more than
it corrected. Lavalleja, Maggesi, Larranaga and Rivera's office are all
really on the plates. Only Rivera's spelling was the machine's.
A zero here is a statement about today, not a property of the archive.

commits.subject: Sixty-one rows rested on a machine transcript. Now none of them do.
commits.body:
The last eight plates, and the sweep is finished: 153 of 153 register
rows carrying a source have been read off an image.
The 1922 dispensation No. 14610 gives JUAN CARLOS GONZALEZ LERENA a date
- 8 November 1922, not "the 1920s" - and the bride's name is left unread
rather than guessed, because the hand will not settle it.
The 1903 Pocitos act turns "Amelia Lerena m. DEL SUANDO" into EDUARDO
ZALSAMENDI, a Basque name no search for the other would ever have
reached, and hands over five people the transcript never carried: the
child Maria Margarita, born 21 June 1903; Eduardo's parents Juan
Zalsamendi and Dolores Pou; the godmother; and ADOLFO LERENA, the only
Adolfo in this register, standing at his likely sister's daughter's font.
The 1789 baptism is the earliest record of Sancho here and it spells him
LLERENA. "Fueron padrinos SANCHO LLERENA y JULIANA JOSEFA" at the font of
Juana, daughter of Nicolas Benteno, indio natural de la ciudad del
Tucuman, and Leonarda Correa of Buenos Aires. Three more people entered.
The 1910 San Nicolas form creates a JUAN CARLOS LLERENA at Buenos Aires -
born 16 July 1910, son of Rafael Llerena and Maria Carlota Amadeo Lastra,
with ALEJANDRINA LLERENA signing as godmother in her own hand. He was two
years old when Pablo Armando's enrolment card was written. He is entered
so the next search meets a dated row instead of a fresh hope, and the
same-name pair against Pablo Armando's father is declared with the
arithmetic on the line.
Act 90 of 1913 looked like a wrong citation and was not: it is her
SISTER's wedding to Jose Pedro Massera, and Maria Julia is in it as a
witness - "Fueron testigos, do[na] ... JUANICO DE HERRERA", which is the
only plate-level support this archive has for the Herrera marriage.
The 1840 baptism adds a second set of grandparents, "ambos naturales de
la COLONIA", and names Sancho and Maria Fernandez for the seventh time
today.
And the Ponteceli/Rivero conflict flagged this morning is resolved the
way it looked: the notes were right and the ark was crossed. Their act is
Dominga Josefa's own baptism on film 008166571 image 01130 - "Padrinos
JOSEF PONTECELI y [Agueda Rivero], de la misma Villa" - not the
confirmation list their rows cited. Corrected, and logged.

commits.subject: A way out to the Record Atlas, which seven of eight maps did not have
commits.body:
Every archive draws its map with the kit's Atlas, and until today exactly one
of eight passed recordAtlas. That link is the estate's one connection between
a family's own places and the worldwide research, and seven maps were a dead
end. One prop.
The year control is NOT switched on here, and that is measured rather than an
oversight: none of this archive's 36 atlas places carries a date the
component can read, so the slider would render only "No place here carries a
date". True, and a data gap to fix rather than a feature to ship. Give the
places spans and it turns on with one word.
Verified on an isolated --outDir build: exit 0, the atlas page built, and the
Record Atlas link in the output.

commits.subject: Where the family lived, and where the name Fidel probably comes from
commits.body:
Two Canelones plates, both on film 008166571, both cited here for a week
and never opened.
Image 01176, 11 December 1806: "bautizo solemnemente a un parvulo de un
dia de edad y puso por nombre JOSE LORETO, hijo legitimo de SANCHO LERENA
y de MARIA FERNANDEZ, VECINOS DE ESTA VILLA. Fue padrino JOSE MARTINEZ DE
LA VEGA, vecino de MONTEVIDEO."
This row quoted the transcript as "Sancho Lorena". The plate says LERENA
- the fourth spelling claim in one day to turn out to be the machine's
rather than the scribe's.
Image 01017, 30 August 1795: "bautize, puse el Santo Oleo y Crisma a
AGUSTINA RAMONA, DE TRES DIAS NACIDA, hija legitima de D.n SANCHO LERENA
y de D.a Maria Fernandez, VECINOS DE LA VILLA. Fueron sus padrinos D.n
FIDEL REY, vecino de MONTEVIDEO, y D.a JOSEFA ... de la misma Villa."
She gains a second forename - RAMONA - and "de tres dias nacida" confirms
the 27 August 1795 this register had only from a tree and a padron.
Two things worth more than the corrections. VECINOS DE LA VILLA in 1795
and VECINOS DE ESTA VILLA in 1806: Sancho and Maria were RESIDENTS of
Canelones, not visitors, across at least eleven years - which joins up
with Dominga's baptism there in 1804 and Justa Pastora being called
"natural de Canelones" - and they had moved to Montevideo, calle San Juan
No 60, by the padron of 1812. Both godparents were fetched the other way,
from the capital.
And DON FIDEL REY stood at Agustina Ramona's font in 1795. Sancho's son
FIDEL was born about 1799. This family names children for whoever stands
at the font, in five other acts read here, so the likeliest source of the
forename Fidel in the Lerena is this man - an inference from a pattern
and not from a record, and it does not touch whether the Fidel Lerena who
married Maria Ruedas is Sancho's son.
Eleven transcript-only rows left of sixty-one.

commits.subject: An act this archive had cited for a week, and never opened, holds a child
commits.body:
Film 007713376 images 01176-01177, the Catedral baptism of 19 October
1833. The register had carried the GODFATHER of this act since 14
September and never the CHILD.
AURELIO EUSEBIO BARROS LERENA, born 14 September 1833 - a second son of
Justa Pastora Lerena and Manuel Zeferino Barros, brother of Juan Facundo
Frutuoso, grandson of Sancho. His godparents are his mother's own brother
and sister: "Padrinos ABELINO LERENA y DOMINGA LERENA".
So the transcript's "Abelino Serena" is LERENA on the plate, and the
S-for-L this archive called "one more instance" was the machine's. That
is the third assertion about this family's spelling to fail the same way
today, after the LORENA of an 1889 margin and the FRUCTUOSO RIVERA
printed over the 1831 act's own FRUTUSO RIBERA.
The co-godparent is worth more than the spelling. Dominga Josefa Llerena
Fernandez is a documented daughter of Sancho, so the two at this font are
a documented Sancho daughter and the Abelino this archive has been trying
to place - at the baptism of a third Sancho daughter's child, twenty-five
years before the 1858 acts settled it. Corroboration, not proof: a cousin
can stand beside a sister.
The act was performed "con licencia del Cura y Vicario D.r D. DAMASO
LARRANAGA" - the first Vicar Apostolic of Montevideo, and the fourth
famous name checked against a plate today, and the fourth to be really
there.
And one line needs care. The act gives the child's maternal grandparents
as "Fran.co Lerenas y M.a Fernandez". The wife is right; the husband is
called FRANCISCO where five other plates call him SANCHO. The obvious
reading is a priest's slip - Sancho was dead by 1832 and the man writing
in 1833 never knew him. It is recorded anyway, because FRANCISCO is not a
neutral name in this archive's Spanish question, and it is recorded
explicitly so that it is on the record and not used. One act against five
is not a second name.
Thirteen transcript-only rows left of sixty-one.

commits.subject: One line on a page of one-line entries, and it is the whole of what he has
commits.body:
Three more plates. Fifteen transcript-only rows left of sixty-one, and a
hundred and nineteen seen on one.
Film 007713376 image 01498, the Catedral baptism of 4 July 1837. Every
reading in the row survives: born 20 February 1837, daughter of Don Pedro
Antonio Lerena, mother natural del Cerro Largo, paternal grandparents Don
Sancho and Dona Maria Fernandez, and godparents "D. LUIS LERENA y D.na
CAROLINA ORIBE" - the uncle and his first wife, on the plate. The margin
writes the family LERENA with one L where 1811 and 1831 write LLERENA
with two.
Film 008165032 image 00505, the Canelones confirmations of 1804: "JOSE
ESCLAVO DE MAN.L LOPEZ PADRINO SANCHO LLERENA". One line on a page of
one-line entries, and it is the whole of what any record gives him. The
entries around him have the same shape - a forename, a parent, a
godfather - so the form is the register's and not a slight peculiar to
him. What is peculiar to him is that where the others read "hijo de", he
reads "esclavo de".
And opening that page exposed a citation this archive had crossed. Joseph
Ponteceli and Agueda Rivero are noted as godparents at the BAPTISM of
Dominga Josefa Llerena on 15 May 1804, but their source cites the
CONFIRMATION list, on which neither appears in the portion read. Dominga
Josefa's own row cites a different ark for that baptism - film 008166571
image 01130, the right parish and the right year, which was also opened.
The likely reading is that the ark on their rows is simply wrong, two
records taken down in one sitting off one search. It is not assumed: the
alternative is that the note is wrong and they are confirmation
godparents. Both rows now carry the conflict and a named test.

commits.subject: The archive read a margin as though it were the sentence
commits.body:
Film 008165116 image 01442, Montevideo civil death registration No. 622
of 1889 - Victor Lerena, alpargatero. Three register rows stood on a
machine transcript of it.
The row for his father said the surname "is written LORENA for him and
LERENA for his son and his father in the same sentence", and built a
claim about this family's spelling on it. The sentence says LERENA
throughout: "el finado era hijo de PEDRO LERENA y JOSEFA SEGUEIRA,
orientales, finados". LORENA is the MARGIN - "Num. 622 Victor Lorena" -
the clerk's index entry, not the text. The family's confusion of L and Ll
is real; this instance of it was the archive reading an index.
SEGUEIRA, not Seguera. Galician, and a different search.
The plate also carried what the transcript had dropped. A cause of death:
TUBERCULOSIS PULMONAR, per the medical certificate. The fact that the
registration is "de oficio", which is why no relative signs it. And a
third generation - "maternos JOSE SEGUEIRA y RAMONA" - two people nobody
had entered.
Ramona keeps a forename and no surname. The act breaks the line after her
name and the next line opens with the single word "apellido" and nothing
before it. That may mean she bore her husband's surname or it may be a
label printed on the form, and this archive will not guess a surname onto
a woman who has only a forename.
And Josefa Segueira had been a name inside somebody else's note since 14
September without ever being a person. The evidence gate caught it the
moment an edge pointed at her.
Nineteen transcript-only rows left of sixty-one.

commits.subject: Juana's name is the only thing any record gives her, so a person read it
commits.body:
Two more plates. Sixty-one transcript-only rows are now twenty-two, and a
hundred and nine have been seen on one.
Film 007713376 image 00601, the 1827 baptism at the Iglesia Matriz. The
name at risk was General Francisco de Paula Maggesi - the third famous
name checked today, and the third to hold. The act says "Fueron padrinos
el Exmo. Sr. Gral. ... ULA MAGGESI y D.a Carolina Amalia", and gives the
child's own birth, 24 April 1827, her mother Dona Dominga Llerena, and
her paternal grandparents the Mayor Don Joaquin Ruiz de Carvallo and Dona
Juana Suarez. Six rows move.
Film 007713375 image 02628, the baptism of 26 September 1812 - the plate
that mattered most for the fewest rows. "que nacio antes de ayer, hija de
JUANA, negra esclava de D.n Sancho Lerena y de D.a Maria Fernandez:
Madrina CATALINA MARTINEZ." A machine is worst at proper nouns, and this
woman's name is the only thing any record gives her, so it was the one
that most needed a human to read it. It is Juana, in the priest's hand.
The plate also carries a trap the archive walked past: the act
IMMEDIATELY BEFORE hers baptises ANOTHER Maria Mercedes on 25 September
1812, "hija de TERESA ABELLEYRA, negra esclava de D.n RAMON ABELLEYRA".
Two enslaved girls of one name, two households, consecutive days, one
page - and this register holds a Teresa of Sancho's household from the
padron who must not be run together with her. Catalina Martinez is
entered as a person: the act gives her no Dona, no husband and no origin,
and she is the only one beside that child who was not her owner.
And Rodrigo Fernandez lost the word "presumed" within the hour of gaining
it. data/padron-1812-image.tsv already recorded him closing Sancho's
household "at 63, ASTURIANO" - so Asturias is attested, his birth is
about 1749, and two documents of successive years put Sancho's
father-in-law under his son-in-law's roof.

commits.subject: The priest drew the family tree, and it holds two people we never entered
commits.body:
Film 007713362 image 02473, the 1911 Lerena-Cardozo dispensation - six
register rows stood on it. The folio is not prose at all. It is "Esquema
explicativo de los grados de parentesco": two kinship diagrams the priest
drew himself, circles for each degree and the names written beside them.
The name this archive had wrong is FLORINDA, not Florencia. Written twice,
in two separate diagrams, in the same hand. Five register rows, the
working log and the last-attested file carried the machine's reading.
And the apex of each schema is a person the transcript never carried into
the register: BERNABE LERENA THE ELDER, father of Bernabe and Maria, and
CUSTODIO CARDOZO, father of Florinda and Eliseo. A whole generation above
the 1911 couple, drawn only because the priest had to prove the
impediment. They exist in this archive because a man drew a circle and
wrote a name beside it, and they have no dates, no places and - for the
Lerena - no wife, because a kinship schema draws only the line it needs.
It also explains the groom's name. CUSTODIO Lerena is named for CUSTODIO
CARDOZO, his mother's father, whose two children's marriages created the
impediment he then had to petition against.
The register held one Bernabe Lerena where the plate shows two, which is
the two-Avelino fault again - and a parish clerk had already solved that
one in 1861 by writing "Avelino Lerena (hijo)". The third Bernabe, of
Trinidad, stays unmerged with a named test on the line.
A hundred rows have now been seen on a plate; thirty are still on a
transcript.

commits.subject: The twins are twins, and the parish was the index's, not the act's
commits.body:
Film 007713378 image 02598, the two Moratorio baptisms of 8 March 1880 -
the plate five register rows stood on. Two findings, opposite in sign.
The first settles a test this register flagged as cheap and unrun. Both
acts state the child's own birth: "que nacio el VEINTE Y CUATRO DE
FEBRERO ultimo". They were born 24 February 1880 and carried to the font
twelve days later. They ARE twins - which is the opposite answer to the
one the same reasoning got in 1858, where Ana Rosario and Alfredo
Justiniano shared a font and were born twenty-one months apart. A shared
baptism date means nothing on its own; it happened to mean twins here.
Declared in consistency.py under a deliberately high bar: a pair goes in
only when BOTH children's own acts state the same date.
The second is a retraction. This archive placed these baptisms at the
UNION, across six register rows, the working log and /uruguay/. The act
reads "con licencia del infrascripto Cura Parroco DE ESTA BASILICA MENOR
Y CATEDRAL DE MONTEVIDEO, bautice solemnemente EN ELLA". They were
baptised in the Catedral. The Union was the INDEX'S PLACE FIELD, copied
as though it were testimony - and it had grown a conclusion on it, that
Avelino Pedro Joaquin Silvestre was christened at the Union in 1866 "the
same parish where his cousins the Moratorio girls were baptised fourteen
years later". That sentence is withdrawn in the open on /uruguay/ rather
than deleted quietly.
The other test on the plate came back empty, which is also an answer. The
Mercedes Lerena row said she could be joined to Mercedes Micaela only if
the 1880 act gave her age or her parents. It gives neither. The rows stay
apart, but now because a page was read rather than never opened.
Two new people the transcript never carried: Francisco Azanola and
Manuela Otondo, godparents to one twin. And a repair the rename broke -
renaming Carolina JUAREZ to SUAREZ silently un-declared her checked pair
in consistency.py, which is now noted in the entry itself.
Ninety-two rows seen on a plate, thirty-six still on a transcript.

commits.subject: Both halves of Sancho's household were Spanish, and the register said otherwise
commits.body:
Two more plates opened off the transcript-only list. Forty-nine rows to
forty-one, and eighty-four now seen on a plate.
Film 007713686 image 02847, the two acts of 12 March 1858 that attach the
Lerena Traibel branch to Sancho. The name most at risk was LAVALLEJA - a
machine that meets a famous Uruguayan surname will write it whether or
not the page says so, which is exactly how FRUCTUOSO RIVERA got printed
over the 1831 act's own FRUTUSO RIBERA. The page says JUSTINIANO
LAVALLEJA, and CONSTANTINO and ANA, in a hand that also spells LERENA and
TRAIBEL correctly on the same line. Ana Rosario's "CATORCE DE ENERO de
mil ocho cientos cincuenta y cinco" is read, not transcribed, and the
parents are "naturales de esta Republica". Seven rows move.
Film 007713375 image 02410, the 1811 baptism of Luis Escolastico - the
only record here naming Sancho's own parents. Four readings survive word
for word and one does not. The transcript gave "Abuelos paternos FELIZ
GERENA y ROSALIA AGUILAR"; the page gives "Ab.s pat.s FELIX LLERENA",
with the double L, in the same hand that writes SANCHO LLERENA two lines
above.
And the plate exposed two failures of propagation, which is this
archive's oldest fault. Maria Fernandez is "nat.l de ASTURIAS" on that
act; the working log has said so since 14 September and her register row
said MONTEVIDEO, with a pin on the atlas to match. Her parents RODRIGO
FERNANDEZ and ROSA FERNANDEZ were read the same day and never entered as
people. Both fixed, and the correction logged.
It changes the family's shape. Both halves of Sancho's household were
Spanish immigrants from opposite ends of Spain - Andalusia and Asturias -
meeting at Montevideo. The register had been telling a different story,
against this archive's own evidence.
tools/plate-read.py does the same edit the same way every time, and
refuses to write if a name is missing or the result would be ragged.

commits.subject: Work list rows 181 and 182: the transcript audit, and Alfredo's wife
The machine wrote the history book's spelling over the page's own
commits.body:
tools/transcript-only.py, written after three surnames turned out to be a
machine's, asks how many register rows cite FULL-TEXT TRANSCRIPT READ and
name no image. Sixty-one did - more than half the rows carrying a source.
It ranks the unopened plates by how many people depend on each, because
one image settles seven rows at once.
The top plate was the 1831 baptism at the Cordon where the President of
Uruguay stood godfather to Sancho's grandson: the most consequential
proper noun in this archive, and a machine had read it. Film 007713388
image 00726, folio 133, opened:
  "padrinos Dn. FRUTUSO RIBERA, PRESIDENTE DE LA REPUBLICA y su esposa
   Da. BERNARDINA FRAGOSO"
Frutuso Ribera, with a B. The transcript printed FRUCTUOSO RIVERA, which
is the spelling in the history books and not what the page says. The
finding holds and is stronger for the check, because the act states the
man's office and names his wife - two independent facts on one line,
either of which identifies him alone. The same page spells the
grandfather LLERENA with the double L, and confirms Pernambuco,
Canelones, and Ana Maria Cabalgante word for word.
So both of today's transcript failures are one failure pointing opposite
ways. A machine invents a plausible name where it cannot read one, and
writes the famous name over the page where it can. The rule is not
distrust transcripts; it is that a transcript is a finding-aid for
everything except the names, and the names are usually why you went.
Seven rows moved off transcript onto plate. Forty-nine remain, and the
tool prints the number.

commits.subject: Three surnames were a machine's, and the archive never opened the page
commits.body:
The rule this archive keeps stating is that an index is not evidence and
the image must be opened. The 1892 marriage act of Alfredo Justiniano
Lerena Traibel was recorded as FULL-TEXT TRANSCRIPT READ - which means a
machine read it - and the plate was never pulled. Three register rows, a
dispensation table, a working log and the last-attested-alive file all
carried the machine's reading for a week.
Film 007713383 image 02601, folio 340: "hija legitima de Don GERONIMO
GAVAZZO y Dona CAROLINA SUAREZ". GAVAZZO, not Gavarro. SUAREZ, not
Juarez. Corroborated by a second image forty-eight years later - her own
Montevideo death registration, which writes her Hermenegilda Gavazzo de
Lerena with the same two parents. Two images against one transcript.
Gavazzo is a known Montevideo surname and Gavarro is not, which is the
sort of tell that should have prompted the check earlier.
And she has a death: 20 June 1940, Montevideo, certificate 632, at R.
Masini 3273, "de estado VIUDA", of a fractured neck of femur. So Alfredo
died between February 1892 and June 1940 - the first thing this archive
has ever known about the end of his life.
The index of that death act is a catalogue of its own failures. It
attaches three children to the couple and there are no children on the
act: one is JOSE M. REYES CORVALAN, the registrar, whose name follows
"ante mi", and two bled across the column rule from the adjacent act,
which concerns a family with English names. It also gives her birth as
1934 for a woman who died in 1940, her nationality as mexicana, her age
as "cu anos de edad" and her birthplace as "Minteridco". Every field is
wrong except the maternal grandparents - and that pair is the only reason
she was found.
The fifteenth false zero, and the rule caught this one. Alfredo with
Hermenegilda GAVARRO returned 0; deleting the mother's surname returned
the three records, because the index writes her "Navarro de Terenadel".
The Villademoros zero cost an afternoon and was caught only by luck. This
one cost a single query, sixty minutes after the rule was written down.

commits.subject: A control licenses the shape of a query, not the value you put in it
commits.body:
The rule this archive published says a null is not written down until a
control in the same form and the same session returns a known result. On
21 September that rule was satisfied and the answer was still a lie.
Avelino Lerena with Celedonia Villademoros returned a clean zero. The
control - the identical shape on Alberto Lerena with Maria Ines Larriera,
minutes earlier - had returned sixteen. Larriera has one spelling in this
register and Villademoros has four, so the control was asked about the
one surname that could not go wrong. What caught the zero was not method:
it was that two of the hidden records were already published here.
So the older rule is sharpened rather than replaced. A nil from a derived
index is first of all a fact about the index, and coverage is not one
thing - it can fail at the collection, as it did for Andalusian parish
registers; at the query shape, as it did for the compound Lerena y
Armenta; or at a single field the source failed to parse, as here. Three
different failures, one identical-looking zero. A published null needs a
date, a control, and a statement of what the instrument could have
reached.
And the gate itself is hardened, because three of today's runs were
killed mid-build by another archive's publish script matching a bare
"astro build" pattern. The build log is now private to the run, since the
shared path let a parallel build in a different project print its failure
as ours; and an exit of 128+N now says the build was TERMINATED BY SIGNAL
and that nothing in the output is evidence about this archive's data.
Two rounds went into looking for a fault in the register before anyone
thought to run ps.

commits.subject: A simpler way into a film image, written down where the next reader looks
commits.body:
tools/fsimage.js pastes a tile-mosaic loader into a console. It still
works, but seven acts were read today without it: resolve the ark through
manifest.json, navigate to dist.jpg, take the img off its fit-to-window
leash by setting an explicit natural width and height, and scroll. The
tab title reports the true pixel size, and dist.jpg is one whole opening
at full resolution.
Two traps go with it, and both cost time today. A hidden browser pane
throttles timers, so `await fetch` never settles and the tool call times
out - navigate and read the page text instead; synchronous JS is fine.
And the screenshot must be its own call, exactly as __view already warns,
or you get the previous view or a black rectangle.
Also recorded: dist.jpg and the tiles are both 401 to curl. They need the
browser session, so none of this can be done from the shell.

commits.subject: Work list row 180: the sweep, and the zero that no control could catch
A parent's surname that removes the records it matches
commits.body:
A parent-pair query on Avelino Lerena and Celedonia Villademoros returns
a clean zero - rows rendered, page settled, read twice. Delete the
mother's SURNAME, keep only "Celedonia", and it returns seven, two of
which are christenings this archive has held since 20 September. That is
how the zero was known to be false. No control would have caught it: the
control for this shape, Alberto Lerena with Maria Ines Larriera, had
returned sixteen records in the same session, which is precisely what
made the zero look trustworthy. Recorded as the fourteenth false zero.
The likely mechanism is that the mother's whole name sits unparsed in the
given-name field, so asking for a surname excludes every record the
parser failed on. One of the seven displays its mother as "Celedonia
Villademoros", spelled exactly as asked, and was still excluded.
What the zero was hiding: Pedro Segundo Lerena Villademoros, dead at
Montevideo 23 August 1936 aged 66, wife Paulina Prando Algar; an Avelino
Lerena dead 5 January 1914 aged 45, wife Carmen Lorente, whose mother is
written VILLADEMORO without the s - a fourth spelling; and marriage
registrations of 1921 for two more. Whether that is four sons or two is
not settled and is not guessed: a man who died in 1914 does not marry in
1921, and the ages come from death certificates.
It also weakens a null this archive published. "LERENA with spouse
surname VILLADEMOROS returns 6,352 records and not one marriage act" was
controlled with LERENA x JUANICO. Juanico has one spelling and
Villademoros has at least four. The control proved the query shape works;
it did not prove this surname is reachable through it. The null is not
withdrawn - it is now stated as the weaker claim it always was.

commits.subject: The errand was done before it was written down, and it found a ninth child
commits.body:
Act No. 246, Montevideo, 2 March 1921 - film 008165205 image 01604, read
off the image. "Que el finado era hijo de Avelino Lerena, fallecido, y de
Ambrosia Treibel, fallecida." The chain from Zelmira Carlota to Sancho
now rests on an image at every step that matters.
And the act does what the index could not. It counts them: "era casado
con Maria Ines Larriera, de cuya union quedan NUEVE HIJOS llamados: Maria
Adelina, Zelmira, Eleiza, Alberto, Carlos, Maria Ines, Maria Consuelo,
Maria Antonieta y Miguel Avelino." Eight of those nine are the eight
found yesterday's way. The third is a daughter no index here has matched,
and her name is not securely read - Eleiza or Eloiza, at three times
magnification, and the archive cannot choose. She is entered as a person
with the uncertainty in her name, because a child named on her father's
death act exists whether or not a birth registration has been found.
Which is the point about eight index entries: they look like eight
confirmations and they are one indexing project reading one set of
registers. One death act, declared by two men who knew the household, is
a different occasion and a different mouth.
The act also gives what no index carried - born at Montevideo, not in San
Jose where his children were; profession RENTISTA; dead at six in the
morning at the calle Juan Paullier of a carcinoma certified by a Dr
Lussich; and the declarants neighbours rather than kin, which is why they
made him sixty-nine fifteen days early.

commits.subject: Copying multiplies the entries and adds nothing to the evidence
commits.body:
Two index entries, two collections, two films, two indexers, agreeing on
a 13 August and on a set of godparents. Any reasonable reader would call
that independent confirmation. It is one act, certified twice.
Stated as a rule on /method/, and instantiated a second time from this
archive's own past: the three baptisms at La Mauricia in January 1846 all
give the year in the identical words, including one for a different
family. Three acts agreeing, one priest, one sitting, and the agreement
means nothing - the children cannot all have been born that year.
One hand, one occasion, one witness.

commits.subject: The archive wrote her off on 14 September, and she is ours
commits.body:
Zelmira Carlota Lerena Larriera, born in the Departamento de San Jose on
4 November 1880, was tested a week ago and closed: "she is NOT ours." The
same row named the one thing that would overturn it - who her father
Alberto Lerena was - guessed Alberto Octavio Lerena Lenguas, and refused
to draw the line on a forename and an age.
It is the other grandfather. Alberto Lerena's Montevideo death
registration of 2 March 1921 names his wife Maria Ines Larriera and his
parents Avelino Lerena and Ambrosia Treibel, so her father is Pedro
Alberto Ysabelino Lerena Traibel of the Aguada, and Zelmira is a
great-granddaughter of Sancho.
And she is one of eight. Asking for Alberto and Maria Ines as a pair
returns a whole household born in San Jose between 1879 and 1898 - Maria
Adelina, Zelmira Carlota, Alberto Julian, Carlos Ambrosio Florencio,
Maria Consuelo, Maria Antonieta, Angel Miguel Avelino, and a Maria Ines
who died at Montevideo eleven months after her father. Three of the eight
carry names out of the household at the Aguada, which is corroboration
and is not the evidence.
The retraction is in corrections.tsv, the chain is written out so it can
be attacked, and the weak link is named: the 1921 registration has been
read at index level only and the image is now an errand.
Thirty-five same-name pairs reviewed and declared - the sharpest being
two Maria Adelina Lerenas fourteen years apart, an aunt and the niece
named for her.

commits.subject: The succession reading is a proposition now, not a note in a working file
commits.body:
Seven certificates, four parishes, one week of November 1896, and a
father dead since August 1890. That belonged on /hypotheses/ with a named
test and a chip that says untested, not in the comment block of a TSV
where the reader this archive is written for would never meet it.

commits.subject: Seven certificates in a row, and grown siblings do not all want one by chance
commits.body:
The film was walked both ways. The Lerena certificates are consecutive -
numbers 147 to 153, pages 78 to 81 - and all seven are children of
Avelino and Ambrosia: Mercedes Micaela, Josefina, Pedro Alberto
Ysabelino, Ana Rosario, Juan Arturo, Andres, Maria Adelina. They are
drawn from four different parishes and lodged within days of each other
in November 1896. Their father died on 22 August 1890. That is what
proving filiation looks like, and it is offered as a hypothesis with a
named test: the Montevideo succession records of 1896.
Two rows move off the index and onto a document. Mercedes Micaela's act
reads "que nacio el ocho de Mayo del ano mil ochocientos sesenta y tres"
with Sancho and Maria Fernandez named as her grandparents. Josefa's
baptism gains a day - 5 December 1852, libro primero al folio 212 - from
the opening of her act on the image before the one already read.
And two readings at fit width were wrong on this film within one hour.
"Noventa y seis" looked like "noventa y cinco" until it was magnified,
and a margin reading SERENA CARLOS two pages from seven genuine Lerena
certificates is DE LA SERNA - a Santander father and an Arequipa mother,
and the father is called Pedro Antonio, which is the name of Sancho's
second son. It was read before it was dismissed.

commits.subject: The certificates were made under a law, and the law is on every page
commits.body:
Film 008166435 image 02852, the second opening. Every certificate opens
"yo Luis Cincinato Bollo, Director General del Registro del Estado Civil,
he certificado, de acuerdo con lo dispuesto por la Ley de 9 de Julio de
1888". Uruguay took registration off the parishes in 1879 and then had
the older baptisms copied across, so a family's whole set of acts sits in
one 1896 volume and the index dates every one of them to 1896. That is
not a fault in one record; it is the shape of a collection.
Andres Lerena Traibel, baptised at the Cordon on 31 December 1861 - the
same day as his brother Juan Arturo, aged four against ten months. His
godfather is written "Avelino Lerena (hijo)", which is the parish saying
in one parenthesis what this archive spent two days deciding.
Maria Adelina, born 13 August 1865, baptised 31 December 1865. Her 1946
death registration says 1861 and the act refutes it - and the reasoning
that doubted the registration was right for the right reason. Her
godparents are Ambrosio Lerena and Carlota Munoz, which are the two names
on the "Marta Adelina, born 1918" record indexed off a different film. It
is one baptism, certified twice, indexed as two children born fifty-three
years apart. The untested item on /method/ is now tested.
And the contradiction gate earned its keep within the minute. Andres's
act says born 16 March 1857 and Alfredo Justiniano was born 2 October
1856. The words were re-read at double magnification and are not
ambiguous, so the fault is not in the reading - it is that Andres's year
survives only in a copy, while Alfredo's comes from the original register
and is corroborated by the age he gave at his own wedding. Andres's birth
column is deliberately empty. The day and the baptism are kept; the year
is not.

commits.subject: A child born six years after his father died, and the index meant it
commits.body:
A parent-pair search on Avelino Lerena and Ambrosia Traibel returned ten
records, three of them dated 1896 and 1919. Avelino died in 1890.
The dates are the certificates'. Film 008166435 image 02850 is an opening
of a register of certified copies issued in 1896, and the indexer takes
the year off the certificate and the day and month off the act inside it.
Read at full resolution, the act says 21 November 1852, born 16 March
1852: Pedro Alberto Ysabelino Lerena, godparents Pedro Antonio Lerena and
Vicenta Vega - his uncle and aunt, and a man born in 1793 who could not
be in a room in 1896. He is the Alberto who died at Montevideo in 1921.
The same opening carries Josefa's own baptism. She has a day at last -
born 10 February 1851 - and her name at the font is Josefina.
Nine children now where the archive held six. Juan Arturo born 16 Feb
1861, Mercedes Micaela born 8 May 1863 with Sancho and Maria Fernandez
named as her grandparents, and Maria Adelina who married Carlos Alberto
Fein. Twenty edges wired, nineteen same-name pairs reviewed and declared.
The trap is on /method/ with the tell that catches it: two children of
one couple indexed with the same birth date.

commits.subject: Asking after the mother found the son's death
commits.body:
Two more work-list rows, both parent-pair questions, and the method
answered them in opposite ways.
ROW 70 — the children of Luis Lerena and Carolina, his first wife. A
parent-pair query returns ZERO, read TWICE because the same session had
a (0) turn into 22 an hour earlier. The control is the same shape on
Luis × Justiniana Lenguas, which returns the two children this archive
holds. So the null is a null: if that first marriage produced children,
they are not in the Uruguayan index, and the parish books are where to
look.
ROW 71 — Justa Pastora's children after 1827. Querying on the MOTHER
rather than the child turned up a DEATH for a man this archive already
had:
  JUAN BARROS LERENA, died 3 May 1915 at Montevideo, aged
  EIGHTY-THREE, registered 4 May, certificate 261
He is JUAN FACUNDO FRUTUOSO BARROS LERENA, Sancho's grandson, baptised
at the Cordón on 13 December 1831. The arithmetic is exact: a man born
27 November 1831 is eighty-three on 3 May 1915. The registration names
his mother JUSTA LERENA and his father "MANUEL C BARROS" — which is the
Manuel Zeferino Barros of Pernambuco already in this register, the C
standing for Ceferino.
AND IT NAMES A WIFE NOBODY HAD: EMILIA ANTELO, now in the register as
the surviving spouse and nothing more, because the record gives her
nothing else.
Exact death dates in this archive: 17 → 19. Of 300 people, 22 are now
known to have died at all.
Register 299 → 300. Two pairs declared.

commits.subject: Two parents searched as a pair find children either name alone buries
commits.body:
Work list row 52, run across the register's twenty couples. It is a
method rather than a lookup and it earns its place: searching two
parents as ONE PAIR surfaces children that either name alone loses in a
crowd of the same surname.
PEDRO LLERENA AND SOFÍA CLAVIJO — six records where this archive held
ONE child. Isabel (b. 14 Nov 1895), Celina (d. 11 May 1917), Telma
(b. 2 May 1900) and Tomasa Cantidia (b. 12 Feb 1903) are now in the
register beside Susana, and Sofía Clavijo has an entry of her own after
being a bare node on the charts. Four of the five are indexed under the
compound LLERENA CLAVIJO, which names both parents in the surname
itself — the evidence is in the name.
MAURICIO LERENA AND CASIMIRA MONTAÑO — twelve records, and one is
explicit: CIPRIANO LERENA MONTAÑA, whose 1928 death registration at
Flores gives the parents outright. He is entered. FOUR MORE ARE NOT:
Manuel, two Ignacias and Clara match the pair query but their own
entries do not name the parents, and this archive does not enter a
child on a query shape alone. The dates fit a marriage of 1837 and they
are written down as candidates.
Luis Lerena × Justiniana Lenguas returns only what is already held.
Francisco Llerena × Rafaela Daraz returns only Baldomero.
AND THE METHOD HAS THE OLD TRAP IN IT. Bernabé Lerena × Casimira Peláez
read "(0)" and, four seconds later, 22 — on a couple whose four
children this archive has held since 13 September. It was caught only
because the answer was already known to be wrong, which is exactly what
caught the first one on 14 September. It is the thirteenth entry in the
false-zeros catalogue on /method/.
Register 293 → 299. Six new people, ten edges, two pairs declared.

commits.subject: The corpus moved under a published null, and it is our own document
commits.body:
Work list row 157 — re-run any exact-forename null recorded against a
two-forename person. The archive's own note says none could be found by
grep, "because the searches were written down in prose without naming
the parameter", so the sharpest available version was run instead: the
CENTRAL null, in the fuzzy-forename / exact-surname shape.
The trap is real. Fuzzy "Juan" with exact LERENA returns 29 distinct
given-name forms, among them JUAN CARLOS ESTEBAN LERENA, JUAN A. LERENA
and JUAN P. LERENA — the three-forename and initial shapes a
whole-string exact match cannot reach. None is the father; the Esteban
man married in 1932.
BUT THE RE-RUN FALSIFIED TWO PUBLISHED ZEROES ON /direct-line/.
  "Father exactly 'Juan Carlos Lerena', mother unconstrained — 0 — no
   indexed child of ANY man recorded exactly as Juan Carlos Lerena"
  "Juan Carlos Lerena as a named person, any role, any country, any
   collection — 1 — and it is not him"
Both return TWO now, and the second one is:
  Juan Carlos Lerena · Father · Argentina, Military Records 1911-1936
  spouse MARÍA LERENA · child PABLO ARMANDO LERENA
which is ark 1:1:6TH8-DVXH — the 1908 enrolment card, a record THIS
ARCHIVE HAS CITED SINCE IT FOUND IT. The archive tested for its own
document and was told nothing was there.
NOTHING WAS WRONG WITH THE SEARCHES. They ran on 17 September and the
Argentina Military Records index has since gained the card; the
FamilySearch citation on that record reads 16 September 2026.
WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE: Juan Carlos still has no record of his own — no
birth, no marriage, no death. The new hit is his son's record naming
him as a father.
WHAT DOES: he is findable by name now, where before he was reachable
only through Cajón 985. And the index places him at "Rosario de Lerma,
SALTA" — the error this archive corrected on 13 September — so anyone
searching will find him in the wrong province.
THE LESSON IS NOT ABOUT THE SEARCH. A null is true on the day it is run
against the corpus of that day, and an index that grows can falsify one
without anybody making a mistake. A published null needs a DATE. Ours
now carry one.

commits.subject: The connections were written in prose and never wired, so nothing drew them
commits.body:
David asked whether the findings are laid out as lines the way the
Defranceski site does it. The answer was no, and the reason is not
presentation.
293 people, 111 relationship edges, and 226 of those people were
ISLANDS — linked to nobody. The Trinidad kindred, the Gualeguaychú
Larenas, the Martínez Lerenas: all of them written up in prose, none of
them wired. A chart can only draw an edge that exists.
Twenty-three are wired now, taken only from notes that OPEN by stating
their own subject's parentage — "Child of Bernabé Lerena and Casimira
Peláez, baptised at Trinidad…". Islands 226 → 193, groups of two or
more 11 → 22.
I TRIED IT TWICE THE WRONG WAY FIRST, and both attempts would have put
false parentage into the register:
  A regex matching "child of X and Y" ANYWHERE in a note made ADELA
  CAMIGLIA the daughter of Julian Martínez and Carolina Lerena —
  because her note MENTIONS a Carlos Martínez Lerena who is. It made
  Sancho the son of his own wife, from a sentence describing the
  baptism of somebody else's daughter.
  Then a fuzzy last-two-words fallback matched the wrong register row:
  Juan Antonio Larena's father became "Juan LARENA (arr. 1910)" instead
  of the Gualeguaychú head, and Baldomero's became the 1923 arrival
  instead of the Córdoba man.
  And even exact matching got the Moratorio girls wrong, because
  keys() strips parentheticals and "(the elder)" IS the disambiguation
  — he is their GRANDfather, and their actual father has no row. Those
  two father-edges are dropped; the two mother-edges to Josefa Lerena
  Traibel are right and kept.
So: exact unique name match only, no fallback, and 43 names left alone
because no single register row carries them. A name that cannot be
resolved is better left unresolved than attached to the nearest thing
that looks like it.
193 islands remain. Many are genuinely alone — unplaced CEMLA
arrivals, people named once in a census line — but not all, and the
rest need the same treatment one row at a time.

commits.subject: Repin: the living check now reads the JSON an atlas serves
commits.body:
An atlas fetches its places from a .json in dist and a search box fetches
its index the same way. Both are served to anybody with the URL, and
check:living walked past every one of them - it read only .html. Raised by
the Luwinski session. Measured across the estate before changing anything:
no archive is leaking, because every living name in a served JSON is also a
published dead person's name and the gate already subtracts namesakes. The
blind spot was real and the leak was not.
Also: namefold no longer implies the commonest spelling of a name is the
right one, and says when nothing on the site is reading the map it built.

commits.subject: A peer's fixes went out under my commit messages, and I did not notice
commits.body: A session working on the landing site found nine structural faults in these pages and fixed them. Verified each before accepting it, and one thing needs saying first. THE FIXES LANDED INSIDE FOUR OF MY COMMITS. `check:templates` first appears in a81916b, "Two brothers married two sisters"; the page repairs are in 8bad9ad and a5b1eca. Their work was in my working tree when I ran `git add -A`, and my commit messages describe entirely different work and never mention it. The history now misattributes it and I cannot rewrite what is pushed, so this commit says so instead. THE DEAD LINK WAS REAL AND MINE. /direct-line/ said: enrolment card Quoted, so a literal string and not an expression. It shipped as href="{u(" — the inner quotes end the attribute — and rendered as words that still looked like a link, pointing at the document that page calls its own best evidence for Pablo Armando. It is fixed and now resolves to /TheLerena/enrolment-card/. AND MY OWN CHECKER'S SAFEGUARD IS WHAT HID IT. check-links.py says in its docstring that it skips any href containing a quote, because those are JavaScript template strings in inline

commits.subject: Fourteen records name him and four require him to be standing there
commits.body:
The last substantive finding still sitting in a working log where no
reader could reach it. It is on /uruguay/#s-sancho-alive now.
A man can be named in a document for sixty years after he dies, so the
question asked of each of the fourteen records naming Sancho Llerena
was narrower: does this one require him to have been IN THE ROOM?
FOUR DO, AND THE LATEST IS 1812.
  1789  godfather at the Iglesia Matriz — a godparent stands at the font
  1798  sworn witness at Canelones, where he took an oath and could
        not sign it
  1804  padrino at the Canelones confirmations
  1812  the padrón, calle San Juan No 60 — "Sancho, andaluz, 45" — and
        A CENSUS ENUMERATES THE LIVING
The other ten name him without requiring him. Fathers are named on
their children's baptisms whether present or not; grandfathers on
grandchildren's. His daughter Justa Pastora's marriage act of 1830 does
NOT write him difunto, which is suggestive and is not evidence. He is
named as an ancestor as late as 1850, sixty-one years after that first
christening.
So 1812 is a floor and the trees' 1832 death is not a fact.
It belongs on a page because it is the worked example of the rule the
whole register is now held to — the one last-alive.py enforces, and
which reports that of 293 people here only twenty are known to have
died at all. Being named in a later record is not evidence of being
alive for it.
THAT CLOSES THE UNPUBLISHED-RESEARCH SWEEP for anything that is a
finding about this family. What remains in the working logs is working
material: how to target an image on a reel, which levels a viewer will
serve, library errands, and catalogue shelfmarks. A working log is
allowed to hold those.

commits.subject: The test was named at nine and run at ten, and it came back empty
commits.body:
Both Villademoros rows now carry the result of the test written on them
an hour earlier, which is the point of naming a test.
LERENA with spouse surname VILLADEMOROS, Uruguay: 6,352 records, and
not one of them is a marriage act. Every hit is a parent entry on
somebody else's baptism or civil registration.
THE CONTROL IS THE ONE THAT WORKED TWO HOURS EARLIER. The same query
shape on LERENA with spouse JUANICO puts the marriage act of 19
December 1864 at RANK ONE. So the shape finds a marriage when there is
one to find, and this null is a null rather than an instrument failing
quietly — which is the whole of what /method/ spent today cataloguing.
So neither Villademoros marriage is in the indexed record, and the
brothers-and-sisters reading stays an inference with its evidence
stated: the surname on both mothers, one Joaquín standing godfather at
both baptisms, and an Angélica godmother named for Celedonia's own
mother. What would settle it is the parish marriage books of the Cordón
and Unión, which have not been walked.
Published at /uruguay/#s-villademoros rather than left in a note, so
the reader who sees the inference also sees what was tried against it.
Also saved to memory: this archive repeatedly writes "same man" in a
note and leaves both rows standing. Seven of today's merges came out of
identifications the archive had already made and never acted on.

commits.subject: Two brothers married two sisters, and the godfather signs both acts
commits.body:
Kept sweeping the Cordón after it decided the Villademoros fork, and it
produced a second marriage into the same family.
ALEJANDRO JOAQUÍN NARCISO LERENA, born 29 October 1872, christened at
the Cordón on 29 May 1873 — son of ALEJANDRO LERENA and ELISA
VILLARDEMOROS. So in one decade at Montevideo, two Lerena men married
two women of that surname.
THREE THINGS TIE THE TWO BAPTISMS TOGETHER:
  the surname on both mothers
  a JOAQUÍN standing godfather at each — indexed "Joaquín Requena" on
    the 1866 act and "Joaquín Regusa y García" on the 1873 one, which
    is one name and a machine mangling it
  the godmother here is ANGÉLICA VILLADEMOROS, and Celedonia's mother
    is ANGÉLICA MÉNDEZ — a daughter named for her
The reading is two brothers marrying two sisters, which is the same
shape as the two Lerena siblings who married two Cardozo siblings and
whose children petitioned to marry each other in 1911.
IT IS NOT PROVED AND IS NOT MERGED. The 1873 act does not name
Alejandro's own parents, so he is NOT joined to ALEJANDRO LERENA
TRAIBEL — Avelino and Ambrosia's eldest, born 1843 or 1845, who would
be twenty-seven or twenty-nine in 1872 and fits perfectly. A surname
and an age are not an identification; that is the rule that has held
all day, through seven merges and a split. The test is the marriage
act, or any record giving this Alejandro a father.
Three people in, three edges, three pairs declared. Register 290 → 293.
The finding is on /uruguay/#s-villademoros. drift flagged it anyway,
because the page says "two brothers married two sisters" where the
register note says "alliance" and "probably" — so it now carries a
PUBLISHED entry saying where it went and why the matcher trips.

commits.subject: Three Avelinos in three generations, which is how a grandson becomes a second marriage
commits.body:
Row 33 of the work list said "search the Iglesia del Cordón". Today's
work had named that parish three separate times — Carlos Lerena's 1914
marriage enquiry says he was baptised there, Carmen Lerena was buried
at its cemetery in 1841, and a Lerena baptism of 1831 is recorded at
Nuestra Señora del Carmen la Mayor, Cordón. So it was searched.
It answered a different question, and one this archive had explicitly
refused to answer.
On 16 September a sweep forward found a branch indexed LERENA
VILLADEMOROS — an AVELINO EDUARDO LERENA married to CELEDONIA
VILLADEMOROS — and set out two readings without choosing:
  either Avelino Lerena Fernández (b.1815) married TWICE, Ambrosia
  Traibel and then Celedonia
  or Avelino Eduardo is a SON of his, making the Villademoros children
  Sancho's great-grandchildren
IT IS THE SON. Two parish acts give Avelino Eduardo's own father as
AVELINO SERENA/LERENA with AMBROSIA TRAIBEL named on the record:
  Avelino Pedro Joaquín Silvestre — b. December 1865, christened at
    UNIÓN, Montevideo, 5 March 1866, the same parish where his cousins
    the Moratorio girls were baptised fourteen years later
  Pedro Gualberto — b. 19 October 1869, christened at the IGLESIA DEL
    CORDÓN, 15 January 1870
So Avelino Eduardo joins Alejandro, Josefa, Ana Rosario, Alfredo
Justiniano and Mercedes as a child of that marriage, and Celedonia —
daughter of Pedro Villademoros and Angélica Méndez — is a
daughter-in-law.
Four people into the register, seven edges, and the nine same-name
pairs the gate raised are all declared. Register 286 → 290.
INDEX-LEVEL AND SAID SO. Both acts are machine-indexed and neither
image has been opened. What decides the branch is that two independent
entries agree on the GRANDPARENTS, not that either was read off the
page.
And the reason the fork existed is worth keeping: three Avelinos in
three generations. That is how a grandson gets mistaken for a second
marriage.

commits.subject: The backlog is empty: 123 pairs, 123 reasons
commits.body:
The duplicate gate went in yesterday with 133 pairs baselined and the
file said twice that being listed does NOT mean a pair has been
compared. Every one of them has now been compared, and the reason is
written on its line.
WHAT IT COST AND WHAT IT FOUND. Register 292 → 286. Seven merges:
  Carlos Augusto Federico, Carlos LERENA Salvañach and Carlos (arr.
    1926) — one man, identified by his own rows and never joined
  Avelino Carlos — two rows, one of which said "see the CEMLA row for
    the same man"
  Rosa María Eppens — two rows, one of which said "the 'Rosa M. E.
    Lerena' of the CEMLA list"
  Luis F. and Luis Felipe; María A. and María Angélica Julia; María C.
    and María Carlota
The last three are one fault four times over: THE ENUMERATOR WROTE
INITIALS AND THE PRIEST WROTE NAMES. Four of Gilberto's children sat in
this register twice because it read both and never laid them side by
side.
AND ONE SPLIT, which mattered more than the merges. Merging Carlos
exposed relations.tsv giving him a wife and a son the register had
explicitly ruled out on 14 September — "two men, one name". The Mendoza
Carlos now has his own row.
Two pairs were decided by reading an image rather than arguing: the
census ages on lines 10-13 were transcribed here as "6, 6, 5, 2" and
are 8, 6, 5, 2. That one digit was the only thing holding María A.
apart from her own baptism.
WHAT IS NOT MERGED IS AS DELIBERATE. The three Gregorio arrivals and
the two José Llerena crossings may each be one repeat crosser or
several men, and a passenger list cannot tell them apart. The two
Franciscos travelling with Argentine-born sons have corroboration in a
CHILD and it is still not enough. And both Marías who look like
candidates for Pablo Armando's mother are kept apart on purpose —
merging either would answer this archive's central question by
accident.
The header now says a line without a reason is a pair nobody has looked
at, and that there are none today. When the gate adds one it will sit
there bare, which is the signal.

commits.subject: One digit was wrong and it was holding two people apart
commits.body:
Two pairs on the duplicate backlog were blocked on the same thing: the
1895 census schedule's four youngest children, transcribed here as
"6, 6, 5, 2". So the image was opened — film 004149111, image 8, read
at magnification.
THEY ARE 8, 6, 5, 2. MARIA A. IS EIGHT.
At six she could not be MARÍA ANGÉLICA JULIA LERENA SALVAÑACH, baptised
at San Francisco de Asís on 31 October 1886. At eight she is exactly
that, and the merge that had been refused all afternoon goes through.
MARÍA C., six, is MARÍA CARLOTA — baptised 29 October 1890 at about a
year old, which fits six in 1895 — and her nación column reads
ARGENTINA, which is precisely what that baptism row has always claimed
for her: "the first child of this family baptised in Argentina".
So four of Gilberto's children were in this register twice today:
Carlos A. and Carlos Augusto Federico, Luis F. and Luis Felipe, María
A. and María Angélica Julia, María C. and María Carlota. THE ENUMERATOR
WROTE INITIALS AND THE PRIEST WROTE NAMES, and an archive that reads
both ends up holding one child twice — four times over, in one
household, without noticing.
María E., five, has no baptism row and stays a distinct daughter.
María E. C., twenty-six and soltera on line 5, is not a daughter of the
house at all; that was retracted on 14 September because it would have
made Gilberto fifteen. Both declared rather than merged.
The household file carries the corrected ages and says which digit was
wrong. Register 288 → 286. Twelve stale pair lines dropped, 61 of the
remaining pairs now carry a reason.

commits.subject: The census wrote initials and the font wrote names
commits.body:
Twenty-one more pairs off the backlog, one more merge, and a pattern
worth naming.
LUIS F. IS LUIS FELIPE. The register held "Luis F. LERENA, born 1893,
Buenos Aires, son of Gilberto (1854)" from the 1895 census, and "Luis
Felipe LERENA Salvanach, baptised 30 December 1892 at Inmaculada
Concepción" from the parish index. Same father, same mother, same city.
The arithmetic is exact: a child baptised on 30 December 1892 is TWO in
a census taken in 1895, and two is what the schedule gives him.
That is the third of this shape today. Carlos A. in the census was
Carlos Augusto Federico at the font; Luis F. was Luis Felipe. AN
ENUMERATOR WRITES AN INITIAL AND A PRIEST WRITES A NAME, and an archive
that reads both ends up holding one child twice.
MARIA A. IS THE SAME SHAPE AND IS NOT MERGED. She should be María
Angélica Julia, baptised at San Francisco de Asís on 31 October 1886 —
same father, same mother, both born in Uruguay. What stops it is three
years: the schedule gives its four youngest as a grouped "6, 6, 5, 2",
which puts Maria A. about 1889. Luis Felipe was merged because his
census age matched his baptism exactly. This one does not, so it is a
candidate with the test named — read the image for the actual ages on
lines 10-13 rather than the grouped transcript.
Also declared, with reasons on the lines: the three Gregorio arrivals
and the two José Llerena crossings, which may each be one repeat
crosser or several men and which a passenger list cannot tell apart;
the two Franciscos who both travel with an Argentine-born son, where
the corroboration is a CHILD rather than an age and is still not enough
to merge; two Bernabés on different wives in different towns; and Juan
Carlos Lerena against the Juan Carlos González Lerena excluded on 15
September — kept apart deliberately, because merging those two would
invent the answer to this archive's central question.
49 of 133 pairs now carry a reason, from 12 this morning.
Register 289 → 288.

commits.subject: Seven rows were four people, and the archive had already said so
commits.body:
Working the duplicate backlog, which is what it is for. Four merges,
one split, and a file that disagreed with the register for six days.
CARLOS. Three rows were one man: "Carlos Augusto Federico LERENA" (born
9 July 1883, Uruguayan civil registration), "Carlos LERENA Salvanach"
(the Retiro información matrimonial of 1914), and "Carlos LERENA
(b.1885, arr. 1926)" (the CEMLA crossing). The second row's own note
already joined it to the third — "two independent sources, same couple"
— and nobody joined them. The arithmetic settles the first: that act
calls him "de treinta años" on 25 March 1914, and a man born 9 July
1883 is exactly thirty that March. Same parents, same birthplace, and
the CEMLA wife "Rosa M. E. Lerena" is Rosa María Eppens, whom the act
names.
AVELINO CARLOS. Two rows, while the note on one of them read "see the
CEMLA row for the same man". The identification was done; the merge was
not.
ROSA MARÍA EPPENS. Two rows, while her own note read "the 'Rosa M. E.
Lerena' of the CEMLA list".
AND THEN A SPLIT, WHICH IS THE PART THAT MATTERED. Merging Carlos threw
up a contradiction: the 1914 act calls him SOLTERO at thirty, and
relations.tsv gave him a wife ADELA CAMIGLIA and a son AVELINO CARLOS
baptised at Mendoza in 1904.
That was settled here on 14 September and nothing told the edges. The
Rosa María Eppens row says it outright — her Carlos is not Adela
Camiglia's, "two men, one name, and the register now says so on both
rows". It said so on the ROWS. The relationship file went on attaching
Adela and Avelino to the wrong man, and only merging the duplicates
made the disagreement visible.
So the Mendoza Carlos now has the row the register always implied, with
nothing claimed of him beyond the act that names him, and the edges
point at him instead.
Register 292 → 289. Five stale pair lines dropped, three new ones
declared.

commits.subject: I wrote twenty-four claims that somebody looked, and two were false
commits.body:
The allowlist added an hour ago says in its own header that adding a
line without looking is the one way to make the file a liability. I
then did exactly that, twice.
  · "the Bauzá purchase errand is on /errands/" — only the Revista
    IEGU one is.
  · "/register/ carries the Lerenaar and Lerenani exclusions" — they
    were on NO page at all.
So the claims are now checkable rather than trusted. A line names a
page AND QUOTES A PHRASE THE PAGE ITSELF USES, and the tool reads the
page for it:
  gendatabase-sa: 'Lerenani' is a Tswana given name   # /south-africa/ carries "Lerenaar"
The first version of that check was circular — it looked for the
WORKING LOG's rare words on the page, which is precisely what a page
does not repeat and the whole reason the allowlist exists. It flagged
three entries I had verified by hand. Quoting the page's own words
instead fixes it, and would have caught both of my false claims on the
spot.
It then caught three more the moment it worked: "Tucuman" where the
page writes "Tucumán" with an accent, a phrase I had paraphrased
instead of quoted, and the Lerenaar line again — this time because my
reason MENTIONED /register/ while explaining the earlier mistake. A
route is only checked when something is claimed of it.
Proved it still catches a false claim before trusting it: added one
naming a phrase that is certainly not on /taylor/, and it failed.
AND THE SECOND FALSE CLAIM IS NOW TRUE. The two South African
exclusions really were unpublished — a 1928 case naming "Lerenani
Matchubani", which is a Tswana given name, and a notarial protocol
transferring a slave to "Goris Janse Lerenaar", a Dutch Cape surname on
a document that predates any Lerena arrival by a century. Both are on
/south-africa/ now, with the archive's own reason: an exclusion that is
not written down gets made again, and each of these cost an hour.
Also published: the Rosario marriage index. Everything at that end has
been aimed at Pablo Armando's BAPTISM, which would name the parents the
enrolment card already names. His parents' MARRIAGE would name all four
grandparents, the index is filmed — 1091466, DGS 4531036 — and for a
man who appears in no indexed record anywhere it would be the first
document to say who Juan Carlos Lerena's father was. It was sitting in
a film list rather than in the plan. It is on /roadmap/ now.
58 unseen, from 95.

commits.subject: A rare name is evidence and a common one is not
commits.body:
David asked whether the Carmen of his aunt Patricia Carmen might be an
Argentine survival — a given name carried down from the Rosario side
the way Armando was. The answer had been researched and was sitting in
a working log; the question was not on the site and neither was the
answer. Both now are, at /name/#s-the-forename-is-the-sharper-clue.
The answer is no, and the reason is exactly the reason the Armando
argument works. Armando discriminates because it is vanishingly rare —
two in three years of the Rosario baptism index, none in four centuries
of indexed Spain. Carmen is the opposite: one of the commonest female
names in the Spanish-speaking world, and it attaches to this surname in
places with no connection to this family at all — "Lerena, Octavia
Maria Del Carmen Erundina Perez" in a Chicago naturalisation index,
born 1903.
So it is only a question, and the difference between the two names is
the whole point of that section. Recorded because the question was
asked, and an answered question should not have to be asked twice.
62 unseen findings remain, from 95 at the start of this pass. What is
left is increasingly working technique — how to target an image on a
reel, which levels a viewer will serve — rather than findings about
this family, which is the right shape for a working log to end up.

commits.subject: She was in England five weeks, and died four months after she got home
commits.body:
data/passenger-lists.tsv had SIX Board of Trade records for this family
and not one of them had ever reached a page. It holds the saddest fact
on the Taylor page and one of the warmest, and both are now published
at /taylor/#s-crossings.
ON 20 MAY 1935 MARY SEPTIMA LANDED AT SOUTHAMPTON off the Balmoral
Castle, aged 50. Her address in Britain is "c/o Dalling, Fore St,
Northam, Devon" — her elder sister Isabella Temple, who had married
Henry Dalling at Northam in 1900. She sailed for the Cape again on 28
June. She died on 15 November 1935.
Nothing in the paperwork says she knew she was ill and the page does
not claim she did. It says what is documented: she was fifty, she had
not been to Devon in the record since 1909, and she spent one summer at
her sister's house in the parish she was born in, four and a half
months before she died.
AND THE 1909 CROSSING CORROBORATES THE THING THAT PAGE ARGUES HARDEST.
The Guelph landed "Mrs M T Lerena" on 19 February 1909, and on the line
directly below her "Mast. L Lerena" — Master, a boy — almost certainly
Roque Luis at three. She is travelling as MRS LERENA with his son two
years before the wedding at St Dominic's. The purser wrote her ENGLISH
and the boy BRITISH COLONIAL.
THEN IT HAPPENS A THIRD TIME. On 12 April 1957 Juanita Ramona Lerena —
Roque's daughter, born 16 June 1937 — landed at Southampton, single,
occupation BALLET TEACHER, address "Vicosa, Westward Ho, N Devon". That
is the village adjoining Northam. Three generations of this family
crossed to the same four square miles of north Devon.
ALSO: the report now has an allowlist, because it was reporting
findings that ARE published in other words — the Barón de la Laguna
placement is on /hypotheses/ in full, and the double wedding of August
and September 1900 is on /taylor/. drift.py keeps a list like this and
says why: a warning that fires on every build is a warning nobody
reads. An entry is a CLAIM THAT SOMEBODY LOOKED and carries where the
finding was published.
I then checked my own twenty-four claims and one was false. I had
written that the Bauzá purchase errand was on /errands/; only the
Revista IEGU one is. Bauzá needs no errand at all — it was read in full
text on archive.org and III p.285 is quoted on /hypotheses/. The line
now says so, and says it was wrong.
95 unseen findings at the start of this pass, 63 now.

commits.subject: A false positive is caught only by opening the document
commits.body:
Two more findings out of the working logs and onto pages.
THE SANTO OFICIO TRAP reached no page at all. A full-text search for
the exact phrase "Sancho Llerena" returns four pages; page one is this
family and pages two to four are Spanish nobility proofs and notarial
books containing nobody of that name. One was opened to find out why —
a 1599 Order of Alcántara proof whose transcript reads "es familiar del
SANCHO, OFICIO LLERENA". It is SANTO OFICIO ... LLERENA, the
Inquisition tribunal seated at Llerena in Badajoz. The machine reads
"Santo Oficio" as "Sancho, oficio" and the phrase search matches
"Sancho ... Llerena" across two words.
The Inquisition sat there for three centuries, so those words stand
together in thousands of documents. Any search for this family in Spain
will drown in them — and this archive was one step from recording that
Sancho is an attested forename in Spanish Llerena families, which is
false, and which would then have been used quietly to argue against
FRANCISCO.
It sits beside the false-zeros catalogue as its mirror, and makes the
point that table could not: a false zero is caught by a control, but a
false positive is caught only by opening the document — the more
expensive half of the rule, because a hit that agrees with you asks to
be believed.
THE HIDALGUÍA NEGATIVE reached only /worklist/, which is a dump. It now
sits on /hypotheses/ where the argument it completes already runs. The
Spanish full-text corpus is not parish registers; it is nobility and
hidalguía files, chivalric orders and Madrid protocols, back to 1489 —
precisely the records that would hold Félix Llerena and Rosalía Aguilar
if they had been armigerous gentry with a chancillería file. They
return nothing.
That is weak evidence and it points away from hidalguía, and it sits
with the two facts already on that page: a man called Don in 1811 who
could not write his own name in 1798. It is also a zero of an unusual
kind. Every other Spanish null here means "not findable by this
instrument". This one comes from an instrument holding exactly the
right record type, which is the only reason its silence is worth
anything.
Checked before writing: the Bauzá 1817 placement of the Lerenas as
Lecor's men, and the Córdoba la Llana / Córdoba del Tucumán reading,
are both already published — and the published versions argue it better
than the working logs do.

commits.subject: Nine ways of being wrong that a reader could not see
commits.body:
"Ensure everything we have researched is on the site" needed a way to
