ask the question, so tools/unpublished.py asks it: 136 working logs
hold three quarters of a megabyte of research, and it reports which of
their emphasised findings reach no page at all. It uses drift.py's
method, because drift.py paid for it — reduce a claim to its three
RAREST words across the corpus and require them to co-occur on a single
page. Presence in the corpus is not presence of the claim.
First answer: 224 findings no page carried. Most were working material
— catalogue headings like 'CAUSAS VARIAS, SIGLO XVIII', and Spanish
transcripts quoted for the record. A reader is owed what those MEAN,
not the shelfmark, so the report now separates a CLAIM from a
TRANSCRIPT and the real number was 95.
THE LARGEST COHERENT THING IN THAT 95 WAS A CATALOGUE OF FALSE ZEROS.
/method/ already argued that a null needs a control, with five worked
cases. Nine more were sitting in working logs where nobody could read
them, and they are the valuable part, because the mechanisms have
nothing in common:
  a results page that renders "(0)" before it has looked
  a session that silently expired and redirected to the sign-in page
  a Google Books quota error reading totalItems: None
  a block delivered as an empty body
  a zero handed over moments before Error 15 arrived
  a throttle that empties four image transcripts
  three empty transcripts that were NOT the throttle but images
    outside the volume — told apart only by the page TITLE
  an exact-surname query that cannot reach a compound
  a reel whose page title attributes Uruguayan acts to COLOMBIA
Plus two found today: the "(0)" catching me three times in one sitting
on 39, 80 and 63 records, and the personas API that answers 8,549 for
every variant and 102 for an invented surname — an instrument with no
zero to give.
On 15 September a working log noted the same trap had been seen "four
times in a month, in four different disguises". It is twelve, and
/method/ now carries all of them with what each looked like, what it
actually was, and what caught it. In every single case it was a control
query whose answer was already known.
87 unseen findings remain. This is the first pass, not the last.

commits.subject: The map can have the screen
commits.body:
Repin. A full-screen button on the map, and the find box and filters come

commits.subject: Both audit findings closed, and both were in the kit
commits.body:
The two things the audit left open needed changes to TheArchiveKit
rather than to this archive, so they were made there and the pin bumped
to a024103.
DUPLICATE IDS — GONE. Spine hardcoded id={"gen-" + g.gen}. /argentina/
draws four lines of descent and /uruguay/ three, so those pages carried
id="gen-1" four times and three times over. Spine now takes an optional
`idPrefix` defaulting to "gen-", so no archive that does not pass one
sees any change, and the seven spines here pass their own.
SKIPPED HEADING LEVELS — FIVE, NOW NONE. Four were kit components
jumping from the page title straight to h3 or h4; one was local.
  /marriages/  local: a card heading that was h3 under the h1
  /search/     Trees, AncChart, Search h3 → h2
  /timeline/   the real one. The timeline labels a block only when the
               caller groups by decade, and this archive does not — so
               every h2 was skipped and the page ran h1 → h3 fifty
               times. The event title now takes whichever level
               actually follows the one above it.
NOTHING MOVED ON ANY PAGE, and I checked rather than assumed: computed
styles on the two headings whose CSS did not pin a margin come back
11px/uppercase and 1.05rem/weight 600 — the values their classes always
set.
ALSO CORRECTED, a claim I made an hour ago: I said bumping the kit
would drag in seven unrelated Atlas commits. That was a misreading —
I read the version in node_modules, not the one in package.json, which
was already at the kit's head. One unrelated commit came with it, a
basemap change.
The audit now reports ONE finding across 663 pages: a telephone number
on /argentina/, which is the Santa Fe Registro Civil's and is in the
letter on purpose.

commits.subject: Nothing had ever swept the whole estate at once
commits.body:
An end-to-end audit of the code and the built site. tools/audit.py is a
REPORT, not a gate — verify.sh refuses a build, this one only looks.
Every gate here was written to stop one specific thing happening again,
which makes each of them sharp and narrow, and nothing had ever read
all 663 pages looking for anything at all.
THE BIG ONE: 1,093 LITERAL ASTERISKS WERE VISIBLE ON /worklist/.
The work list renders its notes through the kit's md(), which supports
links, **bold** with NO nested asterisk, and «guillemets». It has no
italic and no code spans. But 85 of 177 notes were written in the
archive's OWN TSV convention — *** like this *** — plus *italic* and
`backticks`. None of it rendered. Readers saw:
 **Read at magnification: the castrense man is *"Manuel Sánchez…"*.**
with every marker showing, because md's bold regex refuses an inner
asterisk. Two conventions, one renderer, and no gate between them: the
emphasis parity check covers data/*.tsv, and the work list is JSON.
Normalised to what md() actually understands — 349 *** spans, 185
italics and 280 backticks. Now 0 literal asterisks and 1,460 rendered
<strong> spans. Proved the TEXT is untouched: stripping * and ` from
every note before and after gives ZERO differing rows out of 177.
TWO REAL DATA BUGS, both found by looking for rows whose width differs
from their neighbours':
 dominga-carballo-1836.tsv:14 had FOUR cells against a three-column
 header, and build-pages.py truncates to the header width — so the
 sentence "a third daughter, a household, an occupation, and BRAZIL"
 was being silently dropped on the way to a page it was written for.
 census-1895-lerena.tsv:20 had SEVEN against eight, which put the
 census place in the status column and the note in the census place.
AND THE AUDIT WAS WRONG THREE TIMES BEFORE IT WAS RIGHT. Each is
written into the file so the next person does not repeat it:
 · it reported four pages carrying an "unrendered ${...}" — all of it
  minified JavaScript doing its job. Script and style are code, not
  content, and every text check now strips them.
 · it reported 174 "ragged" TSV rows. These files hold SEVERAL tables;
  the second one starts with its own header. Only a width that occurs
  exactly ONCE in a file is a stray tab.
 · it reported 88 "phone-shaped numbers", 87 of them microfilm ids,
  and on the second attempt it caught page ranges and centuries.
  Strict now: an international + or a trunk 0 and a separator.
It also flagged a lone *** on /changes/ — inside the changelog entry
that says "a lone in prose is not an unconverted field… flagging it
would train me to ignore the check". The check now honours the rule its
own archive wrote about it, and looks for PAIRED spans.
Institutional and personal email are now separate findings. Six archive
contacts are published on purpose; no personal mailbox appears
anywhere, which is the thing actually worth knowing.
STILL OPEN, and both need a decision rather than a commit:
 · 6 duplicate element ids — /argentina/ renders four Spines and
  /uruguay/ three, and Spine emits id="gen-N" with no prefix. Invalid
  HTML; nothing links to those anchors, so nothing is broken today.
  Fixing it properly means a kit change, like AncChart.
 · 6 pages skip a heading level (h1 → h3).

commits.subject: A gate for places, because the kit only screens dates
commits.body:
The country pills went on the tree pages yesterday and the living row
on the spine was left without one BY HAND, because I happened to
remember. Nothing would have caught it. check:living is the kit's and
it enforces `named-bare` — a living person may be named and no DATE of
theirs may appear. This archive's own rule, written on /direct-line/,
is stricter: "no dates, no places, no photographs". A country is a
place.
tools/check-living-places.py is LOCAL rather than a change to the kit,
because the kit is shared with Falco and Defranceski and imposing a
place rule on their builds is not mine to decide.
FOUR TRAPS. TWO OF THEM SPRANG WHILE WRITING IT.
1. "LIVING" IS A WORD IN RECORDS ABOUT THE DEAD. The 1891 Northam
   census describes GEORGINA BRAYLEY, a widow of 77, as "LIVING ON
   MEANS". A grep for /LIVING/ makes her a living person and the gate
   then guards a Victorian almswoman. The marker must be a STATUS,
   matched as a whole cell.
2. A BARE PLACE NAME PROVES NOTHING. "Johannesburg" is all over this
   archive, attached to the dead. So a place is only a leak when it is
   a place THE DATA ATTACHES TO THAT PERSON.
3. A BACKWARD WINDOW READS THE CARD ABOVE. On the spine, generation 2
   ends with a SOUTH AFRICA pill and generation 3 is the living row.
   Look back 200 characters and you fail an innocent build. The window
   looks forward only, cut at the end of the list item.
4. AND FORWARD PROXIMITY WAS STILL NOT ENOUGH. The first run FAILED
   the build, on a sentence saying she "married into the Defranceski
   family, whose line runs back through JOHANNESBURG to Gracisce".
   That Johannesburg belongs to someone else's line. It is not a leak,
   and failing on it is how a guard gets switched off inside a day.
So a place is a leak only in a FACT POSITION — a country pill, or one
of the containers this site prints facts in. WHAT IT DOES NOT DO is
printed on every pass rather than left to be discovered: IT DOES NOT
SCREEN PROSE. A sentence giving a living person a place in running
text would pass. That is a stated limit, not an oversight.
Proved both ways rather than assumed. Given the living row a country
pill: caught. Given her the withheld birthplace in a fact position:
caught. Restored: passes.
It also folds the two spellings of her name — direct-line.tsv writes
"Cheryl Anne LERENA" and lerena-siblings-gen3.tsv writes "Cheryl Anne
Lerena" — which it reported as two living people until it didn't.
Wired into verify.sh and the npm build chain, so CI runs it too.

commits.subject: Country pills on the spine, and the mapping written once
commits.body:
Carrying the home-page tree's country pills through the other tree
pages — and the first thing that needed doing was to stop hand-typing
the answer.
src/lib/country.js now decides which country a place is in, once, for
every page that asks. Nine hand-typed pills would have been faster and
would have drifted: on 14 September the Taylor page carried its
siblings as a hardcoded array duplicating the TSV, the TSV gained five
husbands' names, and the page went on saying "m. Dalling" for days.
THE DATA SETS TWO TRAPS AND BOTH ARE LIVE:
  ROSARIO IS TWO TOWNS. "Rosario, Santa Fe" is where Pablo Armando was
  born, in Argentina. "Rosario, Colonia" and "Rosario / Colla, Colonia"
  are in URUGUAY, and this register holds people from both. A substring
  match on "rosario" gets one of them wrong every time, so Colonia is
  tested first - and BARE "Rosario", which this register also holds,
  returns null, because it genuinely could be either.
  CORDOBA MUST STAY AMBIGUOUS. Sancho is "natural de Cordova la Llana"
  and whether that is Andalusia or Argentina is one of this archive's
  open questions. "Cordoba, Argentina" is explicit and safe; bare
  "Cordoba" returns null rather than picking a side. A pill is an
  assertion and this archive does not make that one.
Run across all 292 people: 166 Uruguay, 84 Argentina, 14 Spain, 12
South Africa, 3 Brazil, 2 England, 1 Italy, 1 Peru. The only unmapped
strings left are the seven Cordobas and the two bare Rosarios, which is
exactly right.
WHAT EACH PAGE COULD TAKE:
  /direct-line/  real pills. Spine renders its note with set:html.
  /tree/         TEXT ONLY - "Cape Town · South Africa". AncChart
                 renders a place as plain text with no per-node hook,
                 and it is shared with two other archives, so a
                 coloured pill there needs a kit change rather than a
                 fork. The information is on the chart; the colour is
                 not. Say so rather than half-do it.
  /bloodline/    nothing. Component, graph builder, styles and client
                 script are all the kit's; the page supplies only
                 people.json.
AND THE LIVING ROW GETS NO PILL. Generation 3 of the spine is Cheryl
Anne, living, and that page's own rule is "no dates, no places, no
photographs". A country is a place. check:living only screens dates, so
this one is on the author, not the gate.
The tag and pill CSS moved from index.astro's scoped block into
public/styles.css, because four pages use it now and a rule copied into
four scoped blocks is a rule that drifts.

commits.subject: The tree now says which country holds each record
commits.body:
Country pills on the home-page tree, so the migration is visible
without reading a word of it: Uruguay at Canelones and Montevideo,
Argentina entering with the 1866 Rosario act and the enrolment card,
South Africa from Pablo Armando down, and England arriving sideways
with Mary Septima Taylor.
Deliberately quieter than the evidence tags. The tier is the thing a
reader must not misread; a country is context. So the place pills are
outlined and tinted rather than filled, and their colours avoid
--accent and --terra entirely so they never compete with Documented
and Inferred for the eye. Light and dark values for each.
Two decisions worth recording:
TEXT, NOT FLAG EMOJI. Regional flag emoji degrade to bare letter pairs
on Windows, and England's subdivision flag is barely supported
anywhere. A pill that renders as a boxed "ZA" for some readers is
worse than the word.
AND THE PILLS ADMIT THEIR OWN ANACHRONISM. They use today's borders,
which is wrong for the top of the tree: Canelones in 1791 was the
Banda Oriental of the Spanish empire, and Uruguay did not exist for
another thirty-seven years. The legend says so rather than letting the
pill quietly assert it.
The break carries NO country pill. There is no record there to place,
and giving the gap a country would be the one thing that panel exists
to prevent.
Checked at 375px and in both colour schemes: pills wrap, no horizontal
overflow.

commits.subject: Two birth dates were in an act this archive read six days ago
commits.body:
I went looking for Justo Lerena, the man the Cordon burial turned up,
and the search printed a birth date beside a baptism for somebody else:
Alfredo Justiniano Lerena, christened 12 March 1858, BORN 2 OCTOBER
1856. So I opened the image - film 007713686 image 2847 - and read both
acts on the opening.
  Alfredo      "que nacio el dia DOS de OCTUBRE ... cincuenta y seis"
  Ana Rosario  "que nacio el dia CATORCE de ENERO ... cincuenta y cinco"
The register had 1858-03 for both, which is the baptism date written
into the birth column, and it called them "probably twins". They are
TWENTY-ONE MONTHS APART. She was carried to the font at three years
old and he at seventeen months.
And it dissolves a puzzle this archive had blamed on the record.
Alfredo's row said his 1858 baptism "sits oddly against the 35 he gave
at his 1892 marriage", and consoled itself that ages at marriage are
the weakest date in genealogy. A man born 2 October 1856 is exactly
thirty-five on 3 February 1892. The record agreed with itself the
whole time; the register did not.
"Probably twins" is an inference from a shared baptism date, and this
family demonstrably baptised in batches years late - at La Mauricia in
1846 among children of various ages, and here again in 1858. The same
inference is attached to the two MORATORIO girls of 1880 and is now
flagged there as untested, with the cheap test named.
JUSTO LERENA, meanwhile, exists in exactly one record on earth. Surname
exact, forename Justo: 39 in Uruguay, 220 worldwide with spouse surname
Quintana. The only one that is him is his daughter's burial, read the
same evening. No marriage, no baptism of his own, no second child. A
controlled null - the queries returned records, so they ran - and he
can be neither placed against Sancho nor ruled out.
The rendered "(0)" caught me three times in one sitting: Justo, Alfredo
and the Gilberto sweep all read zero on first load and were 39, 80 and
63. Reading twice is already in the habits and it still nearly
manufactured three false nulls in one evening.

commits.subject: Row 111 read like an instruction and was actioned as one
commits.body:
David asked why Anne had been told to stop. The row never said stop.
It found that ONE document of a six-estate Pretoria pull is already in
the house: the death notice of TAB MHG 1095/48. Everything else stood.
What was actually cancelled was the whole trip - including the will and
liquidation account of 1095/48, which nobody holds, and five entire
estates: 3734/46, 769/52, 5155/51, 10/57 and 52653.
This archive wrote the row that caused it. Its headline read "tell Anne
before Tuesday, its death notice is already in the house" - which, read
at a glance on a work list, is an instruction to call something off.
The limits were all in the note, where a person scanning a list does
not read them. A row that needs its note read to avoid being actioned
wrongly is a badly written row.
The note also said "the other four on her list" and then listed five.
Six estates, minus 1095/48, leaves five. The list was right and the
word was wrong.
Headline now states the scope, the count is fixed, and the row carries
what it cost. Tuesday is the 22nd.

commits.subject: A sweep for one dead man found a household instead
commits.body:
Both halves of the Fidel test are run, through the search UI this time,
and both come back empty.
  control  LERENA + LUIS + spouse JUANICO, Uruguay -> 471 records, and
           the marriage act of 19 December 1864 is the FIRST result.
  test     the same shape on FIDEL + RUEDA / RUEDAS -> 331 records, and
           the only Fidel in them is the 1889 Victor Lerena death
           registration already held.
  test     LERENA + FIDEL, Uruguay, deaths 1815-1840 -> 11, none his.
  control  RODRIGUEZ, same window -> 62,026, with real burials at Las
           Piedras 1840 and San Jose de Mayo 1844. The shelf is full.
The surprise is which way it cuts. The trees give Sancho's son Fidel a
death in 1822, and that death was the ONE thing keeping him apart from
the Fidel Lerena named with Maria Ruedas as a grandfather on the 1889
registration. It is not in the record either. Still not merged - an
unevidenced death is not evidence of survival - but nothing separates
them now except silence, and both rows say so.
AND THE BURIAL SWEEP PAID FOR ITSELF TWICE. Its top Lerena hit was
"Carmen Lerena Lerena", buried at the Cementerio del Cordon - which is
the compound surname this archive has been hunting since 14 September,
because a child of two Lerenas would show that Pablo Armando's parents
could have been kin.
The act says otherwise. Film 007713392 image 2511: the margin reads
"Carmen Lerena." in the clerk's hand, one surname, and the body reads
"de edad de tres an[os], hija legitima de JUSTO LERENA y de Juana
Quinta[na]". One Lerena parent. A fifth transcription doubling - and
the FIRST of them checked against the parish image rather than a
transcript, which is the strongest level this test has reached.
The index is also a year out. It gives 14 August 1840; the act reads
"Mil ochocientos cuarenta y uno", and the burial below it agrees.
What it leaves behind is a household this archive did not have: JUSTO
LERENA and JUANA QUINTANA of Montevideo, and their daughter CARMEN,
born about 1838 and buried at three by the cura Santiago Estrazulas.
All three are in the register. No tie to Sancho is asserted - he had a
daughter JUSTA, and an echo of a forename is not an argument; the 1812
padron lists six children and no Justo, and its child lists are known
to be incomplete, so he can be neither placed nor excluded.
Register 289 -> 292.

commits.subject: The son the identification predicted turns out to exist
commits.body:
I went back to run the test I named yesterday - does the Argentine
military record's date of birth match the Gilberto Lerena who landed
off the CAP. NORTE in 1928? It does not settle it. It found something
better than a guess.
If the traveller is Gilberto Lerena Salvanach, born Montevideo 1878,
then the son walking down the gangway beside him should exist in a
record. He does.
  marriage  19 May 1906, Nuestra Senora del Pilar, Recoleta
  bride     CIPRIANA SAENZ PENA - a woman this archive did not have
  child     "Gilberto de Jesus del Corazon"
And his Argentine nationality stopped being an inference: he is
carried on DISTRITO MILITAR 2 in March 1922, born 1878 at Montevideo.
A Montevideo-born man on an Argentine district roll is exactly what
the passenger list's "ARGENTINE" requires.
IT STILL DOES NOT CLOSE, and the rows stay apart. That child has no
indexed birth year. A search of Argentine Lerena births 1910-1920
returns ten records and none is he - on a filter that demonstrably
works, since it cut sixty-three to ten. A son who exists is not the
same as a son who is THAT son.
The son is also NOT added as a new person. The register already holds
"Gilberto LERENA (b.1916, arr. 1928)", and writing in a second row for
a child who may be him is precisely the mistake made with Dominga
Llerena. He is cross-referenced instead, and the duplicate gate then
fired on the two cross-references I had just written - correctly, and
both were declared in a minute.
Checked before adding: all six Salvanach children the search returns -
Maria Carlota, Horacio Alfredo, Luis Felipe, Cesar Alberto, Raul,
Carlos - are already in this register. Only Cipriana is new.
One more thing fell out. The 1895 census INDEX returns that household
as Gilberto 1854, Maria E. C., Maria Luisa, Carlos A., Raul A. and
Maria E. - and NOT the seventeen-year-old, who is filed under
SALVANACH rather than Lerena. That is why /argentina/ carried a table
of nine names against a schedule of sixteen. The correction went in
earlier today; now the cause is recorded too.
The rendered "(0)" caught me again on first load and read 63 four
seconds later. Reading twice is in the habits for a reason.

commits.subject: A search endpoint that cannot return zero
commits.body:
The duplicate backlog named a cheap test - a Montevideo marriage of
FIDEL LERENA to MARIA RUEDAS, which would decide whether the Fidel of
the 1889 death registration is Sancho's son. I went to run it through
/service/search/hr/v2/personas, which answers quickly, and ran a
control first out of habit.
The control had different parameters and returned the same number.
  surname Lerena, Uruguay            8549
  + givenName Fidel                  8549
  + spouseSurname Rueda              8549
  control: Luis, spouse Julia Juanico 8549
The `results` field moves only for the SURNAME and the COUNTRY -
Argentina 6032, no country 589678, surname exact 1652. Given name and
spouse are ignored completely. And an invented surname, Zzzqqxx,
returns 102.
So the endpoint has no zero to give. The count is the size of a fuzzy
pool; the extra parameters only re-rank it. No null can ever be drawn
from it, and I nearly drew one.
THIS DOES NOT TOUCH THE NULLS ALREADY RECORDED HERE. The Breton query
at the head of the same session file got a real ZERO from a
spouse-surname search on the same day, which this endpoint is
incapable of returning - so the search UI filters and this API does
not, and they are two different instruments. Recorded that way rather
than as a blanket doubt.
What the endpoint did give, by looking rather than counting: the only
two Fidel Lerenas in Uruguay are the 1889 Victor Lerena death
registration already held - which names Fidel Lerena, Maria Rueda and
Victor's father PEDRO LORENA, and gives Victor born 1861 against a
death on 10 October 1889, confirming the twenty-eight this archive
carried - and one unrelated Cordon entry of 1842.
The Fidel test stays unrun, and the pair stays undeclared, with the
reason written on the line instead of a verdict that was never earned.

commits.subject: The year on that page is one formula written three times
commits.body:
I went to check why a father and son both carried 9 February as a
birth day. The date turned out to be fine. The page it sits on did not.
Film 007713524 image 1741, pages 96-97, La Mauricia, 7 January 1846 -
re-read end to end at magnification instead of trusting the two
transcripts already in this archive. All three acts concerning this
family give the birth year in the identical words:
  Justiniana Mauricia  "el treinta de Julio del pasado ano cuarenta y tres"
  Luis Eugenio         "el nueve de Febrero del pasado ano cuarenta y tres"
  Alejandro            "el veinte y nueve de Mayo del pasado ano cuarenta y tres"
and the third is for a DIFFERENT COUPLE, Avelino Serena and Ambrosia
Traibel. The phrase argues with itself - the acts open "En siete de
Enero de mil ochocientos cuarenta y seis", so "el pasado ano" is 1845
and the numeral says 1843 - and it cannot be literally true, because
Justiniana Mauricia and Luis Eugenio are children of one couple and
30 July and 9 February of one year are five months and ten days apart.
On 14 September this archive called that "a year carried down a
column". That is close and too kind. A carry-down is a slip on one
entry; this is every act on the opening, across two families, in one
hand.
WHAT IT COSTS. Luis Eugenio's 1845 stands, but on ONE leg instead of
three: his sister's 1843 came from the same formula and is worth
nothing as corroboration. What is left is his death act of 24 December
1901, "de cincuenta y seis", which is evidence from outside the page.
One good leg is enough and the conclusion does not move.
Alejandro has no leg at all. Nothing outside this page dates him, so
his birth is undetermined between 1843 and 1845 - and his row was
using it to push Avelino and Ambrosia's marriage back "before May
1843". The safe floor is before May 1845. Two years this archive does
not have. Justiniana Mauricia's own date is marked soft for the same
reason.
AND IT COST A GOOD LINE ON /hypotheses/. The Guerra Grande passage
said the three children were "born in February, May and July 1843 -
the first of them in the month the siege began". That is gone. The
finding was never the years: it is that children born under the siege
were not christened until a bishop ordered a legajo of loose papers
copied into a book three years late. The delay survives the years
entirely.
Also: the 14 September retraction of "9 February 1843" had never been
carried back to the files the reading came from. Five of them still
asserted it six days later, one in a paragraph headed WHAT THIS
SETTLES, and the correction's `retired` column was empty so no gate
enforced it. All five now say 1845 or quote the old reading, and the
gate is armed. A correction that does not reach the file the reading
came from is not a correction.
That also kills "Eleven months before Luis Eugenio was born on 9
February 1843. The fit is exact." The marriage of 3 March 1842 is
followed by Justiniana Mauricia sixteen months later. It still fits.
It fits a different child.

commits.subject: The published table had nine names and the schedule has sixteen
commits.body:
Working the duplicate backlog by signal strength rather than
alphabetically. Eight pairs compared, and one of them was being held
apart by a sentence that was not true.
/argentina/ said the Gilberto Lerena who landed off the Cap Norte on
27 February 1928 was "not in the 1895 household", and reasoned from
there that he was an unresolved namesake attached to nobody. The table
it reasoned from was built by hand from the SEARCH INDEX and carried
nine people. The schedule carries sixteen, and line 6 is "Salvanach
Lerena, GILBERTO", varon, 17, soltero - the eldest son, born 1877 or
1878 against the traveller's 1879. The schedule had been read as a
household on 14 September. The page went on reasoning from the index
for six days, because the table was typed rather than generated.
It is generated now, from data/1895-census-gilberto-household.tsv,
which was sitting in the working-log list and is now on the site. The
section carries the retraction, and with the objection gone the two
records agree on every axis available: a birth year one apart,
Argentine nationality that the Salvanach son demonstrably holds, Buenos
Aires, a marriage of 1906, and a son born 1916 who is exactly the
twelve-year-old estudiante beside him on the gangway. NOT MERGED. Both
are index-level, and the military record's date of birth would settle
it in one query.
Also read, and written onto the lines so the next reader gets the
reason and not just the names:
- the two Moratorio girls share an ark because ONE ACT NAMES BOTH.
  The strongest signal this gate has is also its most ambiguous.
- the two Luises are father and son on the son's own marriage act -
  but both rows carry 9 FEBRUARY as a birth day 34 years apart, and
  the son's birth-to-baptism gap is eleven months where the father's
  was one day. His date wants re-reading.
- the two Fidels and the three Josefas stay apart on purpose, tests
  named.
- the Josefa question is sharper than this archive had said: the 1895
  enumerator writes wives as [maiden surname] "de L.", so his widow
  married a LERENA, and Josefa Lerena Traibel married a MORATORIO on a
  parish act. Her row claimed both candidacies without noticing they
  fight. It now carries the counter-argument.
The godmother row's "nothing else in this archive names her" is left
standing, because it is true. What was wrong was the pointer, not the
sentence, and calling that a correction would have been inflation.
--baseline was destructive and I only found it by testing it properly.
It skipped declared pairs when collecting, so rebaselining rewrote the
file from the leftovers: 131 pairs would have become 1, reasons and
all, and the gate would have passed afterwards. My first test of the
fix was vacuous - with every pair declared the baseline branch never
ran at all. It now sees every pair, carries reasons forward, and the
header counts reviewed against unreviewed instead of asserting a
number that rebaselining then overwrote.

commits.subject: Two Carolinas were one woman and Bartolome was never a person
commits.body:
The duplicate gate went in yesterday with 131 pairs baselined, and
baselining is not reviewing. Four pairs read, four verdicts:
Carolina LERENA and "Carolina LERENA (de Martinez)" are the same
woman. Both are recorded as the mother of a groom named Julian
Martinez. I found her on 10 September and found her again on 13
September without noticing she was already here. Merged.
"Bartolome LLERENA - Cordoba origin" was never a person. Its own note
read "Cross-reference: the Rosario 1869 man was born in Cordoba" and
its source field read "See the Cordoba Llerena family below". A note
about a man had been sitting in the register as a man. Removed.
Emilia LERENA b.1886 in Spain and Emilia LERENA Vega b. c.1815 in
Montevideo are two women seventy-one years and two countries apart.
Declared distinct, with the reason written on the line.
Felisa arriving 1911 born 1893, and Felisa arriving 1923 born 1891,
are left open on purpose. A woman who sailed once and came back with
a family is an ordinary thing, and two years of drift in a stated age
is less than this archive sees every week. Neither merged nor
declared - it stays on the backlog because it is genuinely unsettled.
Register 290 -> 288.
The reasons broke the gate within a minute of being written: declared()
split each line on || and read everything after it as the second name,
so "Emilia LERENA Vega (b. c.1815)  # REVIEWED ..." stopped matching
the pair it had just been written for. The file header I wrote
documents that exact format. The parser now strips the reason first.

commits.subject: A gate for redundant data, because every other one catches broken data
commits.body:
An hour ago this archive added a duplicate of Dominga Josefa Llerena, one hour after
refusing to add duplicates on principle. Nothing caught it, and the reason is worth stating:
every gate here catches BROKEN data, and a duplicate person is perfectly well-formed. It
renders, it carries evidence, it passes every check. So this is the missing one.
tools/check-duplicates.py flags two register rows that share a forename and a canonical
surname - all seven of this family's spellings fold to one - AND something only the same
person would share: a shared ark, three uncommon terms in common, or birth years within six.
The second condition is the whole design. Forename plus surname alone fires 382 times on a
register of 290, because this family reuses Carlos, Luis, Maria and Avelino in every
generation. With corroboration required it drops to 133, and the output stops being noise:
Bartolome Llerena against Bartolome Llerena - Cordoba origin, both born 1824. Felisa arr.
1911 against Felisa arr. 1923, born 1893 and 1891. Emilia LERENA against Emilia LERENA Vega.
VERIFIED BY PUTTING THE MISTAKE BACK. Re-adding the Dominga duplicate makes it fail and name
the pair, with the shared terms that give it away - antonio, carballo, carvallo, dominga.
Removing it, the gate passes. It would have stopped me.
133 pairs already existed and are baselined in data/_person-pairs.txt so that only a NEW
pair fails the build. The file says plainly, twice, that being listed does NOT mean a pair
has been compared - it means the gate has seen it. Marking one reviewed means writing the
reason on its line. A row carries the backlog and names the four that look most suspect.

commits.subject: I added a duplicate one hour after refusing to add duplicates
commits.body:
Chasing which parish register rows 167 and 168 were blocked on, I looked up how this
archive got its exact dates for the Lerena Lenguas children - and found that I had been
wrong about something bigger.
THE DOMINGA OF THE 1836 CENSUS WAS NEVER A CANDIDATE. This archive proved her on 14
SEPTEMBER: DOMINGA JOSEFA LLERENA FERNANDEZ, born 13 May 1804 at Canelones, daughter of
Sancho Llerena and Maria Fernandez, married CAPITAN DON ANTONIO RUIZ [RODRIGUEZ] DE
CARVALLO - from the Catedral act of 12 May 1827, which names her outright as "Dona Dominga
Llerena de Carvallo" and baptises the very LUCINDA who stands beside her in the census.
I published her as "a candidate, not a finding", "attached to Sancho by nothing", and added
a new person to the register for her. The duplicate has been removed and its evidence
folded into the woman who was already there. The register is back to 290.
The sting is the timing. One hour earlier I declined to add three children of household 97
precisely because they might duplicate people already in this register, and wrote that this
archive had spent the week unpicking duplicates rather than making them. Then I made one,
by not spending thirty seconds on a lookup.
WHAT SURVIVES IS STILL WORTH HAVING, and it is not the identification. The 1836 household
itself - Antonio entered Continente, casado, HACENDADO; a second daughter also called
Dominga, named for her mother. And JOSEFA CARBALLO, born and resident in RIO DE JANEIRO,
marrying Miguel Carlos Lemus of Rio at San Francisco de Asis on 24 July 1862.
BRAZIL is the one genuinely new country in any of it, and row 171 is re-scoped to say so.
Also corrected: rows 167 and 168 are NOT blocked on "the San Francisco de Asis baptism
register". The siblings were baptised across at least three churches - La Mauricia in Villa
de la Union, S. Agustin in the pueblo de la Restauracion, and San Francisco de Asis - and
the first two are the same town under two names.

commits.subject: Telesforo Lenguas exists in one census line and nowhere else
commits.body:
Row 168 asked who the 34-year-old Lenguas living in Don Luis Lerena's house was. He is not
findable, and the null is tested rather than assumed.
Surname LENGUAS exact, Uruguay, returns 561 records - the surname is well represented and
the query plainly works - and Telesforo is in none of them. "Telesforo Lenguas" across all
countries returns 43, every one of them Colombian, Venezuelan or Mexican noise.
So for this archive he exists in one line of one census. A brother of Justiniana is still
the obvious reading of a man of thirty-four living among her children, and it is still not
asserted: that census gives names, ages and nationality and no relationships whatever.
Blocked on the same parish register that row 167 needs, not on another search - which is
worth saying, because two rows blocked on one document is an argument for reading it.
One thing the control threw up and I am writing down rather than claiming. LUIS PEDRO
LENGUAS and ANTONIA VEIGA of Montevideo had a daughter MARIA EMA LENGUAS, born 18 October
1896. This archive's own MARIA EMA LERENA LENGUAS was born 27 June 1857 - the "Erna" of
household 97. The same two names, forty years apart, in a Lenguas house. Maria and Ema are
both ordinary names and nothing follows from it, but this family's naming has held true
across three generations and two continents before now, and it costs less to note than to
rediscover.

commits.subject: Household 97 will not come out even, and the gap is the interesting part
commits.body:
Row 167 asked for the c.1858 census household to be reconciled against the Lerena Lenguas
siblings this archive already holds. It cannot be done by searching, and trying was the
quickest way to find that out: surname LERENA with mother Justiniana returns 1,301 fuzzy
results and the four hits already known; surname SERENA - the spelling that unlocked
everything else this week - returns 963 and nothing relevant whatever.
Worked against the register instead, three children match cleanly: Luis E. (1845),
Gualberto who is Gilberto, and Erna who is Maria Ema (1857).
THREE IN THE CENSUS ARE NOT IN THIS REGISTER - Maria c.1847, Justiniana c.1849, Josefa
c.1852. AND TWO IN THE REGISTER ARE NOT IN THE HOUSE - Justiniana Mauricia Maxima, who
would be fifteen, and Alberto Octavio, who would be eight. There is no eight-year-old on
the page at all.
The Justiniana conflict has two readings and neither is chosen. Either the census age is
five years wrong, which is a lot even for an age a householder gave - or there were TWO
daughters named Justiniana and the elder had died, which is among the commonest patterns in
any family of this period, would explain the name being used twice, and would explain
Alberto Octavio's absence by the same mechanism.
AND NO NEW PEOPLE WERE ADDED, WHICH IS A DECISION RATHER THAN AN OVERSIGHT. Maria,
Justiniana and Josefa are real, named and in a documented household - but if the ages are
what is wrong, adding them creates duplicates of people already in this register under
other names. This archive has spent the week unpicking duplicates rather than making them,
and three people can wait for the parish register to say who they are.
Blocked on reading the San Francisco de Asis baptisms straight through - which is where the
archive's existing exact dates came from, so it already knows the register.

commits.subject: All fifteen named, and the reel is not in order
commits.body:
Volumen 2 is LIBRO 246, read from its board at image 00126. Every volume on film 007499043
now carries its AGN shelfmark.
And laying them out shows something the image numbers hide. Libros 246, 247, 249, 250, 251,
252, 253, 255, 256, 261 and 262 run almost consecutively - but across volumes 2 to 8, 12 and
15. Libros 147, 148 and 149 sit together in volumes 10, 11 and 13. Libros 334, 444, 464 and
465 are scattered, and Libro 2 and Libro 107 stand alone.
SO ONE REEL CARRIES AT LEAST FOUR SEPARATE RUNS OF THE PADRONES SERIES, FILMED OUT OF ORDER.
That is worth knowing before anyone assumes a neighbouring image is a neighbouring year - and
it is exactly the assumption this archive would have made about Maria Llerena, whose volume
15 sits at the end of the reel and carries Libro 256, in the middle of the 246-262 run.
The table is the deliverable: fifteen volumes, exact image ranges, and the shelfmark that
the AGN's own inventory indexes. Nothing here dates a padron yet. But every one of them is
now a question with an address on it rather than three thousand unlabelled images.

commits.subject: Fourteen of fifteen Libro numbers, and a bridge to a Montevideo reading room
commits.body:
The row said eleven title boards still needed their Libro line, and that each needed the
full image because the upscaled thumbnail gives only the volumen numeral. That was right -
but two full boards render on one page even though four do not, so they were read a pair at
a time, and where one failed to load it was carried into the next pair.
Volumen 1 is Libros 2 y 334. 3 is 444, 247 and 249. 4 is 250, 251 and 252. 5 is 252. 6 is
253. 7 is 261. 8 is 262. 9 is 464. 10 is 147. 11 is 148. 12 is 465 y 255. 13 is 149. 14 is
107. 15 is 256, and it holds Maria Llerena at image 02771.
Volumen 14's number came off its FIN board at image 2724 rather than its own title board,
which refused to render twice. Only VOLUMEN 2 is outstanding, board at image 00126.
Libro 252 appears on both the volumen 4 and the volumen 5 board. That is recorded as read
rather than tidied away: a filmed volume may end and begin mid-Libro, and a neat table is
not worth inventing a boundary the boards do not show.
WHY THIS WAS WORTH THE CALLS. The Libro number is the AGN's own shelfmark and it is what
their inventory indexes. So this table is the bridge between an image on a film and a dated
volume in a Montevideo reading room. Maria Llerena's age of sixty becomes a birth year the
moment somebody says what Libro 256 covers - and the same is now true of fourteen other
volumes, any of which may hold the generation above Sancho.

commits.subject: Fifteen volumes, every boundary seen, two screenshots
commits.body:
The row said each of the fifteen unchecked dark frames would cost one full-image look. It
cost two screenshots for all of them.
thumb_p200 rendered at 194 pixels with heavy contrast makes the big handwritten VOLUMEN
numeral on a filming board perfectly legible - and the numeral is all that was needed to
tell a board from a cover. Forty-one candidates on one page, two screenshots, done.
FIFTEEN VOLUMES. Title boards at images 4, 126, 315, 563, 788, 959, 1215, 1315, 1475, 1574,
1847, 1962, 2155, 2425 and 2725, each preceded by the fin del item card of the volume
before. The twelve other dark frames - 91, 127, 565, 1073, 1216, 1477, 1575, 1848, 1963,
2027, 2156, 2426 - are book covers, spines and blanks, which is exactly why a dark frame
could not simply be called a boundary.
AND THE RULE I WITHDREW AN HOUR AGO WAS RIGHT. Each boundary is FIN carrying the volume it
closes, then immediately the title board of the next. I withdrew it after testing on image
00127 and finding a book cover - but 127 is not part of that pair at all. The pair is
125/126, and 127 is a third frame sitting after it. The rule held; the test picked the wrong
image. Both the withdrawal and this are in the file, because a correction that is itself
wrong is worth more visible than tidy.
Four volumes now carry their Libro numbers - 1 is Libros 2 y 334, 12 is Libros 465 y 255,
14 is Libro 107, 15 is Libro 256 and holds Maria Llerena. The other eleven need the full
image for that line, and a row says which. The Libro number is what the AGN's inventory
indexes, so it is also what will date each padron - which is the question standing over
Maria Llerena's age of sixty.

commits.subject: Eighteen dark frames is not eighteen item boundaries
commits.body:
An hour ago this archive published that film 007499043 has "eighteen item boundaries",
found by measuring thumbnail brightness. That overstates what the method can tell you, and
the overstatement was caught by testing the next inference rather than publishing it.
The scan is sound as far as it goes: dark frames read 16 to 30, ordinary pages read 140 to
156, and nothing falls between. But A FILMING TARGET BOARD IS ONLY ONE KIND OF DARK FRAME.
So is a black book cover. So is a spine.
From the one confirmed pair at 2724/2725 I inferred that every cluster runs FIN, then a
blank, then the START board carrying the title - so the last image of a cluster would always
be the title. Tested on the first untested cluster it failed immediately: image 00127 is a
BOOK COVER, and image 00091 is a FIN DEL ITEM card with no title on it at all.
Only three of the eighteen are confirmed by eye - 00004, a title board for volumen 1;
02724, FIN DEL ITEM for Libro 107; and 02725, the title board for volumen 15.
The scan still earned its place. It reduced 3,208 images to eighteen places worth looking,
in three calls and with no session. What it does NOT do is identify items, and this archive
said it did - on /uruguay/, in the film register and in the row - for about twenty minutes.
All four are corrected and the claim is logged.
Also recorded, because it cost a call: loading four full-size boards into one page to read
them together does not work. They are about a megabyte each and none of them rendered.

commits.subject: The reel is mapped, and not by looking at it
commits.body:
Everything found in Uruguay this week came off six images of a reel of three thousand two
hundred - the Archivo General de la Nacion's Padrones de Montevideo y Extramuros. Until
today nobody here knew where one volume ended and the next began.
It is mapped now. Each thumbnail was drawn to a 32x24 canvas and its mean brightness taken:
filming target boards read 16 to 30, ordinary pages read 140 to 156, and nothing falls in
between. A threshold of 60 separates them cleanly. Scanned at stride 2, which is sufficient
rather than lucky - a boundary is a FIN/START pair of two consecutive images, so one of
every pair is odd.
EIGHTEEN ITEM BOUNDARIES, at images 4, 91, 125-127, 315, 563-565, 787, 959, 1073, 1215,
1315, 1475-1477, 1573-1575, 1847, 1961-1963, 2027, 2155, 2425 and 2724-2725. One thousand
six hundred thumbnails, three calls, no session and no screenshots at all.
That is the part worth keeping beyond this film. The contact-sheet method this archive
already documents finds boards by eye, ninety to a screen; on a 3,208-image reel that is a
morning's work. Measuring brightness finds them by number, and it will work on any film
here.
Three of the eighteen items are named - volumen 1 is Libros 2 y 334, an item ending in
Libro 107 closes at 2724, and volumen 15 is Libro 256, which holds Maria Llerena. The other
fifteen are one image load each, and a row lists exactly which images. Named, the reel
becomes navigable by volume - and the Libro numbers are what the AGN's own inventory
indexes, so they are also what will date each one.

commits.subject: A whole reel of Montevideo padrones, and this archive has read five images of it
commits.body:
The row asked for film 007499043 to be added to the film register with its item boundaries.
Looking properly turned up something larger.
The film runs 1 to 3208 - the last image found by binary probe on the public thumbnail,
which costs eleven requests and no session. Its leader gives the OLD MICROFILM NUMBER,
1263678, which is the cross-reference this archive keeps for every other film it holds. It
is rollo 1 of project URUG NA01S, filmed at the ARCHIVO GENERAL DE LA NACION by Cesar
Graziani in March and April 2006.
And it is not one volume. It is an entire reel of PADRONES DE MONTEVIDEO Y EXTRAMUROS in
numbered volumenes, each covering one or more Libros: volumen 1 is Libros 2 y 334, with its
board at image 00004; an item ending in Libro 107 closes at 02724; volumen 15 is Libro 256,
opening at 02725, and it holds Maria Llerena at 02771.
THIS ARCHIVE HAS LOOKED AT FIVE IMAGES OF THREE THOUSAND. The padrones are enumerations of
the living, with ages and stated birthplaces, running earlier than any Uruguayan work here
- and this single reel has already produced Sancho's household with its four enslaved
people named, two Lerena households with ages, and a Spanish-born Llerena woman of sixty
keeping her own house. The rest of the boundaries are unmapped and a row says so.
The method for mapping them is already proven and written down: thumbnail contact sheets,
ninety to a screen, where the target boards show as dark frames among faint pages. Two
sheets found 02724 and 02725 after a page-by-page hunt had found nothing at all.

commits.subject: Maria Llerena's volume is identified, and her year still is not
commits.body:
Chasing the row opened an hour ago: date the census page that puts Maria Llerena at sixty,
because a Spanish-born Llerena woman of sixty means nothing until you know which decade
she was sixty in.
The film gives the volume and refuses the year.
Her page is film 007499043, image 02771 - taken from the manifest's alternateId rather than
the viewer, which numbers within the waypoint item and has misled this archive once already.
The filming target board at image 02725 identifies the volume: ARCHIVO GENERAL DE LA NACION,
Montevideo, "PADRONES DE MONTEVIDEO Y EXTRAMUROS, LIBRO 256", volumen 15, filmed by the
Sociedad Genealogica de Utah on 5 April 2006. The board at 02724 closes the previous item,
LIBRO 107.
The board carries the FILMING date and the volume's shelfmark. It gives no year for the
padron itself, and her own sheet is headed by a street - "Calle del...", "Ala izquierda" -
rather than a date.
So the question changes rather than fails, and that is the useful part. It is no longer
"when is this census" but "what does the AGN's own inventory say Libro 256 covers" - a
question with an address on it, and the same letter that is already drafted for the Registro
Civil of Santa Fe could ask Montevideo. Re-scoped and handed over.
Found by the contact-sheet method this archive already documents: public thumbnails, ninety
to a screen, and the target boards show up instantly as dark frames among faint pages. Two
sheets found 2724 and 2725 after a page-by-page hunt had found nothing.
And film 007499043 is new here. The DGS audit of 17 September tested 58 numbers and found
them sound; this was not among them, because nothing had ever opened the Uruguayan census
collection. A row adds it to the film register with its item boundaries, so the next person
navigates it by item instead of by probe.

commits.subject: Maria Llerena, sixty, Spanish, head of her own house
commits.body:
The last of the three Llerenas in the census collection, and the one worth the most. She is
the FIRST NAME ON HER PAGE - "Casa 2. Maria Llerena - 60 anos - Espanola" - heading her own
household, with MANUEL, 20, "Africana" and ROSA, 12, "Oriental" under her, both entered with
a ditto mark where a surname would go.
Their names and ages are secure; what they were to her is not. "Africana" means
African-born, and in a Montevidean house of this period that ordinarily means an enslaved or
formerly enslaved person taking the householder's surname. The page states no relationship
and none is asserted - but it is the same shape as Sancho's household in 1812, and this
archive now names those four.
SANCHO WAS ANDALUZ AND FORTY-FIVE IN 1812. Depending on this census's date, a Spanish-born
Llerena woman of sixty stands in his generation or the one above it - which is exactly the
generation row 22 has been stuck on for weeks. She is attached to him by nothing, is in as
UNPLACED - HIGH INTEREST, and is not claimed.
AND THE CENSUS YEAR IS NOT ESTABLISHED, which is said plainly rather than skated over. The
collection spans 132 years and the index gives no year for this sheet. At an 1830s census
she was born in the 1770s - Sancho's own decade; at an 1850s one, the 1790s. The whole
weight of her rests on which, so the next step on her is not another search but the date at
the top of her own page. A row says so, with the rotation and the contrast setting it needs.
On method, since it cost four probes: I scanned her column end to end and she was not in it,
because she was ABOVE where I started. The list ran downward from my first view and I never
looked up. Going back above the starting point found her immediately.

commits.subject: Luis Llerena owned carts, and the collection is not all censuses
commits.body:
The third Llerena in "Uruguay, Census Records, 1726-1858" had an index entry giving a name,
a sex, and nothing else whatever. The page explains why: it is not a census.
It is a PADRON DE LOS PROPIETARIOS DE CARRETILLAS, CARRETAS Y COCHES - a register of the
owners of handcarts, wagons and coaches in a Montevideo district - and LUIS LLERENA is
entry 10, written with the double L. Entry 11 is marked "ydm ydm", which is how these lists
repeat an owner for a second vehicle, so he may hold two. His neighbours on the page are
Pedro Daina, D. Vicente Ponce, D. Manl. Ocampo and Ambrosio Olvega.
THAT IS WORTH MORE ABOUT THE COLLECTION THAN ABOUT THE MAN. A collection called Census
Records holds property registers too, and the index does not say which is which - so an
entry here is not evidence of residence, only of owning something. Three different document
types have now been seen inside it: the 1812 padron, nominal censuses of c.1833, 1836 and
c.1858, and this. Every age or address taken from it has to be read with its document.
THE YEAR IS NOT SECURE AND IS NOT GUESSED. The heading ends "de 18__" and the last two
digits read as 1841, 1842 or 1846. If it falls there, Don Luis Lerena, born 9 February 1811,
would be about thirty - which suits a man of property - but no year is claimed and no
identification is made on it.
He stays unidentified. This archive has two candidate Luises, and the page offers no age,
no household and no parents to choose between them. What it does add is a kind of fact this
archive has almost none of: an ordinary man's property in an ordinary year.

commits.subject: The search was right and the country is wrong
commits.body:
Following the row written an hour ago: find the marriage of Dominga and Antonio R.
Carballo, because a Uruguayan marriage act names both parties' parents and would settle
whether Sancho's youngest daughter has been found.
SERENA exact with spouse CARBALLO, Uruguay, returns exactly one hit - and it is not their
marriage. It is Dominga appearing as MOTHER OF THE BRIDE in her daughter's act. Against a
control of 769 on the loosened form, so their own marriage is genuinely not in Uruguay's
indexed records.
The reason is probably in the record itself. JOSEFA CARBALLO - a THIRD daughter, after
Lucinda and Dominga of the 1836 census - was BORN AND RESIDENT IN RIO DE JANEIRO, and
married Miguel Carlos Lemus, also of Rio, at San Francisco de Asis on 24 July 1862. The
family was in Brazil.
So the act that would name Dominga's parents may be Brazilian, or Montevidean and
pre-1826 in registers this collection does not index. The row is re-scoped and blocked
rather than left looking answerable by another sweep of the same corpus.
And her husband has a fuller name. The FamilySearch Tree attaches him to ANTONIO RODRIGUES
DE CARVALHO, b.1803 - so CARBALLO is CARVALHO, a Portuguese name, which is precisely what
the 1836 census was saying by entering him "Continente" while his wife is "Montevideo".
That identification is a tree attachment and not a document, and it is tiered as such.
It opens ground this archive has never touched. A Lerena-surname woman married into a
Portuguese family and had at least one child in Rio de Janeiro. If Dominga is Sancho's
daughter, one of his children left for Brazil and came back - and nobody here has ever
looked at Brazil.

commits.subject: Dominga, in a household at last
commits.body:
Sancho's youngest child was Dominga, aged seven in the 1812 padron, and this archive has
never followed her past that page. The seven-spelling sweep turned up a Dominga of the
right generation in the 1836 census of Montevideo, and today the page itself was read.
Household 114. She is the wife of D. ANTONIO R. CARBALLO, hacendado, entered "Continente";
both are CASADO; and the two unmarried daughters of the house are LUCINDA and DOMINGA
CARBALLO - a daughter named for her mother, which is the naming discipline this family has
been seen keeping across three generations and two continents.
The census states no relationships whatever. Wife is read from position and status - she
sits directly after the male head, before two children carrying his surname, and her status
column repeats his. That is as far as the page goes and it is said as such.
AND THE PAGE WRITES SERENA WHERE THE INDEX SAYS LORENA. That is the third discrepancy
between this index and its own pages found in a single day, after household 97 and
household 229. The index is not a transcription of the page; it is a reading of it, and a
different reading each time.
SHE IS NOT ATTACHED TO SANCHO. Twenty-eight in 1836 implies 1808, and his Dominga was born
about 1805 - three years out on an age a householder gave rather than a register holds. She
is in as UNPLACED - HIGH INTEREST with both sides of the argument on her row.
What would settle it is the couple's marriage act, which would name her parents outright,
as the 1877 Gilberto act did this week. They are married by 1836 with a daughter old enough
to be entered soltera, so it is likely Montevideo c.1820-1832 - a far smaller search than
the one that found her, and a row now says exactly how to run it, including that the
spelling on the page is not the spelling in the index.

commits.subject: All seven spellings, put to one collection
commits.body:
The sweep row asked for the 1726-1858 census collection to be worked for the generation
above Sancho. All seven of this archive's spellings have now been put to it.
SERENA 10 - and it is the whole reason nothing had ever been found. Two complete
households came out of it: Don Luis Lerena's of about 1858, and Pedro Antonio's of about
1833. LLERENA 3 - Sancho himself, plus Maria Llerena, 60, born Espana, and Luis Llerena,
both unplaced. LERENA 27 fuzzy and mostly noise, and SANCHO IS NOT AMONG THEM, because he
is indexed Llerena. That is the entire argument for sweeping spellings instead of
searching a name.
LORENA 6. GERENA, LERINA and LARENA all zero - and they are tested nulls, not silences,
because Serena returns ten and Llerena three on the identical query.
IT DID NOT REACH THE GENERATION ABOVE SANCHO, which is what the row hoped for, and the row
says so. What it reached instead was two generations of his descendants and one candidate
for a daughter nobody has ever followed.
DOMINGA LORENA, 28, born Montevideo, on a page headed ANO DE 1836 - DEPARTAMENTO DE
MONTEVIDEO. Sancho's youngest was DOMINGA, aged 7 in the 1812 padron, so born about 1805 -
which gives 31 in 1836, not 28. Three years out on a census age, which is what a
householder said rather than what a register holds. A candidate and not a finding, not
attached to Sancho, and worth the chase for one reason: this archive has never followed
Dominga past 1812 at all. She is one of the six children with no later record of any kind.
One thing worth keeping about this collection: it holds DATED censuses, not one blur.
Three have now been seen inside it - the 1812 padron, a c.1833 enumeration, and one headed
1836 - and the index gives none of those dates. They are only on the page. So every age
taken from here has to be read with its census before it means anything, which is exactly
how household 229 got dated and how Dominga can be tested.

commits.subject: Sancho's son, his wife, and three children nobody here had
commits.body:
The same census sweep that found Don Luis's household found his brother's. Household 229:
PEDRO ANTONIO LERENA, son of Sancho, with Da VICENTA VEGA - the wife this archive already
holds, "natural de Cerro Largo", daughter of Don Romualdo and Dona Andrea Maestre - and
three children it did not: EMILIA 18, PEDRO 16, VICENTA 12.
HIS AGE DATES THE PAGE. Born 31 July 1793 and entered at forty, this census is about 1833,
not 1858. And that is the check that makes the whole reading hold rather than a guess: the
couple's one previously known child, Leonarda Margarita, was born 20 February 1837 and is
correctly ABSENT from the page. Three elder children in 1833, a fourth four years later. So
this does not contradict what the archive had; it is four years earlier than anything it
had for them.
The son and the younger daughter are also the answer to what the index entries actually
point at: "Pedro a. Serena, 16" is the SON and not his father, and "Vicenta Serena, 12" is
the DAUGHTER and not the wife. Both were about to be read the other way.
AND IT CORRECTS SOMETHING I PUBLISHED THIS MORNING. /uruguay/ said of household 97 that
"the enumerator wrote the family as Serena throughout". On this page the clerk writes
LERENA perfectly plainly while the index still says Serena - so the substitution may be the
INDEXER's hand, not the enumerator's, and household 97's own handwriting needs re-reading
before that claim is repeated. What is certain, and unchanged, is the practical half:
search this collection under SERENA or nothing comes back. The page now says that instead.
Three people added with their edges, each recording that nothing else about them is known.
Emilia is not the Emilia Lerena of 1886 in Leandro's household, three generations later.

commits.subject: A whole generation on one page, and it was filed under Serena
commits.body:
Sweeping the 1726-1858 census collection for the archive's known spellings, SERENA returns
ten - and seven of them carry consecutive record identifiers, which means one household.
It is Don Luis Lerena's. Household 97, a census taken about December 1858:
  Luis Serena 47 - b. 9 Feb 1811, the age fits exactly
  Justiniana Lenguas 33 - ENTERED UNDER HER OWN SURNAME, not Serena
  Luis E. Serena 14 - Luis Eugenio, b. 9 Feb 1845
  Maria Serena 12
  Justiniana Serena 10
  Josefa Serena 7
  Gualberto Serena 4
  Erna Serena 1 1/2
  Telesforo Lenguas 34
The wife is the proof of the whole thing. The enumerator wrote LENGUAS and not Serena, so
this is the Lerena-Lenguas marriage sitting on a census page - and no Lerena search had ever
returned any of it, because the family is written SERENA throughout. That variant is one
this archive already documents; it had simply never been turned on this collection.
Two clean decodings. "Erna" is EMA - Maria Ema Lerena Lenguas, christened 7 October 1857 -
and at a year and a half SHE DATES THE PAGE to about December 1858, which makes every other
age in the household readable. "Gualberto", aged four, is GILBERTO, born 1854, the man whose
parentage was documented off the 1877 marriage act three commits ago. A clerk's ear, not a
different child - and written down as a reading.
What it leaves open, and none of it forced: Maria Serena, 12, is nobody this archive holds
and would sit exactly between Luis Eugenio and Alberto Octavio. Justiniana Serena, 10,
implies 1848 against the archive's 30 July 1843 for Justiniana Mauricia Maxima - either the
age is wrong, there are two Justianas, or the archive's date is, and it is recorded as a
contradiction rather than resolved. Josefa Serena, 7, may be the Josefa of Gilberto's 1895
household, one year apart, and is NOT merged. And Alberto Octavio, who should be about
eight, is not on the page at all.
One new person: TELESFORO LENGUAS, 34, living in the house, a year older than Justiniana,
among her children. A brother of hers is the obvious reading and is not asserted - this
census gives names, ages and nationality, and no relationships whatever.

commits.subject: A census collection nobody here had opened, and it reaches back to 1726
commits.body:
The 1812 padron came out of "Uruguay, Census Records, 1726-1858" - 162,873 records, never
touched by this archive. Having used it once, it was worth asking what else is in it.
Surname LLERENA exact returns three. Sancho, read yesterday. And two more nobody here has
ever seen: MARIA LLERENA, 60, born ESPANA, and LUIS LLERENA with no age, birthplace or
household in the index at all.
A Spanish-born Llerena woman of sixty is not nothing. Sancho was andaluz and 45 in 1812, so
a Maria born in Spain about 1752 stands in his own generation or the one above it - and she
sits on a different film section, so probably a different census year. She is not claimed
as kin and is attached to nothing. Luis could be Sancho's son of 1811, or Don Luis Lerena
of 1811-1878, or neither.
The larger point is the span. This archive's Uruguayan work begins at the Canelones
baptisms of 1791; this collection reaches back to 1726. Sancho arrived from Andalusia and
his parentage is the wall row 22 has been stuck on for weeks - and an eighteenth-century
census is exactly where an immigrant first appears, with an age and a stated birthplace.
Three rows added, including a sweep of the whole span for Lerena, Llerena, Serena and
Gerena.
One method note that cost twenty minutes and will cost the next person nothing: Maria's
page renders as a faint, wide, apparently unreadable table because IT IS ROTATED 90
DEGREES. Turn it with transform: rotate(-90deg) and a mild contrast(1.5) and it is
perfectly legible - name, age, nationality, occupation, with Oriental, Espanol, Africano
and Francia down the third column. Heavy contrast destroys it: the ink is faint pencil and
blows out to white.

commits.subject: The padron names all four, and this archive said it named none
commits.body:
Following the row opened an hour ago, the 1812 household was read to its end - and the
answer runs in the opposite direction from where I first looked.
Under one bracket: SANCHO LLERENA, MARIA FERNANDEZ, the six children ending with DOMINGA,
then ANTONIO - written out by the enumerator as "negro esclavo" - JOSE, JUANA and TERESA,
and last RODRIGO FERNANDEZ, the father-in-law the transcription puts in the household at
63, asturiano. The next bracket opens at a Teresa Castro, which closes it. Rodrigo standing
at the end is what proves the boundary.
SO THE FOUR ENSLAVED PEOPLE ARE NAMED: ANTONIO, JOSE, JUANA, TERESA. This archive has said
in its data and on its pages that the padron "gives none of them a name". It names all
four, and the claim survived only because it was taken from a transcription that dropped
them. Logged as a SERIOUS correction. Four people this family held were nameable all along.
Antonio, Jose and Teresa are in the register now, each saying plainly that nothing else
about them is known - no age, no baptism, no death, no emancipation. Juana was already
there from the baptism act of 26 September 1812, and is now corroborated inside Sancho's
household by a second document of the same year. Two records, one household, 1812.
AND MY OWN FIRST READING WAS WRONG, published on /hypotheses/ for about an hour. I pointed
at the four standing ABOVE Sancho - Juana 41, Juan "negro esclavo", Gabriel, Maria - and
called that Juana a convergence. Those are house 59, a different address. The tell was
DOMINGA: the children end with her, so everything between Dominga and Rodrigo Fernandez is
the rest of the household, and reading upward was simply the wrong direction. The Juana
aged 41 of house 59 is a different woman, and saying so matters more than the error does -
two Juanas on one page is exactly how a tree acquires a wrong mother. Both logged.
Jose is not Jose Loreto Lerena, Sancho's son of 1806, and Teresa is not Teresa Castro of
the next household. Both traps are written onto their register rows.
The register stands at 285 people.

commits.subject: The 1812 padron could have been read from a desk all along
commits.body:
Row 30 asked for the padron to be read from the image instead of a published transcription
of AGN, Fondo ex AGA, L 251 - on the assumption that the document itself lived only in
Montevideo. It does not. The page is on FamilySearch, in a collection nobody here had ever
opened: Uruguay, Census Records, 1726-1858. It carries the AGN Montevideo stamp, and the
index even spells Sancho's origin "Andaluzia", which is the transcription's "andaluz" in
the register's own hand. Index ark 1:1:61LW-R54J, image ark 3:1:3QS7-99ZR-NKNR.
THE TRANSCRIPTION WAS GOOD. Sancho Llerena, Maria Fernandez su esposa, Juan Agustin, Pedro
Antº, Fidel, Luis, Agustina - seven names under one bracket, all six children present and
in the order this archive has been quoting for weeks.
WHAT THE TRANSCRIPTION DID NOT CARRY is four named people standing immediately above him,
under margin number 59: JUANA - 41; JUAN, "negro esclavo"; GABRIEL; MARIA.
That matters more than it looks. This archive states, in its data and on its pages, that
the 1812 padron "records four enslaved people in Sancho's household and GIVES NONE OF THEM
A NAME". Four people are named right beside him, one explicitly enslaved, and the first of
them is JUANA - which is the name of the enslaved woman the baptism act of 26 September
1812 places in the household of Don Sancho Lerena and Dona Maria Fernandez, mother of Maria
Mercedes born two days before.
AND IT IS NOT BEING ASSERTED. Their bracket is distinct from Sancho's, and the family above
them is a Sargento Veterano de Caballeria with a wife Sabina Balmaceda - so the four may be
his. dist.jpg at 3793x2909 does not settle it, and the filmers themselves captioned the
page "Paginas Rotas / Escritura poco Legible". Four names recorded, attribution left open,
the archive's own "gives none of them a name" flagged rather than quietly overwritten, and
a row that says exactly what would settle it.
If it resolves to Sancho, two more people who were held by this family become nameable.

commits.subject: The 1911 witnesses, read at last - and one guess was wrong at the end
commits.body:
Row 102 has stood since the marriage act was found: two signatures, "something like J. M.
Wathington and A. H. Blackalock", and this archive will not print a guess as a reading. The
page has now been read at full resolution - image ark 3:1:3Q9M-C9BP-73LY-N, 2693x1757.
FIRST WITNESS: J. M. Wathington. The -ington ending is unambiguous at magnification and the
earlier guess was right.
SECOND WITNESS: the earlier guess is wrong where it mattered. The initials A. H. are clear
and the surname ends -BACH, not -lock. Best reading "A. H. Blackabach", and the middle of
it is explicitly NOT secure - the letters between "Black" and "-bach" are one cursive run.
Recorded as a reading with its uncertainty stated, which is what the row asked for.
Neither witness is a Lerena or a Taylor, so the row's hope - that one of them would be the
only social connection to Pablo Armando in the Cape before 1911 - is not met by either name.
What the page gave instead: the officiant is BERTRAM W. GLYNN, R.C. Priest - and he is the
same priest who baptised Roque at Corpus Christi Wynberg on 12 June 1911, three months
before this wedding. One priest, both acts, the same year. The couple were not strangers to
that parish when they married in it.
Method, since it made this possible in four calls rather than a tile assembly: the record
page exposes an image ark, its manifest gives the apid, and dist.jpg on that apid serves the
whole page at full resolution. Where alternateId comes back "null" there is no film-and-
image number to be had, and the apid is the only handle.

commits.subject: Logging a finding was counting as publishing it
commits.body:
Yesterday's drift fix was committed with its catch UNVERIFIED and a row saying so. This
closes that row, and the answer is worse than a bug in the checker.
My own test was broken first, and in the way this archive has a written rule about: the
rebuild ran as `npm run build >/dev/null 2>&1` and the exit code was never checked, so a
failed build would have left the old page in dist and the test would have passed on
nothing. Re-run with the status checked, the build was fine - and the catch STILL did not
fire. The fault was real.
WHAT DEFEATED IT WAS /worklist/. This archive writes its findings into row notes as a
matter of habit - that is what those long notes are - and the worklist page re-prints every
note in full. So the moment a finding was logged, the checker could see all of its words on
a page and counted it as published. Logging was passing for publishing, which is precisely
the gap the check exists to find.
/register/, /people/, /who/ and /search/ were already excluded as register dumps.
/worklist/, /changes/, /corrections/ and /searched/ join them. They are ledgers OF the work,
not places a reader meets the story.
Verified both ways this time, and stated as such: delete the /uruguay/ section that carries
the Mauricio finding and the check reports it by name; restore the section and the check
goes quiet. Build exit codes checked at every step.

commits.subject: Two gates were pulling against each other, and drift was wrong every time
commits.body:
Found by following a drift warning instead of dismissing it. drift.py reads the .astro
SOURCES, so it could see a finding a page had TYPED and was blind to one a page RENDERED.
That was harmless while findings were written into prose by hand. It stopped being harmless
the moment check-onsite.py started requiring every data file to be imported by a page,
because from then on the archive's own two gates pulled in opposite directions - onsite
saying "put the finding in data and render it", drift saying "no page says it" - and drift
was wrong every time. Every data-driven section added this week was invisible to it.
It now reads the built pages as well. A reader does not read .astro.
With one exclusion that matters: /people/, /register/, /who/ and /search/ re-print the
register wholesale, and counting them would make any register finding "published" the
moment it was written down - the opposite of the check's purpose. /register/ was the one
that actually defeated it in testing: the Mauricio finding still passed with the /uruguay/
section deleted, because /register/ was quietly carrying every word of it.
WHAT IS NOT VERIFIED, and a row says so. After excluding the dumps, deleting the /uruguay/
section still did not make the check report the finding again - even though no other
non-dump page and no .astro source holds those words. The blind spot was real and is fixed;
the catch behaviour is unproven. A gate whose catch is unproven is a gate nobody should
trust, so it is written down as an open row rather than left as a green tick.
Also done, which is what turned the warning up: /uruguay/ now carries "Rosario-Colla - not
a gap, an origin", with Mauricio, his parents and Casimira Montano, and the 1837 act.

commits.subject: The fifth name, swept under the surname she actually carries
commits.body:
On 17 September this archive recorded Catherine Tertia Karon's absence from the gazette as
"not a null - a false null averted", because that sweep was keyed on LERENA and she is
indexed under KARON. It could never have found her whatever the truth.
She has now been sought under KARON. The surname returns 28 records in South Africa, so it
exists there and is indexed; Catherine plus Karon returns 281 worldwide and every one of
them is American or Belgian. She is not found.
That is still not confirmation either way, and it is not written as one. But there is a
weak negative worth stating plainly: she is absent from the very Johannesburg cemetery
register that holds the other four, entered consecutively on one day. She may be buried in
another province entirely, and FamilySearch's South African civil death collection stops at
1967 - so the collections that would carry a 1999 death for her are thin. It is the first
evidence pointing away from her being part of the same event, and it is recorded as a lean
rather than a finding.
Also acting on the drift checker, which noticed that the register now describes Mauricio
Lerena as "the patriarch this archive had researched but never made a person" while no
single page says so to a reader. He has a page; the FINDING does not have one. Row added.

commits.subject: It was a catastrophe, and the cemetery register proves it
commits.body:
Found while looking for something else - the 1911 marriage image for row 102.
Rows 11 and 122 have asked since 15 September whether five members of this family carrying
the year 1999 were a family catastrophe or a default-year artefact in a commercial index.
This archive refused to say, twice, and on 17 September narrowed it with the Government
Gazette while recording plainly that the gazette could not reach the wife or the children.
The Johannesburg cemetery register reaches all of them, and it is free.
PIERRE FREDERICK LERENA, born 1948, DIED 12 NOVEMBER 1999. RICHARD LERENA, born 1986,
DIED 12 NOVEMBER 1999 - thirteen years old, the same day as his father. JEFFREY LERENA,
born 1991, eight years old, buried 22 November. GAYLE LERENA, born 1950, buried 22
November. All four share a burial registration of 18 NOVEMBER 1999.
And their four record identifiers are consecutive - 6X6S-M484, M48C, M48H, M48Z. Four
sequential entries, one family, entered in a single act of registration. That is
structural corroboration on top of the dates, and it is exactly what an index loses.
GAYLE IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST HERE. On 17 September this archive wrote that her 1999
"rests on a single index row and must not be published as fact", because a wife married in
community of property leaves no separate estate for the gazette to carry. That refusal was
right, and it is now closed by a different source rather than by argument.
DOREEN MAY LERENA was the last person in this family whose dates came only from the
commercial index - "born 1921, died 1999" stood explicitly as THEIR fact. She died 17
November 1999, five days after the other four, and was buried two days before them. Row 17,
which asks whether gendatabase-derived facts may stay on a public site, is now about very
little indeed.
Also, for free: Careen Maria Lerena died 27 June 1947, which row 106 wanted a day for. Mary
Septima was buried 16 November 1935, the day after she died. And Rhena May and Ricardo Juan
Carlos are matched exactly by a second source - Rhena being the control this archive used
to prove the gazette misses real adult deaths, which is precisely the point: she is in the
cemetery register.
One trap recorded: this collection renders Doreen's year as "0099" and Ricardo's as "0094".
The "19" is dropped, and anything sorting by year puts them in the first century.
Only Catherine Tertia Karon is still untested, and for the reason already logged - she is
indexed under KARON, so a sweep keyed on LERENA was never going to find her.

commits.subject: Two brothers, one parish, thirteen years apart
commits.body:
A parent-pair query on the couple this morning's image documented - Luis and Justiniana -
returns both sons as grooms at the same church. Luis Lerena, 19 December 1864, San
Francisco de Asis, Ciudad Vieja, marrying Julia Juanico; Gilberto Lerena, 11 August 1877,
the same parish, marrying Julia Salvanach. Structural corroboration of what the page had
already said outright.
Worth recording is how badly the machine renders their father on every single entry:
"Luis Lorena Languas", "Luis Lenguas", "Luis". The surname collapses into the mother's both
times - which is exactly why this parentage could not be promoted off an index, and exactly
why opening the image was the right call rather than a formality.
No further siblings could be added: the fuzzy parent-pair search returns 1,254 records and
is far too noisy to close a sibling set honestly. Said here rather than left as a silence.

commits.subject: The patriarch of three departments was never a person here
commits.body:
Re-measuring Colonia for compound surnames turned up the family's own origin, and showed
that my row 156 had the question backwards.
ROSARIO-COLLA WAS NEVER UNACCOUNTED FOR. IT IS WHERE THEY CAME FROM. This archive's notes
already read "RAMON LERENA x MARIA JOSEFA GONZALEZ, of ROSARIO / COLLA, fathering children
