c.1800-1820" and "from Rosario-Colla across San Jose, Flores, Florida, Salto", and the 1837
San Jose marriage gives Mauricio's birthplace as COLLA outright - Colla being the old name
of Rosario in Colonia. I wrote the row from row 120's summary line without reading the file
underneath it, which is the same fault as the Rosario-parishes correction three days ago.
Logged.
What WAS missing is that none of them existed as people. Row 120 identifies Mauricio Lerena
as the man whose children account for San Jose, Flores and Florida, with Salto and
Montevideo besides - and he lived here only inside other people's notes. Four people added
with their edges, from the marriage of 3 February 1837 at San Jose de Mayo, ark
1:1:F21B-SZ5: MAURICIO LERENA of Colla; his father RAMON LERENA of Rosario-Colla; his
mother MARIA JOSEFA GONZALEZ; and his wife DONA CASIMIRA MONTANO, whose own parents Jose
Montano and Ignacia Barredo the act names. Tiered INDEXED, not image-read, and attached to
Sancho's line by nothing.
Ramon of Colla is kept separate from the Ramon LERENA born 1892 in Argentina who was
already in this register, and both rows now say so. The standing warning is carried onto
his row too: the tree's Gabino of Flores is given as a son of Ramon Llerena Cubas and
Margarita Leal, which may or may not be this Ramon, and the two are deliberately not merged.
One more link, and it runs the other way: VITALINO LERENA, born San Pedro, COLONIA in 1870,
son of Vitalino Lerena and Andrea Echeverry - the Trinidad/Flores couple this archive
already holds. Colonia and Flores are joined by a document now, not by inference.
The register stands at 282 people.

commits.subject: Gilberto's parents come off the page now, not off a tree
commits.body:
Row 158 asked whether the 1877 marriage image would document Gilberto Lerena's parents.
It does, and it says so twice.
"...el matrimonio que por palabras de presente contrajo Don GILBERTO LERENA, Oriental,
soltero, hijo legitimo de Don LUIS y de Dona JUSTINIANA LENGUAS: con [Julia] SALVANACH,
del propio estado y nacionalidad, e hija de Don CRISTOBAL y de Dona ANGELA ALVAREZ" -
and the padrinos are "Don LUIS LERENA y Dona ANGELA ALVAREZ". Don Luis is named as the
father and again as the padrino at his son's wedding: the act corroborating itself.
So the father edge moves from TREE to DOCUMENTED, the mother edge did not exist at all and
now does, and Gilberto becomes a documented BROTHER of Don Luis Eugenio Lerena Lenguas,
whose parentage on the same couple already rested on Montevideo act 258 of 1864. San
Francisco de Asis, marriage no. 178, 11 August 1877, DGS 007713525 image 01765.
AND THE INDEX WAS WRONG EXACTLY WHERE IT WAS PREDICTED TO BE. Two days ago the machine
index of this act gave the bride - a Salvanach - a father called "Cristobal LERENA", and
that was flagged as impossible and left unrecorded pending the image. The page shows
Cristobal is a SALVANACH, her own father, and the surname Lerena was carried across from
the padrino line. There is no Cristobal Lerena. None was ever added.
Two method notes, both of which cost time today. An ark's image number is NOT the number
the viewer shows: the viewer said "Image 33 of 250, item 9", and image 33 of that film is a
baptism register. The ark's true position is image 01765, and only the manifest's
alternateId gives it - what is on screen is the position within the waypoint item. And
dist.jpg serves the whole page at full resolution, 4467x3476 here, so no tile assembly was
needed at all.
The emphasis gate caught an unpaired marker in the evidence row before it could render
literally.

commits.subject: The Santa Fe household is not a Santa Fe household
commits.body:
Row 154 held one baptism: Armando Lerena, 1917, Santa Fe city, son of Casimiro Lerena and
Amelia Lepiani - recorded unplaced because the forename Armando is suggestive and nothing
more. Searched properly it has a second child in a second province: VENTURA AMELIA
ARGENTINA LERENA, in the Entre Rios church records, her mother indexed once as "Lapriani".
So it is a littoral family across two provinces, not a Santa Fe one - and it is still
attached to Pablo Armando by nothing whatever. The forename was never evidence and has not
been treated as any.
The useful part is the province. Entre Rios turned up twice in one session from two
unrelated households - Casimiro's daughter, and Gilberto and Julia Salvanach's child
recorded at "Uruguay, Entre Rios, Argentina" in 1885 - and this archive has no Entre Rios
study at all, only Rosario, Buenos Aires and the Uruguayan departments. Entre Rios lies
between them, on the river, which is exactly the route this family used. That is now a row.

commits.subject: The false positive was hiding a family of fifty-two
commits.body:
Row 153 existed only because of a mistake: a full-text search for "Juan Carlos Lerena"
matched ACROSS the compound surname "Juan Carlos GONZALEZ LERENA", and the hit was written
off as a false positive. Swept properly, that variant returns 52 records, and neither of
this archive's two compound-surname files held the form at all.
At the head of it is ESTEFANIA LERENA, who married SERVANDO GONZALEZ - twenty-eight records
name her - with at least six children: Servando Cecilio (1854-1911, Montevideo), Leopoldo,
Francisco, Cesarea (christened 30 April 1872, San Jose), Maria Bernarda and Esperanza. A
Lerena woman with six children, wholly absent from this archive, and the name Estefania
appears nowhere in this register. She is attached to Sancho's line by nothing and is
recorded unplaced.
IT BEARS ON COLONIA, WHICH IS ROW 156. Maria Bernarda Gonzalez Lerena married at CAMPANA,
COLONIA in 1931. Row 156 asks who the 189 Lerena records of Colonia are, and part of the
answer is that they are not all called Lerena - a department counted by exact surname
under-counts a compound family and is then reported as thin. Colonia was measured that way,
so it must be re-measured before anyone concludes anything from the number.
And it closes the false positive properly rather than leaving it as a shrug: Juan Carlos
Gonzalez Lerena, born 1899, married Concepcion Petrona Urbano Orio at Montevideo on 9
November 1922, son of Leopoldo Gonzalez Lerena and Maria Guillerma Giuria - Estefania's
grandson, seventeen years younger than Pablo Armando. Not ours, and now demonstrably so
rather than merely improbably so.
The on-site gate earned its place here: a section insert threw before the file was written,
so the new data reached no page, and the build refused it by name rather than passing.

commits.subject: Three questions to FamilySearch, and the control found more than the searches
commits.body:
FamilySearch is signed in again. Three rows worked, and the most valuable thing came out
of a control query rather than out of a search.
ROW 105, the Bretons who stood godparent by proxy in 1911: surname BRETON exact with
spouse surname LERENA exact returns ZERO, against a control in the identical form -
SALVANACH with spouse LERENA - that returns 19. So no Breton married into this family.
That does not kill the lead, it narrows it: if Jose and Maria Luisa Breton are connected
to Pablo Armando they are friends, compatriots or employers rather than kin, and they
should be looked for beside Lerena in Argentine records instead of in marriages.
ROW 35, where Roque was born in 1905: answered out of this archive's own files. He was
baptised 12 June 1911 at Corpus Christi Wynberg - aged five and a half, and three months
before his parents married on 3 September 1911, with his mother entered as "Mary Septima
OLIM Taylor". So the register's flat statement that he was born at Cape Town is an
inference from where he was baptised six years later, not from anything that says where he
was born. The pattern is legitimation. The question stays open and is better posed.
AND THE CONTROL TURNED SOMETHING UP. The marriage of Gilberto Lerena and Julia Salvanach,
11 August 1877 at San Francisco de Asis, names the bride's parents-in-law - Gilberto's
parents - as "Luis Lenguas" and "Justiniana Lenguas". That is almost certainly a machine
garble of LUIS LERENA and JUSTINIANA LENGUAS, which is exactly the couple this archive
assigns him AT TREE TIER ONLY. A parish register would make it documented.
It is not being promoted, and the reason is in the same record: the page says "indexed by
a computer", and that same entry gives the bride, a Salvanach, a father called "Cristobal
Lerena" while she marries a Lerena. One half of the entry is visibly wrong, which is the
whole argument for opening the image before trusting the other half. Image ark recorded,
row added, no Cristobal added to the register.

commits.subject: Agustina is a real null now, and the first three zeros were not
commits.body:
FamilySearch is signed in again, so row 66 was re-run - the row filed as "untested, not
null" because a session expired mid-search. The recorded query was Agustina LERENA exact,
Uruguay, then LORENA and LLERENA. All three returned zero.
Those zeros were worthless, and finding out why is worth more than the row.
FAMILYSEARCH'S EXACT FORENAME MATCHES THE WHOLE GIVEN-NAME STRING, not the first forename.
A person indexed with two forenames is invisible to an exact search on the first one. She
is Agustina RAMONA. Proved rather than assumed: exact "Maria" returns 53 Uruguayan Lerenas
and Maria Lili Lerena is NOT among them, while exact "Maria Lili" returns her alone - same
surname, same country, same form, only the given-name string changed.
Re-run in the safe shape - fuzzy forename, exact surname, which does match per token - it
returns 35 records and not one is an Agustina. They are fuzzy hits on Augusto, Agustin and
A. That is the null, and this one is real.
AND IT IS THE EXACT MIRROR OF A TRAP THIS ARCHIVE ALREADY HAD. On FreeBMD the printed index
ABBREVIATES the second forename, so "Horace Archibald" finds nothing while "Horace A" sits
there. Two free sources, opposite behaviour, and the habit that is correct on one produces
a false null on the other. They are now written on one page of /method/ for that reason.
Blast radius: 133 of 278 people in this register carry two or more forenames. Any
exact-forename null recorded against one of them is unsafe. None could be found by grep,
because the searches were written down in prose without naming the parameter - which is
the lesson underneath the new row: record the QUERY, not just the answer.
What it does not undo: the central null on "Juan Carlos Lerena" used the full string as the
exact given name, which is the right shape. It stands, but its limit is sharper than when
written - it would still miss "Juan Carlos Maria" or "Juan C.", because the match is whole.

commits.subject: What each source would and would not do today, written down
commits.body:
Three access conditions recorded where this archive already keeps them, so the next
session does not spend an hour rediscovering them.
FamilySearch is SIGNED OUT again, three days after being signed in - /search/ redirects to
ident.familysearch.org and the results frame renders empty. Assume signed out until proved
otherwise. No null was recorded from it today, and the rule that saved that is already in
this file: a rendered "(0)" is not a zero.
But DeepZoom serves anyway: thumb_p200.jpg returns 200 to plain curl with no session,
which is exactly what made the film audit possible on a signed-out day. manifest.json does
NOT - it answers 401 "Unauthorized (anonymous session)" - which corrects this archive's own
method note. And a 401 is not a missing film: access is set per IMAGE, so one film answers
401 at image 1 and 200 at image 100. Only 404 means absent.
gazettes.africa splits: the search index is open and returned 42 documents, but the
document viewer sits behind a bot challenge that did not clear and was not worked around.
Snippets yes, pages no - so a name that fails a gazette search today is untested rather
than absent, because the OCR cannot be checked. Three new records were found from snippets
regardless.

commits.subject: Neither of them went to sea, and the census said so four days ago
commits.body:
Row 148 asked what a ship-by-ship search of the merchant crew lists would cost before
anyone committed to it. It costs nothing, because it must not be started.
The 1891 census had already answered it, and had been in this archive since 16 September.
In their father's household at 2 Fore Street, Northam: WILLIAM J TAYLOR, son, 20, CAB
DRIVER - his father is a cab driver and retired cavalry sergeant - and HORACE A TAYLOR,
son, 19, FOOTMAN, DOMESTIC SERVANT. Two brothers, two land trades, on one page, at exactly
the ages a life at sea would already have begun.
That also gives the ADM 188 null its reason. They are absent from the Royal Navy registers
of seamen because they were not seamen.
The costing is recorded anyway, so nobody reopens this as though it were merely untried.
Crew lists are filed by the ship's official number and not by name, so for the Bideford,
Barnstaple and Appledore registries it would have meant several thousand annual agreements
across a hundred-odd vessels, held in three institutions at once. And it could not have
been done by name in any event: the name-indexed registers of merchant seamen run to 1857
and resume in 1918, and both men's working lives fall inside that gap. There is no index
that turns a name into a ship for 1885-1910. The route was never available, quite apart
from being unnecessary.
What this does NOT touch: the Taylors of Appledore on the Ulelia are still joined to this
family by nothing at all. If anything the gap widens - a cab-driving, footmanning
household in Northam looks less like a shipmaster's kin, not more - and it is still not
asserted either way.

commits.subject: Two rows had been finished for days and left open
commits.body:
Row 72 turned out to be mostly done and unmarked, which prompted a sweep of every
"next" row whose note claims completion. Six matched; four of them say NOT done and
were correctly open. Two were not.
Row 127, the 1891 census at Northam, was finished on 16 September. Its one unsettled
question - the seventh daughter - is row 128 and is already written there. A row whose
remainder lives in another row is finished, not open.
Row 120, the four Uruguayan departments, is answered and answered against itself: three
of the four turned out to be one family spreading in a single generation, and its own
"never searched" claim was retracted to /corrections/. One remainder was too specific to
leave hiding inside it, so Colonia now has its own row - 189 records, no dedicated study,
and the department where the warning about a DIFFERENT Lerena family would show first.

commits.subject: Juana and her daughter were on this site as strangers
commits.body:
Row 72 asked that the enslaved people of Sancho's household be written as people rather
than as circumstances of somebody else's life. Most of it was already done and the row had
simply never been closed: JUANA and MARIA MERCEDES are both in the register, both with
their own pages.
What was missing is the thing the record actually says. The baptism act of 26 September
1812 reads "a MARIA MERCEDES, que nacio antes de ayer, NEGRA ESCLAVA DE DON SANCHO LERENA
Y DE DONA MARIA FERNANDEZ, HIJA DE JUANA" - it names the relation outright, and this
archive had never recorded it. A mother and her daughter stood on the site unconnected.
The edge is in now, both ways, and both women have evidence rows carrying the act itself
(ark 3:1:3Q9M-C9BW-X757-D) so it reaches their pages rather than sitting in a file. The
evidence gate now counts 13 records about 10 named people.
The 1812 padron counted four enslaved people in that household at calle San Juan No 60 and
gave none of them a name. This act names two. The other two stay unnamed, and that is
recorded as a fact about the record rather than a gap to be filled by guessing - which is
the same rule this archive applies to its own ancestors.
Nothing is claimed about Maria Mercedes beyond her first two days: no marriage, no death,
no emancipation is known, and the page says so.

commits.subject: Last demonstrably alive, and the answer is 20 of 278
commits.body:
Row 82: the register records when a person was NAMED, never when they were last ALIVE,
and a man named as a grandfather on an 1880 act may have been twenty years dead. That
confusion is invisible while the two share a field.
tools/last-alive.py computes it, and it does not guess. Dates in this archive live in
prose, and prose carries other people's dates too - "son of X, who died 1873" is not a
date for this person. So it reads only what is unambiguous, in two tiers. DEATH is an
explicit date on the person's own row. DEATH BY is a ceiling taken from a record that
only exists because somebody died - an estate or death-notice file - and it is never
treated as the date, because this archive has already been caught that way once: Anton
Armando died 3 April 2003 and his estate was advertised in 2013, ten years later.
The result is worth saying plainly. TWENTY of 278 people are known to have died at all.
The other 258 carry a birth estimate and nothing more - a floor below which they certainly
existed, not evidence they survived to anything later.
That is the finding, not a failure of the tool, and the register's own inconsistency is
why: it writes "d. 15 Nov 1935" for one person and "SA death cert 1950" for the next, so
half its death dates are only implied by a record type. Ricardo Juan Carlos is left as
birth-only deliberately - his source is his FATHER's 1950 estate, where being named means
he was alive, not dead, and no tool should be allowed to read that the other way.
Rendered on /register/, listing the twenty by name and saying what the other 258 are.
Runs inside the gate chain, so the field cannot drift out of date with the register.

commits.subject: Three gazette records nobody here had, found by running the control
commits.body:
The target was Paul Raymond Lerena's 2001 estate notice, and it was not reached. But the
control query - the one run first so that no zero is believed before the search is proved
to work - returned 42 documents for "Lerena", and three of them this archive did not hold.
Transvaal Provincial Gazette 4793 of 11 December 1991, page 75, and 4796 of 18 December
1991, page 50: a two-week township advertisement naming RICARDO JUAN CARLOS LERENA, in
his lifetime - he died 21 December 1994 - and carrying the amendment scheme number
WYSIGINGSKEMA 2595, which is the one hard handle in it. This archive holds no property
fact for him at all.
South Africa Government Gazette, Legal Notices B 18373 of 24 October 1997, page 165:
ABSA Bank Beperk versus LERENA in the Witwatersrandse Plaaslike Afdeling. The snippet
cuts off before the respondent's forenames, so it is deliberately attributed to nobody.
All three are recorded as SNIPPET ONLY and tiered as such. The search index is open; the
document viewer sits behind a bot challenge which was not worked around. And a caution
that belongs with every gazette snippet this archive ever reads: OCR reads straight across
the gutter of a two-column notice, so "John Landman, Ricardo Juan Carlos Lerena" appearing
side by side in a snippet is NOT evidence that the two names sit together on the page. No
relationship between them is asserted.
Paul Raymond himself is left as UNTESTED, NOT ABSENT. A name search returned nothing, and
that is not a null - the control proves the search works, but OCR of a name is exactly
what a search misses, and the page could not be opened to check. Reading page 35 of GG
22032 would do two jobs: settle whether P. R. Lerena Racing Stables of Randburg is Paul
Raymond, which row 50 has only ever held as a reading, and take another person off the
commercial index that row 17 is about.

commits.subject: Every film number tested, and the archive's numbers are sound
commits.body:
Row 40 held that any DGS taken from a catalogue rather than from opening the film was
suspect, because two Montevideo attributions had already failed inspection. All 58 were
tested, at three images each. Fifty-seven resolve. Not one points at a film that does not
exist. The suspicion is cleared.
Done with FamilySearch SIGNED OUT, which is the useful part of the method: thumb_p200.jpg
is public and needs no session at all. And a correction to this archive's own method note
while I was in there - manifest.json is NOT public. It answers 401 "Unauthorized
(anonymous session)". Verify a film by fetching its thumbnail, not its manifest.
Two traps recorded, because both would have produced false corrections against good data.
FIRST: a 401 does not mean the number is wrong. Access is set per IMAGE, not per film. DGS
008166573 answers 401 at image 1, 200 at image 100, 401 at 500 and 200 at 2167 - one film,
both answers. Only a 404 means the film is not there, and the bogus control 999999999
returns exactly that. Probing image 1 alone and believing its 401 would have condemned a
film that is demonstrably fine.
SECOND, and it caught me: the first pass matched "film" as well as "DGS" and reported six
failures. All six are old microfilm roll numbers, and all six are correctly labelled by
this archive - it writes "DGS 7713373 (film 2124160, items 5-13)" and "DGS 8166578, items
11-13 (old film 2274694)", the DGS beside the old roll number exactly as it should. The
fault was in my regex. Six false corrections avoided by reading the citation before
believing the test.
One open item: DGS 008166571 gave no 200 at any image probed, so it is restricted rather
than proven. Left as the single loose end, settleable by one signed-in fetch.
FamilySearch itself signed out again between sessions, so no null from it was recorded
today - only this audit, which does not need it.

commits.subject: The letter to the Registro Civil, and the premise it was built on was wrong
commits.body:
David asked for the letter and where to send it. Drafting it changed what it asks for.
THE PREMISE WAS WRONG AND I GAVE IT TWICE. Row 152 and last night's recommendation both
said a birth in February 1882 "should have been registered civilly whether or not he was
baptised", and called it the main line on the central question. Civil registration in
Santa Fe province begins in 1886 - four years after he was born. That act does not exist
and no letter would produce it. Checked before drafting rather than after sending, which
is the only reason it cost nothing. Logged as a correction.
THE REBUILT ASK IS STRONGER THAN THE ONE IT REPLACES, and the best part of it is not
about Pablo Armando at all. Juan Carlos Lerena and Maria Lerena would in all likelihood
have died AFTER 1886, so their deaths WOULD have been registered even though his birth
was not - and an Argentine acta de defunción names the parents and the spouse of the
deceased. That reaches the generation above the wall, from records that ought to exist.
The letter therefore asks for, in order: the parents' death acts; a late birth
inscription for Pablo Armando, since he held an Argentine passport and was enrolled in
1908 and both needed proof of a birth for which no baptism exists; their marriage act if
there is one; and failing all of it, a certificado negativo - which for an archive that
records tested nulls is a document rather than a disappointment.
WHERE IT GOES. Registro Civil de la Provincia de Santa Fe, Ministerio de Gobierno e
Innovación Pública, San Luis 2950, CP 3000, Santa Fe - verified on the province's own
site today and matching the address the FamilySearch wiki gives, which is why it is
trusted rather than copied. The province also runs Registro Civil Digital at
santafe.gob.ar/rcdigital, which issues actas and certificados negativos; its request form
would not load here, so whether it takes a requester with no Argentine DNI is recorded as
UNTESTED rather than assumed.
The Spanish text is rendered in full on /argentina/, not left in a data file.

commits.subject: All three routes walked, and one of them should never have been offered
commits.body:
Named last night as the only live routes to Pablo Armando's parents. All three walked
today. None finds them, and that is written down on /argentina/ so the next person does
not spend the same day finding out.
ROUTE 2 WAS DEAD BEFORE IT STARTED, and the archive's own file said so in a column
headed "does it reach February 1882?". Of the five Rosario parishes, four open in 1888,
1896, 1899 and 1899. The Catedral was the ONLY parish in existence when he was born, and
its register is the one already walked act by act - 750 consecutive acts, no Lerena.
There are no "other parishes" to search. I recommended it without reading the file.
Logged as a correction against this archive.
ROUTE 1 IS REAL AND IS NOT ON THIS SITE. FamilySearch has no Santa Fe civil registration
collection at all: of 42 Argentine collections, Buenos Aires City, Buenos Aires province
and Catamarca each have one and Santa Fe does not. A February 1882 birth should have been
registered civilly whether or not the child was baptised, so the question stands - but it
has to go to the province directly. That is now a row, and it is a letter rather than a
query. Also tested: Argentina, Santa Fe, Catholic Church Records, 783,111 indexed records,
holds exactly THREE Lerena entries. One is new - Armando Lerena, baptised 1917 at Santa
Fe city, son of Casimiro Lerena and Amelia Lepiani. It carries the name Armando, which is
suggestive and nothing more; recorded unplaced and attached to nothing.
ROUTE 3 GAVE TWO FALSE POSITIVES AND ONE PRIZE. Full text for the exact phrase "Juan
Carlos Lerena" - the parents' generation, which earlier full-text work had never been
aimed at - returns two hits. A 2001 Montevideo death, and entry N. 14610 of 8 November
1920, where the Vicar General dispensed "Don Juan Carlos GONZALEZ LERENA" the three banns
for his marriage to Concepcion Petrona Urbano. The phrase matched across a compound
surname; he married an Urbano, not a Lerena, forty years too late. Written down as a
false positive so it is not rediscovered as a lead.
The prize: opening that hit gave the viewer's own header, and with it DGS 007713367,
item 13, 247 images - the film number for the Montevideo marriage-dispensation register,
which row 32 has been open asking for. Found sideways, while looking for something else,
and not by the catalogue, which was still erroring. And GONZALEZ LERENA is in neither of
this archive's compound-surname files, so that sweep is short by at least one variant -
also now a row.
WHERE THE CENTRAL QUESTION STANDS. Not baptised at Rosario across 750 acts. Not confirmed
there across 2,500 children. His father absent from every indexed record FamilySearch
holds, control run first. And the civil registration that might hold the birth is not
digitised here at all. The next move is not another search on this site.
Also: walked straight into the import.meta.url trap that Base.astro documents - a
statement reading import.meta.url must sit below every import, or the build dies pointing
at an innocent line seventy rows away. Same warning now written into argentina.astro,
where it actually bit.

commits.subject: The name on the card is absent from every indexed record FamilySearch holds
commits.body:
FamilySearch is signed in again, which unblocks the central question - so the central
question is what it was pointed at.
The 1908 enrolment card names Pablo Armando's parents, JUAN CARLOS LERENA and MARIA
LERENA, and it is the only document in this archive that does. Put to the whole indexed
corpus: father exactly "Juan Carlos" Lerena with the mother's surname also Lerena - 0.
The same without the mother - 0. "Juan Carlos Lerena" as a named person in any role, any
country, any collection - ONE, and it is an infant, Lerena Caraballo, died 21 February
1983 at Montevideo aged 0, certificate 177. A century adrift of a man whose son was born
in 1882.
The control was run BEFORE the zeroes were written down, not after, and it is recorded on
the page beside them: the same query form with Gilberto Lerena and Julia Salvanach
substituted returns 11. The form works. The zeroes are the corpus.
The limits are stated as plainly as the result, because this is the kind of null that
gets over-read later. It tests the EXACT string "Juan Carlos" - a record indexed as
"Juan C.", "J. C." or plain "Juan" would not match, and the fuzzy form returns 47. And it
tests INDEXED records only; unindexed images are a separate corpus.
WHAT IT IS GOOD FOR. Taken with the 1882 Rosario walk - already proved complete across
750 consecutive acts, February to July, with no Lerena, so he was not baptised at the
Catedral - two independent results now say the same thing: the parents' generation is not
in any indexed corpus this archive can reach. That is worth knowing because it closes off
a direction. Further index searching is not where the next hour goes. A row says so, and
names the three routes that are still live: unindexed images and full-text, Argentine
civil registration, and the other Rosario parishes.
Rendered on /direct-line/, the page about what stands above him, rather than left in a
data file - the new gate would have refused the build otherwise, which is the point of it.

commits.subject: The register search folds the spellings this archive actually holds
commits.body:
Built by the kit's namefold.py from this archive's own corpus, and narrow on
purpose: it folds only forms that are one word two keyboards wrote
differently - an accent, a capital. Anything that changes a LETTER is
printed by the tool and left off, because whether two spellings are one
family is this archive's judgement and not a rule's.
Folding is a search rule. It widens what a query matches and merges no
record, no person and no line.

commits.subject: Findings reach the reader now, and the build refuses one that does not
commits.body:
David: "make sure anything you find is always referenced and available on our site."
He was right to press it. The morning's audit had found 129 of 168 TSVs read by no
build script, and the day's own findings went straight into that hole - the National
Archives search, the 1999 deaths, the Devon addresses, all sitting in data/ where no
reader could reach them.
THE DOCUMENT FIRST. David signed the archive into a TNA account and ordered
ADM 188/195/140021 himself, free. It does not merely confirm the rejection of that
William Taylor - it replaces the argument. The rejection had rested on a census age.
The record gives two harder reasons. The form asks for "Names in full" and the answer
is plain "William Taylor", while ours is William JOHN Taylor. And conclusively: on
census night, 5 April 1891, this man was borne on HMS Impregnable at Devonport, having
joined her 20 May 1890 and left 4 October 1892, while William John Taylor was
enumerated at home in Northam aged 20. One man cannot be in two places on one night.
Two men, proved. Also read off the record: 5 ft 1 in, brown hair, brown eyes, fresh
complexion, a burn mark on his back, entered as a Boy on Lion in January 1887 aged
fifteen, promoted Acting Gunner, pension traced to 1909.
And a detail that strengthens a candidate rather than killing one: the Royal Marines
attestation of John Walker Brayley says he joined FROM THE SOUTH DEVON MILITIA. A man
born in Middlesex serving in a South Devon regiment is a Devon family's son born in
London, which is exactly this family's shape. Still not asserted to be him.
ON THE SITE. New page /national-archives/, in the nav, rendering both National Archives
files in full rather than summarising them. The 1999 deaths now render on /south-africa/,
the three Devon addresses on /taylor/. Six files that were exported to JSON but which no
page ever imported - half-wired, someone had meant them to show - were given real homes
on /uruguay/, /name/, /taylor/ and /naairs/ instead of being quietly written off.
THE GATE, so this holds after today. tools/check-onsite.py requires every data/*.tsv to
be one of exactly two things and to SAY which: rendered on a page - in the export list
AND imported by an .astro file, because a JSON nothing imports is the same silence in a
different directory - or named in data/_not-on-site.txt as a working log. Anything in
neither fails the build by name. Verified by adding a new TSV: it exits 1 and names the
file. The 136 already in that state were declared rather than deleted or hurriedly
published; they are genuine search transcripts and film registers, and the count sits at
the top of that file so the debt stays visible instead of dissolving into a passed gate.
Licensing recorded and being followed: TNA downloads are licensed for private study and
non-commercial research, this site is public, so the line is cite the reference and
transcribe the facts, never republish the scan. Links expire 30 days from the order.

commits.subject: The Taylor men were not Royal Navy, and that is a tested null
commits.body:
Northam parish contains Appledore, so if these men went to sea ADM 188 should hold
them. It is indexed man by man and gives an exact date of birth, which makes it
testable against a tree instead of merely suggestive.
The sweep of Northam and Bideford returned five men by name and date: Taylor,
William, b. 14 Oct 1871 Northam; Taylor, Joshua, b. 28 Aug 1881 Northam; Taylor,
Robert, b. 17 Mar 1869 Bideford; Taylor, Richard Henry, b. 7 Apr 1899 Bideford;
and Brayley, William Ewart, b. 29 Nov 1885 Northam - the only Brayley of Northam
in the whole series. Not one of them is a man of this family.
That the method returned five is the control, which is why the absence of William
John Taylor (b. Nov 1870) and Horace Archibald Taylor (b. Apr 1872) is recorded as
a tested null rather than left as silence. If they went to sea it was the merchant
service, and merchant crew lists are indexed by SHIP and not by man - a far harder
search, costed in a row before anyone starts it.
The near miss is written down on purpose. Taylor, William, born 14 October 1871 at
Northam, has the right surname, the right parish and the right decade, and the next
person to find him will want him to be ours. He is not: the 1891 census, taken 5
April, makes our William John twenty, which fits November 1870 and rules out
October 1871, when he would have been nineteen.
Recorded as context and claimed as nothing: a seafaring Taylor family of Appledore
on the Ulelia - T Taylor mate b.1846, J W Taylor master b.1888, T G Taylor b.1893,
previous ship Annie of Bideford. Same parish, wrong generation, no document joining
them to ours.
Two operational facts logged. The JSON API answered about twenty queries and then
began returning 202 with x-amzn-waf-action: challenge - AWS bot detection. It was
not worked around; the control query itself had started failing, so every zero
collected at that moment was thrown away rather than written down, and the rest was
read in a browser at reading pace. And the part that does the genealogical work -
name, exact date of birth, birthplace, year of entry - is free. The scanned record
is £3.50 or free to a signed-in account, which is David's call; no account was
created and nothing was bought.

commits.subject: The UK National Archives, searched for the first time, and it corrects a null I wrote this morning
commits.body:
David asked whether this archive had ever looked at nationalarchives.gov.uk. It had
not. Three mentions of "National Archives" in the whole corpus and all three are
nationalarchives.gov.ZA. Discovery's JSON API answers 200 unauthenticated - no login,
no CAPTCHA - which clears both walls that stop CEMLA and the GRO, and it aggregates
about 2,500 UK repositories rather than Kew alone: on the control query TNA held
4,791 records and other archives 11,719.
Control first: "Bideford" returns 16,510, so the zeroes below are tested zeroes.
THE LERENA SURNAME IS A NULL IN BRITAIN. Two hits, one an 18th-century Seville street
plan dedicated to a Spanish finance minister, one an incidental crew-list match.
Llerena returns one Peninsular War letter about the Spanish town. Absent, as a family
that went Rosario to the Cape without touching Britain should be.
THE BRAYLEY SIDE IS THE OPPOSITE - 639 records, and this is the wife's line: Mary
Septima Taylor, who married Pablo Armando, was a Brayley through her mother. Three
Brayley wills of Northam, two of them within living memory of Mary Septima. A Brayley
family of standing in Bideford and Northam from 1767 to 1861, in deeds nobody here
has opened. And ADM 157/197/182, a Royal Marines attestation for a John Walker
Brayley BORN MIDDLESEX, attested 1861 aged 18 - against this archive's John Walker
Brayley born 1845 at St Paul's, London, whose death index already implied about 1847
and left a two-year gap open. Three sources, three years. Not asserted to be him.
AND IT CORRECTS ME. This morning row 123 recorded 23 Geneva Place and North Street as
"NOT TESTABLE FREE" because FreeCEN holds neither 1871 nor 1881 for those parishes.
The census sentence was true; the verdict on top of it was not. Geneva Place is a
COUNCIL SCHOOL, and North Devon Record Office 629C holds its log books and admission
registers for 1885-1949 - which give child, date of birth, father and ADDRESS, and
which cover Lucy Elizabeth, Mary Septima and Agnes Walker Taylor. One route was
tested and the verdict was written as though all had been. Logged as a correction.
The limit of the source is recorded too, because it matters more than any single hit:
Discovery does NOT name-index ordinary civilians. "Horace Archibald Taylor" returns
eight documents that merely contain those words. It indexes people only where a series
was catalogued name by name. A civilian's name searched here must never be written
down as a null about that person.
Four rows added: the attestation, the three wills, the school registers, and the
untested question of whether the Bideford gentry Brayleys are kin at all.

commits.subject: A retracted fact was still doing corroborating work, and now the build refuses it
commits.body:
The Mazza hunt turned up a second shape of the same disease. The first was evidence
in a file the build never read, so a page said nothing was known. This is its mirror
image: a correction applied only where it showed.
David read the enrolment card off the original and reported Serie "E 3555". The page
was corrected, the correction was logged, and the old number sat on in data/ twice -
in enrolment-card-1908.tsv as the Serie value, and in direct-line.tsv inside what
reads as a transcription of the card, which is the worst place for a wrong number to
hide because it looks like the record talking.
Worse: racing-dynasty.tsv still asserted "Roque Luis Armando Lerena married Rosalina
Wilhelmina CHAPPELL... Frederick Chapell is her kin" and offered it as a
CROSS-CONFIRMS of the parish register - a claim a SERIOUS correction had withdrawn
seven days earlier. She was Roseline Wilhelmina FORBES, a widow, so Chappell enters
this family by her first marriage and not by blood, and two sources agreeing she was
called Chappell corroborate nothing beyond her widowhood. Rewritten, with the
open question left standing: whether that jockey is the same man as Frederick
Christian Chappell has not been checked.
Fourth, lerena-lenguas-siblings.tsv carried "Alberto Otario" in its NAME column - a
superseded index spelling in a key, where it breaks name matching.
The gate. corrections.tsv gains a `retired` column and check-corrections.py enforces
one rule, which is the archive's own habit made compulsory: a retracted reading may
appear in data/ only inside quotation marks. Quoted it is history; bare it is an
assertion, and the assertion is false. That rule separated all six real occurrences
from all six innocent ones with nothing left over. It is opt-in - only a correction
with its `retired` column filled is enforced - because guessing retired values out of
English prose was tried first and returned "child", "probably" and "Argentine".
Verified by reintroducing all four bugs: the gate names each one and exits 1, and
exits 0 restored. Wired into verify.sh and into the npm build chain, so CI runs it too.

commits.subject: The 1999 cluster is not an index artefact, and a control shows the absences prove nothing
commits.body:
Rows 122 and 11, taken as far as free sources go. NAAIRS was 503 all day, so the
death registration row 122 asks for is still unread.
What the Government Gazette settles: Pierre Frederick Lerena's estate was
advertised 28 January 2000, GG 20821 p.41 Transvaal, re-advertised 3 March 2000.
That is ten weeks after the 12 November 1999 the GEDCOM gives, from a source
independent of both the GEDCOM and the commercial index. A padded or default year
does not reproduce as an exact day in a separate source and then land ten weeks
before a real government notice. The artefact reading is dead for him, and the
same GEDCOM gives his two sons the same day.
What it cannot settle, and why the absences are worth nothing. The control is
Rhena May Lerena: died 1 April 1998 on cemetery records, an exact date, and she
has NO gazette estate anywhere in a 1994-2023 sweep. So this source demonstrably
misses real adult Lerena deaths. The lag from death to advertisement, calibrated
across five Lerenas, runs from ten weeks to ten years.
And one reported absence was never a test at all: the sweep was keyed on LERENA,
while the index carries Catherine Tertia Karon under KARON. Calling that a null
would have been a straight error. It is logged as untested, and the next sweep
must include KARON.
Gayle Lerena stays open on a single index row. Her absence is doubly uninformative
- the Rhena control, and a wife married in community of property sharing one joint
estate wound up in her husband's name, which predicts exactly the one notice found.
Row 17 still governs whether any of this may be published.

commits.subject: Five more records reach their people, and one Devon address in three is confirmable free
commits.body:
The evidence pipe built yesterday had four rows in it. Backfilled to eleven, about
eight named people: Sancho LLERENA Aguilar, Avelino LERENA Fernandez, Justa Pastora
LERENA and Mary Septima TAYLOR twice over. The gate now reports 11 records about 8
people reaching their pages, and the rendering was checked on two of them rather
than assumed.
Row 123, the three Devon addresses. 2 Fore Street, Northam is CONFIRMED off the
1891 return - piece 1787, ED 4, folio 42, page 1, schedule 2. 23 Geneva Place and
North Street are not testable free and the reason is bigger than this row:
FreeCEN has no address field at all, so the method this row assumed only works on
a paid census. Row set to blocked/David rather than left looking answerable.

commits.subject: Evidence reaches the person now, and a gate refuses the build when it does not
commits.body:
The Mazza fault was looked for here and found in a different shape, and
the gate written to catch it found a second, pre-existing one on its
first run.
WHAT THE SHAPE IS HERE. Mazza kept evidence in files its person-builder
never read. This archive had no person-keyed evidence file at all:
build-people.py read lerena-register.tsv and relations.tsv and nothing
else. So a whole session of records — Cipriano's parents, Vitalino's
wife and children, Bernabé's marriage — sat in topic files and on
/uruguay/ while the people themselves had pages saying "No relationships
are recorded for this person. The source names them and nothing more."
AND THE ONE THE GATE FOUND BY ITSELF, which is the real vindication.
/people/carlos-lerena-salvanach/ carried that same sentence while
relations.tsv held FIVE edges for him: father Gilberto Lerena, mother
Julia Salvanach, wives Rosa Maria Eppens and Adela Camiglia, and his son
Avelino Carlos. The cause is written on his own page — the row was
corrected on 14 September from "Retiro baptism" to "información
matrimonial", and the rename fixed the register while orphaning every
edge, because relations.tsv does `if not subj: continue` and drops
unknown names in silence. All five repointed and recovered.
THE FIX. data/person-evidence.tsv, keyed by person name on the same
convention relations.tsv uses. build-people.py reads it and RAISES on a
name the register does not hold rather than skipping it. The person page
renders "What has been read about this person", and the sentence about
nothing being recorded is now guarded so it cannot appear beside
evidence.
THE GATE. tools/check-evidence.py, wired into verify.sh and into
npm run build so CI runs it too. It refuses when a named person is not
in the register, when their page does not carry their evidence, when the
page still prints the false claim, and when relations.tsv names anyone
the register lacks.
Verified by reintroducing the bug three separate ways, each exiting 1:
the build stops reading the evidence file; the template guard is
removed so the false claim returns; an edge is repointed at a name the
register does not hold. Clean state passes — 6 records about 4 named
people reach their pages.
The charts are untouched. This archive draws the export as given, and
the point was never to rewrite the tree — only to stop a page claiming
nothing has been read when something has.

commits.subject: Eight of the nine Taylor children followed to their deaths
commits.body:
In September the nine named children were confirmed in the birth index.
Today they were followed forward, and four married surnames the archive
did not hold have been recovered out of nothing but an absence.
  KATHLEEN GEORGINA never married — Taylor, Kathleen G, 69, Mar 1940,
    Bideford. Born and died in the same town.
  WILLIAM JOHN — Taylor, William J, 80, Jun 1951, Totnes.
  HORACE ARCHIBALD — Taylor, Horace A, 61, Mar 1934, Birmingham.
  IRENE — married HENRY ALBERT BURTON, Bideford 1900, 5b/900; died
    Burton, Irene, 90, Mar 1969, Barnstaple.
  ISABELLA TEMPLE — married HENRY DALLING, Bideford 1900, 5b/901; died
    Dalling, Isabella T, 79, Dec 1953, Bideford.
  LUCY ELIZABETH — married WILLIAM NORRISH SWEET, Totnes 1909, 5b/373;
    died Sweet, Lucy E, 75, Jun 1957, Plymouth.
  AGNES WALKER — married ALFRED S WOOD, Devonport 1918, 5b/588; died
    Wood, "Agnes Walter", DATE OF BIRTH 3 AUGUST 1889, Jun 1974,
    Cheltenham. Not an age that fits — her birthday, to the day.
  MARGARET HELLEN WALKER — married at ST PANCRAS, Dec 1903, 1b/43, and
    the husband is NOT resolved: the page holds Charles William Bell and
    Arthur Wallis, and the tree gives her no death date to choose on.
  MARY SEPTIMA — Cape Town, 1935. Outside the English index. She is the
    one who left.
And a detail that only appears with the pages side by side: Irene
married on 5b/900 and Isabella on 5b/901. Adjacent pages, same quarter,
same district — two sisters married at Bideford within days of each
other in the autumn of 1900, the year their mother died.
Four rules about this index are now written into brayley-bmd.tsv,
because each cost something to learn:
  Search the FIRST forename only. "Horace Archibald" and "William John"
  both returned nothing; both men were there under an initial.
  A woman missing from the death index is a FINDING, not a failure. It
  means she married, and the marriage index still holds her maiden name.
  When a marriage page holds four names, the DEATH resolves the pairing.
  It did for Irene and Isabella, sixty-nine and fifty-three years after.
  The index changes shape twice, and both changes help. From 1912 the
  marriage index names the spouse. From about 1969 the death index gives
  a date of birth instead of an age.

commits.subject: Two sisters recovered through their married names, and a wedding settled by a death
commits.body:
The sisters looked unreachable: a woman who marries leaves the death
index under her maiden name and this archive holds no husbands. That is
not a wall. The MARRIAGE index still holds her maiden name.
  KATHLEEN GEORGINA never married. Taylor, Kathleen G, age 69, March
  quarter 1940, Bideford. Born and died in the same town, a Taylor all
  her life, and 69 is exact for 4 November 1870.
  ISABELLA TEMPLE married at Bideford in the September quarter of 1900,
  5b/901, indexed under her full unmistakable name. The page carries
  four names — Coles Mary Ann, DALLING Henry, ISAAC William Smith,
  Taylor Isabella Temple — so the index could not say which man was
  hers. Her death does: DALLING, Isabella T, age 79, December quarter
  1953, Bideford. She married HENRY DALLING, and her own death
  disambiguates her wedding fifty-three years afterwards.
  LUCY ELIZABETH married at TOTNES in the June quarter of 1909, 5b/373 —
  and that page carries only two names, William Norrish SWEET and
  herself. One marriage, no ambiguity, which is rare enough to note.
  Died Sweet, Lucy E, age 75, June quarter 1957, Plymouth.
Two husbands and two married surnames the archive did not have an hour
ago. And Totnes is not a random town: her brother William John Taylor
died at Totnes in 1951, so two of the ten children ended sixty miles
south of where they were born.
The method is written into the file because Irene, Margaret Hellen
Walker and Agnes still need it. Look for the death under Taylor; if she
is not there, that absence is a FINDING and not a failure. Look for the
marriage under Taylor, take the volume and page, search that page with
no surname, and the page names the husband. Then the death under his
surname, confirmed on age. If the marriage page holds four names, the
death is what resolves the pairing.

commits.subject: Two Taylor siblings' deaths, and a false null that nearly took both
commits.body:
The unfinished half of row 126. The nine children were confirmed in the
birth index in September; their deaths test the same birth quarters from
sixty and eighty years later, because the death index carries an age.
  HORACE ARCHIBALD — Deaths, March quarter 1934: Taylor, Horace A, age
  61, BIRMINGHAM. The tree gives 18 January 1934, which falls in the
  March quarter, and a man born April 1872 is exactly 61 that January.
  The district is the surprise, Birmingham rather than Devon — but he
  was a FOOTMAN at nineteen on the 1891 census, and servants went where
  the places were.
  WILLIAM JOHN, the twin — Deaths, June quarter 1951: Taylor, William J,
  age 80, TOTNES. Quarter, age, initial and county all right. So of the
  twins born in one quarter of 1870, one died in Devon at eighty and the
  other sailed to Cape Town.
And the method note, because it nearly cost both men. The first search
for each returned NOTHING. "Horace Archibald Taylor", deaths 1930–1940:
no rows. "William John Taylor", deaths 1951: no rows. Both nulls were
false and both men were sitting there under an initial — Horace A and
William J.
The GRO index abbreviates second forenames and FreeBMD transcribes what
the index says, so a full-forename search is WEAKER than a first-forename
search. The rule is to search the first forename only and filter the
results by age, which is what does the identifying after 1866 anyway.
The controls held both times — 34 Horace Taylors across the decade, 205
William Taylors in 1951 with all four quarters at >99%. The coverage was
never the problem. The query was, twice, in one afternoon.

commits.subject: José Loreto is a tested null now, and FamilySearch signed out mid-search
commits.body:
Row 5 sent me back to DGS 7713375, the film the 1812 act came off. The
productive move there was not paging it blind but asking the index for
Sancho's children directly — and the answer was that the archive has
already done this properly. sancho-children-reconciled.tsv, written
yesterday, holds all eight children with tiers and image locations.
Justa Pastora's 1830 marriage to Manuel Zeferino Barros of Pernambuco,
which I found and briefly thought was new, is in two files already and
is explicitly marked "already held, and the archive was right".
That is the third rediscovery in two days, and the pattern is worth
naming: the Uruguayan core is genuinely well worked, and a search that
starts from the index rather than from the archive's own files will keep
landing on ground already taken.
So I went to what the reconciled file itself names as unfinished — the
children never followed forward.
  ROW 68, José Loreto. Searched as "José Loreto Lerena", birth 1800–15,
  and then, because the archive found him only through the variant sweep
  on "Sancho Lorena", as "Loreto Lorena" exact. Neither returns him. He
  is not in FamilySearch's indexed Uruguayan records after his baptism
  of 10 December 1806. That is now a tested null rather than an untried
  row, and the routes left are ones an index cannot reach: the Cordón
  and Matriz registers walked by image, or a death under a mangling.
  ROW 66, Agustina Ramona. Attempted and NOT completed — the
  FamilySearch session expired mid-search and this session does not sign
  in. Recorded as untested, not as null, with the exact search to
  re-run: Agustina Lerena exact, Uruguay, 1790–1805, then the same under
  Lorena and Llerena.
FamilySearch is now signed out for this session. Everything below it —
the Uruguayan and Argentine index work — is paused until David
re-authenticates.

commits.subject: Valdemoro is not on FamilySearch, and row 78 finally has a place to go
commits.body:
Row 141 was opened yesterday when the 1812 act gave Ramón's house a hard
Spanish place-name. The first thing to ask of a place-name is whether
its registers are reachable. They are not, from here.
  FamilySearch catalogue, place Valdemoro, Madrid: ONE item, and it is a
  census. The place note reads "SEE: PART OF MADRID".
  Same catalogue, Valdemoro plus subject CHURCH RECORDS: "No Results
  Found."
That null is controlled by the line above it — the place resolves and
returns its census, so the silence is about the holdings and not about
the query. FamilySearch has no parish registers for Valdemoro.
And a warning that has now misled twice in two days, so it goes in the
file as a rule. An indexed search for SERENA filtered to "Valdemoro,
Madrid, Spain" returns 79 hits and NOT ONE of them is Valdemoro: they
are Madrid city, Toledo, Murcia, Almería, Huesca, Barbastro. The place
filter silently widens to the province, exactly as it did for "Santa Fe,
Argentina". A place-filtered result has to be checked against the place
field on the rows themselves.
What is actually wanted is the baptism of Ramón Serena about 1775–85 and
the marriage of Salvador Serena and Ana de Cubas before it. Those books
are in a diocesan archive, not a film vault: Valdemoro is historically
the Archdiocese of Toledo and since 1991 the Diocese of Getafe, and
PARES is the state route.
Both were already row 78 — "try PARES and the Spanish diocesan portals"
— which until today named no place to try them on. It now names one, and
two specific acts to ask for. Row 141 is marked blocked rather than open,
because nothing further can be done on it from this desk.
The caution stays attached to both rows: this is Ramón's house, not
Pablo Armando's. Work it because it is a real Spanish origin the archive
can name, not because it is his.

commits.subject: The tenth Taylor child: FreeBMD cannot settle it, and one GRO search can
commits.body:
Row 128 asked for the infant-death search, on the reasoning that a child
who died before 1891 would be in the birth index, counted among the
family's ten, and in no census — which is exactly the shape of the
person missing. Run: FreeBMD deaths, Taylor, Bideford district,
1881–1891. Thirty-seven entries, fourteen of them aged 0 to 3.
And one fits the gap exactly. ETHEL Taylor, born Bideford in the
December quarter of 1882 and dead at two, falls between Lucy Elizabeth
(September 1881) and Mary Septima (December 1884), and died before any
census could hold her.
She still cannot be attached to this family. Nor can Edith, the earlier
candidate. Nor can Ida, Jane, Susan, Ellen or Ann Eliza, who are the
other Taylor infants dying in the same town in the same years.
The reason is structural and worth writing down once rather than
rediscovering: the FreeBMD birth index carries no mother's maiden name
and the death index carries no parents. There is therefore no field
anywhere in FreeBMD capable of joining a Bideford Taylor child to THIS
Taylor household, and every candidate is a name in the right town in the
right year and nothing more. More searching there will not help.
What settles it in a single search is the GRO's own index, which is not
FreeBMD and gives the MOTHER'S MAIDEN NAME on every birth from 1837:
births, surname TAYLOR, mother's maiden name BRAYLEY, district BIDEFORD,
1870–1890. That returns every child of William Taylor and Mary Ann
Hellen Brayley by definition, with no inference required, the tenth
included. It needs a free GRO account, which this session does not
create, so the row moves to David.
The other half of the row — where Mary Septima was at six in 1891 —
stays open, and is not answerable from FreeCEN, whose Devon 1891 is
transcribed parish by parish.

commits.subject: Isabella vanishes, and the Kilburn Georgina is refuted
commits.body:
Two rows opened when the Lower Gunstone censuses were read, both now
answered, and the refutation is the more useful of the two.
ROW 129 — Isabella Brailey, born London about 1841, last seen aged 20
and unmarried in her widowed mother's house in 1861. No marriage under
Brailey or Brayley in Devon 1861–1890; none anywhere in England and
Wales 1858–1895; no death under either spelling 1861–1925.
The null is controlled: Brayley marriages with no forename, in 1870
alone, return fourteen nationally. The surname is thickly indexed and
the searches were capable of finding her. She did not marry in England
and she did not die in England. Either she emigrated, or she married or
died under one of the manglings this surname is notorious for, and
nothing decides between them.
One thing said carefully. Sue Rowbotham's history has a chapter called
"The mystery of the missing husband and daughter". The missing husband
is now firmly John Brailey. Of the four children, Mary Ann Hellen
married in 1870 and died in 1900, John Walker married in 1876 and died
in 1900, Georgina Margaret lived to about 1940 — and Isabella alone has
nothing after 1861. That makes her the best candidate for the missing
daughter. It is an argument from absence, which is the weakest kind
there is, and it is recorded as a candidate to be tested against Sue's
own text rather than against a guess.
ROW 130 — REFUTED. John Walker Brayley married in the December quarter
of 1876 at Bideford, 5b/978. That is five years after a child born at
Kilburn in 1871, so the general servant at Tower Street cannot be his
daughter by that marriage. The reasoning that produced her — a Brayley
of the right age, in service at Northam, carrying the family's forename
— was a resemblance and nothing more. She is not adopted.
And the search that refuted her supplied something: 5b/978 carries
Bonning Elizabeth, Brayley John Walker, Paddon Elizabeth, Richards John.
Two marriages on one page, so John Walker married an ELIZABETH, either
Bonning or Paddon, and the index cannot say which — exactly as on his
sister's 5b/794 six years earlier.

commits.subject: The missing .two rule, fixed where it belonged — not in the kit
commits.body:
Row 133 wondered whether repinning the kit had brought a .two rule with
it. It had not. And by today the inline workaround had been written into
FIVE pages — enrolment-card, index, uruguay, argentina, family-papers —
which is well past the point where a repeated inline style should have
become a rule.
So .grid.two now lives in this archive's own site/public/styles.css,
directly beside the .grid rule it was always missing from:
  .grid.two{grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fit,minmax(290px,1fr))}
auto-fit rather than a hard 1fr 1fr, so it collapses on a phone without
needing a media query. All five inline overrides removed. Verified that
every .grid two on /uruguay/, /argentina/, /enrolment-card/ and the
front page still renders two columns at 1024px.
This is deliberately NOT a kit change. The kit is shared by six archives
and would need all of them repinned for a bug that only this archive has
hit; a local rule in a local stylesheet costs nothing and blocks nobody.
If the kit ever grows its own .two, this one can go.
Row 139 closed too. It asked for Ramón's marriage in order to read where
he was natural de. The marriage was never found and did not need to be —
the 1812 act says it outright: natural de Valdemoro en Castilla la
Nueva.

commits.subject: Argentina gets its chart: three households that point back across the river
commits.body:
Four descents drawn on /argentina/, in a 2x2, with the same Spine
component as /uruguay/ so the two pages read as one argument.
  The 1866 baptism at Rosario — Luis Lerena Lenguas and Julia Juanico,
  "naturales del E. Oriental" in the clerk's own hand. Their daughter is
  the ONLY Lerena in the Rosario baptism index between 1731 and 1901,
  and she is Uruguayan on both sides.
  The Stud Book household — Gilberto Justiniano Lerena Lenguas, born
  Uruguay 1854, co-founder of the Argentine Stud Book. In the 1895
  census the elder children are born Uruguay and the younger ones Buenos
  Aires: the crossing is legible in one household.
  The family in the army drawer — Alejandro M. Lerena, born Uruguay
  1839, with Julia Bassani. His sons' cards sit in Cajón 985: Hector
  born Montevideo 1886, Roberto Juan Misiones 1891, Romer Rosario Buenos
  Aires 1895. One family, five spellings — and the same drawer that
  holds Pablo Armando's card.
  And the one this archive is for — Juan Carlos Lerena and María Lerena,
  marked as the joint that cannot bear weight because they are named on
  one card and nowhere else on earth, then Pablo Armando.
The panel under them says what the four say together. Three point back
across the river and say so on the record. The Lerenas of Argentina are,
so far as Argentina can show, Uruguayans who crossed. The fourth points
nowhere: no Lerena in the Rosario index for 1881–83, no Lerena or Lerina
household in Santa Fe province in 1895, parents on one card. He is the
only one of the four whose Uruguayan origin is a hypothesis rather than
a line of text.
The contents gate caught the new section before the build passed, which
is the gate doing exactly its job.

commits.subject: The two houses drawn, and Pablo Armando's line drawn beside them
commits.body:
David asked whether the Argentina and Uruguay stories had neat family
trees showing the juxtaposition. They did not. Neither page had a chart
of any kind — /argentina/ has none at all, and /uruguay/ had prose cards
and record tables. Now /uruguay/ has three descents drawn to the same
scale with the kit's Spine component, which is the right one for this
because it marks the joint that cannot bear weight.
  Sancho's house — out of CÓRDOBA. Félix Llerena and Rosalía Aguilar
  (marked weak: named on River Plate acts, found in no Spanish register)
  → Sancho and María Fernández, Canelones 1791 → Avelino and Ambrosia
  Traibel, 1815–1890 → the Lerena Traibel.
  Ramón's house — out of VALDEMORO. Salvador Serena and Ana de Cubas
  (marked weak, same reason) → Ramón Serena, natural de Valdemoro, and
  María Josefa González of Lanzarote → Alejandro and Mauricio, married
  San José 1825 and 1837 → Bernabé and Cipriano, two of the Trinidad
  fathers and first cousins.
Both run four generations and both reach a named couple in Spain. Set
side by side they make the point the prose was making at length: five
hundred kilometres apart in Spain, about ninety in Uruguay, and they
never touch.
And then the third one, which is why this was worth doing at all:
  Juan Carlos Lerena and María Lerena — marked weak, because they are
  named by their son on his enrolment card and there is no other record
  of either of them anywhere on earth → Pablo Armando, born Rosario de
  Santa Fe 22 February 1882, died Newlands 1950.
Two generations, and it stops at a pair of names on one card. Drawn to
the same scale as the other two on purpose, with a panel beside it
saying so: that is not a gap in the research, it is the whole problem,
and it is why the Uruguayan work is done in parallel and in hope rather
than as his line.
One rendering fault caught and fixed: Spine renders the name as text, so
"&" in a name field printed literally. Replaced with "and".

commits.subject: An About page, with the one part of it left for you to write
commits.body:
Three of the seven had one and four did not, which means four archives asked a
reader to trust them without saying who was asking. This is the shape the three
already agreed on: what it is willing to say, what it holds, where the evidence
comes from, and how to tell it it is wrong.
Everything on it is counted from this archive's own data at build time - the
people, the places, the records, the corrections it has made to itself - so it
cannot go stale the way a typed number does. The five words and the rule on
living people are the estate's and are the same on all seven.
What is NOT written is who made this archive and why, and nothing has been
invented to fill it. The page says so plainly, addressed to whoever maintains
it. A fabricated provenance on a page whose whole subject is provenance would
be the worst thing in the estate.

commits.subject: Valdemoro: the 1812 act closes the join and opens Spain
commits.body:
Row 140 said the image was one click away and one phrase in it might
decide everything. Read today, DGS 007713375 image 02668 — which is the
film already on this work list as row 5.
  "…hijo legítimo de RAMON SERENA natural de VALDEMORO en CASTILLA LA
  NUEVA, y de María Josefa González natural de la Ysla de Canarias,
  LANZAROTE. Abuelos paternos Salvador Serena y Ana de Cubas; id.
  maternos Marcial de León González è Ysavel Lorenza."
Valdemoro is twenty-seven kilometres south of Madrid. Sancho was natural
de Córdova la Llana, in Andalusia, five hundred kilometres away. So the
surname entered the Banda Oriental TWICE, from opposite ends of Spain.
Two emigrations, two families, one rare name. The join is closed.
And the coincidence that made it worth asking is discharged exactly as
the page said it should be. This archive had noticed both fathers
written GERENA in Montevideo acts a year apart and called it "a scribal
habit of one place and one time rather than two families independently
choosing the same variant — a reason to look and not a reason to
believe." The act writes SERENA, and both men were baptising children at
the same font, one year apart, having come from opposite ends of Spain.
The resemblance was real and it meant nothing. That is the rule working.
The act beat its own index nine facts to four. The index gave four names
and a wrong church. The act gives the father's birthplace, the mother's
birthplace, the true maternal grandmother — Ysavel Lorenza, whom the
index never named, and for whom the child Manuel LORENZO is probably
named — and the real church: the index says "Unión", the act says the
Iglesia Matriz. The image was free and had sat unopened for a day.
What it costs: the hope that the Uruguayan Lerenas were one kindred with
Pablo Armando somewhere inside it. Two arrivals means two haystacks.
What it buys, and it is more than it costs: a hard Spanish place-name
where there was none. Salvador Serena and Ana de Cubas were married in
Spain and Ramón was baptised there about 1775–85, and Valdemoro is one
parish, not a province. Plus a migration stream nobody suspected — María
Josefa González is a canaria, from Lanzarote, daughter of Marcial de
León González and Ysavel Lorenza.
/uruguay/ rewritten around the act, with the transcription quoted and
the discharged coincidence kept on the page rather than deleted. New row
141, carrying a caution: work Valdemoro because it is real and cheap,
not because it is his.

commits.subject: Uruguay gets a page: two houses, built in parallel, neither of them his yet
commits.body:
David asked for the Uruguayan Lerenas to be researched and painted as a
complete story in parallel, in the hope they eventually join up. New
page at /uruguay/, and it is built as two houses rather than one family,
because that is what the records say.
Two more rungs found first, both on 17 September.
  RAMÓN LERENA's parents are SALVADOR GERENA and ANA DE CUBAS, named on
  the baptism of his son Manuel Lorenzo at Unión, Montevideo, 15
  November 1812 — Montevideo acts name grandparents as a matter of
  course. ark 1:1:6D7Z-BD56. The image is available and has NOT been
  read, and the page says so.
  That also explains the current tree's "Ramón Llerena CUBAS", which the
  tree merely carried and could not account for: Cubas is his mother's
  surname. Second time in two days a record has explained a compound
  name — the first was Clara Lerena Montaño.
And it settles half of row 139. SANCHO AND RAMÓN ARE NOT BROTHERS:
Sancho's father was Félix, Ramón's was Salvador. Different men, both on
records. They may still be cousins, and the single thing that keeps that
worth chasing is the spelling — both fathers are written GERENA in
Montevideo parish acts one year apart, 1811 and 1812. That is a scribal
habit of one place and one time rather than two families independently
choosing the same variant. It is a resemblance and the page says twice
that it is not evidence.
The page sets out: the two houses side by side; the arithmetic that
separates them; Ramón's house record by record; Mauricio and Casimira's
children and why they explain four departments that looked like four
leads; the Trinidad nest with its Basque mothers and its consanguinity
dispensations; and what would join the houses to each other.
And it closes on what it must not be allowed to obscure. Neither house
reaches Pablo Armando. There is no Juan Carlos in either family, in any
generation, in any search that built the page. The Argentine end says
the same from three directions — no Lerena in the Rosario baptism index
for 1881–83, no Lerena or Lerina household in Santa Fe province in the
1895 census, and his parents named on exactly one document and nowhere
else on earth. These families are being built in parallel and in hope,
the hope is reasonable, and the hope is not evidence.
New row 140: read the 1812 act. The image is there, it costs nothing,
and Uruguayan acts routinely say where the father is natural de. If
Ramón is Córdoban like Sancho the two houses are cousins; if he is Banda
Oriental-born they are two arrivals. One phrase decides it.
Uruguay added to the nav beside Argentina and South Africa.

commits.subject: Repin: the long registers are laid out in boxes the browser can skip
commits.body:
A block box per two hundred rows, each holding its own table, sharing one
colgroup so the columns still line up. Measured working this time: twenty
skip-and-restore events across one scroll of the D'Arcy register, where the
previous attempt fired none.
The haystack that the filter reads is no longer built at load, because reading
every row's text was what rendered every row and defeated the skipping.

commits.subject: Ramón Lerena of Rosario — and the Uruguayan Lerenas are two families, not one
commits.body:
Row 138 asked for Mauricio Lerena's parents, on the reasoning that he
was born about 1810–18 and so belonged to the generation of Sancho's own
children, where the two families would either meet or not. Two searches,
and they do not meet.
  ALEJANDRO LERENA, birthplace ROSARIO, married Margarita Fernández
  Álvarez at San José, 16 September 1825. Father Ramón Lerena, mother
  María Josefa Gonsales. Her parents Juan Fernandes Alvares and Bárbara
  Sotura. ark 1:1:F21Y-JRV
  MAURICIO LERENA, birthplace COLLA, married Casimira Montaño at San
  José de Mayo, 3 February 1837. Father Ramón, mother María Gonzales.
  Her parents José Montaño and Ignacia Barredo. ark 1:1:F21B-SZ5
  And their brothers Manuel Lorenzo, born 14 November 1812 at Unión,
  Montevideo, and Luís Manuel, born 25 September 1820.
The 1825 act also closes a circuit the archive opened on 14 September.
the-three-alejandros.tsv recorded an "Alejandro Lerena of the Trinidad
orbit" with "Severa FERNANDEZ; and a Barbara Lerena" and could not place
him. The Fernández is his wife and the Bárbara is his mother-in-law,
Bárbara Sotura — which is how a Bárbara got into the indexes looking
like a Lerena.
So the whole interior hangs from one couple. Ramón Lerena and María
Josefa González of Rosario/Colla, fathering children c.1800–1820, whose
sons Alejandro and Mauricio are the fathers of Bernabé and Cipriano —
two of the six Trinidad fathers, and first cousins to each other. It
also accounts for all four departments the current tree pointed at, and
Rosario in Colonia turns out not to be a fourth lead at all: it is where
the family came from.
And the answer row 138 wanted. Alejandro married in 1825, so was born
about 1800–05, putting Ramón's birth about 1775–85. Sancho was baptised
about 1767, married in January 1791, first child 1793. A man born in
1775–85 cannot be the son of a man who married in 1791. Ramón is
Sancho's contemporary, roughly ten years his junior — not his
descendant.
That costs the comfortable assumption that the Uruguayan Lerenas are one
family. They are two, documented separately: Sancho's, from Canelones
1791 into the Montevideo trunk of Lerena Lenguas and Lerena Traibel; and
Ramón's, from Rosario-Colla across San José, Flores, Florida and Salto.
It buys a better question, which is row 139 and turns on a single
phrase. Uruguayan marriage acts say where the groom is NATURAL DE.
Sancho was "natural de Córdova la Llana". If Ramón is Córdoban too they
are brothers or cousins and the surname entered the Banda Oriental once;
if he was born in the Banda Oriental they are two arrivals and may be
unrelated. His marriage falls about 1795–1810, most likely at Rosario in
Colonia or San José.
None of this touches Pablo Armando. No Juan Carlos appears anywhere in
this family, in any generation, in any search that produced it.

commits.subject: A generation above the Trinidad nest: Mauricio Lerena and Casimira Montaño
commits.body:
Row 137 said to sweep the Uruguayan interior through the free
FamilySearch collections instead of the paywalled index the archive's
Uruguayan layer was read on. Run once, searching BY PARENT rather than
by person, and it worked immediately.
MAURICIO LERENA and CASIMIRA MONTAÑO, with at least seven children found
so far across five departments:
  Ignacia, born 30 July 1850 and dead 6 August 1850, San José de Mayo
  Manuel, b. 1856, married April 1882 at Santísima Trinidad, Trinidad,
    the same marriage also registered at San José
  Ignacia, b. 1864, married 27 April 1882 at Trinidad
  Mauricio junior, b. 1838, married 4 May 1878 at Florida
  Belisario, marriage registered 23 October 1890 at Salto
  Clara, d. Montevideo 3 March 1925, certificate 47, aged 77
  CIPRIANO, death registered 1928 at Flores
Cipriano is the finding. trinidad-flores-kindred.tsv has a Cipriano
Lerena who married Lauriana Beloqui and baptised three children at
Trinidad between 1875 and 1891, and the archive had no generation above
him or above any of the six Trinidad fathers. It has one now.
Graded honestly: the card says "Image Unavailable", so this is an INDEX
and not an act, and the identification rests on a rare forename in one
small department across the right span of years. Strong, not airtight —
two Ciprianos are possible.
Clara is the other one worth having. She is almost certainly the current
tree's "Demetria Clara Lerena Montaño, b. 22 December 1848, San José" —
forename, birth year and the mother's surname all agree — and the record
EXPLAINS the compound name, which a tree never does: she is Lerena
Montaño because her mother was Casimira Montaño. One disagreement left
standing: the tree says she died in 1930, the register says 1925.
And this reframes row 120. Four Uruguayan Lerenas in four departments
were treated as four leads. They are not. Three of the four departments
are accounted for by the children of one couple — San José de Mayo,
Trinidad in Flores, and Florida — with Salto and Montevideo besides. One
family spreading across the interior in a single generation. Only
Rosario in Colonia is still unaccounted for.
What it does not do: it does not touch Pablo Armando, it reaches no
Juan Carlos, and it does not join the nest to Sancho. Mauricio's own
parents are unknown, and until they are found the Trinidad kindred and
the Canelones trunk remain two documented families sharing a surname.
New row 138, and it is one rung and precisely defined. Mauricio was
fathering children by 1838, so he was born about 1810–1818 — the
generation of Sancho's own children. He is either one more child of
Sancho and María Fernández that the Canelones registers did not yield,
or the head of a separate family. His marriage, about 1835–1845 at San
José de Mayo or Trinidad, would decide it.

commits.subject: The bloodline chart fits its box again: repinned to 8e565d9
commits.body:
David asked what was going on with the bloodline chart and I diagnosed
it hours ago without fixing it. The diagnosis was right and the fix was
already upstream.
The chart was drawn at a fixed 1,354px and dropped into a 1,022px box
with overflow:auto, so it could only be dragged sideways — which is why
both edges were clipped and the leftmost generation heading was missing
entirely. Someone has since added width:100%, height:auto, and a
maxWidth/minWidth floor to bloodline.client.js in the kit, with a comment
working through exactly that ratio: 1,354 into 1,022 is 75%, which still
leaves a legible name box, and below 70% dragging beats squinting so the
stage scrolls as before.
Lerena was pinned eight commits behind it. Repinned to 8e565d9 and
reinstalled. Measured on Gilberto's chart at 1440px: the SVG now renders
at 1,022px, exactly 75% of natural size, and stage.scrollWidth no longer
exceeds clientWidth — no horizontal scroll. All four generation headings
are present, and Sancho Llerena Aguilar is visible in the grandparents'
column where the chart used to be cut off.
Full gate passes on the new pin: 629 pages, 0 broken, living/kit/
worklist/covers all clean.
What I have NOT changed, deliberately. The second thing visible in
David's screenshot — the empty vertical band beside a tall column — is
the centring rule, which puts short columns opposite the tallest rather
than at the ceiling. With 13 children against 2 in Gilberto's own
generation that leaves about 270 viewBox units of space above and below
the left-hand columns. It is a deliberate design choice with a comment
defending it, in a stylesheet shared by six archives that another
session is actively working in, and it reads far better now that
nothing is clipped. Not mine to redesign unilaterally.
Row 133 updated: the repin may or may not have brought a `.two` rule
with it, and the enrolment-card grid still carries its inline
workaround.

commits.subject: No new people in the interior — but the wrong index has been doing the work
commits.body:
Chasing names through Flores and San José produced nothing new. Every
person reached was already held: Bernabé Lerena and Casimira Pelaez,
Vitalino Lerena and Andrea Echeverry, Alejandro Lerena and Bárbara
Lerena of San José de Mayo. All in lerena-register.tsv or
trinidad-flores-kindred.tsv already. The interior is better worked than
the record counts suggested, which is the second time today that
measuring a thing and knowing a thing came apart.
What did turn up is a sourcing fact, and it is worth more than a name.
The archive's Uruguayan baptism layer, uruguay-baptisms-lerena.tsv, is a
findmypast FREE RESULT LIST. Its own header says so: "33 index rows...
transcripts are behind findmypast's paywall and were NOT opened."
Twenty-two rows recorded — eleven Trinidad, four Montevideo, three San
