José de Mayo — carrying names, years, and parents' FORENAMES ONLY.
Beside it, free, sit 1,343 exact LERENA records across the same four
departments, carrying parents in full and frequently a "View original
document" link. For Trinidad the 608 break roughly half Catholic Church
Records 1726–2000, half Civil Registration 1879–2020, and only a couple
from Uruguay Baptisms 1750–1900 — which is the very index findmypast was
charging to transcribe.
Fair to the earlier work, because the fairness matters: the register does
cite Catholic Church Records for particular people, so the collection was
not unknown. It was used person by person and never swept.
So the interior has been read through a paywalled index that gives
forenames, and never through the free one that gives full parentage and
images. New row 137: take the four departments one collection at a time
and build the Trinidad kindred upward. That is the difference between
knowing Bernabé married a Casimira Pelaez and being able to put a
generation above either of them — which is the only way the Trinidad
nest gets joined to Sancho, or shown to be a separate family.
One small thing kept from the sweep: Alberto Lerena Traibel, 1852–1921,
held in the trunk file on a tree ID, now has a record behind his death —
Montevideo civil registration, certificate 246, naming Avelino Lerena
and Ambrosia Treibel.

commits.subject: Retraction: the archive searched Flores three days ago and called it the nest
commits.body:
I said Flores, San José, Florida and Rosario-Colonia were "four
departments this archive has never searched", and I reported the Bernabé
Lerena / Casimira Pelaez family of Trinidad as a find. Both are wrong,
and the first one is simply false.
trinidad-flores-kindred.tsv, read 13 September 2026, is titled
"TRINIDAD, DEPARTMENT OF FLORES, URUGUAY — the founding nest of the
surname". It holds eleven children and the Basque mothers Beloqui,
Echeverry and Pelaez, and carries a correction of its own.
lerena-pelaez-trinidad.tsv maps four Lerena–Pelaez consanguinity
dispensations in the same town. Bernabé Lerena and Casimira Pelaez are
in it by name. Flores appears in fourteen data files.
San José, Florida and Colonia have no dedicated study, only passing
mentions, so for those three "never searched" was merely too strong. For
Flores it was false.
The mechanism matters more than the error. The claim entered through the
GEDCOM import, where a note about what the TREE offered got written as a
claim about what the ARCHIVE had done — without checking the archive.
A sentence of the form "this has never been searched" is a claim about
161 data files, and it has to be grepped before it is written, every
time. Caught about an hour after publishing, and only because the Flores
work led back into the-three-alejandros.tsv, which cites "the six
Trinidad, Flores fathers".
What survives is the measurement, which is new and is the useful part:
  Flores 608, San José 315, Florida 231, Colonia 189 — 1,343 exact
  LERENA records; Canelones, worked hardest of all, returns 191.
So the archive has read a NEST at Trinidad and there is a DEPARTMENT of
608 behind it, and San José, Florida and Colonia hold another 735
between them with no study at all. The picture is not wrong. It is thin
in places nobody had measured.
Corrected in gedcom-import.tsv, uruguay-four-departments.tsv and row
120, and logged serious in /corrections/.

commits.subject: Four departments, 1,343 records, and Flores alone is three times Canelones
commits.body:
Row 120 treated Flores, San José, Florida and Rosario-Colonia as four
names off the current tree. They are four doors, and the archive has
never opened any of them.
  Flores     608 exact LERENA records
  San José   315
  Florida    231
  Colonia    189
Canelones — the department this archive has worked hardest, where the
1791 marriage act was found, where the eight children were read off the
registers, where three burial registers were walked image by image —
returns 191. Flores alone is more than three times that.
Record-backed presence confirmed in two of the four by reading actual
entries: Fausto G. Lerena, married 7 April 1900 at Santísima Trinidad,
Trinidad, Flores, born 1880, son of Bernabé Lerena and Casimira Pelaez.
And Carmelo Anselmo Lerena, born 20 April 1846 and dead 27 April 1846 at
San José de Mayo — seven days old — son of Alejandro Lerena and Bárbara
Lerena. Note the parents sharing a surname, which is the same pattern as
Pablo Armando's own card, where his mother is written "María Lerena".
The tree's own Florida person, Brígida Rudecinda Lerena b. 1 March 1861,
was searched by name and NOT found. One person missing out of 231
records proves nothing; recorded so nobody assumes she was confirmed.
What it is not: 1,343 records is not 1,343 people, and nothing here
touches Pablo Armando. What it changes is the shape of the question.
This archive's Uruguay has been a Canelones marriage and a Montevideo
trunk, and that is the small part of the picture. And the tree's Gabino
of Flores is given as a son of Ramón Llerena Cubas and Margarita Leal —
not Sancho's line at all — so the interior departments may hold a
different Lerena family entirely, which is a useful warning against
reading every Uruguayan Lerena as a relative.
Two things found along the way and kept. Alberto Lerena Traibel,
1852–1921, already in the trunk file on a tree ID, now has a record
behind his death: Montevideo civil registration, certificate 246, 1
March 1921, naming Avelino Lerena and Ambrosia Treibel as his parents.
And a tool caveat: FamilySearch's anyPlace filter works cleanly for
Uruguay and failed silently for "Santa Fe, Argentina", almost certainly
because Santa Fe is both a province and a city. Before trusting any
place-filtered null, run the same filter on a place known to return
something.

commits.subject: The three lists of names say which is which
commits.body:
The People, Every Name and The Register sound identical in a menu and are
genuinely different pages: the people themselves, every name and how many bore
it, and one row per source line. A reader arriving at one had no way to tell.
D'Arcy is where this comes from - its /who/ opened by saying in so many words
what the other two were, and it was the clearest thing on the page.
Each of the three carries the same strip now, with the one you are standing in
marked. The wording is this archive's to change.

commits.subject: The work list was pointing the search at the wrong decade
commits.body:
Row 74 read "the 1908 enrolment card puts him still in Argentina."
The card shows the opposite. Its Oficina enroladora reads CAPETOWN and
both Región Militar and Distrito Militar are blank — the signature of a
man registering at his own consulate because he was already abroad. The
card is evidence he had LEFT Argentina. And the 1908 is unsourced
anyway: no year on the card but the class of 1882, a collection
catalogued 1911–1936, and a Cape Town consular libreta of 1915 on the
passport.
That error mattered more than a wrong fact usually does, because it set
a floor on the search — if he was in Argentina in 1908, his departure is
after 1908 — while rows 74 and 108 were simultaneously hunting a
1901–1905 window derived from his son being born at the Cape in 1905.
The work list was holding two incompatible positions and no page
noticed. Logged serious: a wrong fact on a work list is worse than one
on a page, because a work list tells the next session where to look.
And I withdrew half of what I wrote this morning. I had said Pablo
Armando's absence from the 1895 census at thirteen suggested he had
already left. It suggests nothing of the kind. One person can always be
missed or mangled — and this person's name demonstrably mangles, since
the Argentine army's own index turned his card into "Armand Lorena,
born Rosario de Lerma, Salta."
The control is what separated the two claims, and it is worth keeping.
Gonzalez, exact, Santa Fe returns 88,739 records with the 1895 census
reaching San Cristóbal, Alberdi/Rosario, San Jerónimo and Iriondo. So
the index is dense and covers Rosario itself, which means:
  the SURNAME absent from the province is STRONG — for a surname to
  vanish from a province indexed that thickly it has to be really
  absent, and that agrees with the Rosario baptism sweep from an
  entirely different record type;
  the INDIVIDUAL absent from the census is WEAK, and is withdrawn as
  evidence of anything.
Same census, same search, two completely different evidential weights.
Honest position on his passage out: nothing dates it. Born Rosario
February 1882, son born Cape Town November 1905, twenty-three years with
no record inside them. The live routes remain the ones hypothesis 2
already named — UK outward passenger lists (BT 27, indexed from 1890)
and the consular file behind the 1940 passport — and the archive had
already reasoned that the South African War shipped some 360,000 horses
in, Argentina among the sources, when he was seventeen to twenty and a
horseman.

commits.subject: Turin mapped in detail, and it cannot answer the question — Argentina can
commits.body:
David asked to keep going on Turin in detail. Done, and the honest
result is that this route is structurally incapable of closing it.
The map: 49 Lerina records in and around Torino — the civil registration
of Turin 1866–1924, the Diocese of Torino, Ivrea, and the Piedmont towns
of Montaldo Roero and Costigliole. Recurring fathers Carlo, Giacomo,
Firmino, Luigi, Domenico, Antonio, Innoquiti. Two Carlo Lerinas appear
as fathers. These families post banns in Turin, marry in Turin and die
in Turin across sixty years. They stay put.
Why it cannot work, written down so nobody spends a week on it. The
Turin civil series begins in 1866, so a man born in the 1840s or 1850s
has no birth record in it at all — he can only appear as a father, a
groom or a corpse, and the diocesan books are indexed only in patches.
And the fatal one: an emigrant leaves no later Italian record by
construction, so "a son who vanishes from the Turin record" cannot be
distinguished from an unindexed death, a move to another province, or a
register that was never filmed. Enumerating Piedmontese Lerinas produces
a map of the people who STAYED, which is exactly the complement of what
is wanted.
So the question went to the other end instead, and that produced
something. LERINA in Argentina, a spelling this archive had never swept:
26 records, and exactly one person of that surname ever appears in Santa
Fe province. Set beside the archive's existing Lerena sweep, that gives
a clean joint negative — in 1895 there was no Lerena and no Lerina
household, under any spelling, anywhere in Santa Fe province, thirteen
years after Pablo Armando was born there. It is the same answer the
Rosario baptism sweep gave, arriving from a census rather than a parish,
and it is the strongest negative this archive has on the Argentine end.
And a fact already held now reads differently: Pablo Armando is not in
the 1895 census at all, at thirteen, and he is at the Cape by 1905. New
row — rows 74 and 108 hunt his passage out in a 1901–1905 window, and
that window may be far too late.
One method catch, recorded because it would have become a published
falsity. A search filtered with q.anyPlace=Santa Fe returned ZERO while
the same 26 records unfiltered contain a Santa Fe burial. The place
filter silently failed to match a place demonstrably in the data, and it
was caught only because a record already in hand should have come back
and did not. A null from a filtered query is worth nothing until the
same query is run without the filter.

commits.subject: Repin: an echoed source label, a retired prop, and tr[hidden] said out loud
A Juan Lerina in Santa Fe, written down as a coincidence and not a lead
commits.body:
The archive has worked LERENA hard in Argentina and had never swept
LERINA, which is the commoner Italian spelling. Done now, exact match:
26 records, thinly scattered across La Rioja, Santiago del Estero, the
1895 census, cemetery and military records. No family group, no cluster,
nothing resembling a household at Rosario.
One is worth writing down, and worth writing down carefully:
  JUAN LERINA, age 64, estimated birth 1862, buried 4 April 1926 at
  Santa Fe, La Capital, Santa Fe, Argentina. Cemetery records,
  1:1:6575-KRRP. Image unavailable.
For it: the Italian spelling of the surname, Santa Fe province, and a
birth about 1862 that is not impossible for a man whose son was born in
February 1882. Against it, and heavier: he is Juan, not Juan Carlos; he
is at Santa Fe La Capital, 170 km north of Rosario and a different city;
1862 makes him twenty when Pablo Armando was born; and the image is
unavailable, so the entry itself cannot be read. Four loose fits and no
join. This archive has been wrong before by promoting exactly this shape
of thing, so it is filed as a coincidence.
It also does not disturb the standing claim on the front page — "No Juan
Carlos Lerena appears in any indexed record in Argentina or Uruguay" —
which is still literally true: this man is Juan LERINA. The sentence was
checked against the find rather than left to rot, which is the only good
reason to record a find like this.
CEMLA could not be run and that is a hard stop, not a difficulty. The
buscador is an iframe onto search.cemla.com and the form carries
CaptchaCode and LBD_VCID_SampleCaptcha. This session does not complete
CAPTCHAs. New row, owner David — with a prior question attached, because
it may make the search pointless: CEMLA's arrivals database is generally
given as starting in 1882, and if so, an arrival before February 1882 is
invisible to it by construction and finding nothing would prove nothing.
Check the coverage before spending the searches.

commits.subject: Repin: the table chunking did nothing and is gone
commits.body:
Measured in a browser: content-visibility on a tbody inside a table never
skips, with either table layout, while a plain off-screen div does. The
debounce stays.

commits.subject: Antenati has the Turin images and cannot search them for these years
commits.body:
David asked whether Antenati holds anything. It was the right place to
ask about — the caveat on yesterday's FamilySearch work was that
FamilySearch's Italian coverage is uneven, and Antenati is the Italian
State Archives' own portal, the source rather than a mirror of it.
  LERENA, whole national name index: ONE record. Cesare Lerena, death
  register 1915, Brescia, spouse Rosa Barbaleni. Lombardy, not
  Piedmont, and not our man.
  LERINA: eight, and most of them are "Di Lerina", which is a different
  surname. No Carlo, no Giovanni, no Giovanni Carlo.
But that null is worthless, and the control is what shows it. Antenati
holds 2,621 registers for Torino — the images are there. Searching its
name index for ROSSI restricted to Torino returns 102 people called
Charles, Marguerite and Jacinte, in the years 1805 to 1811. The Turin
name index is Napoleonic only, kept in French during the French
annexation of Piedmont, and it does not reach the 1840s–1880s at all.
So for Piedmont in the period that matters, Antenati's images exist and
are not name-searchable. A surname search there was never capable of
finding him. That is the same lesson as the Rosario typescript index
and the FreeREG Devon parishes: the null belongs to the finding aid and
not to the past.
What is searchable for the right years is FamilySearch's "Italy,
Torino, Torino, Civil Registration (Tribunale), 1866–1899", which is
where the 66 Lerena and 114 Lerina came from. Antenati's 2,621 Turin
registers remain the fallback — browsable by comune and year, image by
image, the way this archive read Rosario and Canelones. Expensive, and
possible.

commits.subject: No Juan Carlos in Italy — but the surname lives in Piedmont, where the DNA points
commits.body:
David asked whether there is a Juan Carlos Lerena or Lerina in Italian
records. Tested under both spellings.
The direct answer is no. There is no Giovanni Carlo or Gian Carlo
Lerena or Lerina anywhere in FamilySearch's Italian index. Carlo and
Giovanni both occur; they never occur together.
Method note, because the default search would have produced nonsense: a
fuzzy search for LERENA in Italy returns 9,112 and is worthless — the
results are Lorino, Loreno, Lorena, Lorosano, Lorrai. Exact match
returns 66. Every figure below is exact-match, and the zero for "Carlo
Lerena" is controlled by the same search without a forename returning
66, so the mechanism works and the surname is in the index.
What the search found instead is better than a name:
  LERENA, exact, Italy — 66 records, clustered in the DIOCESE OF
  TORINO. Bartolomeo, Teresa, Eduardo, Luigi, Paolo, Giovanni,
  Giuseppe, Giacomo, Maddalena. All Italian forenames, in Piedmont.
  This archive did not know the surname was Italian at all.
  LERINA, exact, Italy — 114, more than Lerena. Torino again, plus
  Ivrea. This is the commoner Italian spelling, which matters because
  CEMLA has Lerinas landing at Buenos Aires.
And that is the same corner of Italy the DNA already pointed at. The
archive's own DNA page reasons that Cheryl's 11.1% Italian, with three
non-Italian grandparents, implies about 44% in Pablo Armando — one
Italian parent — and that the split is northern-dominant, 6.1 against
3.6. The Italian Lerenas and Lerinas are in Turin and Ivrea. That is
the north. Two independent things, an admixture estimate and a surname
distribution, now point the same way, and neither names anybody.
Recorded as convergence, not proof.
The one age-plausible Carlo is written down as a coincidence and not a
candidate: Carlo Domenico Lerina, baptised Ivrea 30 May 1858, parents
Antonio Lerina and Giuseppa Pean-Conto. Nothing whatever ties him to
Argentina.
And the null is weaker than 66 and 114 make it look. FamilySearch's
Italian coverage is uneven by province, a man who left before 1882 may
have no indexed Italian record at all, and if he was baptised Giovanni
and became Juan Carlos on the far side of the Atlantic then the Carlos
never existed in Italy to be indexed. That is the ordinary shape of an
emigrant's name.
New row: work Piedmont properly, and re-run CEMLA for both spellings
before 1882, which is the arrival that would matter.

commits.subject: Mary Septima gets her own block, and the sons get a line of their own
commits.body:
Following the Luwinski archive's layout: a row rail on the left, cards
on a line, an eyebrow label on each saying what the person is, and the
status pill kept.
  1882 → 1950 — Pablo Armando Lerena beside MARY SEPTIMA TAYLOR, who
  until now was a clause inside his entry and is now a block in her own
  right: her name is a count, she was the seventh daughter of ten, her
  birth is registered at Bideford in the December quarter of 1884,
  5b/506 — and her line is documented three censuses further back than
  his, to a mason born at Westleigh about 1777 and a Scotswoman who died
  in the Northam alms house. The Lerena side stops at two names.
  Their sons — three cards on one line. Roque Luis Armando, whose 1911
  baptism is what proves Pablo Armando and Robert Paul are one man, and
  who was born six years before his parents married and baptised three
  months before the wedding. Ricardo JUAN CARLOS, who carries the name
  on the enrolment card and so corroborates it from eleven thousand
  miles away. And Nuno Fernando, David's grandfather, marked as the
  descent.
The standalone 1882 node went with it — he was appearing twice once the
marriage row existed. Checked in the built HTML: one instance in the
tree, the other two are ordinary prose elsewhere on the page.

commits.subject: Repin: the bloodline chart fills its box and scales down
commits.body:
Raised from the Lerena session, fixed in the kit and rolled to all seven rather
than pinned on one - the same component rendering two ways across the estate is
the drift the kit exists to stop.

commits.subject: One tree with status pills, and a page that was contradicting itself
commits.body:
David: "this is also confusing... we may as well keep as one tree with a
status of inferred or documented as pills/colour legends."
The front page ran two parallel lanes, and in four of its six rows one
lane held nothing but an em-dash. Half the grid was placeholder, which
is what made it hard to read. It is now ONE tree, oldest first, with a
legend and a pill on every node:
  Documented  a record was read, and it says this
  Inferred    this archive's reading, with no record behind it
  Not proved  the join nothing supports yet
Every generation is present and in order — 1791, 1793–1815, 19th c.,
then the break, then by 1882, 1882, 1911→ — and the Juan Carlos and
María generation, which the lanes never gave a row of its own, now has
one. The argument the two lanes existed to make is not lost: it is
carried by a single full-width dashed break, "And here the tree
breaks", sitting exactly where the evidence stops, and by an Inferred
note on the Montevideo trunk saying plainly that Pablo Armando's
descent from it is this archive's reading and not a record.
Heading changed with it: "Two lines, and they do not yet meet" became
"One tree, and the joint that is missing".
I broke the stylesheet doing it and am recording how, because it was
nearly invisible. Deleting the old lane CSS line-by-line removed the
first line of two multi-line rules and left their second lines behind as
orphans — `opacity:.6; padding-top:14px; text-align:right; }` sitting
outside any selector. That is a parse error, and everything after it in
the block, including the .tag pill styles, silently stopped applying.
The build passed throughout. Fixed, and braces now balance 25/25.
And the reason this page was worth rereading in full: /direct-line/ said
at the bottom "Above him there is nothing. His parents are unnamed in
every document held here" — while its own opening paragraph said an
enrolment card names his father and mother. The page has contradicted
itself for six days. Now reads "Above him there is one generation and no
more". Logged in /corrections/ as SERIOUS, because it is not a slipped
digit: it is the archive telling a reader the opposite of what it knows,
on the page whose job is to state the line.

commits.subject: What the card actually is — a conscription registration, made at the Cape
commits.body:
David asked for the explanation to go on the page, and he was right that
it belongs there: the obvious reading of a military document is the
wrong one here.
New section, "What this card actually is":
  It is a registration every Argentine man had to make. Argentina
  introduced compulsory service in 1901 and enrolled men in a clase
  named for their birth year, so "Clase de 1882" is his cohort, not a
  date. Marked on the page as background rather than something this
  archive has sourced, because it is.
  The blanks are the evidence. Región Militar: nothing. Distrito
  Militar: nothing. A man enrolling in Argentina is placed in a region
  and given a district; he has neither, and his enrolling office is
  Capetown — which for an Argentine abroad meant his consulate.
  So the card is the reverse of what it looks like. Not a soldier
  arriving at the Cape, but a man already living there doing his
  Argentine paperwork. That is what makes it evidence he had emigrated
  before he filled it in.
  Matrícula, Domicilio, Casilla and N.º de órden are empty too: he
  registered, he was never mustered. The only numbers are the filing
  ones, Serie E 3555 and Sección I 3322.
And a caution panel, because the date will not stand up. This page calls
it the ficha of 1908 and nothing on the card says 1908 — the only year
on its face is the class, 1882 — and the archive has never written down
where 1908 came from. It sits in a collection catalogued 1911–1936.
Against that, page 6 of the passport records the libreta de enrolamiento
from the Consulado General Argentino, Cape Town, with Dist. Militar a
dash, Matrícula a dash, and Año 1915 — the same pattern as this card,
down to the two dashes. Either there were two enrolment events at the
Cape or these are one, and if they are one the date is 1915. Flagged,
not decided.
Also moved the link cards above the "printed card with blank rules"
prose. David could not find them and said so twice: they were sitting at
y≈1047, below the fold on a normal screen. The heading now lands at
y≈666 at 1440x900, so "Go and look at it yourself" is visible without
scrolling, though the links themselves are still a little under.

commits.subject: Serie reads E 3555, not 3885 — David read the original
commits.body:
The card's SERIE field was published as "3885" in the table of what the
card says. It reads "E 3555". The letter prefix was dropped entirely and
two digits were misread.
What should have caught it here, and did not: SECCIÓN directly below was
transcribed "I 3322" — correctly, letter and all. Two adjacent fields of
identical shape, one with its letter and one without, is an internal
inconsistency this archive could have seen without looking at the image
at all.
Neither number carries weight in any argument on the page. No conclusion
moves. Logged in /corrections/ anyway, because a transcription is the
one thing this archive asks a reader to take on trust, and a wrong one
is worse than a missing one.

commits.subject: The record links become a card, and a stray 261 KB file leaves the build
commits.body:
David asked for the FamilySearch links to be prominent rather than a
line of prose. They are now a two-card section, "Go and look at it
yourself": the image on one card, the index entry on the other, each
with its ark underneath.
Reconciled with another session that edited this page at the same time.
That session had already answered, and answered better, the question my
earlier panel left open — where "Serena" comes from. It is the printed
field label SERIE, and the drawer is filed by sound, so Lera / Lorena /
Serena / Sera / Perena were already neighbours before any machine read
them. My panel duplicated that, so it is gone. The one fact in it that
was not covered elsewhere — the record is attached to tree person
GPWH-72S — moved onto the index card. I also left three nested
<section> elements behind when I inserted it; that is fixed.
Two things found while checking the result in the browser:
  There is no .two rule. The stylesheet has `.grid { display:grid;
  gap:14px }` and nothing for `.two`, in any media query. So both
  `grid two` blocks on the site — this one and the front page's "What
  this archive has established" — have always rendered as one column at
  every width. Worked around inline here with an auto-fit minmax, and
  logged as a row: the real fix is in the shared kit stylesheet and
  needs six archives repinned, so it should ride along with row 92.
  site/public/docs/.jpg — a hidden file, 261 KB, byte-identical to
  marriage-1911.jpg and referenced by nothing. It was committed in
  a1eba22, the "six documents published" commit, which is exactly where
  the zsh 1-indexed-array bug struck and produced an empty basename.
  Deleted.

commits.subject: Unblock the deploy, and make the local gate run what CI runs
commits.body:
The site has not deployed since 09:11 this morning. Three pushes in a
row failed and I did not notice, because I checked the gate and the push
and never the deployment. Said the work was live when it was not.
The cause was not in these commits. d1a9811, from another session
working this repo, added work-list rows 131 and 132 with state "open",
which is not one of blocked/done/next/running/struck. check:worklist
rejected it, the build exited 1, and every push after that inherited a
red pipeline. Both rows set to "next", which is what they plainly are.
The reason nothing local caught it is the real fix. tools/verify.sh ran
`npx astro build` directly. CI runs `npm run build`, which chains
check:living, check:kit, check:worklist and check:covers after astro. So
the local gate was a strict subset of CI and could print ALL GATES
PASSED over a build that could never deploy. verify.sh now runs
`npm run build`, and all four kit checks pass locally:
  living     630 pages, no living person reaches the build
  kit        630 pages, 1453 ids, links/anchors/search/sitemap clean
  worklist   ok
  covers     ok
For the record, so the scope is not overstated: last night's Brayley and
census work did deploy and is live. What was stuck behind the red
pipeline is today's two commits — the menu rename and the ark links.

commits.subject: Make the citations clickable: 11 arks were links, now 72 are
commits.body:
David asked where the link to the actual record was on /enrolment-card/
and there wasn't one. The page cited the arks — image 3:1:3QHK-MQL4-NQWN,
index 1:1:6TH8-DVXH — as dead text in a mono span. A citation the reader
cannot follow is doing half its job.
That turned out to be systemic. 72 distinct FamilySearch arks are quoted
across the site and 11 of them were clickable. The register alone had 58
dead ones, the people index 52, the places pages 36.
Fixed once, in the shared helper: arkify() in site/src/lib/text.js turns
a bare ark into a link to familysearch.org/ark:/61903/<ark>, and emph()
now runs it, so every field already rendered through emph() is covered.
It runs after escaping and after the conversion, so it only ever
sees text it has escaped itself and cannot corrupt its own markup. Four
call sites were rendering source strings raw and now go through emph:
register.astro, people/index.astro, places/[slug].astro, and two
hardcoded spans in searched.astro plus one in horses.astro.
Verified against the live build: 72 clickable, one left — 1:1:XPG2-RYP
on /worklist/, which is rendered by the archive-kit WorkList component
and would need the kit changed and six archives repinned. Left alone and
recorded rather than quietly fixed halfway.
And following the link paid immediately. FamilySearch's index of the
enrolment card does not say Pablo Armando Lerena. It says "Armand
Lorena", born 1882 at "Rosario de Lerma, Salta" — a real town seven
hundred miles from Rosario de Santa Fe — with his father as "Juan Carlos
Lorena Serena" and his mother, correctly, María Lerena. So no search for
Lerena at Santa Fe could ever have returned it, which is why it was hard
to find; and it is a plain demonstration of this archive's own rule that
the index is a finding aid and the image is the evidence.
One real question falls out, recorded on the page as open: where does
"Serena" come from? This archive reads the father's line as Juan Carlos
Lerena and nothing more, and an indexer in front of the same handwriting
saw a second word. That wants re-reading at higher resolution before
anyone decides who is right. The record is also attached to a
FamilySearch tree person, GPWH-72S, which has not been examined.
Also renamed the menu entry "The Card" to "The Enrolment Card".

commits.subject: Say "enrolment" in the menu, because David looked and did not see it
commits.body:
The enrolment card page was never orphaned — it is linked from all 629
pages through the nav, with four in-body links from the front page and
four from /family-papers/. The problem was the label. It read "The
Card", sitting between "The Passport" and "The Name", and nothing in
those two words says this is the only document that names Pablo
Armando's father and mother.
Renamed to "The Enrolment Card". It breaks the terse parallel of the
other entries slightly, and the archive's most important document
should be findable by someone who does not already know what it is.

commits.subject: The prose pages that cannot join their siblings, written down where they will be seen
commits.body:
Three shared pages are stuck, and not on anything the UI can fix. /searched/
sits at four of seven, /open-questions/ at two, /sources/ at two, because the
rest of the estate holds those as paragraphs rather than rows. Turning a
paragraph into rows means deciding what each search returned and what would
answer each question, and that is research this archive owns.
Until now that only existed in the shared-pages register, which is my record
and not this archive's. It is on the work list now, where the coverage gate can
see it and where whoever picks this session up will meet it.
The outcome words and the confidence words stay this archive's. The estate
deliberately does not flatten hit, yield, nothing and pending into a shared
five - those are different judgements about what a search did.

commits.subject: Two hundred and seventy-eight people, and the standing becomes a question you can ask
commits.body:
The card grid becomes the estate's table. What this page argues - that a rare
surname produces a majority of unplaced people, and that this is what the work
looks like before the connecting document turns up - was sortable but not
askable. Connected, excluded and unplaced are a filter now, and the trade, the
place and the record that produced each person are columns rather than a line
of run-together text.
The search box goes because the shared table brings one, and it no longer
carries a second copy of every card's text in an attribute beside it.

commits.subject: The alms house at Northam, and a fourth spelling trap
commits.body:
The 1891 household was found by searching TAYLOR. Searching BRAYLEY in
the same parish and year finds two more people, and one of them is the
grandmother. A search under BRAILEY returns zero for Devon in 1891 —
the household that was BRAILEY in 1861 is BRAYLEY again by 1891.
  Georgina Brayley, head, WIDOW, 77, "Living On Means", born Scotland,
  East Lothian — living ALONE in the ALMS HOUSE, Northam. Piece 1787,
  ED 6, folio 72, page 6, schedule 40. A different enumeration district
  and a short walk from her daughter's family at 2 Fore Street.
That completes a sentence the tree only half-wrote. It gives her
occupation as "Monthly Nurse & Shoemaker Wife Pauper", which has always
read like three things run together. Follow her across four records and
the whole life is there: "Shoemaker Wife" in 1851, a married lodger in
her father-in-law's house with her husband five weeks from dying in the
county asylum; "Mangles Clothes" in 1861, a widow keeping her own
household; the alms house in 1891; and a death at Bideford in the March
quarter of 1900, aged 85. The Scottish end of the ascent is now on four
English records.
And a candidate, graded as a candidate. Georgina Brayley, 20, general
servant, born London Kilburn, in a draper's household in Tower Street,
Northam — precisely the pattern of Mary Ann Hellen herself, in service
in a china dealer's house at eighteen, and carrying the family's
forename. The obvious reading is a granddaughter of Georgina Temple,
most likely a daughter of John Walker Brayley. None of it is proven:
the census states no relationship to anybody in this family. Row 130.
The hypothesis that Mary Septima, aged 6, was with her grandmother was
worth testing and it fails — her grandmother is alone. She is not at 2
Fore Street, not in the alms house, and not among the 368 Devon Taylors
born 1882–1886. Where she was is a real open question.

commits.subject: Three Brailey households on one street, and a false null that nearly stood
commits.body:
Lower Gunstone, Bideford, 7 April 1861. Piece 1502, ED 7.
This entry almost did not happen. A search of all 129 Brayleys in
FreeCEN's Devon for 1861 found no William born Westleigh, no Georgina
born in Scotland and no child born in London. The control was clean —
53 Taylors at Bideford the same year, so the parish-year is properly
transcribed — and the null was one sentence from being written down as
"the family left Bideford between 1851 and 1870."
It would have been false. Searched again as BRAILEY, every one of them
came back, on the same street as in 1851. That is the third false zero
this one spelling produced in a single evening. A controlled null is
only as good as the spelling it was run under.
  Schedule 27: Georgina Brailey, head, WIDOW, 45, "Mangles Clothes",
  born Scotland — with Isabella, 20, NEEDLE WOMAN, born London, St
  Andrews; John, 16, DRUGGIST PORTER, born St Pancras; Georgina, 10,
  scholar, born Bideford; and a lodger.
  Schedule 38: Ellen Brailey, servant, 18, "HOUSE SERVANT", born London
  (City), in the household of Michael Prust, china dealer. The current
  tree gives Mary Ann Hellen the occupation "House Servant" and nothing
  to support it. Here it is, written by an enumerator — and she went
  into service four doors from her mother.
  Schedule 48: William Brailey, head, WIDOWER, 84, "Formerly A Mason",
  born Westleigh, living alone. Peggy died in January 1858 and he is a
  widower at the same address.
What the two censuses together establish: the family did not leave.
Lower Gunstone in 1851 and in 1861; Mary Ann Hellen marries at Bideford
in 1870; her mother dies there in 1900 aged 85; she and her brother die
there the same year. Four generations on one street for fifty years.
Isabella is confirmed a second time, ten years on, with the same
birthplace — a real person, not a transcription ghost. John is sixteen,
putting his birth at 1845 for the third time: two censuses now against
the single 1900 informant who implied 1847.
Both censuses agree the old mason was born about 1777 — 74 in 1851, 84
in 1861 — where the tree says 1 March 1778. Two records against one
tree. And Peggy's four-year gap is recorded as still open: she died in
1858, eight years before the death index began carrying ages, so it
cannot be closed from an index at all and needs Braunton's baptisms.
The three households now render on /family-papers/ in date order.

commits.subject: Section 9: the evening's records reach the page, not just the data directory
commits.body:
The index and census findings were sitting in data/ as TSV and JSON with
nothing rendering them. They now have a section on /family-papers/:
 the sixteen graded claims, tree against index;
 a panel on why the NAMES are the find and not the dates;
 the household at 2 Fore Street, Northam, 5 April 1891;
 the household at Lower Gunstone, Bideford, 30 March 1851.
Two rendering faults found and fixed while checking the built page
rather than assuming it:
 Emphasis leaked in the relation and age cells, which were the two
 columns not wrapped in em(). Three tables' worth of reached the
 HTML; the gate caught it.
 The repeated header lines inside the TSVs were being rendered as data
 rows, and — worse — the children block of the 1851 file carried six
 columns against the header's seven, so every child's OCCUPATION cell
 held their birthplace and their BIRTHPLACE cell held the commentary.
 Fixed in the data, not papered over in the template: the four
 grandchildren now carry their real census occupations (three
 Scholars, and a blank for the eight-month-old).
Verified in the browser against the running dev server: three tables,
18/10/7 body rows, no stray markers, columns aligned.

commits.subject: Lower Gunstone, Bideford, 30 March 1851 — four generations in one house
commits.body:
Piece 1895, folio 108, page 8, schedule 34. The best single record of
the day, found free, in a database that had been sitting there all
along. The Brayley ascent was published as eleven generations of pure
tree; this page puts four of them in one house with their birthplaces
written down by an enumerator.
  William Brayley, head, 74, MASON, born Westleigh — generation 4, and
  it was unsourced until tonight. His trade matters: the ascent has
  John Reed, STONEMASON, three generations up and Gregory Reed, PAUPER
  SHOEMAKER, two. The tree did not need to invent that.
  Peggy Brayley, wife, 78, born BRAUNTON — generation 4w, with the
  nickname on the record. And the house is LOWER GUNSTONE, which is the
  address the tree gives for her death in 1858. Her age is four years
  off the tree's 1777, which is more than ordinary census slippage and
  is recorded as a discrepancy, not smoothed over.
  Georgina, lodger, married, 35, "Shoemaker Wife", born HADDINGTON,
  EAST LOTHIAN — Georgina Temple, and this is the 1851 census the tree
  already cited for her. She is in her father-in-law's house with four
  children and no husband.
Put that beside the other record found tonight. The census is 30 March
1851; John Brailey died 4 May 1851, indexed in the St Thomas district,
which contains the county asylum at Exminster. He was alive on census
night and he was not in the house. Sue Rowbotham's history has a
chapter called "The mystery of the missing husband and daughter". Here
is the household he is missing from, dated.
The four children resolve two open questions and raise a person:
  John, grandson, aged 5, born St Pancras. A boy of 5 on 30 March 1851
  was born April 1845 – March 1846, which fits the tree's 22 June 1845
  and not the 1900 death index's implied 1847. That two-year gap, left
  open earlier tonight, resolves in the tree's favour — the informant
  in 1900 was wrong. The census says St Pancras where the tree says St
  Paul's, and that disagreement stands.
  Georgina, granddaughter, EIGHT MONTHS, born Bideford — so born about
  July 1850, and the tree's "1851" is a year late. Three elder children
  London-born and the baby Bideford-born also dates the family's return
  to Devon: between 1845 and mid-1850.
  Ellen, granddaughter, 8, born City of London — Mary Ann Hellen as a
  child, in the house, a year high like everyone else on this page.
  Isabella, granddaughter, 10, born London, ST ANDREW — a daughter this
  archive did not have. Mary Ann Hellen named her own second daughter
  Isabella Temple in 1874, for this sister and for their mother's
  maiden name. New row 129. Whether she is Sue Rowbotham's missing
  daughter is not established and is written down only to be tested.
Controlled: Westleigh 1851 was searched for Brayley first and returned
zero. A Taylor search in the same parish and year returns 12, so the
parish is transcribed and the zero is real — and expected, since the
tree already had William at Bideford by then.

commits.subject: 2 Fore Street, Northam, on the night of 5 April 1891
commits.body:
FreeCEN holds Northam for 1891. Piece 1787, ED 4, folio 42, page 1,
schedule 2 — the first time this archive has seen Mary Septima's family
in a household return.
  William Taylor, head, 65, "Cab Driver / ret'd Army Srgt", born
  Worlingworth, Suffolk. That confirms the birthplace and solves
  something filed as a data error: the tree attaches "Sergeant-Major in
  the army" to the infant who died at nine months in 1825. The trade
  was real and had drifted onto the wrong William. It belongs to this
  man, on a census return, in his own house.
  Mary A. H. Taylor, wife, 47, born ST BARTHOLOMEWS, London (City).
  That is the birthplace FreeBMD could not find a registration for,
  control passed. Three independent records now agree she was born in
  1843 and not one of them is her birth certificate.
  William J. and Kathleen G., both 20, both born Bideford. The twins,
  confirmed a third time — tree, birth index, census.
  Horace A., 19, footman. Margaret H. N. (the initial is W, for
  Walker), 14. Irene, 12. Lucy E., 9. Agnes W., 1, born at this
  address. And a visitor, Agnes Harrison, dressmaker, of Macclesfield.
What it did not settle. There is no Edith of the right age in Northam,
so that candidate for the tenth child is weakened — but Mary Septima,
aged 6, is missing from her own parents' household too, and a
county-wide check of all 368 Devon Taylors born 1882–1886 does not find
her either. A census cannot tell a child who was elsewhere from a child
who never was, and a child who died before 1891 would fit every fact
there is. The count still demands a seventh daughter.
The null is soft and is recorded as soft: FreeCEN's Devon 1891 is
transcribed parish by parish and is not complete for the county.
Northam itself is, which is the only reason her absence from it counts.
New row 128: where was she on census night, and who is the tenth child.

commits.subject: Nine of nine Taylor children, and the names carry the ascent inside them
commits.body:
One search — births, surname Taylor, Bideford registration district
(which contains Northam), 1870–1890. Every child the tree names is in
the index, in the right district, in the right quarter. Not one miss.
Including the one that matters to this archive: TAYLOR, Mary Septima,
Bideford, December quarter 1884, 5b/506. The woman who married Pablo
Armando at St Dominic's, Wynberg, on 3 September 1911 now has her own
birth registration located.
The tree's odd-looking pair of November 1870 births turns out to be
right, not a data error: Kathleen Georgina at 5b/490 and William John
at 5b/489, same quarter, adjacent pages. They are almost certainly
twins. The tree was right and it looked wrong.
But the names are the find, not the dates. Isabella TEMPLE (1874),
Margaret Hellen W[ALKER] (1876), Agnes WALKER (1889). Those are not
forenames. They are the surnames of the two women at the Scottish end
of the ascent — Georgina Temple, born Haddington 1814, and HELEN
WALKER, who married George Temple at Haddington in 1813 and who, per
gedcom-graded.tsv, cites nothing at all.
She is still not on a record. But three of her descendants were
registered with her surname as a given name, by a clerk, in 1874, 1876
and 1889 — and that is on a record. The naming pattern this archive
noticed and guessed at is now documented even though the woman behind
it is not.
New row 127, out of the count argument: the tree says ten children and
names nine, and SEPTIMA MEANS SEVENTH. Counted off the index Mary
Septima is only the sixth daughter, so a daughter is missing between
1881 and 1884. The index offers exactly one — TAYLOR, Edith, Bideford,
September quarter 1882 — and this archive already knew of a sister
Edie at 26 Fore Street, Northam, in 1935. Graded a strong candidate and
not a find: the birth index gives no mother's maiden name before 1911.
The 1891 census at Northam would settle it, the twins, and John Walker
Brayley's two-year age gap, in one household line.

commits.subject: Three deaths in Bideford in nine months, and one age that will not fit
commits.body:
Second pass at the GRO index, same evening.
  Georgina Temple — CONFIRMED, and the age confirms Haddington.
  BRAYLEY, Georgina, age 85, Bideford, Mar quarter 1900, 5b/421. A
  woman born 23 August 1814 is 85 all through that quarter. The tree's
  vague "about January 1900" lands in exactly the right quarter. She is
  indexed BRAYLEY though her husband was registered BRAILEY.
  John Walker Brayley — the death is confirmed and the birth year is
  contradicted. BRAYLEY, John Walker, age 53, Bideford, Dec quarter
  1900, 5b/305. Distinctive name, right quarter, right district. But 53
  at 22 October 1900 means born about 1847, and the tree says 22 June
  1845. Two years out, in a family whose other two reported ages have
  just proved exact to the month — which points at the tree rather than
  the informant.
  So mother, daughter and son all die in Bideford inside nine months:
  March, June and December quarters of 1900.
  And neither sibling has a registered birth. No John Walker Brayley
  anywhere in England and Wales 1843–1850; no Mary Brayley or Brailey
  in June 1843. Two siblings, two missing registrations, is no longer
  two nulls — it is a household that did not register births, which was
  lawful before the 1875 Act. That weakens both nulls as evidence and
  points where the tree pointed all along: the parish baptism registers
  of St Paul's and St Bartholomew's.
  A near-miss is written down so it is not later mistaken for a find:
  John BACKWAY Brayley, Bideford, June quarter 1847, fits the age of 53
  and the district. The middle name is wrong, so he is not adopted.

commits.subject: Three of four Brayley links now rest on the index, not on a web site
commits.body:
Work-list row 124. The Brayley ascent was published unsourced below 1843.
Four of its claims have now been put to the GRO civil index via FreeBMD.
  John Brailey's death — CONFIRMED. Deaths, Jun quarter 1851: BRAYLEY,
  John, St Thomas, 10/177. The Devon County Asylum stood at Exminster,
  in the St Thomas district. A search under BRAILEY returns nothing in
  1851 at all; the family spells it both ways and one spelling finds
  nothing.
  The 1870 marriage — CONFIRMED. BRAYLEY, Mary Ann H, Bideford, 5b/794,
  double-keyed. TAYLOR, William is on the same page. That is the join
  that attaches the whole ascent to the Taylor line. The page carries
  four names, so the pairing is near-certain rather than certain.
  Her 1900 death — CONFIRMED, and it pays a dividend. TAYLOR, Mary Ann
  H, age 56, Bideford, 5b/363. Age 56 on 21 April 1900 is exactly a
  birth of 20 May 1843, corroborating the birth year from a second
  direction forty-three years later — and killing the 2018 backup's
  1844, which would have made her 55.
  Her 1843 birth registration — NOT FOUND. The control passed: June
  1843 births are transcribed and other Brayleys appear in the quarter.
  But registration was not compulsory until 1875, so the null is weak,
  and "St Bartholomew's" may be a baptism, which is not in this index.
Everything above generation 3 is still unsourced and still needs the
Westleigh parish register, which no free tool reached tonight:
FamilySearch record search was blocked, and FreeREG holds none of
Westleigh, Coldridge, Braunton, Bideford or Shirwell. Recorded in
devon-tooling.tsv so the evening is not spent twice — including that
FreeBMD's submit is an <input type=image>, which is why form.submit()
silently re-renders the search page.
New rows 125 (buy the 5b/794 marriage certificate — it names both
fathers) and 126 (run the remaining Taylor vitals through FreeBMD).

commits.subject: Six of 244 cite a record
commits.body:
Work-list row 121 asked a narrow question: where did the tree get Felix de
Llerena's Andalusia from? Answering it meant reading every SOUR citation on
every Lerena, Taylor, Brayley and Brailey person in the current export, and
the narrow answer came with a much larger one.
THE NARROW ANSWER. Felix's Andalusia is sourced to "Carvalho Calcagno Web
Site" and "Familia Martinez Camino" - two other people's MyHeritage trees.
This archive wrote, four hours ago, that the tree agreed with its own reading
of "Cordova la llana" as the Spanish city "from a direction that owes the
archive nothing". It owes the archive nothing because it is two strangers'
trees, which may perfectly well have copied the same reasoning from the same
place. No support.
THE LARGER ANSWER. Of 244 people on this line in the tree:
  6 cite a record
  94 cite only other people's family trees
  144 cite nothing at all
The entire documentary foundation is three citations of the 1911 census, one
each of 1871 and 1901, one death index and one baptism. 97.5% of the line
rests on nothing, or on somebody else's tree.
WHICH MEANS the eleven-generation Brayley ascent published two hours ago is
almost entirely unsourced. Matthew Reed of 1643 rests on "Lightning Web Site".
John Brailey on "Moore-Christian Web Site". HELEN WALKER - the woman who
explains the Walker given name and the DNA match sharing Temple and Walker -
cites NOTHING AT ALL. This archive flagged the ascent "tree, not record",
which was right, and did not say how thin. It is this thin.
And the three deaths of 12 November 1999 carry zero citations. The warning
that they should be checked against a death registration before being stated
as fact now has a number behind it and is binding.
WHAT THIS DOES NOT MEAN: that the tree is wrong. An unsourced entry can be
perfectly correct. It means the tree is a set of LEADS and not a body of
evidence - and that a lead carrying a parish and a date is worth far more than
one without, because it can be tested.
The register stays at 278. Nothing is promoted on the tree's say-so.
Row 124 opened with the densest target in the ascent: Westleigh, September
1799, where one parish register page should carry Robert Brayley's baptism on
the 21st, his burial on the 23rd, and his mother Ann Snow's burial the same
day.
- data/gedcom-graded.tsv; /family-papers/ gains section 7d
- row 121 closed

commits.subject: The current tree imported: 245 people, 122 the archive did not have
commits.body:
The re-import, finished. From the 15 September export: 245 people carry a
Lerena, Taylor or Brayley name; 122 are not in this archive's register of 278;
41 of those are dead.
THE URUGUAYAN TRUNK IS IN THE TREE, and it reaches the people this archive
read off registers. FELIX DE LLERENA, born about 1725 at Cordoba in
ANDALUSIA - the archive's own Felix, from the Canelones marriage act of 8
January 1791, which says only "naturales de dicha Cordova". This archive
argued from the phrase "Cordova la llana" that the Cordoba meant was the
Spanish city. The tree agrees, from a direction that owes the archive nothing.
And FIDEL LLERENA, dead 30 January 1822, son of Sancho Francisco Llerena
Aguilar and Maria Josefa Teresa Fernandez - the archive's Sancho and Maria,
with fuller names than the act gives, and the same 1822 the Geneanet trees
carry.
But a tree is not a source, and agreement from an unknown source is worth
nothing while feeling like a great deal. Row 121 is to find out where that
Andalusia came from before any of it is leaned on.
FOUR URUGUAYAN DEPARTMENTS THIS ARCHIVE HAS NEVER SEARCHED: Flores, San Jose,
Florida, and Rosario in Colonia - each with a named Lerena and a date. It has
worked Canelones and Montevideo and nothing else.
THE BRAYLEY FAMILY ENTIRE, with the parish attached to nearly every line.
Robert Brayley lived two days and his mother Ann Snow died on the same date,
23 September 1799 - a birth and two deaths in one Westleigh household in three
days. Five children of William Brayley and Peggy Reed between 1803 and 1817,
two of them dead as infants. All of it confirmable in one sitting at Westleigh.
THE TAYLOR SIBLINGS with three Devon street addresses the archive lacks - 23
Geneva Place Bideford, North Street Northam, and 2 FORE STREET, NORTHAM, which
is a few doors from the 26 Fore Street where Mary Septima stayed on her last
visit home in 1935. An address is what a census is searched on, and this
archive already has five censuses and the 1939 Register worked.
AND THREE DEATHS ON ONE DAY. Pierre Frederick Lerena, born 10 May 1948, dead
12 November 1999 - with his sons Richard, born 2 January 1986, and Jeffrey,
born 2 January 1991, both dead the same day, aged thirteen and eight. This
archive knew only that his estate was advertised in 2000. Recorded plainly,
with no speculation as to cause, and to be confirmed against a death
registration before it is stated as fact anywhere else.
Also: an unnamed infant of Roque Luis Armando, born 17 May and dead 22 May
1932, which makes three of his children dead in infancy. And Jeanette Marie
Lerena, Cheryl's eldest sister, died 6 June 2021.
- data/gedcom-import.tsv; /family-papers/ gains section 7c
- four work-list rows

commits.subject: The 2018 GEDCOM is withdrawn, and the Brayley line goes back to 1643
commits.body:
David: "Do not use the 2018 gedcom. That is an old backup only. And is
incredibly wrong and out of date." He was right, and the current export
proves it point by point. Everything published from the backup is withdrawn
and re-derived.
WHAT THE BACKUP GOT WRONG.
  The Australian birth does not exist. The backup put Paul Lerena at DAPTO,
  WOLLONGONG, NSW on 3 November 1951. The current tree has Paul Raymond
  Lerena, born 11 March 1951 at Johannesburg, and no Australian place anywhere
  in that generation. This archive had flagged that entry as "a date that
  cannot be true" because his sister was born in Johannesburg six months
  later. The flag was right and the cause was the backup.
  Careen Marie was published as born and died 1945. She was born JUNE 1947 and
  died 22 JUNE 1947 - three weeks old. Which is exactly what Cheryl told her
  English cousin in 2020. The family were right and the backup was wrong.
  And the backup carried him as "Roberto Paul (Llorens) Lerena, born EST 4 SEP
  1872, Argentina" - the unsolicited Buenos Aires candidate baked into his
  name, his birth date and his parents. The current tree has restored Pablo
  Armando / Robert Paul Lerena, born 22 February 1882 at Rosario.
THE LESSON, which this archive should not have needed: a file's DATE IS PART
OF ITS PROVENANCE, and "found on the disk" is not a source. It was treated as
one because it was large and internally consistent. Two errors WERE caught by
internal arithmetic - the impossible date, and a man dead at 117 - and both
were written up as isolated slips when they were symptoms.
AND WHAT THE CURRENT TREE GIVES INSTEAD. rootschat-assessment.tsv says Brayley
"is the one this archive could not push past". It goes back to Matthew Reed,
born 1643 at Braunton.
Eleven generations with parishes and dates: Mary Ann Hellen Brayley, born 20
May 1843 at St Bartholomew's in the City of London, a HOUSE SERVANT, married
26 January 1870 at St Mark's, Bideford. Her father John Brailey, born 1814 at
West Leigh by Coldridge, married at St Martin-in-the-Fields in 1839, DIED 4
MAY 1851 AT THE DEVON COUNTY ASYLUM at thirty-six - very probably the "missing
husband" of Sue Rowbotham's chapter title. Her mother Georgina Temple of
Haddington, "Monthly Nurse & Shoemaker Wife Pauper". Back through Westleigh
and Braunton and Shirwell to Matthew Reed and Anne Heddon, married at Braunton
in 1671.
AND THERE IS THE WALKER. This archive guessed a Walker grandmother from a
naming habit - Margaret Hellen WALKER Taylor, Agnes WALKER Taylor. She is five
generations up: HELEN WALKER, who married George Temple at Haddington, East
Lothian, on 6 January 1813. So is the other name: Helen Walker to Mary Ann
HELLEN Brayley to Margaret HELLEN Walker Taylor. Which is why a South African
DNA match shares TEMPLE AND WALKER with Cheryl. The tree and the chromosome
arrive at the same woman from opposite ends.
A WARNING, not a retraction: the current tree still carries his parents as
Roberto Llorens and "Francisca Fernandez Lerena" while his birth reads Rosario
1882. Those cannot both be true, and the mother's surname appears in no
register. Work-list row 119, David's, to fix before the next export.
- data/gedcom-2018.tsv and gedcom-harvest.tsv deleted
- data/gedcom-current.tsv, data/brayley-ascent.tsv
- /family-papers/ sections 7 and 7b replace the retracted one
- two corrections; row 118 struck; row 119 opened

commits.subject: The GEDCOM breaks the Brayley wall, and the Brayley reading does not survive it
commits.body:
Three jobs in the order David set them: mine the tree, fetch three media,
test the Brayley convergence. Two done, one blocked, and the convergence went
somewhere other than where it looked.
THE TREE. 2018-07 Defranceski.ged: 8,286 individuals, 2,532 families, 4,001
media - against 278 in this register. Never opened before today.
  THE BRAYLEY WALL IS NOT A WALL. Six generations, with parishes. Mary Ann
  Helen Brayley, b. 1844 at St Bartholomew's, MIDDLESEX - London, not Devon -
  d. 21 April 1900 at Sweet Home Terrace, Northam. Her father John Brayley,
  b. 14 Aug 1814 at West Leigh by Coldridge. His father William Brayley, b. 1
  March 1778 at Westleigh, who married Peggy Reed of Braunton. His father John
  Brayley, b. 1747, d. September 1815 at Westleigh. And the Reed marriage at
  Braunton, 21 November 1771, to Margaret Wybourn. rootschat-assessment.tsv
  says Brayley "is the one this archive could not push past". It was being
  pushed past in a file on the same disk.
  ANTON ARMANDO IS PLACED. Son of Ricardo Juan Carlos and Doreen May Chappell,
  born 5 June 1952 - and his J193 identity number begins 520605. Exact. This
  archive carried him as "unplaced" throughout and ranked a Pretoria divorce
  file FIRST to place him.
  CAREEN IS EXPLAINED, and it is not a scandal. Careen Marie, b&d 1945,
  daughter of RICARDO. The third grave at Newlands is a granddaughter in her
  grandparents' plot, not an old man's secret - and it agrees with the 1950
  death notice's "nil" against other marriages.
  And a date that cannot be true: Paul born Dapto, New South Wales, 3 November
  1951, with a sister born Johannesburg 21 May 1952. Six and a half months, to
  one mother. Recorded as a contradiction inside the tree, not as a finding -
  but an Australian birth in that generation would be entirely new.
THE THREE MEDIA: BLOCKED, by the application and not by permissions. The tree
view is a canvas carrying 8,286 people and it froze the renderer three times.
A lighter route is needed. Said plainly rather than quietly dropped.
THE CONVERGENCE, TESTED - AND THE ANSWER IS NO. The GEDCOM handed over the
actual surnames, so they went through the match list. BRAYLEY returns 4: an
Australian at 23.0 cM sharing Brayley and Baker, and an Englishman actually
surnamed Brayley at 16.2 cM. TEMPLE returns 22, including a South African who
shares TEMPLE AND WALKER - and Walker runs through the Taylor line as a given
name. The maternal English line is real, corroborated, and sits at 14-25 cM.
The Bailey cluster sits at 61-116 cM in the United States and NONE OF ITS
THREE MEMBERS CARRIES BRAYLEY. This morning this archive wrote that cluster 14
was "probably" Brayley. It had no business writing "probably" and the claim is
corrected on /dna/ and in /corrections/.
And the absence proves nothing either: those trees hold two people and four
people, and no shared surname can be computed from a tree with two people in
it. The link is UNTESTED, NOT REFUTED. One message to the 116 cM match would
settle it, and that is David's to send.
What the convergence actually delivered: for Mary Septima Taylor's mother's
family, a wall became a documented ascent of six generations in an afternoon.
For Pablo Armando it moved nothing at all.
- /family-papers/ gains sections 7 and 8
- data/gedcom-harvest.tsv, data/brayley-convergence.tsv
- one major correction; three work-list rows; row 112 closed

commits.subject: Where the name is, drawn by density because that is what the page argues
commits.body:
The estate's distribution chart ranks by bearers and picks the first bar out in
the accent, on the reasoning that the largest is almost always the answer. Here
it is not: the section under this chart says so in so many words - Spain has the
most Lerenas and Uruguay carries them at six times the density, which is the
signature of founder emigration. So the bars are density and Uruguay leads them.
Bearers, incidence and national rank all travel beside each bar.

commits.subject: Four generations onto the shared spine, and not one joint marked
commits.body:
This page's claim is that there is no inferred link left in the descent, and
the shared spine says that by leaving every joint unmarked - which only means
something because the same component marks Booyzen's seventh generation and
Blazevic's third. Cheryl Anne stays a name and a relationship.

commits.subject: Thirty-six places onto the shared register
commits.body:
The card grid becomes the estate's places table, which brings the search this
page did not have. The prose above it - that the surname clusters in the River
Plate and that Rosario, the one place the family names, is the thinnest - is
the argument and stays.

commits.subject: Six documents, published - and the tree, counted at last
commits.body:
THE SITE HAS IMAGES NOW. This archive has been text since it began. Six
document scans are published at /family-papers/, every person named on them
dead: the 1911 marriage register, the 1950 death notice, the 1950 death
certificate, the baptisms of Roque and Nuno at Corpus Christi Wynberg, and the
Buenos Aires candidate.
The 1971 and 1973 death notices are deliberately NOT published. They list
living children with their birth dates, and this estate names the living and
nothing more. Their transcriptions stay; the scans do not.
A near-miss worth recording: the first pass through the resizer wrote all six
under the wrong names, because zsh arrays are one-indexed and the loop was
not. Every caption would have sat under the wrong document on a public
genealogy site. Caught by checking the aspect ratios against what each
document actually is.
THE LLORENS PROVENANCE, CORRECTED. This archive wrote that "somebody pulled
that deliberately" - an intention nobody had stated, invented to fill a gap
where a file sat with no note attached. David says it arrived unsolicited, in
the mail, from a researcher in Argentina, and that he regards it as likely no
relation. The working is kept, because the archive reached the same verdict
from the documents before he said so - and because the name has already leaked
into the family tree, where he is entered as "Roberto Paul (Llorens) Lerena".
A stranger's guess becomes a fact when nobody refutes it in writing.
AND THE GEDCOM, WHICH HAD NEVER BEEN OPENED. 2018-07 Defranceski.ged, 7.5 MB:
8,286 individuals, 2,532 families, 400 sources, 4,001 media objects - against
278 people in this register. Eighty-one carry a Lerena or Taylor name and
forty-two of those carry photographs. It is the largest unmined source in the
whole project and it is sitting on the disk.
The media are not. The FILE references point at MyHeritage's servers; only 169
cached thumbnails survive locally, at 60x80, too small to read a document
from. So the text is free and the images need the live tree.
Three titles already earn their place on the work list:
  "Mary Ann Taylor Death Certificate", hanging on Mary Septima - her MOTHER's,
  the death that orphaned her at fifteen. This archive does not hold it.
  rootschat-assessment.tsv says Brayley is the line it could not push past,
  and the DNA subtraction produced a paternal cluster of Bailey trees at 116
  cM the same day. Three roads now point at Brayley.
  "Lerena Grave", hanging on Nuno - which may settle Newlands against the
  death certificate's Maitland without writing to anybody.
  record-image_3Q9M-C913-K98Q-J - one page of MOOC 6/9/17017 that the local
  folder does not hold.
- site/public/docs/, six scans, 1.8 MB
- data/gedcom-2018.tsv; llorens-1872.tsv provenance corrected
- one correction; four work-list rows

commits.subject: A rival identification, a death certificate, and a Falco page in the wrong folder
commits.body:
The nine unopened images in the family's own Lerena folder, read.
THE DEATH CERTIFICATE, which is not the death notice. Union of South Africa
A 214036, Wynberg, entry W612/50. It registers him as ROBERT PAUL LERINA -
the spelling this archive has been treating as a clerk's slip is on the civil
register itself. Birthplace: SOUTH AMERICA. No country, no town. Age: 76.
Occupation: Race Horse Owner. Cause: coronary thrombosis and angina pectoris,
six weeks and about three years - and his son Nuno died of a coronary
thrombosis at forty-six, twenty-one years later. Intended burial: MAITLAND
Cemetery no 1, which contradicts what the family were told at Newlands.
Informant: W. FRASER, of Main Road, Observatory, qualification "causing
burial". An undertaker. So the notice was completed by a woman of no relation
and the certificate by the undertaker, and NOT ONE DOCUMENT MADE AT HIS DEATH
WAS FILLED IN BY ANYBODY WHO KNEW WHERE HE CAME FROM.
AND A RIVAL IDENTIFICATION NOBODY HAD MENTIONED. Filed among the estate
papers, two photographs of the Libro de Bautismos de la Parroquia de San
Miguel, Buenos Aires, 1872: ROBERTO JUAN ROQUE LLORENS, born 16 August 1872,
son of Roberto Llorens and Francisca Fernandez, both of Spain, of Calle
Chacabuco 156. Somebody pulled that deliberately and this archive had never
seen it.
It is set out for and against because it is not silly. FOR: both South
African death records make him mid-seventies, and 1872 fits where 1882 does
not; and the names Roberto, Juan and Roque all recur in his own sons.
AGAINST: his own passport and his own enrolment card, the only two documents
in the whole question he filled in himself, both say Rosario de Santa Fe, 22
February 1882 - and the parents do not match at all.
Verdict recorded: not the same man on the evidence as it stands, and the age
problem is real and is not dismissed. The cheapest open question in this
archive is now to trace Llorens forward in Buenos Aires. If he lived and died
in Argentina it closes in an afternoon.
The remaining images are pages of the 1950 estate file, already transcribed -
except one, which is a 1991 burial index for the FA- surnames carrying FALCO
Carmine Antonio, Caterina, Filomena and Raffaele. Misfiled. Noted, left where
it is, and not touched: this estate does not mix its families.
AND ONE FOR TUESDAY, WHICH IS NOT THIS ARCHIVE'S. The Barry & Booyzen folder
holds the death notice of GEORGE DOWNING MOUNTJOY BOOYZEN, estate TAB MHG
1095/48 - one of the six Booyzen estates Anne is booked to pull at Pretoria on
22 September. Its companion 2945/44 that archive has already read. The other
four on her list are NOT in the folder, so the rest of the trip stands. Work
list row 111, owner David, because it needs saying before Tuesday.
- /family-papers/ gains the certificate and section 6
- data/llorens-1872.tsv; death-notice-1950.tsv extended
- one correction on the nine-year age gap; three work-list rows

commits.subject: Repin: the chronology picks its headings from the span
"Father: not known. Mother: not known."
commits.body:
David asked whether it was worth scouting his whole Documents folder for the
subject's own name. A filename sweep this archive had never once run found
Photos from Email/, and in it the document this archive has been chasing since
it began.
THE DEATH NOTICE OF ROBERT PAUL LERENA, 1950. KAB MOOC 6/9/17017. This
morning it was called "the single most valuable file in this entire archive,
because it asks for HIS parents - the one document that could name Juan Carlos
Lerena", and there is an open request for it at the Western Cape Archives.
Item 3 reads: Father, not known. Mother, not known.
The informant was ROSE LILIAN THEYS, who signed as "Present at death" and
"Executrix Nominate" - the woman he lived with at No. 7 Forth Road, described
in the liquidation account as a spinster and NO RELATION. She could not name
his parents. Neither did any of his three living adult sons. Cheryl wrote to
her English cousin in 2020: "My Father never discussed his parents with me or
my siblings." That silence is now dated. It had closed by March 1950.
So the 1908 Argentine enrolment card is now, definitively, the only document
on earth naming Juan Carlos and Maria Lerena.
It also gives: Argentine, nationality only, no town. Racehorse Trainer.
Widower, no surviving spouse - so he did NOT marry Rose Theys, whatever the
family believed. Three sons, all majors, no other marriages. And age "77
approx", which is nine years out against the passport and is recorded rather
than smoothed, because the woman who guessed it did not know his parents
either.
AND THE DEVON FAMILY CALLED HIM SOMETHING ELSE. Sue Rowbotham's Taylor family
history, held unopened in the Taylor folder: Mary Septima "went out to South
Africa to work for a widower by the name of ROBERT (or ROBERTO) MARINO". The
three sons she names - Louis, Cardo, Nuno - are exactly right, so the memory
is anchored in real people; it is the surname that drifted, or was never
Lerena. Marino is one of the commonest surnames in Italy, and two companies
independently put Italian ancestry in his granddaughter. Wholly separate lines
of evidence, neither aware of the other. Corroboration, not proof, and
recorded as the former.
TWO BAPTISMS, from Corpus Christi Wynberg. Roque born 25 Nov 1905, baptised
12 June 1911 - at five and a half, and three months before his parents
married, by the priest who then married them, who wrote "conjugum" early. A
legitimation, and it explains why the register calls them bachelor and
spinster. His godparents were JOSE BRETON and MARIA LUISA BRETON, both BY
PROXY - the first Hispanic names ever found around him in the Cape, and proxy
is what a parish writes when the sponsors are overseas.
Nuno baptised at six weeks, and against his mother the priest wrote MATER
ANGLICANA. The Catholicism was his father's.
AND FROM CHERYL'S 2020 LETTERS: they are buried at Newlands in an unmarked
grave carrying only the word LERENA - and there is a third person in it, a
baby girl CAREEN MARIA LERENA, born and died 1947, whom this archive has never
heard of. A newspaper cutting in north Devon reports Roberto fined five pounds
for shooting at two boys stealing from him. And "Uncle Louis married Uncle
Cardo's wife's mother" - which is precisely the relationship the AutoClusters
produced hours earlier, from chromosomes, in ignorance of the letter.
- /family-papers/ now leads with the 1950 death notice; five sections
- data/death-notice-1950.tsv, data/family-memory.tsv
- the Western Cape errand closed; two corrections; six work-list rows

commits.subject: Eighteen fixed points, off the table and onto the shared chronology
commits.body:
The four-column table becomes the estate's timeline shape. This archive was
the one printing what each row rests on, and the shared component carries
that column - it was the others that had dropped it.

commits.subject: The papers in the house, which nobody had opened
commits.body:
David asked whether this archive had searched his own folder. It had not.
Twenty minutes in Genealogy & Family History/Lerena produced more than the
last three days of reading registers, and it also produced an expensive
embarrassment.
WHAT IT COST. This morning this archive drew up a ranked pull list for a
researcher at the National Archives in Pretoria on 22 September, where the
first file costs R2,850, and put two Transvaal death notices first and second.
Both had been photographed and saved since November 2021. Worse: the second
was ranked on the promise that it would NAME NUNO FERNANDO'S PARENTS, and item
19 of that notice carries the single word "Deceased" and a ditto mark. No
names at all. Both are struck; the list now leads with two divorce files.
WHAT CAME OUT OF IT.
The 1911 marriage, which was ON THE WORK LIST as a thing to go and find.
Wynberg, 3 September 1911, St Dominic's, by an R.C. priest, after banns. He is
29, a BACHELOR, and a HORSE-DEALER - the trade documented nine years earlier
than anything else held, and a DEALER before he was ever a trainer. Both
parties of Diep River. And the first religious affiliation this archive has
for him: he was a Catholic. The form has no column for fathers, so its silence
about Juan Carlos is a fact about the printing and not about the family.
Rogue Luis Armando's death notice: PLACE OF BIRTH, CAPE TOWN. Not Argentina.
That was precisely the question this archive proposed to send somebody to
Pretoria to answer, and the answer had been on the disk for five years. His
father is written ROBERTO LERENA by his own widow, which ties Pablo Armando
and Robert Paul together in a family document rather than a clerk's index.
Neither son followed him onto the turf: a retired railwayman and a salesman.
And page 6 of the passport, which this archive transcribed a week ago without
turning over. "Acta del Registro Civil (o fe de bautismo) extendida por ____"
- THE LINE IS BLANK. In 1940, at his own consulate, he produced no birth
certificate and no baptismal certificate. This archive has read the Rosario
registers act by act looking for his baptism. Here is contemporary evidence
that he did not have one either. What he did produce was a libreta de
enrolamiento issued at CAPE TOWN IN 1915 - a second Argentine enrolment,
seven years after the ficha of 1908, never looked for.
THE RULE, on /method/, so it binds: before any list of documents to acquire,
list the documents already held. This archive kept a careful register of what
it had READ and none at all of what it already HELD, and the two are not the
same thing.
Also fixes /changes/, which had been shipping five dangling day anchors and
fifty unrendered emphasis markers - the same omission as /corrections/ had
this morning. Kit repinned to 49295ca, which lets a day carry an id.
- new page /family-papers/, linked under Evidence
- data/marriage-1911.tsv, data/death-notices-read.tsv, passport extended
- the Pretoria pull list corrected before a rand was spent
- one correction, four work-list rows

commits.subject: The change feed runs on the shared shape
commits.body:
A dated note saying what was done and what it turned up — the same job on
every archive that keeps one, written four different ways. This page keeps its
own words and its own grading; what is shared is that a day groups its
entries and that doing and finding are two different fields.

commits.subject: A pull list for Pretoria, 22 September
commits.body:
A researcher is at the National Archives in Pretoria on Tuesday and charges
R2,850 for the first file. Five TAB references, ranked, with the pages that
matter and the ones to drop.
THIS ARCHIVE HAS NO SAB REFERENCES AT ALL and the list says so.
And it says what no file on it can do: a South African death notice asks for
the deceased's PARENTS, not their grandparents, so the death notices of Pablo
Armando's sons will name him and Mary Septima Taylor and will NOT name Juan
Carlos Lerena. Nothing at TAB answers the central question directly.
Best of them is MHG 1518/73, Rogue Luis Armando, for his PLACE OF BIRTH: born
6 December 1905, fifteen years before his next-known brother and three years
before his father's Argentine enrolment was filed at Cape Town. Argentina or
Cape Town, either answer dates the emigration.
Caveats recorded rather than smoothed: the four court references carry no
volume number in NAAIRS; WLD sits in Johannesburg though NAAIRS places the
files at TAB; and the modern estates known from gazettes should still be with
the Master rather than the archives, which this archive has not verified.

commits.subject: The subtraction finds one paternal cluster, and it is a Taylor one
commits.body:
Jeanette's AutoClusters arrived, which is the instrument this page has been
asking for since the morning. She is the granddaughter's maternal aunt - Cape
and nothing else - so any cluster of the niece's with no counterpart on hers
belongs to the FATHER: Pablo Armando or Mary Septima Taylor.
THE TRAP FIRST, because this nearly went in wrong. Run naively the subtraction
says five of fourteen clusters are paternal. That is a floor artefact. The
aunt's chart begins at 75.3 cM and the niece's at 50.6, so four of those five
have no member that could ever have appeared on the aunt's chart whatever
their ancestry. Only 15 of the niece's 107 clustered matches clear the floor,
and those 15 are all this test can speak about.
DONE PROPERLY: eight testable clusters. Six confirmed Cape. Two candidates.
Six clusters silent.
CANDIDATE ONE IS A FALSE POSITIVE AND IT WAS CAUGHT. Cluster 8, one match at
80 cM, a Kroon tree, absent from the aunt's clustered chart - but MyHeritage's
own Theory of Family Relativity for that match names the shared surnames as
KRUGER, VENTER and NEL. Cape. Absence from a CLUSTERED list is not absence
from a match list, and this is the case that proves it.
CANDIDATE TWO STANDS. Cluster 14: three matches, 61 to 116 cM, all BAILEY
trees. Its 116 cM member clears the aunt's floor comfortably and is not on her
chart. It is a genuine paternal cluster.
AND IT IS NOT PABLO ARMANDO'S. Mary Septima Taylor's mother was MARY ANN
HELLEN BRAYLEY of Bideford, Devon. This archive's rootschat-assessment.tsv
already says in terms that Brayley "is the one this archive could not push
past", and wikitree-searches.tsv records Brayley queries coming back swamped
by Bradley, Bayley, Burley, Barley. A 116 cM paternal cluster of Bailey trees
is the best lead that wall has ever had. Bailey is not Brayley, and it is
written down as a candidate.
A second pointer the same way: cluster 12 is Jullien and Walker, and WALKER
