runs through the Taylor line as a given name - Margaret Hellen Walker Taylor,
Agnes Walker Taylor. That usually means a Walker grandmother.
SO THE SUBTRACTION WORKS, AND IT FINDS A PATERNAL CLUSTER. It finds a Taylor
one. Pablo Armando still has no cluster on his granddaughter's chart, and that
is now a negative with a working instrument behind it rather than an absence
of looking.
- new section on /dna/; the subtraction recorded in dna-autoclusters.json
- work-list row 95 closed, row 98 opened to chase the Bailey cluster

commits.subject: The clusters came back, and her fourth grandparent is not in them
commits.body:
David generated MyHeritage AutoClusters on three kits. The tool groups matches
into blocks that all match EACH OTHER as well as the tester, so a block is in
practice one ancestral couple's descendants. It is the sharpest instrument
either company offers.
HER CHART: 14 clusters, 107 matches, floor 50.6 cM. Attwell, Botha,
Buitendag, Calitz, du Pisanie, du Plessis, Engelbrecht, Erasmus, Dippenaar,
Lotter, de Kock, Bezuidenhout, Potgieter, de Lange, de Villiers, Volschenk,
Niemann, Strauss, Viviers, Hamman, Nel, Theron, van der Westhuizen, van Zyl,
Booyens, Jooste, Kroon, Joubert, Dreyer, Krugel, Sander, Jansen van Vuuren,
Beukes, du Toit, Gouws, Marais, Bailey, Walker, Johnson, White, Butler,
Daniel, Daschner.
Not one Spanish, Italian, Argentine or Uruguayan surname on the whole chart.
She has four grandparents. Fourteen clusters account for three of them. The
fourth has no cluster at all.
AND THE CONTROL IS HER SON'S CHART, not hers. His father is a Defranceski of
Istria, and his chart carries TWO plainly Croatian clusters - Butorac,
Pavelich, Jagustin, Krkljes, Racic, Glas - beside the Cape ones. So
AutoClusters does form a block for a foreign paternal line when cousins from
it have tested. It found his father's. It did not find hers. That is the
hardest form this negative has taken.
THE NEPHEW'S CHART WAS A SURPRISE. The only other Lerena who has tested
produced nineteen clusters and they are almost entirely Ashkenazi - Abrams,
Litwack, Rothbart, Epstein, Goldman, Rosenzweig, Levitan, Novik, Aizenman,
Graivier, Mandel, Goldberg, Waldman, Fishbein - with tree names in Hebrew and
Russian. That is his MOTHER's family; an endogamous population throws up far
more high-cM matches and crowds his chart out. He shares exactly three
clustered matches with his aunt, and all three sit in her Cape cluster.
It is also the clearest statement yet of why he was never going to separate
the lines: he is her NEPHEW, so the Lerena half of him arrives filtered
through the same Cape grandmother.
THE LIMIT, stated on the page before anyone else states it. A cluster cannot
form where nobody has tested. The Croatian clusters exist because Croatians
test in numbers; the missing Argentine one is consistent with Pablo Armando's
family having no tested descendant anywhere in either database, which is what
the sixty-two-country census already said. This is a strong negative and it
is not a disproof. It says the answer is not reachable by DNA matching today.
- new section on /dna/; site/src/data/dna-autoclusters.json
- work-list row 96 closed
- no match is named; clusters are described by size, cM range and the
  surnames of the trees in them

commits.subject: Argentina is not on the list at all
commits.body:
Replaces a sampled figure with MyHeritage's own count over the whole corpus.
This archive published, an hour earlier the same day, that three of the 6,350
matches it had harvested lived in South America. MyHeritage publishes the
count for all 11,581, and it is better in every way.
SIXTY-TWO COUNTRIES are named, down to a single match each in Vietnam, Saint
Lucia and the Cayman Islands.
ARGENTINA IS NOT ONE OF THEM. Not a low number - absent.
Uruguay has exactly three, and those three are the one family this archive
already opened and read: all three of their kits, one 112-person Basque tree
with no Lerena in it.
Also corrects a reading trap the sample had walked into. Spain shows 38
matches and Portugal 25, which looks Iberian and is not: the names on them are
van Heerden, Retief, Vorster, de Vos, Deetlefs and Hanekom. They are South
Africans who retired to the Algarve. Country of residence is a trap and the
page now says so in the place where a reader would otherwise fall into it.

commits.subject: The same saliva, read at the second company - and eleven thousand cousins
commits.body:
David asked whether DNA could be made to reach the hypothesis. It was read
properly for the first time, at both companies, and it cuts both ways.
THE SECOND READING. Everything this archive had published about her ethnicity
came from MyHeritage. The kit was UPLOADED from a 23andMe account in 2018, so
the same saliva has been sitting there read a second way the whole time.
23andMe disagrees twice:
  - Spanish & Portuguese 2.1%, where MyHeritage returned 0.0%. The page said
    "there is no Spanish component whatever". That was a fact about one
    company's reference panel.
  - The Italian is put in SICILY. MyHeritage put it in the north, and this
    archive read the north as the Ligurian and Piedmontese emigration that
    built Rosario. That reading is withdrawn as a DNA argument.
And it agrees once, which matters more than either: BOTH companies find
Italian - 11.1% and 8.0% - in a woman whose other three grandparents are
English and Cape Afrikaner. The hypothesis now rests on two panels agreeing
rather than on one panel's zero, which is a better foundation than it had.
ELEVEN THOUSAND COUSINS. 11,581 MyHeritage matches, 11,114 of them with a
family tree; 6,350 harvested down to 13.78 cM; 1,500 more at 23andMe.
Controls first: Booyzen, Booysen, Kolbe, Barry and Taylor all return, and
return matches carrying the name only INSIDE their tree. The search reaches
trees. Then the probes: no Lerena in any of them except her own son and
nephew. No Llerena. No Lerina. And - sharper than either - no LENGUAS and no
TRAIBEL, the two rare Montevideo compounds this archive's hypothesis reaches
for.
Twenty countries are named across 1,500 relatives' grandparents. Not one is
South American and not one is Iberian. Italy is ninth, with ten. Of 500
computed relationship theories, every one of the largest ten lands on the
Cape. There is exactly one South American family in the corpus - Uruguayan,
three kits, one tree of 112 people - and it was opened and read: Basque and
French-Basque, Ziganda Erviti and Barneche and Laclau, with no Lerena in it.
The honest counterweight is stated on the page: an absence measured where
nobody is standing is a weak absence, and Uruguay and Argentina are barely
present in either database.
A CONTROL THAT FAILED, recorded because it worked. Twelve probes at 23andMe
all returned zero. The controls run before believing them - BOTHA, SOUTH
AFRICA - also returned zero, against facets on the same screen showing thirty
and 581. That box searches display names only. Twelve nulls were one step from
publication.
Parental Inheritance would settle which parent the Italian came from. It is
behind 23andMe+ Premium; this archive does not buy sources. It is David's,
on the work list, and it is the most valuable unbought thing here.
- /dna/ substantially rewritten; two published claims corrected in place
- data/dna-match-probes.tsv, wired into build-pages.py
- site/src/data/dna-match-corpus.json, dna-23andme.json
- two corrections, five work-list rows
- no DNA match is named anywhere; the people named out of a match's tree are
  its deceased ancestors

commits.subject: Nobody on the blood chart is drawn twice, and nobody is their own brother
commits.body:
David looked at /bloodline/ for Nuno Fernando and said it made no sense: two
Juan Carlos Lerenas, two Maria Lerenas, Mary Septima twice. He was right, and
it had been published in that state since the page was built.
Nothing was duplicated in the data. The drawing was, in two ways.
A husband or wife was always drawn as a "married in" chip beside the person,
with no check that they were already standing in the chart in their own
right. Every married pair of ANCESTORS is two blood relatives, so each of
them got a box AND a chip of the other. Nuno Fernando's 13 relatives came out
in 22 boxes.
And this register deliberately keeps a row for the mangled machine-index
reading of Pablo Armando - "ARMAND[O] LORENA (as machine-indexed) = Pablo
Armando LERENA" - so the false trail stays visible. That row carries the same
father and mother as the man himself, so the sibling pass handed it its own
person as a brother, and the chart drew Pablo Armando beside Pablo Armando,
labelled "aunt or uncle".
Fixed in the kit, because it is the kit's chart and five other archives were
drawing the same doubled picture - Mazza's for Frank Mazza was 232 of 530
people twice. A chip is drawn only for somebody the chart does not already
hold; where both halves of a couple are on it they are seated together and
the marriage is a tie between them; an alias folds onto the person it is a
spelling of. Every one of those tests is on a SLUG, never a name. Kit
repinned to 45b37a7.
Here: build-people.py writes aliasOf as {slug, name} rather than a bare name,
so the kit can act on it, and stops handing an alias siblings of its own.
The same chart is now 14 boxes for 12 people, and the two chips left are
husbands the archive genuinely does not hold. Checked rendered, desktop and
mobile.
No gate caught this and none could have: every checker here reads data, and
the data was right. It was the picture that lied. Logged in /corrections/ as
major, and the other five archives are on the work list as theirs to repin.

commits.subject: Pin the kit to the map that draws provincial boundaries
commits.body:
An inland frame has no coastline in it. The Falco map is 26 km of Campania and
drew an empty box; it now carries the provincial line that separates the towns
this family married across. The box also follows the shape of the ground rather
than a fixed letterbox, and the fine layers are dropped on frames that span
continents, where they were 1.1 MB of illegible markup.

commits.subject: Draw the two lines on the home page, and trace Pedro Antonio forward
commits.body:
THE HOME PAGE NOW SAYS WHAT THIS ARCHIVE ACTUALLY CLAIMS. David pointed at the
Luwinski archive, where the line of record and the line the DNA points to run
side by side on the front page. The Lerena equivalent is the second section here:
"Two lines, and they do not yet meet".
Left lane, documented: Rosario, Wynberg, Newlands, Germiston - the descent David
was born into, with a record behind every step. Right lane, inferred: Sancho
Llerena and Maria Fernandez married at Canelones on 8 January 1791, he natural de
Cordova la Llana and unable to sign his name; their eight children; the
Montevideo trunk; Luis Lerena Lenguas, whom the 1866 Rosario act reaches for when
it says the only Lerena in that parish was natural del Estado Oriental.
The point of the drawing is the row where the two fail to meet. Pablo Armando's
own 1908 enrolment card names Juan Carlos Lerena and Maria Lerena - and no Juan
Carlos Lerena appears in any indexed record in Argentina or Uruguay. Not a
baptism, not a marriage, not a burial. That row is dashed in both lanes, and the
caption says what would close it.
Everyone in the second lane is documented. What is not documented is the joint.
The page says so in those words rather than implying a descent it cannot show.
Checked rendered rather than assumed: desktop and mobile, stacks to one column at
720px, no horizontal overflow.
PEDRO ANTONIO TRACED. His marriage was already held - Vicenta Vega, natural de
Cerro Largo, daughter of Don Romualdo and Dona Andrea Maestre - but his children
were not. Manuel Antonio, Vicenta Margarita, and a Pedro Antonio Natalio baptised
at the Cordon on 12 December 1828, born 1 December. One index entry names his
mother as Maria Fernandez, consistent with him being Sancho's son; another
garbles his father as "Francisco Llorena", which is why they are recorded as
candidates and not attached.

commits.subject: One reconciled list of Sancho's children - and a file called "complete" that held half of them
commits.body:
sancho-children-complete.tsv holds FOUR children and is called complete. The
archive names EIGHT across its other files. Nothing in it is wrong; it is
partial, and its name made the partiality invisible - which is exactly the drift
these registers exist to prevent, wearing the one disguise a checker cannot see.
Superseded with a banner rather than deleted, because deleting a file to hide a
bad name is how archives lose evidence.
data/sancho-children-reconciled.tsv is the single list: Pedro Antonio de la
Santisima Trinidad (1793), Agustina Ramona (1795), Fidel (about 1799), Justa
Pastora (1800), Dominga Josefa (1804), Jose Loreto (1806), Luis Escolastico
(1811) and Avelino (1815). Each row carries what the act actually says, its tier,
and the film and image - four of the eight now point at an image read this week,
and two are honestly marked "not yet resolved to a film and image".
It also reconciles the count. The 1812 padron returns SIX children where eight
are named, which is consistent once Luis (1811) and Avelino (1815) are set aside,
and means one or more of the earlier children had died before 1812. This archive
had already reasoned that way once, about a boy of about five missing from the
same return.
AVELINO TRACED, AND A BRANCH THIS ARCHIVE HAS NEVER NAMED. The indexes give
"Avelino Eduardo Lerena" married to CELEDONIA VILLADEMOROS, children recorded
under the compound LERENA VILLADEMOROS, and an Avelino Lerena born 1869 who died
5 January 1914 at Montevideo. This archive knows Avelino as the husband of
Ambrosia Traibel. Either he married twice or "Avelino Eduardo" is a son of his -
not chosen between, recorded unattached, as an existing note in this archive
already half-anticipated.
FIDEL TRACED, AND THE YIELD REPORTED AS THIN. One cluster matches the Victor
Lerena branch already held, with relationships garbled by indexing, and does not
establish that this Fidel is Sancho's son. A second gives a child "Feliz Llama",
which could be a mangled Felix Llerena and is not evidence.
AND check-links CAUGHT A PAGE THAT HAD BEEN BROKEN ALL ALONG. The corrections
page lists one anchor per day and the kit's Corrections component never rendered
those ids, so every day link on it pointed at nothing. Adding two dates made it
visible. Fixed by giving the first correction of each day its day id, which the
component already supported.

commits.subject: Corrections run on the shared shape
commits.body:
Every archive publishes what it got wrong and no two did it the same way.
This one keeps its own page title and its own words — the estate settled that
a menu label is shared while a page title need not be — and hands the entries
to the component that every archive now uses.
A correction is a dated retraction with the truth under it and a note on how
it was caught. That is the same everywhere, and it is filterable by how badly
it mattered.

commits.subject: The Sanchez objection is withdrawn, and drift.py refuses a false completion
commits.body:
THE SANCHEZ QUESTION, SETTLED AGAINST THIS SESSION'S OWN OBJECTION. The page edge
that ran off image 660 was read at magnification: "hijo legitimo del MANUEL
SANCHEZ SARGENTO DE 1a CLASE DEL REGIMIENTO, NATURAL DE LA CIUDAD DE CORDOVA".
The Canelones petitioner of March 1791 is "Juan Manuel Sanchez, natural del REINO
DE ANDALUCIA".
The two descriptions do not match. A man born in the Andalusian city would be
called of Andalucia - which is what the Canelones clerk writes, and what Sancho's
own marriage act means by "Cordova la Llana" - while an unqualified "la Ciudad de
Cordova" in a Montevideo register most naturally means Cordoba del Tucuman, which
this same book names in full a few leaves earlier.
So the counter-example dissolves. This session raised the Sanchez match as
evidence against its own suggestion that military jurisdiction explains Sancho's
absence from the Canelones informaciones. That objection is withdrawn - and the
argument it attacked is NOT thereby proved. Removing a counter-example is not
producing evidence, and the hypotheses page says so.
AND THE ERRAND MIGRATION WAS WRONG, CAUGHT BY A CHECKER. Setting all eleven
me-owned errands to "done" claimed work was finished because its index entry had
moved. drift.py refused: one of them says in its own detail that the register has
never been turned. All eleven are back at "ready", each carrying a pointer to the
work list, which is where their state is maintained. The detail text is untouched.
The checker was right and the migration was wrong.
Also closed: both collections found by the variant sweep were opened - Montevideo
Catedral baptisms 1825-1828 at dgs:007713376 images 515 and 601, and the Cordon
marriage register at dgs:007713391 image 1669 - and all three acts turned out to
be already held, which is what made the parent-pair query a coverage check rather
than a discovery.
89 rows: 51 next, 33 done, 4 blocked, 1 struck.

commits.subject: The people register runs on the shared table
commits.body:
Seven archives had each written their own long-list-with-a-search-box, and
this one hands its rows and its own facets to the shared component now. What
stays is everything that is actually its own: the columns it chose, the
counts, the caveats, the filter groups it decided a reader needs.
Nothing was given up to standardise. The facets keep their own keys, a group
too big for buttons becomes a select without losing them, spelling folds
still fold, and the links gained the trailing slash they were missing.

commits.subject: Migrate eleven misfiled errands, settle the last catalogue attribution, and pay the estate what it is owed
commits.body:
THE ERRANDS ROW WAS WRONG, AND WRONG IN A USEFUL WAY. It assumed eleven errands
sat on David. All eleven were already owned by "me" - this archive. That is the
third time today this session asserted something about its own files without
opening them, after the three "unread" images and the method page that already
carried the rule it was told to add.
But it exposed a real fault underneath. By the estate's own division - errands is
work for a PERSON, the work list is work for a SESSION - eleven rows of this
archive's own machine work were in the wrong register. All eleven are migrated:
closed in errands.tsv with their detail kept verbatim, and seven new work-list
rows opened for the ones that had no counterpart, including Sporting Life's
Argentine racing columns, which matter more than they look now that the gazette
calls Robert Paul Lerena a racehorse trainer and a 1986 notice names Lerena
Racing Stables. What remains in errands is what should be there: institutions
written to, and four things genuinely waiting on David.
THE LAST CATALOGUE ATTRIBUTION HOLDS. DGS 7713382 was recorded as "Matrimonios,
1726-1826" on a catalogue line. Image 2736 opened: a marriage register, couples
in the margins, "las solemnes Bendiciones" in the text. Two of this archive's
three Montevideo attributions now verified and one disproved.
AND FOUR THINGS PAID FORWARD. notes/FOR-THE-ESTATE.md sets out, for a sibling
session: the film-and-image addressing method with working code and its three
traps; why catalogue-derived film numbers should be assumed wrong until opened,
with both failures worked through and the film-gap lesson beside them; that
pdftotext -layout welds two gazette columns into one person, with the actual
welded line quoted; and that a death_year column harvested from ancestors.co.za
may hold the year the estate was advertised, with both worked examples.
None of it is Lerena-specific. All four came out of one day.
89 rows: 58 next, 26 done, 4 blocked, 1 struck.

commits.subject: Every Name runs on the shared component now
commits.body:
Three archives' /who/ pages were byte-identical apart from the line that
imports the data, and two more differed only in wording — a copy-paste fork
sitting there waiting to drift, which is the thing the kit exists to stop.
It gains a search box and a facet for the names held by more than one, which
is the distinction the page exists to draw: a name is not a person. Every row
is still in the HTML and visible before any script runs.

commits.subject: The living-person tick was passing over an empty set - so the set was counted
commits.body:
checkliving.py finds living people from an explicit flag: living,
presumedLiving, alive, isLiving, or conf:"living". people.json carries none of
them. So the green tick this archive has been shipping was passing over nothing
at all. The kit's own docstring says that is "correct rather than a gap" FOR AN
ARCHIVE THAT GENUINELY HAS NO LIVING PEOPLE - which had never been established
here, only assumed.
So it was established. Of 278 people, three are born 1930 or later with no death
recorded. Rieta Maria (1936) and Antoinette Septima Lynette (1943) are both over
eighty and presumed deceased by the rule the checker itself applies. Anton
Lerena, born 1952, was not - and he was the one person this archive published who
might have been living.
He is not. The J193 read today gives his death as 3 April 2003, and his register
row is updated from "named in the tree; not yet corroborated by a document" to a
documented death, with the internal inconsistency kept rather than smoothed: the
typed birth date says 05-05-1952 while the identity number encodes 1952-06-05, so
the year is certain and the day is not.
drift.py then did its job and refused to let that finding sit in the data without
appearing on a page. So the South Africa page gains a section on the gazette work
- the three sons with their exact dates, the twenty-one-year agreement between
the 1950 liquidation account and Nuno Fernando's 1971 notice, Rogue Luis Armando
born 1905 and what that asks about the eight unaccounted years, Anton Armando's
documented death, and Robert Paul Lerena described by the state as a racehorse
trainer.
Also cleared a stale site/dist that was failing the build with a missing
open-questions.astro.mjs - unrelated to content, fixed by removing dist and
.astro and rebuilding.

commits.subject: A gate for stale errands - the failure that started all of this
commits.body:
tools/check-errands.py, wired into verify.sh. It fails the build when an errand
whose status is still open carries a detail that announces the errand is
finished. That is exactly what happened on 15 September: "Sancho's 1791 marriage
- FIVE FILMED BOOKS" sat at ready, addressed to David, for hours after the act
had been found and published, still telling him to go and find it. Nothing was
checking, so nothing complained.
It threw a false positive on its first run, which is the useful part. An errand
said the work "cannot be closed online at all" - meaning the TASK was impossible,
not that the errand was over - and a bare \bCLOSED\b matched it. The patterns
were tightened to phrases that can only mean this errand is finished: "CLOSED 15
September 2026", "THIS ERRAND IS CLOSED", "DO NOT REDO IT", and so on. A noisy
check gets switched off, and the docstring already said so before the run proved
it.
Then tested both ways rather than assumed. Planting the real case - the 1791
marriage errand set back to "ready" - makes it exit 1 and name the row and the
phrase. Restoring it returns to green. 40 errands checked, none finished-but-open.

commits.subject: Sancho is last seen alive in 1812, not 1798 - and the siege did not burn the registers
commits.body:
TWO MORE ROWS DONE, AND THE FIRST CORRECTS THIS SESSION TWICE.
Fourteen records name Sancho Llerena. Only four require him to have been standing
there: godfather at the Iglesia Matriz in 1789, sworn witness at Canelones in
1798, padrino at the 1804 confirmations, and enumerated in the 1812 PADRON at
calle San Juan No 60, household 59, as "Sancho, andaluz, 45".
A census enumerates the living. So the last document in the world that shows
Sancho Llerena alive is the padron of 1812 - not the deposition of 1798, which
this session asserted twice today, including in the very worklist row that set
out to answer the question. Everything after 1812 names him as father,
grandfather or ancestor, up to 1850, and a dead man can be all three. The
unaccounted gap before the trees' 1832 is twenty years, not thirty-four.
Written up record by record in data/sancho-last-alive.tsv, with a column that
does nothing but ask whether the document requires him to be alive. That column
is the whole point, and the archive did not have it.
AND THE COVERAGE TEST. Montevideo church burials are indexed continuously across
the period - 1832, 1833 and 1838 in the first window; 33 indexed burials for one
surname across 1839-1848, including 1841 and 1842; and 1852 in the next. The
siege of 1843-51 did not destroy the registers. So Sancho's absence from the
burial index is not explained by register loss, which strengthens the negative
and justifies walking the images rather than abandoning them.
One honest limit recorded with it: indexing density is not register survival. The
1850s window returns seven where the 1840s returns thirty-three, and that may be
thinner indexing rather than fewer burials.

commits.subject: Four infrastructure rows done: the ark map, the film register, the tool, the rule
commits.body:
RESOLVE EVERY ARK. 78 image arks, 51 films. 73 resolved to a film-and-image, two
restricted (HTTP 403 - access denied, not absent), two with no DeepZoom id, two
Argentine enrolment cards on a different id scheme. data/ark-to-film.tsv. Every
one of them can now be reopened through the tile service while www is blocked.
THE FILM REGISTER. data/film-register.tsv, 51 films, built from resolved arks
rather than catalogue lines - which is the point, since two of this archive's
catalogue attributions failed inspection today. Nine are identified in detail,
including the two-block structure of 8166573 and the correction that 7713386 is
not the 1726-1800 index. The other 42 are listed as "not yet identified", which
is the honest state and a queue in itself. This archive had named perhaps nine
films before today; it can now reach fifty-one.
THE TOOL. tools/fsimage.js - mosaic reader, contact sheet, ark resolver, extent
prober - with the three traps written as comments where they will actually be
read: never cache-bust a failed tile, wait after naturalWidth, never batch the
view and the screenshot. Plus the rule that is not about code: do not read names
at fit-width, with the four misreadings of 15 September named in full.
THE RULE - and this row was wrong. The method page has carried "A null is not a
finding until a control says so" since 14 September; assuming it did not was the
same error as assuming three already-read images were unread. So it was
strengthened rather than duplicated, with the four times the rule decided a
question today: once it saved three hundred images of hand-reading, twice it
voided nulls that looked clean, and once - only once - it confirmed a negative
worth keeping.

commits.subject: The errands key belongs in the TSV, because build-pages rewrites the JSON
commits.body:
Second archive with the same trap, and the gate caught this one loudly
instead of going quiet. errands.json is generated from data/errands.tsv by
tools/build-pages.py, so the stable keys written into the JSON lasted until
the next build — and the gate then refused, saying the declared key was on
0 of 40 rows and naming the likely cause.
That refusal is the fix working. Before today it would have reported nothing
to count and exited 0, which is how Mazza sat at "nothing outstanding" with
twenty-four outstanding searches.
The key is now a column in the TSV, which is the record, and the generator
passes every column through untouched. 40 errands, 40 unique keys.

commits.subject: Twenty-six more on the work list, most of them opened by today's failures
commits.body:
The list goes to 82 rows: 59 next, 18 done, 4 blocked, 1 struck. Seven groups,
and the largest came out of things that did not work.
THE BURIAL HUNT, WIDENED. Sancho's death is now the live question and the Cordon
is only one parish. Rows for the Iglesia Matriz and Canelones burial registers,
for Santa Lucia where his wife's people were vecinos, and one that has to come
first: test whether the registers of the 1830s and 40s even survive, given the
siege of 1843-51 and that civil registration does not begin until 1879. An
absence proves nothing until coverage is established - the same discipline as the
Berroeta control.
And one that changes the question rather than answering it: establish the last
date Sancho is attested ALIVE. He is named in acts of 1831, 1836 and 1850, but in
every one of them as somebody's father or grandfather, which a dead man can be.
His last certain appearance as a living person is the deposition of 9 January
1798, where he stood in a room and could not sign his name.
INFRASTRUCTURE THIS SESSION PROVED AND SHOULD NOT LOSE. A film register - every
DGS, what it actually is rather than what a catalogue said, its image range, and
what has been read; two attributions failed inspection today and one film turned
out to have two blocks. Resolve all seventy-nine stored arks to film-and-image,
because an ark alone cannot be reopened when the viewer is down. Put the mosaic
reader in tools/ with its three traps written as comments. And publish the
control-before-null rule on the method page, where it is not stated, having today
saved a day of work once and voided three nulls.
THE CHILDREN, INDIVIDUALLY. Agustina Ramona, Fidel, Jose Loreto, Avelino and
Luis' children each get a row, plus Justa Pastora's after 1827 - the archive
already notes a thirteen-year gap between two of hers that almost certainly hides
others.
THE PEOPLE IN THE HOUSEHOLD WHO WERE NOT FREE. The 1812 padron puts four enslaved
people in Sancho's house; Juana and Maria Mercedes are named in acts as belonging
to him and his wife; the castrense register is full of baptisms of enslaved
children of the regiment's officers. They are in this archive as circumstances of
somebody else's life. Their names survive in the same records this archive reads
for its own purposes.
SOUTH AFRICA AND ARGENTINA. A Lerena birth in Argentina in 1905 would close the
declared gap between Northam and the Cape. Pablo Armando's arrival in South
Africa connects nothing to nothing at present. The 1911 Taylor marriage record
would state his father's name, which is the whole question here.
SPAIN, WITHIN THE CONSTRAINT. The Santander collection is the only free route
that touches Asturias. PARES and the diocesan portals were never tried - this
morning established what FamilySearch does not have, not that nobody has it. And
the catalogue back route, from an image's own Information panel, which worked for
Canelones when catalogue search was down.
QUALITY. Merge the overlapping accounts of Sancho's children while they still
agree. Lift consistency.py's sibling coverage above 106 of 277 using the
parent-pair query. And give every person a last-attested-alive date, because the
archive currently records when someone was NAMED, not when they were
demonstrably living - which is exactly the confusion the Sancho search exposed.

commits.subject: Pin the kit to the gate that refuses a key on no rows
commits.body:
A declared key that matched nothing was being skipped silently, so an archive
with outstanding work could report none. It now fails and says so.

commits.subject: Give the register rows a stable key, and start counting what is outstanding
commits.body:
The work-list gate can only see a row that is MISSING if it has an exact key
to count against, and these rows had none — which is why this archive has
been printing "nothing declared to count the work list against" on every
build since the gate arrived.
Every row now carries a key, seeded once from its most stable fields and
frozen in the file, so editing a title later cannot move it. Nothing is
derived from the title at build time, deliberately: a gate that guesses from
names calls a genuinely unopened source stale, and a gate that cries wolf
gets switched off.
Enforcement is on, with the backlog declared rather than pretended away. The
number of outstanding items with no covering row is printed on every build
and the build fails if it grows. Writing a row lowers it; a row may cover
several items at once.

commits.subject: The timeline, on this archive too
commits.body:
Dated events laid over who was in charge — the Defranceschi chart, promoted
to the kit because the idea was never about marriages: it is what this family
was doing, and what was happening to them while they did it.
What a dot IS stays this archive's to say, and the caption says it. Four of
the seven have real marriage dates; the other three plot the years they
actually hold and say so, because a chart quietly plotting births while
claiming marriages would be worse than no chart.

commits.subject: Search for Sancho's death - a controlled null, in the right parish and decade
commits.body:
No indexed death or burial exists for Sancho Llerena in Uruguay under any
spelling. Across 401 loose results he appears only as father, father of the
bride, spouse or "other" - never as the principal of a death. The two
death-flagged hits are an S/v Lorena of Artigas in 1902 and a Castilla Llerena of
Flores in 1924.
The control passed, and it is a strong one. A surname-Rodriguez search for
Montevideo deaths 1828-1838 returns church burials from "Uruguay, Catholic Church
Records, 1726-2000" at NUESTRA SENORA DEL CARMEN LA MAYOR, CORDON, dated 1832,
1833 and 1838. That is the exact parish and the exact decade: Justa Pastora
married at the Cordon in 1830, the 1831 godfather act is at the Cordon, and
Dominga lived there. So burials in his own family's parish, in the years he is
supposed to have died, ARE indexed - and he is not among them.
Maria Fernandez is absent on the same terms, searched 1810-1870. One gain from
it: FamilySearch's index gives her "Parents Rosa Fernandez, Rodrigo Fernandez",
which is a third independent witness to what the 1811 baptism and the 1791
marriage act both say. Three sources, one couple, no disagreement.
What the null does not mean, written down before anyone assumes it. The index is
name-based and an eighteenth-century surname mangled by a transcriber is
invisible to it; and the Cordon is one parish of several - he could be at the
Iglesia Matriz, at Canelones, or at Santa Lucia where his wife's family were
vecinos. He is not in the INDEX. That is not the same as not in the REGISTERS,
and the trees' 1832 remains a tree.
So a new row: walk the Cordon burial register by image for 1826-1845. The Cordon
marriage register is already anchored at dgs:007713391 image 1669, so the burial
volume is findable from the same reel's item boards.
56 rows: 33 next, 18 done, 4 blocked, 1 struck.

commits.subject: Search the Granada index for Felix and Rosalia - a controlled null, after two fake ones were thrown away
commits.body:
Exact-surname searches returned zero twice: "Llerena" + spouse "Aguilar", and
"Lerena" + spouse "Aguilar", Spain 1720-1800, both with the "No Results Found"
line present. Both were DISCARDED. The control - the same exact-match shape run
for 1750-1760 - fails to retrieve the 1754 act that is KNOWN to be in that
collection, because the indexed surname is the compound "Lerena y Armenta", which
exact matching will not reach. A null from a query that cannot find what is there
is not a null, and the temptation was to report two clean zeros and move on.
The working shape is non-exact surname, exact given names, place Spain, dates
1735-1785. Run for the known couple it returns 263 results including the Granada
Catholic Pre-Marriage Investigation Files and the full 1754 marriage record, so
the shape works and that collection is reachable by it. Only then is a null worth
anything.
And it is a null. The same shape for Felix Llerena and Rosalia Aguilar, Spain
1735-1785, returns 305 results and not one Andalusian collection among them -
nothing from Granada, Cordoba, Sevilla, Jaen or Malaga. What comes back is Spain
Catholic Church Records, Spain Baptisms, Gerona Municipal Records and the Diocese
of Santander.
So their marriage is not indexed by FamilySearch anywhere in Andalusia in the
fifty years that must contain it; their son was born about 1767. Taken with this
morning's mapping - that Cordoba's parish registers are not on FamilySearch at
all - the searchable routes are closed. What is left is the Archivo General del
Obispado de Cordoba, which is a letter and is already logged as David's.
It also means the Canelones marriage act of 8 January 1791 remains the only
document in the world this archive has that names Felix Llerena and Rosalia
Aguilar.

commits.subject: Chase the 1754 pre-marriage file - it cannot be read, and my own lead deflates
commits.body:
The expediente has its own record: Spain, Granada, Catholic Pre-Marriage
Investigation Files 1556-1899, ark 1:1:XPG2-RYP. It is "Image Unavailable" like
the marriage record beside it, no image ark is exposed, and the collection's own
FamilySearch Wiki page has no text at all - so no film number can be recovered
and the film-and-image trick has nothing to bite on. Its index entry is thinner
than the marriage index this archive already held: names, date, place, nothing
else. A controlled negative - the record exists, was opened, and yields nothing.
And the more useful result is the second one, which is against this session.
Yesterday's turn found "Felix Llerena and Rosalia Aguilar, naturales de dicha
Cordova" on the 1791 act and called the 1754 marriage "two Lerena-Aguilar unions
in Cordoba and Granada in one generation". That over-read it. The 1754 bride, Ana
Maria de Aguilar, is of LA MALA - La Malaha, in GRANADA province - and this
archive had already recorded exactly that, including the modern identification.
Our Rosalia Aguilar is explicitly of Cordoba. Only the groom is Cordoban. Aguilar
is among the commonest surnames in Andalusia and a town in Cordoba province
besides.
So the convergence is one common surname in two different provinces, not a
family. An earlier session had already run the decisive test - a structured
search for a son "Sancho de Lerena y Aguilar", returning a controlled "No Results
Found" - and was right to close the file. This session was wrong to reopen it on
that basis, and the reasoning is kept because it is the useful part.
Every field on the marriage record was already here too, including the bride's
parents Francisco de Aguilar and Beatris Franco and the original event place of
Santa Ana, Granada. Nothing was gained. That is worth recording as plainly as a
find would be.

commits.subject: The families who married in, on the front page too
commits.body:
All seven home pages now carry the same five sections: where this family can
actually be put, the families who married in, what this archive has
established, the archive in numbers, and what is still missing. Before this
only four of those were shared and the diagram was on none of them.
The grouping rule moves into src/lib/marriedin.js so the front page and
/marriages/ read the same answer to "how does this family reach this line".
A rule copied into two pages is a rule that will be two rules by next month.
Each archive keeps its own rule — descent, ahnentafel, route, status, or the
line already assigned in the data — the lib only stops it being written
twice.

commits.subject: Rank the families instead of drawing a wheel of them
commits.body:
The radial chart came from the archive with seventy-four in-law surnames,
where a ring is a reasonable shape. At thirteen it was indefensible: a large
empty hole, every name sideways or upside down, type shrunk to fit a
circumference nothing needed, and most of a wide page unused.
A ranked bar reads at any count. The name is horizontal and legible, the bar
is the count so the comparison is a length rather than the area of a dot, and
the rows fill the width. One scale across every group, because two bars of
the same length meaning different numbers is how a chart like this lies.

commits.subject: Map what is filmed for Cordoba and Asturias - and the answer cuts both ways
commits.body:
THE BAD HALF. Cordoba's parish registers are not on FamilySearch. The Research
Wiki's Church Records section for the province lists no FamilySearch collection
at all, only MyHeritage indexes behind a paywall; the registers are with the
Diocese of Cordoba. Asturias is the same, with one partial exception - "Spain,
Diocese of SANTANDER, Catholic Church Records 1538-1985, contains some records
for Asturias". Full text for Andalusia is nobility and notarial only.
So Sancho's baptism is not sitting on a film waiting to be addressed by number.
That route is a letter to a diocesan archive, not a search, and it is logged as
David's with the exact citation to quote.
Also tested rather than assumed: "Spain, Cordoba, Municipal Records, 1509-1947"
does exist with images, but a search for Llerena in Cordoba returns 5,031 results
of which every visible one is a municipal CENSUS of 1919-1924. Its 1509 start
date is not where its indexed content is.
THE GOOD HALF, which corrects this session's own pessimism of an hour ago. The
provincial wiki pages are not the whole picture. A record search for Llerena in
Spain, 1730-1800, returns 228 results from national collections the Cordoba page
never mentions: Spain, Catholic Church Records 1307-2005; Spain, Baptisms
1502-1940; Spain, Marriages 1565-1950; and Spain, Granada, Catholic Pre-Marriage
Investigation Files, 1556-1899 - the same record type walked at Canelones this
morning, indexed, for Andalusia, covering the right century. The eighteenth
century is reachable by INDEX even where it is not reachable by IMAGE.
AND A FILE THIS ARCHIVE CLOSED, WHICH THE 1791 ACT RE-OPENS. The index gives
"Sancho de Lerena y Armenta, married 17 November 1754 at Granada to ANA MARIA DE
AGUILAR, born CORDOBA, son of Sancho de Lerena y Velasco and Maria Antonia de
Armenta y Guebara". This archive found that act, examined it, and correctly set
it aside - it settles Cordoba versus Granada for the 1754 groom and not for ours,
and this archive has already corrected itself once for overstating exactly that.
What changed is the other side of the comparison. The act of 8 January 1791 gives
our Sancho's parents as FELIX LLERENA and ROSALIA AGUILAR, naturales de dicha
Cordova. So there are now two Lerena-Aguilar unions in Cordoba and Granada in one
generation, with the given name Sancho recurring across them. That is not proof
and is not being treated as any. It is a reason to read the 1754 pre-marriage
file itself rather than its index entry, and to search the same Granada files for
a marriage of Felix and Rosalia about 1750-1766.
55 rows: 36 next, 14 done, 4 blocked, 1 struck.

commits.subject: Run the parent-pair query on Felix Llerena and Rosalia Aguilar - and run the control first
commits.body:
"Llerena y de Rosalia Aguilar" returns ZERO. The page rendered and reported a
count of 0; it was not a blocked page. "Felix Llerena" returns results, all of
them modern Latin America - Cartagena, Peru, Mexico - where the name is common.
"Rosalia Aguilar" returns forty collections, of which two are in Spain at all:
La Carolina, Jaen, notarial records of 1829-1837, wrong province and forty years
too late.
On its own that would mean nothing, so the control was run BEFORE the null was
believed rather than after. Searching "ciudad de Cordova" and reading the
collection names shows what FamilySearch full text actually holds for Andalusia:
Nobility Records for Granada 1489-1718 and Ecija 1529-1907, Madrid notarial
protocols, and Orders of Chivalry induction files. The only "Cordoba" that
appears is Cordoba, VERACRUZ, in Mexico.
So the full-text index for Andalusia holds nobility and notarial records, not
parish registers. An eighteenth-century Cordoba baptism or marriage is not in the
corpus being searched, and the zero above is "not findable by this instrument",
not "not there". Recorded that way.
This is the Berroeta lesson applied forwards instead of backwards. There, the
control came after a day of hand-reading had been planned on an unchecked
assumption. Here it came before a single conclusion was drawn.
One thing the null does support, weakly. The corpus that IS indexed - Spanish
nobility and hidalguia files, chivalric orders, Madrid protocols, searchable back
to 1489 - is exactly where an armigerous couple would appear, and Felix Llerena
and Rosalia Aguilar are not in it. Weak evidence that they were not gentry with a
Chancilleria file. It bears on this archive's long argument about "de Llerena" as
a toponymic, and it sits with the 1811 act calling Sancho "Don" while the 1798
deposition records that he could not write his own name.
Mapping what is filmed and indexed for Cordoba and Asturias is therefore promoted
to running, and is the gating item for the whole Spanish programme: four people
wait behind it, and until it is done every Spanish null this archive produces is
uninterpretable.

commits.subject: Read the three images - and every one of them was already in the archive
commits.body:
dgs:008166571 image 1130 is the baptism of DOMINGA JOSEFA, 15 May 1804,
godparents Joseph Ponteceli and Agueda Rivero. dgs:007713376 image 515 is
FRANCISCO JUAN RAMON, 22 March 1826, son of Capitan Don Antonio Rodriguez de
Carballo and Dona Dominga Llerena. dgs:007713376 image 601 is LUCINDA GREGORIA
DEL CORAZON DE JESUS, 12 May 1827.
All three were already read and recorded here, and the last two in fuller words
than FamilySearch's index gives - the archive has the Capitan, the Mayor Don
Joaquin Ruiz de Carvallo, and a General standing godfather, none of which the
index carried.
So the worklist row calling them unread was wrong, and this session wrote it. The
inference was "the collection is not in sources-consulted, therefore the act has
not been read", and that does not follow: the same act reaches this archive under
different arks by different routes. An unread COLLECTION is not an unread ACT.
Logged in corrections.
Which reframes the parent-pair query, and in its favour. Every document the
phrase "Llerena y de Maria Fernandez" returned, the archive already had - five
for five. That is an independent instrument, aimed at the exact question "who are
the children of this couple", run against an index this archive did not build,
and it found nothing missing. The coverage of Sancho and Maria's children is
better than this session assumed when it opened the row. The query keeps its
value where coverage is NOT established - Felix Llerena and Rosalia Aguilar in
Cordoba, Rodrigo and Rosa Fernandez in Asturias - where a clean pass would mean
something different.
One thing the exercise did add. The 1826 act names the father "Antonio RODRIGUEZ
de Carballo" and the 1827 act names him "Antonio RUIZ de Carvallo"; this archive
had already logged that split as a discrepancy recorded rather than smoothed.
FamilySearch's own extraction splits the same way, which argues the difference is
in the registers and not in this archive's reading of them.
52 rows: 36 next, 12 done, 3 blocked, 1 struck.

commits.subject: The marriages page has one shape, and the map has a coast
commits.body:
Two complaints, both right. The marriages page was standardised in its
families section and left different everywhere else — measured after the
fact: one archive had a metrics row and six had none, two had a chart and
five had none, two had no register of couples at all, and the couples sat
above the families on five and below on two. And the place map was a scatter
of dots in an empty box, which cannot be read as anywhere.
The order is no longer this page's to arrange. Metrics, the wheel, the
spine, the couples and the families are handed to the shared component and
rendered in that order, so seven archives cannot drift into seven layouts
again.
The wheel is the radial chart that was local to one archive. It draws
labelled groups of named things with counts, which is what the component is
already given, so an archive that can list its families can now draw them.
The map now carries real coastlines and national borders — Natural Earth,
decoded at build time and clipped to this frame, so the page ships its own
corner of the world and not an atlas. The line saying there is no coastline
here has gone, because there is one.

commits.subject: Run the gate that can see a work-list row that is missing
commits.body:
The existing gate checks the rows this list has; nothing checked for the rows
it was missing, which is how a sent letter — the one that named three further
doors — stayed off a list where every visible row looked fine.
This archive now runs checkcovers on every build. An archive declares where
its outstanding work lives and a row declares what it answers for, and the
gate refuses in both directions: work with no row, and a row pointing at
something that no longer exists.
Declaring nothing does not pass quietly, because silence is the failure the
gate exists to end: it prints what is going uncounted, and says where a list
needs a stable key before it can be counted at all. It does not fail the
build for that, so this can be adopted without the archive going red first.

commits.subject: One name per page, in the menu and on the page itself
commits.body:
A reader who clicks The Register should land on a page called The Register.
Across the seven archives they often did not: the same estate route carried
a different title on nearly every site, and sometimes a different one from
the menu entry that led to it.
/corrections/ had five titles, /searched/ five, /who/ four, /direct-line/
three. /people/ was The People, The people or Everyone depending where you
stood. /register/ was The register on five sites, The Register on one and
Register on another. /worklist/ was the reverse case — all seven pages
agreed on The work list while all seven menus said The Work List.
The canonical name for each route is not a preference imposed on them; it
is what the archives already mostly said, counted across all fourteen slots
per route — seven menu labels and seven page titles — with the six names
that were decided directly kept as decided. Where that count was a tie the
tie is broken and said so: /worklist/ goes to the pages, because the title
lives in worklist.json and the menus were the outlier; /bloodline/ is left
alone entirely, because all seven agree on both sides and the menu's extra
word, drawn, is doing real work.
Five titles are deliberately not canonical and stay: For Michael, What was
taken back and What This Archive Got Wrong for three corrections pages, The
Search Register, and The Names. Menu labels are estate-wide so that a reader
learns them once; a page title may keep the archive's own voice.

commits.subject: Open Canelones 1776-1794, and correct a claim I made this morning
commits.body:
The volume is DGS 8166573 images 72-478 - the SAME FILM as the informaciones
matrimoniales, in a separate block. This archive already held an ark into it,
3:1:3Q9M-CS2Z-WH52, and had never resolved it.
Which disproves something this session published this morning. The informaciones
walk said "images below 1057 return nothing at all, so whatever else is on film
8166573, this archive cannot reach it by number". That came from three probes -
images 1, 500 and 1000 - all of which happen to fall in the same gap. The film
has TWO blocks, 72-478 and 1057-3295, and block one is the baptism register.
Three samples are not a survey. Corrected in place and logged.
Pedro Antonio's baptism read from the image rather than the full-text transcript
the archive had been relying on: "El Capellan del Regimiento de Infanteria de
Buenos Ayres Don Bartolome Munoz bautizo, puso oleo y crisma a PEDRO ANTONIO DE
LA SS.ma TRINIDAD, que nacio ayer, hijo legitimo del Soldado Dragon Sancho
Llerena y de Maria Fernandez. Fueron padrinos Don ANTONIO ALEMAN y su mujer."
New: the full baptismal name, and the godparents. Confirms 31 July 1793.
And a query worth more than the volume. Full text for the phrase "Llerena y de
Maria Fernandez" returns six documents, three of them this family - because that
phrase only occurs when a document names BOTH parents, which happens when a child
is baptised, when a child marries, or when a GRANDCHILD is baptised. It resolves
to Canelones baptisms 1794-1810 (dgs:008166571 image 1130), the Cordon marriage
register (dgs:007713391 image 1669), and two Montevideo cathedral baptisms of
1825-1828 (dgs:007713376 images 515 and 601). Three of the five are still unread
and the worklist says so.
The Cordon one turned out to be Justa Pastora's marriage, which this archive
already holds - and holds correctly. At fit-width the heading read "Noviembre de
1836" against the archive's five records of 3 November 1830, which briefly looked
like a contradiction. At magnification it is plainly 1830. The archive was right
and the session was wrong.
That is the fourth fit-width misreading today - Mendoza for Berroeta, Llerena for
Juarez, Rosalia Illera for Petrona Illescas, and now 1836 for 1830. None reached
the site, because each was magnified before it was believed. The rule is holding.
The habit of trusting a small image is not.
52 rows: 1 running, 36 next, 11 done, 3 blocked, 1 struck.

commits.subject: Pin the kit to the marriages component all seven now use
commits.body:
The shared page picked up a chip grid, structured group detail, a per-group
count label and a count noun while it was being rolled out, and each of
those came from an archive that needed it. Without the repin, CI installs
the sha from before them and builds a page the local one does not match.

commits.subject: The Marriages: the couples, and what has been decided about everybody else
commits.body:
This archive had no marriages page. It has one now, on the estate's shared
shape, and it is grouped by this archive's own judgement rather than by
descent or by name.
The subject here is a NAME, not a family. 183 of 278 people carry some
spelling of Lerena and most have no proved relationship to the line, and
sorting out which do is the entire reason the archive exists. Grouping by
descent would claim what the evidence cannot support; grouping by surname
would assume the very thing in question. So the groups are the status field:
22 connected, 6 of high interest, 12 of interest, 230 unplaced, 8 excluded.
The excluded are the point. Lola Lerena, Italian-born, where the name is
coincidental; Catherine Buys, where Lerena is a given name and not the
surname at all. An archive that grouped on the name would have swallowed all
eight. They stay visible rather than deleted, so the next person to search
this name finds the answer instead of doing the work again.
The count in a group heading is people, not families: 230 unplaced Lerena
are not 230 families, and the shared component now takes the noun from the
archive.

commits.subject: Close the Berroeta control on both limits - Sancho is not in the regiment's book
commits.body:
LIMIT ONE, the hits are that film. Six arks from the 22 results were resolved
through the tile service's manifest. Five return dgs:007713373 - images 657, 667,
676, 716, 831 - and image 657 is a page this session had already read by hand.
So the collection labelled "Montevideo. Military Award Records 1812-1814" IS the
Regimiento de Infanteria de Buenos Ayres book, whatever its label says. The sixth
returns dgs:007713382 image 2736, the Montevideo marriage register, which is a
new anchor.
LIMIT TWO, the sweeps are run. "Sancho Llerena" 68 results, "Sancho Lerena" 143,
"Sancho Lorena" returns results too. Their Uruguayan collections are Canelones
and Montevideo cathedral baptisms and marriages. Not one hit, under any of the
three spellings, comes from DGS 7713373.
So Sancho Llerena does not appear in the regiment's chaplaincy book as indexed.
The book IS indexed - the control proves it - so this is a real absence and not a
gap in coverage. The standing caveat does not go away: machine transcription of
eighteenth-century hands is imperfect, so an index absence is weaker than a page
absence. Eleven images read by hand agree with it.
Row 1 is therefore retired rather than performed, and says so on its face. Images
663-950 were never read and now will not be. "Done" is the nearest of the five
states to what happened; if anything later contradicts this, the 290 images are
still there.
The sweeps also threw up four bodies of record nobody here has opened, and one
of them should go to the front: CANELONES BAPTISM RECORDS 1776-1794. This archive
has been working from the 1794-1810 volume and did not know an earlier one
existed. Sancho married in January 1791 and Pedro Antonio was baptised in August
1793 - both inside that book. Also opened as rows: Montevideo cathedral Religious
Marriage Records 1782-1797, and cathedral baptism volumes for 1811-1813,
1831-1833 and 1840-1842.
And the free gazette produced one more: "N84/085959 ... Lindana Boys ... P. R.
LERENA RACING STABLES, P.O. Box 425, Randburg", 8 August 1986. The 1951 gazette
calls Robert Paul Lerena a racehorse trainer at Newlands; this is a Lerena racing
stable at Randburg thirty-five years later, in the town where Ricardo Juan Carlos
lived and died. "P. R." is most likely one of his sons and Paul Raymond is the
obvious reading of the initials - recorded as a reading, not a fact. Nothing is
said here about any living member of this family.
50 rows: 36 next, 10 done, 3 blocked, 1 struck.

commits.subject: Twenty-seven more items on the work list, arranged as a roadmap
commits.body:
The list had twenty rows, most of them loose ends from today. This turns it into
a programme, in seven groups.
SPAIN, which the 1791 marriage act opened and nobody has walked into. Five rows.
The act names four people as natives of Spain - Sancho of Cordoba, his parents
Felix Llerena and Rosalia Aguilar of the same city, and Maria Fernandez with her
parents Rodrigo and Rosa Fernandez of Asturias - and this archive has never
opened a single Spanish parish register. The enabling row is mapping what is
actually filmed and indexed, and deliberately not from a catalogue line, because
two of two catalogue attributions failed inspection today. Then Sancho's baptism
about 1767, his parents' marriage, the Asturian Fernandez family who emigrated
and lived in his household, and the Llerena-Aguilar compound tested where it
would actually occur.
URUGUAY, finishing Sancho's own life. Five rows: his death, still only a tree's
1832; Maria Fernandez's death, never looked for; a closed sibling list read
straight out of the Canelones registers instead of assembled from scattered
searches; Pedro Antonio forward from 1793, who is "Mayor Don Pedro Antonio
Llerena" by 1826 and is the generation where this family changes class; and the
1812 padron read from the image rather than a transcription.
ERRANDS THAT ARE NO LONGER ERRANDS. Eleven rows sit in errands.tsv at "ready"
and owner David because when they were written this archive could not drive the
viewer and full text was down. Both are solved. One row to go through them and
leave David only what genuinely needs a person.
SOUTH AFRICA, from people the gazette produced this afternoon. Catherine Mary
Sophia Lerena, a wife nobody knew Nuno Fernando had. Where Rogue Luis Armando was
born in 1905, which tests a declared gap - the eight years between Northam and
the Cape. Rose Lilian Theys, who was "no relation" and yet lived at the
deceased's address, executed his will and took a quarter of the residue. A
Taylor and Booyzen sweep, since the pipeline works and costs nothing. And the
Rapeport thread - one firm, four estates, twenty-five years.
METHOD. Make the build catch a stale errand, which is the failure that started
all of this. Audit the other catalogue-derived film numbers. And check that
check:living's green tick was a question asked rather than assumed, now that
people who died in 2022, 2023 and 2024 have been added with addresses and
identity numbers.
OWED TO THE ESTATE. Two warnings, both learned the hard way here: pdftotext
-layout interleaves the gazette's two columns and a bare grep will weld two
strangers into one person; and a column labelled death_year in an
ancestors.co.za harvest may hold the year the estate was advertised, which is
invisible until you fetch the gazette the row points at.
DECIDED NOT TO DO, recorded rather than left implicit. No accounts and no
payments, with the visible cost named - Doreen May is the one person who could
not be taken off a commercial index. No routing around the FamilySearch block,
with its costs named too, including the rule that every zero from a blocked page
was discarded rather than recorded as a null. And no reading 290 more images
until the Berroeta control's two limits close.
46 rows: 34 next, 8 done, 3 blocked, 1 struck. 39 on this archive, 4 on the kit
and estate, 3 on David.

commits.subject: Four menu labels brought to the house style
commits.body:
The estate writes menu labels in sentence case — 257 of 368, and it is every
archive’s own majority. These four were the shared pages where archives
disagreed with each other: What Changed against What changed, Photograph These
against Photograph these, What We Cannot Close, and The Namesakes against
Namesakes.
Only case and one article. The six shared pages that carry genuinely different
WORDS — /people/ as The People or Nine lives in full, /who/ as Every Name or
Everyone, a page each — are left alone: those are a decision about voice, not a
tidy-up.
Also: /tree was the one menu link here without a trailing slash.

commits.subject: Finish the gazette re-sourcing, and find a column that was lying
commits.body:
Four of the five notices read, the fifth a real null, and two corrections that
matter more than any of them.
ROGUE LUIS ARMANDO LERENA, in full: "1518/73 - LERENA, Rogue Luis Armando,
6/12/05, 331/402089, 20 Park Lane, Florida, 29/1/73." Born 6 December 1905, died
29 January 1973. That makes him the ELDEST of the three sons by fifteen years -
Ricardo Juan Carlos 1920, Nuno Fernando 1924 - and forty-four when his father
died in 1950, comfortably the "LOUIS LERENA, major son" of that account. It also
opens a question this archive has not asked: Pablo Armando was born at Rosario in
1882 and the eight years between Northam and the Cape are still unclosed. A son
born in 1905 may not have been born in South Africa at all.
ANTON ARMANDO LERENA: born 1952, died 3 April 2003, estate 15127/2013.
Which kills the contradiction this session invented yesterday. There was never
one and there is one man. The archive's row read "2013 ... 68"; 2013 was the
GAZETTE year and 68 was the PAGE NUMBER - both columns in its own file - and this
session read them as a death year and an age. gendatabase was right.
And pulling that thread found the bigger fault: THE COLUMN LABELLED death_year IN
data/sa-deceased-estates.tsv IS THE YEAR THE ESTATE WAS ADVERTISED. Every one of
the eleven rows had it equal to the year of its own notice. Ricardo Juan Carlos
died 21 December 1994 and was filed under 1996. Renamed to gazette_year, true
dates recorded, both errors logged in corrections.
Also read: Roberto Juan Roque (b. 20 March 1944, d. 20 February 2022), Brigitte
(b. 16 October 1951, d. 18 May 2023, Johannesburg), Belinda Maud (b. 16 January
1957).
Two anomalies flagged rather than smoothed. Anton Armando's typed birth date says
05-05-1952 while his identity number encodes 1952-06-05, and every other entry on
that page agrees with its own number - so the year is certain and the day is not.
Belinda Maud's death field reads 7 August 2024 in a gazette published on 2 August
2024, which is impossible; recorded as "died 2024, day unreliable" rather than
quietly corrected to something that looks sensible.
DOREEN MAY could not be re-sourced. Estate 16409/00 returns exactly two J187
accounts and no J193, so gendatabase's "born 1921, died 1999" stands as THEIR
fact, not this archive's. A real null - the search ran and returned results, it
did not error.
One thread worth pulling later: Rapeport Incorporated of 107 Oxford Road,
Rosebank acted for Doreen May in 2001, Anton Armando in 2013, Roberto Juan Roque
in 2022 and Belinda Maud in 2024. One family solicitor across a quarter-century.
Worklist moved with the work: rows 9 and 19 done, row 20 opened for Doreen May's
missing J193 and for the 1986 Lerena Racing Stables notice.

commits.subject: Pin the kit where the work list pills filter
commits.body:
Ten or twenty rows and no way to ask the one question anybody opens that page
with: show me only what is blocked. The pills are buttons now — one active at a
time, count stays on the pill, and the choice goes into the URL as
?show=blocked so a filtered list can be sent to somebody.
Every row is in the page and visible before the script runs, so a reader without
JavaScript gets the whole list rather than an empty one.

commits.subject: Re-source the South Africans from the Government Gazette, and get more than the index gave
commits.body:
David chose re-sourcing over arguing fair citation. gazettes.africa is free and
official, and the Form J193 estate notice carries the estate number, forenames,
DATE of birth, identity number, address, DATE of death, surviving spouse and
executor. gendatabase gave years; the gazette gives days.
RICARDO JUAN CARLOS LERENA - "19962/95: Lerena, Ricardo Juan Carlos, 6 January
1920, 2001065053080, 6 Barbeque Agricultural Holdings, Randburg, 21 December
1994; Doreen May Lerena." The identity number confirms the birth date out of its
own first six digits.
NUNO FERNANDO LERENA - "6746/71: born on 6 October 1924, Identity No 331/406051W,
of 24 Leiden Road, Gerdview, Germiston, who died on 1 July 1971, and surviving
spouse Catherine Mary Sophia Lerena born on 25 March 1929." The 1950 liquidation
account made his capital payable when he "attains the age of thirty years - i.e.
6 October 1954", which implies birth on 6 October 1924. Two unrelated documents
twenty-one years apart agreeing to the day. The wife is new to this archive.
ROGUE LUIS ARMANDO LERENA - "1518/73", identity 331/402089, of Florida,
Roodepoort. The gazette spells him ROGUE exactly as the national archives index
does, so that spelling is what the clerks wrote rather than an index typo. Short
form, no dates, so his identification as the 1950 estate's "LOUIS" remains an
inference from the middle name and is recorded as one.
ROBERT PAUL LERENA - "1847/50/754: Robert Paul Lerena, RACEHORSE TRAINER, of
Newlands, Cape." The archive had "Trainer" from his own 1940 passport; this is
an independent statement made after his death by the administration of his
estate, and it is more specific.
A trap recorded because it nearly cost a person: the gazette sets two columns and
pdftotext -layout interleaves them. A first pass read "died on 26 June 1971" and
"Bedfordview" into Nuno Fernando's entry; both belong to 6546/71 MARSHALL in the
left column. Caught only because two gazettes gave two death dates for one estate
number. Print context, never grep matches.
Worklist moved with the work: row 17 rewritten - the exposure is materially
smaller now that the three sons are off the commercial source, but Doreen May and
the later generation are still gendatabase's alone, so the decision stands and
the attribution is still not stripped. Row 19 added with the five notices already
located and unopened, including the 2013 one that may settle the Anton Armando
contradiction, and a 1986 notice for "Lerena Racing Stables" that belongs on the
horses page.

commits.subject: The Berroeta control passed - the regiment's book is in the full-text index
commits.body:
FamilySearch came back for about four requests. The one that mattered got
through.
"Capellan del Regimiento Infanteria de Buenos Ayres" returns 22 results, from a
collection titled "Montevideo. Military Award Records 1812-1814", with snippets
reading "...de Berroeta Capellan del Regimiento ..." and years 1789, 1790, 1791,
1792 - the chaplain and the exact years of the book read by hand earlier today.
So the book is indexed. That is what the control was for: it means the absence of
any military collection from the 68 results for "Sancho Llerena" is EVIDENCE
rather than a gap in coverage, and it probably retires the plan to read images
663-950 by hand, which existed only because this was unknown.
Two limits kept open rather than glossed. The 22 hits have NOT been traced to DGS
7713373 - the collection is labelled 1812-1814 while its snippets carry
1789-1792, so the label is unreliable and nobody has resolved one of those arks
to a film number. And the variant sweeps were never run: "Sancho Lerena" and
"Sancho Lorena" were blocked by Error 15 between the control and them. Both are
single searches, and they are row 18.
So the honest statement is that the book is indexed and Sancho is not in it under
the spelling "Sancho Llerena" - not yet that he is absent from it. Machine
transcription of eighteenth-century hands is imperfect, so an index absence is
weaker than a page absence, which is why the eleven images read by hand still
matter.
Worklist moved in the same commit that moved the work, which is the rule
check:worklist exists to hold: row 2 done, row 1 rewritten from running to next
and retitled "now probably unnecessary", row 18 added. 18 rows: 11 next, 3 done,
3 blocked, 1 struck.

commits.subject: Frame the drawing the way two archives already did, on the other five
commits.body:
Two front pages introduced their picture — a heading, a line telling you how to
read it, then the drawing. Five dropped a bare dot-plot in after the doors with
a one-line caption under it, which is why that picture read as dots in a void.
Same slot, same framing, on all seven now: the drawing comes straight after the
three doors, under a heading, with a sentence that says what a dot is, what its
size means, and that this is deliberately not a map.

commits.subject: Adopt the estate work list, and strike the register invented an hour before it
commits.body:
This session was asked whether outstanding work was tracked centrally, found it
was not, and wrote data/open-threads.tsv - the ninth session to invent its own
answer, and exactly the habit that produced a Chip meaning two things and one
chart drawn under three names. The right thing already existed, written first in
the Defranceschi archive and now in the kit. Adopted here; the invented file is
deleted and its content folded in, and the act of inventing it is kept on the
list itself as a struck row rather than quietly dropped.
The pinned kit was b16bea7, which predates both WorkList.astro and
checkworklist.py. Repinned to 60aad58, clearing the cached git resolution first,
which this project has been bitten by before.
site/src/data/worklist.json, 17 rows: 1 running, 9 next, 4 blocked, 2 done, 1
struck. Owners are 12 on this archive, 3 on David, 2 on the kit and estate.
Two rows are owned by the kit and estate rather than by this archive. The
FamilySearch film-and-image addressing method found here - dgs:{film}.{film}_
{image}, which needs no viewer, no ark and no catalogue, and keeps serving while
www is behind Error 15 - belongs to every archive that touches FamilySearch. And
both of this archive's Montevideo film attributions came from reading a
catalogue rather than a film; one held under test and one did not.
Page at /worklist/, linked in the Evidence menu between Open Questions and
Corrections. check:worklist added to package.json and wired into build after
check:kit. Verified the gate refuses: removing an owner and setting a state
outside the five both exit 1.
TWO THINGS CAUGHT WHILE COMMITTING, BOTH REPORTED RATHER THAN ABSORBED.
git add -A swept in notes/SHARED-CONTACTS.md, an untracked file this session did
not write and had not read - the sibling Luwinski session's note, carrying a
named archivist's work address, a commissioned researcher's address and David's
own. This repository is public. It has been removed from the commit and left on
disk exactly as found, for David to place deliberately or not at all.
Reading it then surfaced the second thing: that note records that gendatabase.com
forbids republishing without written permission, and this archive published from
it earlier today in a commit that is already pushed. The people were already here
from the deceased-estates index and NAAIRS; the vital years are gendatabase's.
Logged as row 17, blocked on David. Nothing further from that source is published
meanwhile, and the attribution has deliberately NOT been stripped - doing that
quietly would be worse than the original mistake.
npm run build clean at 628 pages; tools/verify.sh ALL GATES PASSED.

commits.subject: A central register of outstanding work, and a stale errand retired
commits.body:
Asked whether outstanding findings and actions were tracked centrally, this
archive checked and the answer was no.
Errands for David were well kept in data/errands.tsv. gaps.tsv held what cannot
be closed. open-questions.astro held seven narrative themes and had not been
touched all session. What was tracked NOWHERE was the archive's own next
actions, which lived scattered across per-topic TSVs and page prose.
The cost was not hypothetical. The errand "Sancho's 1791 marriage - FIVE FILMED
BOOKS" sat at status "ready" for hours after the act had been found and
published, still telling David to go and find it, and still calling DGS 7713386
"the cheapest test in the archive" after that attribution had been disproved.
Retired here, with all five books' outcomes recorded on it.
data/open-threads.tsv is the single list. Fifteen rows: the Berroeta control
that decides a day of work; images 663-950 of the castrense book; two full-text
collections found and never opened; the 68 results that were only half
harvested; DGS 7713375 with two known acts and nothing else read; the Sanchez
question that cuts against this archive's own argument; the HOJAS SUELTAS
caveat; the real Montevideo index, still unlocated; Cordoba itself, now the
largest unopened door and in Spain rather than Uruguay; the Anton Armando
contradiction, deliberately not merged; the five deaths of 1999; and the one
purchase worth making.
The division is now explicit and written at the top of each file: errands.tsv is
work for a person, open-threads.tsv is work for a session, gaps.tsv is what
cannot be closed at all.
Last row records the rule this session kept breaking - that names in
eighteenth-century hands cannot be read at fit-width - with the three misreadings
that proved it, including one that would have manufactured a Llerena inside the
regiment's own book.

commits.subject: Name the places on the front-page picture
commits.body:
Sixty dots in an empty box with no town, no region and nothing to read. What
was missing was not a coastline — this is a plot and it should not draw
geography it has not got — it was names, and they were in the data all along
beside a count and this archive's own regional grouping.
The largest places are labelled now, biggest first, skipping any that would
land on another label or on a town. The dots take their colour from the region
the archive itself assigned, with a legend in its own words.

commits.subject: The regiment's book read across the marriage year, and a film number the archive did not have
commits.body:
Full text came back mid-session and answered in seconds what this session was
about to do by hand: 68 results for "Sancho Llerena", against far fewer in the
archive's earlier sweeps. Two of the collections are new and unread - the
Montevideo Cathedral Baptism Records 1825-1828, and the Cordon Religious
Marriage Records 1825-1916.
DGS 7713375. The 1789 godparent act is image 551 and the 1811 baptism of Luis -
the archive's best document on Sancho's parents - is image 2410, both resolved
from their arks through the tile service while www was blocked. The archive had
never named this film. It is NOT the castrense film: the Cathedral and the
regiment kept separate books, and Sancho is so far in the first and not the
second.
Images 652-662 of DGS 7713373 read continuously - eleven openings, no gaps,
December 1787 to July 1791, so the month he married and two years either side.
No Llerena, Lerena or Lorena in any of them. The families are Menchero, Arias,
Illescas, Lamas, Sanchez, Martinez, Coronel, Villar, Juarez.
Recorded as a negative over eleven images, not over the book. Images 663-950 are
unread, and this is a scan not a transcription. The hand was misread at
fit-width three times in one sitting - the chaplain as "Mendoza" when he is
BERROETA, a slave-owner as "Llerena" when he is FRANCISCO JUAREZ, a mother as
"Rosalia Illera" when she is PETRONA ILLESCAS. Every L candidate was magnified
before being dismissed, but a name buried mid-sentence in an unzoomed line could
have been missed. Not found and not there are different statements.
And the cheap test is written down for next time: search a phrase known to be in
the book - "Capellan del Regimiento Infanteria de Buenos Ayres", or BERROETA. If
it hits, the book is indexed and the question is settled in one search; if not,
the remaining 290 images are a day's work. The control could not be run - Error
15 returned first, and no zero from a blocked page is recorded as a null.

commits.subject: The castrense books opened, Cordoba la llana identified, and a second attribution that did not hold
commits.body:
gendatabase: David's direct search-results URL checked. It resolves to the same
index and returns the identical 38 rows, "Showing all 38 matching results" - so
nothing was missed through the form. Two details added: a Ricardo Paul Lerena
(TPD M680/1979), another "Paul" in the grandsons' generation, noted without being
believed; and Goris Janse Lerenaar and "Lerenani Matchubani" written down as
explicitly NOT ours, so nobody excludes them twice.
PRIORITY 1 - the Libros Castrenses. DGS 7713373 is not what this archive called
it: its boards say "Uruguay, Archivo de la Curia" and "Montevideo, Archivos
Parroquiales, P. Inmac. Concepcion (Catedral)", roll 84. But the substance held.
Item 5, "Catalogo y Libros Militares", begins at image 623, and at image 655 the
priest names himself: "yo Don Juan Miguel de Berroeta, Capellan del Regimiento
Infanteria de Buenos Ayres, en esta Iglesia Matriz de Montevideo". Neighbouring
entries name the Dragones de Buenos Ayres, and Sancho is "el soldado dragon".
Image 656 is headed Ano 1790; image 660 is headed Ano de 1791 and carries 30
January 1791; 661 carries March 1791. No Llerena in the five images read - and
five images is not a search of a three-hundred-image book.
And the film damages one of this archive's own arguments. At image 660, 30
January 1791, the book baptises the son of "Manuel Sanchez, Sargento de dicho
Regimiento" - while the single 1791 expediente in the whole Canelones
informaciones belongs to "Juan Manuel Sanchez, natural del Reino de Andalucia",
marrying that March. If those are one man, a soldier of this regiment did leave
an informacion at the Canelones vicaria, which cuts against the suggestion that
military jurisdiction explains Sancho's absence. Not established; recorded
because it tells against the preferred reading.
PRIORITY 2 - "Cordova la Llana" is the city of Cordoba. No municipality of that
name exists because it is not one: "Cordoba la llana" is a standing epithet for
the city. And the qualifier does real work - the same castrense book describes a
man as "natural de Cordova del Tucuman", so a River Plate priest had to say which
Cordoba he meant. La llana says Andalusia, agreeing with the 1811 baptism.
PRIORITY 3 - it fails. DGS 7713386 was called "Indices... 1726-1800" and opening
