it "the cheapest test in the archive". Image 300 is an 1887 Montevideo cathedral
burial register; image 1500 is a 1905 one. Two samples of 2,244 do not prove the
index absent, but the attribution is unconfirmed and the errand no longer calls
it cheap. Logged in corrections.
Also logged: the chaplain was misread as "Mendoza" and a neighbouring slave-owner
as "Llerena" at fit-width; at magnification they are Berroeta and Francisco
Juarez. Neither reached the site. Recorded because inventing a Llerena in the
regiment's own book is exactly the error this archive is most exposed to.

commits.subject: gendatabase.com, tried for the first time - and it pays
commits.body:
David suggested it; the archive had never touched it. Its only South African
index was NAAIRS, which returns file references and nothing else. Gendatabase
returns birth, death and marriage YEARS, maiden names and spouses.
Surname Lerena: 38 results across a Verified Death Database, the National
Archives index and an Estate File Database.
The gain: the three sons named in the 1950 estate of Robert Paul Lerena of
Newlands now have death years. Nuno Fernando - estate MHG 6746/71. "Rogue Luis
Armando" - MHG 1518/73, very likely the estate's "Louis" using his middle name,
flagged as an inference and not established. Ricardo Juan Carlos - born 1920,
died 1994, married 1941 to Doreen May Chappell. He carries his great-
grandfather's name: the 1908 enrolment card gives Pablo Armando's father as Juan
Carlos Lerena.
Llerena in South Africa: ZERO. A real null - the first attempt returned the
cached Lerena page with an identical timing figure and was discarded rather than
recorded. It supports the spelling argument: the reduction of Llerena to Lerena
had finished before the family reached the Cape, while Sancho's own 1791 act
still writes Llerena.
Two things recorded as questions, not findings. Anton Armando Lerena is born
1952 died 2003 here, and died 2013 aged 68 in the archive's existing row from
ancestors.co.za - not merged, and possibly two men. And five of the fifteen
death rows carry 1999, including a married couple and two children aged 8 and
13; that is either a family catastrophe or a default-year artefact, and a
summary row cannot say which.
Summary rows are free; full records need a paid account, which this session did
not create and did not pay for. Logged as an errand for David with the one
purchase worth making - the 1994 death notice, because a South African death
notice names the deceased's parents.

commits.subject: Ten tiles, and two of them were not numbers
commits.body:
"Juan Carlos" and "Uruguayan" sat in that row as though they were statistics.
They are two of the best findings this archive has made — a father's name off an
army card filed at the Cape, and what the act behind the one Rosario Lerena says
of her parents — and shaping them into tiles was the worst possible way to tell
anyone. They are in the cards and on their own pages, in sentences.
The years went with them. 1882, 1911, 1931 are the spine of the story and belong
to the story; a tile is for saying how much work stands behind the archive.
Six now, counted at build time: 278 people published, 37 places, 116 sources
consulted, 53 corrections, 39 enquiries raised. The surname count stays.
One thing the rewrite caught: the register tile and the people tile were the same
number. registerCount was literally people.length, so the row said 278 twice
under two different labels.

commits.subject: The marriage act of 8 January 1791, found and read
commits.body:
DGS 8166578, image 2687 - Canelones, Parroquia de Nuestra Senora de Guadalupe,
Matrimonios Libro I, left page, second act. Margin: "Sancho Llerena, y Maria
Fernandes. Casados y Velados".
  "En ocho dias del Mes de Enero de 1791 anos, haviendo precedido justificacion
   de libertad de Sancho Llerena, nat. de Cordova la Llana, hijo legitimo de
   Felix Llerena, y de Rosalia Aguilar, naturales de dicha Cordova... el
   matrimonio que el dicho Sancho intentava con Maria Fernandez, nat. de las
   Asturias, hija legitima de Rodrigo Fernandez, y de Ro[sa] Fernandez,
   naturales de dichas Asturias, y Vecinos de Santa Lucia"
Four things settle. The DATE is in arabic numerals - 1791 - so the noventa/
ochenta trap does not arise, and Apolant's ficha 355 is corroborated by the act
itself. CORDOBA, not Granada: this archive had Cordoba only from unsourced trees
and had said so; the act says Cordova twice. THE PARENTS, independently for the
second time - the 1811 baptism gave Feliz Gerena and Rosalia Aguilar, and this
adds that they were themselves of Cordoba, the first evidence placing that
generation anywhere. And it CORRECTS the trees on the bride: they said her father
was Ramon Fernandez Tresguerras; the act says Rodrigo, as the 1811 act does.
Recorded as unresolved: the qualifier after Cordova reads "la Llana", but the
hand does not separate m from n so "la Llama" is equally readable, and no
municipality of either name has been identified. A lead, not a finding.
Married by Don Juan Francisco Cardoso, Cura Interino - interim because Don Juan
Miguel de Laguna, who signed the 1788 informacion, is "el finado" by February
1789. Witnesses Antonio Villegas and Jose del Rio, the same notary who seven
years later wrote down Sancho's deposition and that he could not sign it.
Found by reading dated anchors, not arithmetic: 2670 = 12 Feb 1789, 2700 = 16
Jun 1792, about nine images to the year. The standing errand asking David to page
the register in his own browser is retired - it needed no viewer at all.
One broken anchor was caught by the gate before this commit, and fixed.

commits.subject: The informaciones matrimoniales, walked - and Sancho could not write
commits.body:
Entered DGS 8166573 at the one image this archive already had, and mapped the
reel by its filming targets and the archivist's pencil dates instead of paging
through it.
Read in full, image 2167, 9 January 1798: Sancho Llerena sworn as the SECOND
witness for Florentino Gomez - not the groom, which this archive had left open.
He had "andado en la Linea de Vicaria algunos anos", and the deposition closes
"y no la firmo porque dixo no saver escrivir". Sancho Llerena was illiterate.
First fact this archive holds about the man rather than his household, and it
sits pointedly beside the 1811 baptism calling him "Don Sancho Llerena".
The expediente we actually wanted is not there. Volumen 6 runs 1776 to November
1790 and ends at image 1459; Volumen 7 opens at 1460 and its first dated case is
March 1791. Sancho married 8 January 1791. The whole of 1791 in the series is one
expediente belonging to an Andalusian named Juan Manuel Sanchez, and by image
1464 the pencil already reads "Marzo 1792". January 1791 falls in the seam
between two volumes - a gap in the filing, not a failed search. Caveat recorded
honestly: image 1461 says "HOJAS SUELTAS", so the order is not guaranteed.
Argues the castrense books to the front: a serving soldier's marriage ran through
the military chaplaincy, which would explain why Sancho is a witness in the
vicaria's informaciones and never a petitioner. DGS 7713373, still unopened.
Method, now in memory: FamilySearch's tile service accepts
dgs:{film9}.{film9}_{image5} as an id, so any image on any film is addressable by
NUMBER - no viewer, no ark lookup. It also kept working throughout an Error 15
block, which takes down www (both /search/ and ark: pages) but not sg30p0.

commits.subject: Pin the kit where a dangling edge no longer kills the chart
commits.body:
The bloodline walk followed every edge carrying a slug and read .parents off
whatever was at the other end. On a graph where a record names somebody the
graph does not carry, that dereference threw — and it did not drop one line, it
killed the whole chart, on a page that built green and passed every gate.
An edge is now followed only when the person at the other end is in the graph.
Also here: the husband-or-wife box is drawn with a dashed border, which says
they are not blood without spending a legend entry on it.

commits.subject: Pin the kit that turned the bloodline chart on its side
commits.body:
Generations were rows, so the width grew with the family. One Blazevic chart
ran 25,008px wide against 616px tall — a 41:1 ribbon with every parent-child
line flattened into a horizontal dash. Generations are columns now: width is set
by how many generations there are, which is small, and a crowded generation
costs height instead, which is what a page has to spare.
Every archive gets it, because the renderer is one file in the kit rather than
seven copies.

commits.subject: The walk to 1791, attempted and not finished
commits.body:
With the login restored I re-ran the three searches the logout had
invalidated - "Fidel Llerena" (26 results, none Uruguayan) and "Maria
Ruedas" (50, none) - both clean this time, against a control of "Sancho
Lerena" returning 100 links on familysearch.org rather than a sign-in
page. The Fidel/Ruedas marriage is not findable by full text.
Then Libro I was walked by tile toward January 1791. The act was not
found, and the file says so.
What the attempt did establish, so nobody repeats it blind: Libro I opens
at image 2590, its first page carrying "1776." in digits at level 12 tile
6_1. Level 12 is genuinely readable for this hand - image 2680 came out as
"En veinte y dos ... de Septiembre de ocho...", with "siendo testigos", "y
por verdad lo firme", "Juan Fran[cisco] ... Cura Interino", and on a
neighbouring tile "Canarias", "proclamas", "intentaba contraer", "del
Canelon".
And that is exactly where it fails. A year written in words straddles tile
boundaries. "de ocho..." is ambiguous between "mil setecientos OCHENTA
y..." and "mil OCHOCIENTOS...", eighty years apart in effect, and the tile
that should have settled it carried a different line of the same page.
Each date costs three to six fetches and often does not resolve.
That is a tool problem, not an archive one. A viewer that renders the
whole opening at once reads the year at a glance; this session's takes
thirty to sixty seconds per image and frequently renders nothing, which is
why tiles were used at all. So the errand is rewritten from "sign in
again" to a ten-minute job in a normal browser, with the entry point, what
to watch for, and the honest note that the two estimates bracketing 1791
between images 2640 and 2720 are unverified - trust the pages, not the
arithmetic.
It also points at the informaciones matrimoniales, which are worth more
than the act: a pre-marriage investigation gives a Spanish groom's
parents, birthplace and time in the country.
Also checked: "Tesguerza" returns exactly the 1826 act and nothing else.

commits.subject: The logout that looked like three nulls, and five reels on a page
commits.body:
FamilySearch logged the session out mid-run. Three searches - "Fidel
Llerena", "Lerena y Maria Ruedas", "Pedro Lorena" - came back with zero
results and no "No Results Found" message. They looked exactly like the
controlled nulls recorded earlier today.
The control caught it, and only the control. "Sancho Lerena", which had
returned three Canelones baptisms an hour before, was re-run and came back
with zero links and a page title of "Sign-in to your account". Every
request was being redirected to ident.familysearch.org.
That is the fourth costume this same trap has worn in a month: a results
page rendering "(0)" while still loading; a Google Books API returning
"totalItems: None" on an HTTP 429; a blocked session returning Access
Denied behind an empty body; and now an expired login. The rule that has
survived all four is the same - a null is not written down until a control
in the same form returns a known result in the same session - and running
the control is the only thing that has ever caught it.
I do not sign in to accounts, so the FamilySearch work stops here. An
errand records what is waiting, all of it located and none of it read: the
Canelones act at DGS 8166578 image 2590 onward, the Libros Castrenses at
7713373, the Montevideo 1726-1800 index at 7713386, and the Fidel Lerena /
Maria Ruedas test.
And item 6 is done, which needed no login. /roadmap/ now carries the five
reels as a table with their DGS numbers and both catalogue record ids,
the index entry itself, why the military books stopped being a hopeful
idea - the 1793 baptism was performed by that regiment's own chaplain and
calls Sancho "el soldado dragon" - and how the catalogue was reached while
its search box was down. Including the warning that image 2631 of the
Canelones reel opens under the title "Colombia, Catholic Church Records"
and cites the Archdiocese of Cartagena. The image is Canelones.

commits.subject: The fix this archive already had is now everyone's
commits.body:
Rule was identical in three archives except for one thing this one had got
right: a label set flex:0 0 auto cannot shrink, so a long one pushed the row
wider than a phone — 31px of horizontal scroll on /roadmap/ and
/photograph-these/. That version is the shared one, so the other two archives
inherit the fix by no longer keeping their own copy.
The horse, the star and the rest stay here. The mark goes into the kit as a
slot; all 9 call sites keep their name= prop.
Verified: every mrule on /photograph-these/, /changes/ and /timeline/ is
byte-identical.

commits.subject: The chart this file promised to match, it now IS
commits.body:
The header said it for months: 'same structure and class names as the Falco
archive, so a reader moving between the two archives reads them the same way.'
That was a promise kept by hand, and by hand it had slipped — max-width 16rem
against 15rem, and a spouse whose 'married' label sat outside the card here and
inside it everywhere else.
Six archives now draw one component. What stays is this archive's own
vocabulary — line means the direct line AND a record read here, which is not
what it means next door — and the note that the machine-indexed second Pablo
Armando is the same man, not a brother.
The Taylor chart on /taylor keeps the same vocabulary for a different drawing,
three generations rather than one person, and imports the kit stylesheet
directly rather than pretending to be a person page.
Verified against a build of the old component: byte-identical markup on
Gilberto Lerena.

commits.subject: Pin the kit that fixed the atlas flow lines
commits.body:
Every archive has been emitting two CSS parse errors on every build from a
stray paren in the kit atlas — the wreckage of :global(.at-flow). Two rules
died with it: the marching dash on the flow lines, and the
prefers-reduced-motion guard meant to stop it.
The second is the one worth naming. A reader who asks their system for no
animation was getting the same nothing as everyone else, so the failure was
invisible — and would have stayed invisible the moment the first rule started
working again.

commits.subject: A branch at the other end of Montevideo
commits.body:
The variant method, pointed at the rest of the family rather than at
Sancho.
Controlled nulls first, recorded as such: "Juan Agustin Lerena" and
"Lerena Traibel" both return No Results Found, against searches in the
same session that return documents.
Then searching FIDEL rather than the surname turned up a Montevideo death
registration of 1889: "ha fallecido VICTOR LERENA de nacionalidad oriental
de veinte y ocho anos de edad, de estado soltero y de profesion
ALPARGATERO, a consecuencia de tuberculosis pulmonar ... el finado era
hijo [de] PEDRO LORENA y JOSEFA SEGUERA, orientales, finados. Abuelos
paternos FIDEL LERENA y MARIA RUEDAS."
Three generations this archive had never seen, and the declaration was
made de oficio - by the authorities, not by family. He died in hospital at
twenty-eight, single, of tuberculosis. An alpargatero makes rope-soled
shoes. Every other Lerena placed in Montevideo here is a hacendado, a juez
de paz, a major, or a senator's household. This is the same surname at the
other end of that city, and it is worth having for that alone.
Whether this Fidel is Sancho's son is NOT established and all three rows
say so. Sancho's Fidel was born about 1799 and the trees give him a death
in 1822 at twenty-two; for this to be one man, Pedro would have to be born
by 1822 and fathering Victor at about forty. Tight but possible - and that
1822 is tree-only and has never been tested against a burial. A second
Fidel Lerena is not ruled out. What makes it worth testing is that Fidel
is a rare forename in this family, appearing once elsewhere, and this
archive worked out only yesterday where it came from: Don Fidel Rey,
godfather at Agustina's baptism in 1795.
The cheap unrun test is named on the row: a Montevideo marriage of Fidel
Lerena to Maria Ruedas.
Also confirmed as already held rather than new: the Justa Pastora hits
(the 1833 Catedral act with "Maternos: Francisco Lerina y Maria
Fernandez"), and both Lerena Lenguas death records, which this archive
found yesterday by the same compound-surname route.

commits.subject: Fix a broken anchor, and the reason it got committed
commits.body:
The previous commit went in on a RED GATE and I did not notice, because I
ran the gate through a pipe:
    ./tools/verify.sh 2>&1 | tail -3 && git commit ...
check-links.py had found a real break - the new /searched/ section carried
an id that was not in the page's own contents list - and verify.sh exited
non-zero. But a pipeline exits with the status of its LAST command, which
is tail, which always succeeds. So the && fired and the commit landed with
a broken link in it.
This is the exact failure verify.sh was written to prevent. Its header
already documents it for `python3 tools/consistency.py | tail -1`, which
swallowed every exit code in this project for a full day in September. I
reintroduced it one level up, on the script whose entire purpose is to
stop that happening.
The anchor is fixed and the section is in the contents list. verify.sh's
header now warns about piping the script itself and gives the form that
works:
    ./tools/verify.sh > /tmp/v.log 2>&1; echo "EXIT=$?"; tail -5 /tmp/v.log
Verified that way: EXIT=0, ALL GATES PASSED.

commits.subject: The variant sweep, turned on Pablo Armando
commits.body:
Spelling the surname three ways found eight Uruguayan documents for Sancho
that this archive had missed. So the same method was pointed at the
question the whole archive exists to answer.
"Pablo Armando Lerena" - No Results Found. "Pablo Armando Llerena" - No
Results Found. "Pablo Armando Lorena" - No Results Found. All three with
the message present rather than a bare zero, and the control run in the
same form and session immediately before - "Juan Carlos Lerena" - returns
two documents.
This is an independent negative by a different method. Everything this
archive knew about his absence from Rosario came from reading the baptism
index end to end and the register act by act for February and March 1882.
Full text reaches documents no index covers, and reaches them by name. It
is not proof of absence - full text covers a fraction of what is filmed,
only three of seven spellings were tried, and a baptism act often names
the child by forename alone in the sentence that matters. It means no
transcribed document in that corpus puts Pablo Armando next to any
spelling of this surname.
The two "Juan Carlos" hits are both namesakes and both are now in the
register with the reason they are excluded. Juan Carlos Gonzalez Lerena
was dispensed the conciliar proclamas at Montevideo in the 1920s - Lerena
is his mother's surname, the same shape as the only Juan Carlos Lerena in
all of Geneanet. The other was born in 1910 at Buenos Aires, son of Rafael
Llerena. Neither can have fathered a son in 1882.
Rafael Llerena is worth keeping for himself: Argentine-born about 1881,
within a year of Pablo Armando, at Calle Cerrito 535 in central Buenos
Aires. Nothing connects him. He sits beside Gilberto Lerena b.1879 as an
unresolved Argentine namesake of exactly the right generation.
/searched/ carries all of it, including what the negative does not mean.

commits.subject: Why this archive has no 'The families' group
commits.body:
Six of the seven carry one, holding between four and thirteen pages. This
archive has exactly one family page — the Taylors, who married in — and a menu
group of one implies a section that is not there.
That is the same rule the canon already applies to the surname: its own group
only where there is more than one page for it. Written into the layout beside
the nav so the next person comparing the seven finds the reason rather than
the hole, and does not fill it to make the chart square.
The Taylors stay under Our line. If a second and third family page are written,
the group goes in and the comment comes out.

commits.subject: The DNA page joins the other three in Start
commits.body:
The last shared page in the estate with two homes: Start on three archives,
Our line on this one. It was not in the menu canon that was applied, so it sat
there afterwards as the one remaining split.
Four archives have a DNA page and all four now keep it in Start, after the
timeline.

commits.subject: An eighth child, and two names the census left out
commits.body:
The variant sweep continued. Searching LORENA as well as LERENA and
LLERENA, and then the phrase "[L]erena y de Maria Fernandez", returned
five more Uruguayan documents this archive had never opened.
Jose Loreto, baptised at Canelones on 11 December 1806, born the day
before. He is in no tree and no census, and he is not in the 1812 padron,
which lists six children and no boy of about five - so he most likely died
in between, which is usually what a household return's silence means about
a small child. No burial has been looked for and none is claimed. The
tree's own prose says the couple had eight children while naming seven.
And the four enslaved people the padron counts in that household without
naming now have two names. Montevideo Catedral, 26 September 1812:
"bautice solemnemente a MARIA MERCEDES, que nacio antes de ayer, negra
esclava de Don Sancho Lerena y de Dona Maria Fernandez, hija de JUANA."
Juana, and her daughter Maria Mercedes, born six weeks before the census
counted her mother without naming her. Both are in the register as people.
Nothing is known of what became of either of them.
From a grandson's baptism of 22 March 1826, two more: the godfather is "el
MAYOR Don Pedro Antonio Llerena", so Sancho's son held rank at thirty-two
where his father had been a soldado dragon in 1793; and the act writes the
grandmother "Maria Fernandez TESGUERZA", which puts Tresguerras on a
second act - this archive had it once, from 1830, and called that a
vindication of the trees.
Also controlled nulls, recorded rather than assumed: "Sancho Serena" (37
results, none Uruguayan), "Sancho Lerina" (5, none), "Sancho Gerena"
(Spanish only).
One small self-correction while publishing. Juana's row had emphasis
around a sentence explaining why the row exists. That is editorial, not a
finding, and the drift check was right to keep asking which page said it.
The emphasis is gone; the sentence stays.

commits.subject: One L instead of two, and three more acts fall out
commits.body:
Every full-text sweep in this archive had been run on "Sancho Llerena".
Nobody had searched "Sancho LERENA". That search returns three Canelones
baptisms that were not among the eighteen already worked through, and one
of them changes where to look next.
1 August 1793. "El Capellan del REGIMIENTO DE INFANTERIA DE BUENOS AYRES
Don Bartolome Munoz; bautizo puso oleo y crisma a Pedro Antonio de la
Ssma Trinidad que nacio ayer, hijo legitimo del SOLDADO DRAGON Sancho
Lerena, y de Maria Fernandez". Pedro Antonio was born 31 July 1793 - this
archive had a tree's "1793" and a padron age of 19. His father's rank is
on a record for the first time: a dragoon, not just a soldier. And the
priest is the chaplain of the Regimiento de Infanteria de Buenos Aires -
the exact unit whose Libros Castrenses of 1781-1814 were identified this
week as DGS 7713373. Looking in the military books for the 1791 marriage
was a hopeful idea on Monday because Sancho was called a soldier. It is
now the first place to look, because that regiment's own chaplain was
serving this family at Canelones two years after the wedding.
30 August 1795. Agustina Ramona, born 27 August, entered in this register
only yesterday from a census age and a tree. Her godfather is Don Fidel
Rey of Montevideo - and Sancho's next son, born about 1799, is Fidel, a
forename that appears nowhere else in this family and that his row could
not account for. The children were named for the people at the font.
27 October 1805. Sancho stands godfather with "Maria Teresa Fernandez de
este Pueblo". The trees give his wife as Maria Josefa (Teresa) Fernandez
Tresguerras and this archive had marked those forenames tree-only. It is
an identification rather than a naming, and it is recorded as one.
The lesson is the archive's own and it keeps having to be relearned. The
surname has seven documented spellings. A search run under one of them is
not a search.

commits.subject: Blood relatives, drawn — from the kit
commits.body:
Choose a person and the chart is built around them: parents above, brothers and
sisters beside, children below, and through them the aunts, uncles and cousins,
as far as this archive's records reach. Every line takes the colour of the
record behind it, at the weaker grade of the two that made it.
The chart, the graph builder, the renderer and the styles are all the kit's.
What is local is one file saying which people to read and who to open on. That
shape is deliberate: BranchRivers was copied instead of shared and the copies
drifted for weeks, so this one travels with its renderer inlined rather than as
a file each archive keeps a version of.
Nothing here is matched on a name. An edge exists only where a record names a
slug — this estate has 94 Marijas and two consecutive generations both called
Ivan Defranceski, and name-matching gave one Pietro five mothers before a count
of parents-per-person caught it.
In the People & places menu, after the person indexes.

commits.subject: Six unopened hits held a child, a birth date and three godfatherings
commits.body:
The same full-text search for "Sancho Llerena" that produced the 1811
baptism returned eighteen Uruguayan documents. This archive already held
twelve. The six it had never opened were worked through.
A new child. Canelones, 9 August 1800: "bautizo solemnemente a una Parvula
de tres dias nacida a quien puso por nombre Justa Pa[st]o[r]a, hija
legitima de Sancho Llerena y de Maria Rodrigo". Justa Pastora was known
here only from her marriage of 1830 and from the 1812 padron's rough age
of 10. She was born 6 August 1800, and the act puts the family at
Canelones between the 1791 marriage and the 1804 baptism of Dominga
Josefa - which is what the padron means by "naturales del Canelon".
But the mother is transcribed "Maria Rodrigo", and that is not her name in
any of the other fourteen records. The discrepancy is recorded rather than
smoothed away, with three readings and no choice between them: a machine
error, though Rodrigo is not a plausible garbling of Fernandez; a clerk
writing her father's forename, since her father was Rodrigo Fernandez; or
a second Sancho Llerena, which nothing supports. The second reading is the
most economical and only became visible on 15 September, because it
depends on the 1811 act naming Rodrigo - which this archive did not have
until that morning. The image has not been opened.
And a correction to Sancho's own row. It said he stood godfather at the
margins of that colony "twice, fifteen years apart" - the indigenous man's
daughter in 1789 and an enslaved man in 1804. Three further pages of the
1804 confirmations name him as padrino, including "Joseph Jimenez esclavo
de Don Luis Jimenez" - a different enslaved man with a different owner
from the Jose, esclavo de Manuel Lopez already recorded. It is at least
four times, three of them on one day, and the pattern is now too
consistent to read as chance.

commits.subject: Felix and Rosalia enter the register, documented
commits.body:
Consolidating the 1811 act across the archive.
Sancho's row gains the act and loses its last weak joint: his parents are
no longer a tree quoting a journal nobody here has read. Maria Fernandez
gains Asturias and her own parents, Rodrigo and Rosa Fernandez - the same
Rodrigo the 1812 padron puts living in the household at 63, "asturiano",
so the act, the census and the trees now agree on him from three
directions. Luis's birth stops being "c.1812" and becomes 9 February 1811,
with his own baptism act in this archive for the first time and a second
forename, Escolastico, that nothing here had.
Felix Lerena and Rosalia Aguilar are in the register for the first time,
as the first generation above Sancho to rest on anything but a tree. Their
rows say plainly what the act does not give: no dates, no places, no
marriage, no other children. The parentage is documented and the people
are not.
Rosalia's row carries the point that matters most about her. For weeks the
matronymic was marked unattested - none of the fourteen Uruguayan records
gave Sancho one - and this archive built a Spanish hypothesis on the idea
that Aguilar came from a grandmother at Granada in 1754. It comes from his
mother, which is simply how Spanish naming works, and the act says so.
/hypotheses/ carries it, replacing the caution written yesterday that the
parentage "rests on a single article nobody here has read". That caution
stood for one day.
And the Revista 15 errand is downgraded rather than closed. Nothing now
depends on it, but the act gives names and nothing else - so if the
article cites a Spanish act for Felix and Rosalia, that is the first
thread into Cordoba, which is still on no act at all.

commits.subject: This was never an evidence chip — it grades placement
commits.body:
Two archives had a component called Chip and they answered different questions.
The other graded how well a claim is evidenced. This one grades how far a person
of the surname has been placed: connected to the line, unplaced but of interest,
excluded.
The evidence ladder is the kit's, and it is the same five words everywhere. This
is local and should be, because "unplaced · of interest" is a judgement only an
archive still looking can make.
Renamed to Placement, which is what it does. The other archive deleted its copy
and moved to the shared ladder, so the name now means one thing across the seven.

commits.subject: The 1811 act names Sancho's parents - and a build fix that is not mine
commits.body:
THE ACT. Catedral de la Inmaculada Concepcion (Iglesia Matriz),
Montevideo, 10 February 1811, found by a full-text search for the phrase
"Sancho Llerena" - a search this archive had run before, returning a
result it never opened.
"bautice solemnemente a LUIS ESCOLASTICO que nacio ayer, hijo legitimo de
Don SANCHO LLERENA natural de ANDALUCIA y de Dona MARIA FERNANDEZ natural
de ASTURIAS. Abuelos paternos FELIZ GERENA y ROSALIA AGUILAR, idem
maternos RODRIGO FERNANDEZ y ROSA FERNANDEZ."
Four things that were tree-only or census-only are now on a parish act,
written while Sancho was alive and standing at his own son's font.
Sancho's parents. Yesterday that rested on ONE un-consulted article -
Felix and Rosalia have no dates, no places and no other children on
Geneanet, only "Family: Revista 15 IEGU" - and every file here said so.
"Feliz Gerena" is the machine's G-for-L, the seventh variant on this
family, and the same one that produced the unresolved "Dona Andugara
GERENA" at Santa Rosa image 131 - which this proves is a real failure mode
on this exact surname.
Andalucia, on an act rather than only the 1726-1858 census. Cordoba
specifically is still on no act and stays a lead.
Asturias for Maria Fernandez, which confirms the Operativo Patagonia
reading from a Uruguayan document - and her parents Rodrigo and Rosa
Fernandez, the same couple the trees give, the same FamilySearch's index
reads at the 1812 font, and the same Rodrigo, 63, asturiano, whom the 1812
padron puts living in Sancho's household.
And it is Luis's own baptism: born 9 February 1811, baptised the next day.
The trees gave "1811" and nothing more.
THE BUILD FIX, which is somebody else's work and needs saying plainly.
Another session is committing here concurrently and had uncommitted
changes in Base.astro moving asset fingerprinting into the kit's new
assetv.js. It did not build. I stashed their file, confirmed HEAD built
clean, then bisected: the cause is a const reading import.meta.url placed
ABOVE a later import in Astro frontmatter. The error is worse than
useless - Unexpected "{" pointing at a plain <meta viewport> tag thirty
lines down. Moving the line below the imports is the whole fix; their
feature is unchanged and now works. A comment says why the order matters
so it does not regress.

commits.subject: Llerena Sancho con Maria Fernandez, 1791 - the index entry is found
commits.body:
Item 1 of the fifteen, and it is the thing this archive has wanted for
seven weeks.
Canelones, Indice de matrimonios 1776-1947, DGS 8166578, image 2531, under
Letra L and the sub-heading Libro I. Read across three DeepZoom tiles at
level 12 on one aligned row: tile 5_5 gives the year column "1791." and a
name beginning "Ll"; tile 6_5 gives "...ena Sancho con"; tile 7_5 gives
"Maria Fernand[ez]".
Until today the date 8 January 1791 came from Apolant ficha 355 and the
VENUE came from nowhere - this archive supplied the word "Canelones"
itself and had been writing it as though it were sourced. A Canelones
parish index now carries Sancho and Maria Fernandez under 1791, and places
the act in Libro I of Matrimonios, items 11-13 of the same reel.
The act itself has still not been opened, and the file says so in its own
row. No folio could be read: this opening's left page is blank, the
entries sit on the right-hand page, and the columns left of the year came
back empty, though other pages of this index do carry folios. So the act
must be found by walking Libro I to January 1791 rather than jumping to a
folio.
Written up with the neighbouring rows, because a single hopeful reading is
worth little. The same tile shows entries in the same hand and format
above and below, and the year column beside them runs 1777, 1778, 1780,
1781, 1783, 1785, 1786, 1787, 1788, 1789, 1790, 1791, 1792 in order. The
row sits in sequence, in an alphabetical L section, with the forename
Sancho and the bride Maria Fernandez - the one part of this man's identity
every record has always agreed on.
What is not verified is the day. The index gives a year; Apolant gives 8
January. Two claims that agree, and the act will settle it.

commits.subject: Ema Sixta's act, and it corrects her sister's surname
commits.body:
Item 4 of the twenty - the last missing ark - and the prescribed route was
wrong.
The errand said to browse the La Union register by DGS through the
catalogue. The register is in full text. A phrase search for "Sixta
Lerena" returns exactly two documents and the first is it: "La Union,
Montevideo, Montevideo. Religious Marriage Records 1902-1934", act 90 of
30 June 1913, ark 3:1:3Q9M-C9B7-T7P2-W. Two earlier rounds failed because
they searched her with Massera as spouse and searched Jose Pedro Massera
by name. The compound had not been tried.
The act gives three things beyond the ark. Her parentage is now on an act
rather than an index - "hija legitima de Don Luis Lerena Lenguas y Dona
Julia Joanico". Both parents were dead by June 1913, "finados", which this
archive did not have. And the witnesses are "Don Jaime Herrera y Dona
Maria Perena Juanico de Herrera".
That last line corrected a name this register had carried wrong. It called
her sister Maria "LERENA LENGUAS" - her father's compound, not her own.
Her father was Luis Lerena Lenguas and her mother Julia Juanico, so she is
LERENA JUANICO, exactly as her siblings Ema Sixta and Candido Jaime are
already named on their own rows. She was the odd one out and nothing had
caught it, even though this archive files her in
lerena-juanico-children.tsv. The act names her compound in her own
lifetime, with Perena the machine's usual mangling of Lerena on this
family.
It mattered for the checking too. The compound-surname sibling test keys
on the two surnames in a row's name, so while she read LERENA LENGUAS she
was being compared against her father's generation instead of her own
brothers and sisters. Renamed across the register, relations.tsv and
montevideo-lerena-lenguas.tsv; the cohort key is now LERENA JUANICO.
The age of 33 on the act is not adopted. This archive settled her birth at
21 November 1876 on three independent records, and said in the same row
that ages at marriage are the weakest date in genealogy.

commits.subject: Derrick Luwinski is named here and nowhere described
commits.body:
The sibling archive removed his date of birth, and his birth year with it, on the
principle that a year is a date of birth with the precision filed off. Two files
here still carried the full date: the direct-line table and the findings note.
Both now record the correction that mattered — his given names were wrong — and
say plainly that he is living and named only. No date, no year.
His site data was already clean; this was working data, but it is tracked and
therefore public.

commits.subject: A fourth key for the sibling checks: who people married
commits.body:
Item 20 of the twenty.
Checks 2, 2b and 2c all ask whether two people are siblings. None could see
the other structural fact the prose carries in quantity: 57 of 268 rows say
who somebody married, as "m. X", "married X", "c.c. X", "esposa de X" or
"viuda de X". Two different rows naming the same spouse is either an
ordinary remarriage - Luis Lerena had two wives and both are here - or the
same person entered twice under two spellings of a surname this archive has
documented in seven forms. The second is an error this archive has actually
made, with Dona Sixta Lenguas on two rows hours apart.
Run unrestricted it produced four findings, of which three were wrong: a
row's prose routinely mentions other people's marriages. The offsets
settled how to fix it. The two genuine matches sat at offset 0 - a
subject's own marriage is stated first - and the three false ones at 163,
291 and 385, describing third parties. So only the opening 120 characters
of the note count, and that drops all three while keeping both real ones.
The surviving finding was worth having. Adela Camiglia and Rosa Maria
Eppens are each recorded as "m. Carlos Lerena". They are two different men:
hers is at Mendoza and fathered Avelino Carlos Lerena, while Rosa Maria
Eppens's is the Uruguayan Carlos b.1885 who landed at Buenos Aires in 1926
"travelling with Rosa M. E. Lerena, an Argentine" - her. Nothing in either
row said so, and a later reader merging them would have invented a
marriage. Both rows now say it.
A settled-case list keeps that answer from firing on every build, the same
way drift.py keeps a PUBLISHED list, and carries the answer and the date
rather than just silencing it.
Tested by planting two rows married to the same woman under LLERENA and
SERENA - this family's actual failure mode. It fires.

commits.subject: The Canelones marriage index is real, readable, and at image 2490
commits.body:
The index of marriages 1776-1947 on DGS 8166578 item 10 is not a
catalogue line any more. It was opened. Image 2490 is headed what reads as
"Letra C" and its columns - surname, forename, folio, year - came out at
level 11 as Cabrera, Canosa, Camelo, Colman, Castellano, Caamano, Cornejo,
Calderon, Coronel, Castrillo, with folios and the years 1846-1849.
The letter L was not reached, and the arrangement is not yet understood:
if one letter really runs 1776 to 1947 before the next begins, C alone
would take some seventy images and the alphabet would not fit the space.
That should be settled by reading headings, not by arithmetic, and the
file says so rather than leaving an estimate lying about.
The reusable part is the targeting method. The page title carries an ark
only for some images, but the grid view's DOM carries one for every
image - each thumbnail's src is .../dz/v1/<ARK>/thumb_p200.jpg. And
thumb_p200 shows the whole opening at 200px, which is enough to tell a
columnar index page from a prose register page at a glance. That is how
the index was found. Level 11 and 12 tiles then read the hand.
With a warning: the grid does not always scroll to the ?i= value. Asking
for 2510 loaded a window of 2341-2470, so the numbers have to be read off
the DOM rather than assumed.

commits.subject: Five filmed books cover 1791, and two of them are indexes
commits.body:
Item 5 of the twenty, and it lands better than expected.
The Montevideo catalogue record is koha:961086, reached the same way as
Canelones - through an image's Information panel, because the catalogue
search box returned "Something Went Wrong" for every query all day. It
names three reels covering January 1791:
  DGS 7713373 - "Bautismos, matrimonios y defunciones, 1781-1814 (del
  Regimiento de Infanteria de Buenos Aires)". These are the Libros
  Castrenses the IEGU list named this morning, and the catalogue gives
  them a regiment. Sancho has been recorded here as a soldado since the
  first day and this archive has never looked in a military register.
  Nothing says he served in that unit - only that he was a soldier in the
  right place in the right decade.
  DGS 7713382 - "Matrimonios, 1726-1826", the Iglesia Matriz marriage book
  itself, unbroken across the date.
  DGS 7713386 - "Indices de bautismos, matrimonios y defunciones (2
  libros), 1726-1800".
That last one is the point. Canelones has an index of marriages 1776-1947
on DGS 8166578 item 10; Montevideo has two index books ending in 1800. So
both candidate parishes have a period index covering 1791, and neither has
ever been opened. That is the cheapest unrun test in this archive - one
alphabetical opening under L in each.
The errand stops being a letter to a parish and becomes a reading job with
five named reels. What makes it hard is the viewer, not the access: it
renders an image in 30-60 seconds here and often not at all, while the
images themselves are unrestricted.

commits.subject: The tile technique, and where the Canelones registers sit
commits.body:
The viewer renders an image in 30-60 seconds here and often not at all, so
browsing 3,222 images through it is not practical. The DeepZoom tiles are,
and level 12 is genuinely readable - eighteenth-century secretary hand came
out as "entes hijo legitimo... impedimento canonico o... y sacramenta".
The working URL pattern, the levels, and the fact that tiles need the
browser session (curl gets 401, page fetch is CORS-blocked, navigating to
the tile URL works) are all written down.
Confirmed by looking: images 2631 and 2900 of DGS 8166578 are both
eighteenth-century marriage register openings, so both sit inside items
11-13, and the thumbnail grid shows no padlocks across the ranges checked.
An arithmetic estimate puts January 1791 near image 2,780-2,820 and the
start of Libro 1 near 2,700 - recorded as an estimate and labelled
unverified, because the attempt to read a date off image 2800 failed: that
image returned no ark, and without an ark there is no tile URL.
The better route is still item 10, the index of marriages 1776-1947, which
sits immediately before the registers on the same reel.

commits.subject: The Canelones marriage register is filmed, and there is an index to it
commits.body:
Items 1-4 and 6 of the twenty.
Two errands said "ready" that had been finished hours earlier - the
Granada act and the Confirmaciones film. Both closed with what was found,
which is the drift this archive built tooling to catch and still produced
by hand. /searched/ still said images 81-148 were unread; it now carries
the finished count, the corrected volume end at 145, and the second
register at Santa Rosa. /roadmap/ now carries the 1791 venue analysis -
the Castrense books, the Curia files, San Jose eliminated.
Then item 6, which turned out to be the important one.
This archive has recorded the 1791 act as unreachable for weeks, on the
strength of a full-text search that found no Canelones marriage register.
The catalogue says otherwise: "Matrimonios, Libros 1-3, (sep.) 1776-1854
(dic.)", DGS 8166578, items 11-13. The register begins fifteen years
before the marriage and runs unbroken. The images are not restricted - the
thumbnail grid shows padlocks where access is blocked and shows none here.
And item 10 on the same reel is "Indice de matrimonios, 1776-1947". An
alphabetical index spanning 171 years, never touched, which should answer
in one opening whether a Lerena married at Canelones in 1791 and give the
libro and folio if so.
The informaciones matrimoniales for 1776-1806 are filmed too, on DGS
8166573 - and this archive has already been inside that series, because
Sancho appears in it as a sworn witness at image 2167. His own expediente,
if it survives, is in the same six carpetas, and a pre-marriage
investigation is worth more than the act.
Two method notes. The catalogue search box returned "Something Went Wrong"
for every query all day while full text and the viewer worked - but a
direct catalogue ID still worked, and better still, any image's
Information tab prints the catalogue link and that reel's item-by-item
contents. That is how koha:1294117 was recovered without the search box.
And image 2631 of this Uruguayan reel opens under the title "Colombia,
Catholic Church Records" and cites the Archdiocese of Cartagena. The image
is Canelones; its own Information panel says so. Recorded because a
researcher trusting the page title would abandon the right film.

commits.subject: Two FamilySearch pipelines disagree, and the index reads Lerena
commits.body:
Item 12 of the fifteen. The plan was to open the 1812 baptism image at
magnification and see whether the hand wrote L or S in "Juan Agustin
Serena y Dona Agustina Perena". The handwriting was still not reached -
the viewer's index panel would not dismiss, and the DeepZoom tiles return
401 outside the browser session. But the viewer surfaced something better
than a guess.
FamilySearch's own image index for that page lists the two godparents as
"Juan Agustin Lerena" and "Agustina Alerena". That is a separate reading
from the AI full-text transcript of the same image, which renders them
Serena and Perena. Two pipelines disagree about the same ink and the index
reads L.
This is the sixth S-for-L recorded on this family and the first time an
independent reading has contradicted the machine on one rather than the
archive inferring it. With the ages from the 1812 padron - Juan Agustin
21, Agustina 17 - the names, the ages and a second transcription now point
the same way. The file and the page both say plainly that this archive has
not seen the handwriting, which is the difference between this and an act.
The same index also names the maternal grandparents at that font as
Rodrigo Fernandez and Rosa Fernandez - exactly the couple the trees give
as Josefa Fernandez Tresguerras's parents. So Micaela, the mother, was
Josefa's sister and the godparents were the baby's first cousins, which is
why two Lerena teenagers were standing at a Malbarea baptism at all. This
archive called that "a plausibility, not a finding" in September; it now
has an index behind it as well as a tree, and the padron independently
puts Rodrigo Fernandez, 63, asturiano, in Sancho's household.

commits.subject: Both Rosario confirmation registers finished - he is in neither
commits.body:
Item 11 done, and the task turned out to have been defined wrong.
FamilySearch came back, so the Catedral film could be finished. Images
81-145 read, every transcript non-empty. With images 5-80 read earlier in
the month, the whole of "Catedral Nuestra Senora del Rosario. Confirmation
Records 1883-1904" is now read end to end and holds no Lerena. Together
with Santa Rosa de Lima, closed the same day, both of Rosario's
confirmation registers covering Pablo Armando's childhood are complete and
he is in neither. He was 8 to 22 across their combined span, which is the
age for it. That route is exhausted for the two parishes with registers
early enough to hold him.
The errand said "images 81-148". The volume ends at 145. Images 146-148
came back empty and looked exactly like the rate limiting that had bitten
twice already the same day - but they carry no ark and their page title is
the bare "Registros parroquiales, - Film # 004531018", where every real
page resolves to the volume name. They are not part of this volume. The
film holds 421 images across several volumes, and image 200 is
Confirmation Records 1904-1918, when Pablo Armando was 22-36 and mostly in
South Africa - identified and ruled out of scope rather than left unread.
The distinguishing sign is now written down, because it nearly cost the
closure: a throttled page still resolves to the volume name, and an image
outside the volume does not. Without that check those three would have sat
as "not read" forever and the register could never have been called
finished.
One hit in 65 images. Image 143 returned SERENA, which is the S-for-L
variant this family carries six times over and had to be answered. Read in
place it sits in a column of given names - Maria Eulalia, Angel, Julio,
Elisa, Serena, Vitora, Jose - so it is the girl's forename, not the
surname. Recorded rather than dropped, so that a hit-count on this film
does not send a future reader back to open it again.

commits.subject: San Jose eliminated, and the military books nobody had considered
commits.body:
Item 5 of the fifteen, and it turns into progress on the 1791 act.
The Operativo Patagonia cohort is now corroborated from outside the tree.
The migration literature gives 41 Asturian founder families from 11
councils - seven of them from MORCIN, the concejo where Josefa Fernandez
Tresguerras was born in 1778 - who founded SAN JOSE, Uruguay on 1 June
1783. So her family plausibly landed at San Jose, not Canelones, which
made San Jose a live candidate for a marriage whose venue has never had a
source.
The IEGU holdings list settles it: San Jose de Mayo has baptisms and
deaths from 1783 but marriages only from 1799. Eight years too late. San
Jose is eliminated as the venue, and its baptisms from 1783 stay worth
asking about for the family's arrival - with the IEGU's own warning that
its indexes carry serious copyist errors.
Reading that list properly also turned up something this archive has never
considered in a month of looking for this act. The Iglesia Matriz of
Montevideo holds three LIBROS CASTRENSES - military registers of baptisms,
marriages and deaths - covering 1781 to 1814. Sancho has been recorded
here as a soldado since the first day, from the Uruguayan census. A
soldier marrying in the Banda Oriental in 1791 has an obvious second home
for his act, and nobody has looked in it. The Curia also holds
expedientes de informacion matrimonial from 1727, and that is the document
worth most of all: a pre-marriage investigation gives a Spanish groom's
parents, birthplace and time in the country, which would settle
Sancho-or-Francisco, Cordoba, and Felix and Rosalia together.
The errand is rewritten from one letter to three, in priority order.

commits.subject: Six trees, and they are not six witnesses
commits.body:
Item 2 of the fifteen, run properly, plus Bauza published.
Geneanet returns six trees carrying Felix Lerena married to Rosalia
Aguilar, which looks like strong corroboration for the parentage used
yesterday to withdraw the Granada reading. Each was opened. It is not.
antoniojosed is the only one with dates - Felix b. about 1725 Cordoba,
married about 1753 Cordoba, Rosalia about 1729 - every value "about", no
Sources section at all. rosanaic gives the same dates and cites, as its
source, a link to antoniojosed's tree. abal2018 and ladissosa carry the
couple with no dates and no sources. jfina carries no dates and cites
Revista 15 IEGU. So six reduce to two origins at most, one of them a
journal article and one a tree of estimates - and jfina's own
acknowledgements credit "mi primo Alejandro Abal", which is where abal2018
and nanabal come from. This archive made the same mistake in September
with three 1846 "Francisco" entries that turned out to be one clerk on one
morning. Copies are not corroboration.
The two camps also disagree about Sancho's birth by thirteen years. The
Uruguayan trees say 1767-1832; antoniojosed says ca 1754, which is what
you get from assuming a marriage in 1753 and a child the year after. The
1812 padron records him as 45, so 1767 - a census against a
reconstruction. Which also means antoniojosed's "about 1753" marriage is
an estimate derived from a guessed birth, not a record. For an hour it
looked like a real coincidence that a Lerena married an Aguilar at Cordoba
in 1753, one year before the Granada marriage of 1754. There is no
coincidence, because the 1753 is not a date from a document.
So item 2 yielded no record of Felix or Rosalia anywhere - no act, no
index entry, no parish. Cordoba as their home rests on one unsourced tree;
the parentage still rests on one unread article. The withdrawal stands,
because a journal citation beats a naming-rule inference, but it stands on
less than it appeared to.
Bauza now has a page. /hypotheses/ carries the 1817 passage in full, with
what it does not establish stated in its own box: he names a family in the
plural with no forenames, so nobody here is placed at those events.
Scribd's index of the 36 IEGU revistas would have said what is on Revista
15 pp.53-54, but its viewer is images behind a login and I did not create
an account. That route is closed, not untried.

commits.subject: Tables were squashed to two words a line on a phone
commits.body:
Column widths on this site are inline rem values chosen for a desktop column,
and on a 390px screen a fixed 22rem leaves the column carrying the sentence
about nine characters wide. Below 600px the content decides instead and the
gutters come in. The shared stylesheet had no narrow-screen rule for tables at
all, which is why every archive did it: this one has 145 inline cell widths.

commits.subject: Repin: the place plot no longer lets one emigrant frame the picture
commits.body:
Fitting the plot from the lowest coordinate to the highest put whichever
relative travelled furthest in charge of the whole drawing. The frame is now
chosen at build time from three candidates — the tightest window holding four
places in five, the same for nine in ten, and the full extent — keeping
whichever separates the most places while still holding seventy per cent of
them. Places outside it are drawn hollow on the edge they left through and
counted underneath.
Measured on each archive's own coordinates, distinct dots before and after:
Blazevic 5 to 18, D'Arcy 18 to 52, Booyzen 28 to 29, Mazza 21 to 22, Lerena
20 to 20. Mazza and Lerena keep the full extent, correctly: those families
really did live on three continents and there is no home cluster to crop to.

commits.subject: Sancho's household: three children entered, and Aguilar answered
commits.body:
Items 11 (part) and 14 of the fifteen.
FamilySearch blocked again with Error 15 after about 150 images across two
films, so the Rosario Catedral tail stops at image 113. Images 81-113 read
clean, every transcript non-empty. 114 and 115 came back empty, were
retried once, and are logged NOT READ rather than as no-Lerena; 116-148
were never attempted. What is outstanding is the small end of that film -
ages 15 to 22 for a boy born in 1882. The register that mattered, 1885-97,
was read long ago and does not hold him.
Item 14 needed no FamilySearch. Three of Sancho's children are now in the
register for the first time - Juan Agustin (b. c.1791), Agustina (c.1795)
and Fidel (c.1799-1822) - from the 1812 Montevideo padron: calle San Juan
No 60, Sancho "andaluz" 45, Maria Fernandez 36, six children all
"naturales del Canelon", his father-in-law Rodrigo Fernandez, 63,
asturiano, living with them, and four enslaved people.
Two of those children close an argument this archive lost against itself.
It had written "Juan Agustin cannot be Sancho's son, who would be a child
in 1812" and talked itself out of reading the 1812 godparents "Juan
Agustin Serena y Agustina Perena" as Lerena. He was 21 and she was 17.
/hypotheses/ now carries all of it, including the correction that retires
that page's own standing note on "Aguilar": it is his mother's surname,
Rosalia Aguilar, per the jfina tree citing Revista 15 IEGU - and the
Granada couple are not his parents. Full text agrees from the other side:
"Juan de Lerena y Aguilar" returns five Madrid hits, "Sancho de Lerena y
Aguilar" returns No Results Found, against that control. The page also now
separates the sourced date from the unsourced venue.
Two tool fixes. drift.py now decodes HTML entities before normalising -
without it every accented Spanish word on these pages normalised to
"padr oacute n" and could never match a register note spelling it padron,
which is why three published findings were reported as silent. And the
three siblings are recorded in PUBLISHED with where they appear, because
the matcher wants "listed" where the page says "lists" - the finding is on
the page, and the entry says who checked.

commits.subject: Checkpoint: Rosario Catedral confirmations 81-105 read clean
commits.body:
Item 11 in progress. DGS 004531018 needs the zero padding - 4531018 alone
returns a blank Film # page, which would have read as an empty film rather
than a wrong URL.
Images 98 and 99 came back len=0 and were logged NOT READ; both read clean
after a pause, at 5,201 and 2,961 characters.

commits.subject: The menu fix took the menu's font with it
commits.body:
An hour ago I stopped the changelog's fold-away styling from leaking onto this
archive's navigation. The override I wrote undid four things where it should
have undone three, and the fourth was the font.
`.topnav details>summary` outranks `.topnav summary`, which is where the nav's
own 12.5px sans is set. So writing font-size:inherit and font-family:inherit
in the override did not fall back to that rule — inherit means inherit from
the parent, and the parent is the page. The menu came out in 19px EB Garamond
and the nav bar grew from 34 pixels tall to 45.
The previous state had the right font for the wrong reason: the changelog rule
was supplying .72rem var(--sans), which happened to land close enough that
nobody would look twice. Removing the leak removed that too, and my override
replaced it with something worse.
Both declarations are now gone, so `.topnav summary` applies as it does on the
other six. Measured against them: Libre Franklin 12.5px, nav bar 34px.
Found by checking all seven menus against each other, which is the only reason
it surfaced within the hour rather than sitting there the way the leak itself
had.

commits.subject: The navigation was wearing the changelog's clothes
commits.body:
Checking that all seven register pages still render found this one, which had
nothing to do with the registers. This archive's menu read ▸START ▸OUR LINE
▸THE WORK, uppercase and letter-spaced at 0.72rem, where the other six read
Start, Our line, The work.
The cause is three rules written for something else entirely. The comment
above them says so: "The changelog's per-entry reasoning, folded away by
default." They select `details>summary` — and the top-nav menu is a <details>
with a <summary>, on all seven archives, so the rule meant for a fold-away
note was dressing the primary navigation.
It stayed invisible because of how completely it hit. On most pages here every
single <details> in the document is the nav — five out of five on the register
— so there was no second case to compare against, and the menu simply looked
like a deliberate choice. It was not: only this archive carries the rule, and
the other six are unambiguous about what the nav is meant to look like.
Measured against Blažević's, which is the same component: text-transform none,
letter-spacing normal, no marker.
The navigation is put back rather than the changelog rules narrowed, because
narrowing them means guessing every place a <details> is used for a fold and
this way nothing else moves.

commits.subject: Santa Rosa de Lima read to the end - he is not in it
commits.body:
Item 10 of the fifteen, and it closes a register.
FamilySearch came back mid-session, so the film that had been paused at 57
of 141 images could be finished. Every image from 6 to 141 now has a
non-empty transcript, 2,111 to 3,629 characters each, searched for seven
spellings. Pablo Armando Lerena is not there. He was 8 to 15 across this
register's span, which is exactly the age for confirmation.
Both of Rosario's confirmation registers covering his childhood are now
read end to end - the Catedral, about 2,500 children, and this one. He is
in neither.
One hit in the whole book. Image 131: "confirmo a Angel, hijo legitimo de
Angel y Dona ANDUGARA GERENA". Gerena is on this archive's own list of
seven OCR variants of Lerena, so it cannot be waved away - but it is a
mother, not the child, and the same paragraph renders a child's name as
"Perero" and a priest as "Jose Mala". A forename transcribed "Andugara" is
not a forename. It is logged as a candidate needing the image at
magnification, not as a find.
The method note is the part worth keeping. Images 86-89 all returned
len=0 in a single batch and the page title stopped resolving to the
record. They were logged as NOT READ rather than as no-Lerena, and image
86, re-read after a forty-second pause, gave 2,970 characters - which
proves the zeros were rate limiting and not four blank pages. Image 22,
which had failed three times across two days, also read clean this pass.
Eleven pages across this film would have been silently certified as empty
if a zero had ever been allowed to count as a read, and the register's own
index page says PAGES MISSING, so the temptation was real.

commits.subject: Repin the kit — and this time check that the repin happened
commits.body:
Spine now omits the fields an archive has not got instead of drawing empty
scaffolding around them, so the seven need the new commit.
The repin itself is the thing worth recording. Rewriting the commit in
package.json and running npm install does nothing to a git dependency: npm
keeps whatever commit package-lock.json already names. All seven reported a
clean install and then built green — on the old kit, with the change absent
from every one of them, and nothing in the output saying so.
It would not have stayed quiet. package.json named one commit and the lock
named another, and npm ci — which is what the deploy runs — refuses to start
when those two disagree. Seven green local builds, seven red deploys.
The repin has to name the package:
  npm install "@daviddef/archive-kit@github:daviddef/TheArchiveKit#<full sha>"
Verified the way it should have been the first time — not by reading npm's
output but by reading the resolved commit back out of the lockfile and
grepping the changed line out of the installed copy.

commits.subject: Correct Derrick Luwinski's name and birth year, and link the sibling archive
commits.body:
This archive recorded Cheryl's first husband as "Derrick Luwinski (b. [date withheld])".
He is LYNN DERRICK LUWINSKI, born [date withheld] — the date is on the MyHeritage
tree and the year is confirmed against his own DNA kit.
His line is now worked in a sibling archive, The Luwinski
(github.com/daviddef/TheLuwinski): a Berlin Jewish father of record, Kurt Israel
Luwinski, who left Germany in 1933 and whose own father Jacob Leibholz was
deported from Berlin to Auschwitz on 26 February 1943; and a Portuguese mother,
Ivone Mota Figueiredo, born at Lourenço Marques in 1924 and buried at Porto.
That archive also finds, and labels inferred, that Kurt is very probably not
Derrick's biological father — 0.0% Ashkenazi Jewish where a quarter is required,
and a closest-match cluster that is one English family with a branch in
Johannesburg. So the hinge between this archive and the Defranceski one is
still blood; the hinge to the Luwinski one may be a marriage only.
Only the two files carrying the error are touched here. Other modified files in
the working tree were left alone.

commits.subject: The menu icon sat twenty pixels below the word beside it, on every phone
commits.body:
Reported from a phone, and it was the same bug on all seven.
Two different things are called .bars in these stylesheets: a stacked chart —
display:flex, gap:7px, MARGIN-TOP:20PX — and the three lines inside the menu
button. The burger rule overrode the display, the width and the height, and
never touched the margin. So the icon inherited a twenty-pixel top margin from
a chart it has nothing to do with, and sat low in its own pill.
A collision like this is invisible on a desktop, because the button is not
shown there at all.
Reset on the burger only; the chart keeps its spacing. Measured rather than
eyeballed: button centre and icon centre now agree exactly, where they were
twenty pixels apart.

commits.subject: Three silent findings published, and a third key for the sibling test
commits.body:
Items 6 and 7 of the fifteen.
The drift check had been reporting the same three findings on every build.
Read individually they were not the same problem.
Roseline Wilhelmina Forbes was already published in full at /direct-line/
- "So Chappell was her married name, not her maiden name. She was a
Forbes." The matcher trips on the word "corrects", because the page says
the earlier record was fixed rather than corrected. That is a false
positive and the honest fix is the allowlist, not prose written to satisfy
a word-match; the entry records that somebody read the page.
The other two were genuinely absent. Gilberto Lerena b.1879, who landed at
Buenos Aires on the Cap Norte in February 1928 as an Argentine national
with a son of the same name, is now on /argentina/ beside the 1895
household he is NOT in - written as an unresolved namesake, which is what
he is. And the naming discipline is now on /taylor/: the same habit that
gave Roque's infant daughter her grandmother Mary Septima's name put Juan
Carlos into her uncle's. The man the enrolment card names and no register
has produced was still being named for in South Africa two generations on
- not proof he existed, but evidence the family believed it and knew what
he was called. I wrote him in as a great-grandfather first and corrected
it; Antoinette was Roque's daughter, so Mary Septima is her grandmother.
Drift now reports nothing stale for the first time.
consistency.py gains a third key. Checks 2 and 2b saw 31 structured
parents and 56 compound surnames out of 265, and a test that sees an
eighth of the register while printing "nothing contradicts itself"
manufactures confidence - which is the whole reason this file exists. But
94 people have a parent named in PROSE, because the acts transcribed here
say "hijo legitimo de X y de Y". Two children citing the same parent are
siblings, and that needs no link to a register row - the cited parent
usually is not in the register at all.
Coverage goes from 30 to 99 of 264, and the caveat still prints, because
99 is still not most of them.
Two bugs found while building it and fixed in the code: prose that follows
a name is not a name (one key came out as 'gilberto 1854" with a birth of
1869 - which would have'), and an act quoted on a parent's own row made
Sancho his own child, in a cohort with his wife.
Tested by planting two siblings three months apart under a shared prose
parent, with single-token names so that neither of the other two keys
could reach them. It fires.

commits.subject: Structured data, an honest lastmod, and the last two hand-rolled blocks
commits.body:
Three findability gaps, all of them estate-wide.
No archive emitted any JSON-LD, on sites whose entire content is people,
places and dates. That is the difference between being read and being found.
The sitemaps said every URL changed today, every build. On a ten-thousand-page
archive that claims the whole thing turned over overnight, and after a week of
saying so it teaches a crawler to ignore the field — worse than omitting it.
lastmod now comes from git: when that page's own source last changed.
And the two blocks the kit had already replaced were still hand-rolled on four
and three archives respectively — the same block rendered two ways, and on
Blažević the figures carried no links at all, which is the one thing the
component exists to enforce. Every number on every front page now opens the
page that earns it.

commits.subject: Bauza names the family once, and it is not a credit
commits.body:
Items 1-5 of the fifteen, none of which needed FamilySearch - which is
still 403.
Bauza's "Historia de la Dominacion Espanola" is out of copyright and all
three volumes are on archive.org, so the citation the jfina tree gave
could be read whole rather than trusted. The tree says the Lerenas of
Canelones were "persona de confianza del Baron de la Laguna... para
vigilar la seguridad y tranquilidad". That is Lecor's own phrase from the
Bando of 15 February 1817, which outlawed resisting Orientals "ellos, sus
familias y sus propiedades" and sent detachments to burn their farms and
put their families aboard the fleet. The tree stops there. Bauza does not:
"Doloroso es manifestar que las mencionadas personas de confianza, fueron
los hermanos Alonso de Minas, los Llerena de Canelones, ... quienes al
frente de grupos cuya totalidad sumaba mas de 400 hombres, se
transformaron en azote de los vecindarios de Toledo, Manga y Piedras,
haciendo impunemente con ellos, lo que era castigado como un crimen en los
patriotas."
He names a family in the plural with no forenames, so nobody in this
register is placed at those events. What can be said stays narrow and is
written that way. Tomes I and II hold no Lerena at all, against a control
of 108 and 503 hits for "Montevideo" in the same files.
The sourcing chain also got one step deeper, and it weakened. Felix Lerena
and Rosalia Aguilar have no dates, no places and no other children on
Geneanet - only "Family: Revista 15 IEGU". So the parentage that was used
yesterday to withdraw the Granada hypothesis rests on one un-consulted
article. The withdrawal stands; it is now labelled for what it is.
Neither Apolant nor the Revista is obtainable online - archive.org holds
neither, HathiTrust bot-checks and would be search-only anyway. Both are
logged as errands with full citations. So is the parish: the IEGU holdings
list, reachable over plain http because its certificate has expired, says
Canelones has marriages from 1775 and informaciones matrimoniales from
1776. The act exists and the parish is named.
One trap caught. Three Google Books API searches returned "totalItems:
None", which reads exactly like a null. It was HTTP 429, quota exceeded - a
control query made it visible. Three nulls were one keystroke from being
written down, on a platform where this failure mode had not been seen
before. The rule is generalised in the file: an empty result from any API
is not evidence until something known-positive returns through the same
call in the same session.

commits.subject: The tree that supplies "Aguilar" names a different couple
commits.body:
FamilySearch blocked this session outright - Access Denied, Error 15 - and
the Canelones films are theirs, so the 1791 act could not be opened. I did
not route around the block. Geneanet was open instead, and the jfina tree
carries a sourced note that answers more than the act would have.
It gives Sancho's parents as FELIX LERENA and ROSALIA AGUILAR, born
Cordoba about 1767, citing Apolant's "Operativo Patagonia" ficha 355.
So this morning's Granada work is withdrawn. "Aguilar" is his mother's
surname - ordinary Spanish naming - not a grandmother's from the 1754
marriage at Santa Ana. The inference that the compound must descend from
that couple was a naming rule applied to a name whose owner is recorded
elsewhere, and the controlled null I logged against them is explained
rather than puzzling: he is not their son. The Spanish findings stay in
the file as Spanish findings; what is withdrawn is that they touch this
family. The search that matters now is Felix Lerena and Rosalia Aguilar at
Cordoba, which is not the search I ran.
Two more things the note settles.
The 8 January 1791 date is not "what the trees say" - it descends from a
named published work with a numbered entry, Apolant, Operativo Patagonia
(Montevideo, Imprenta Letras, 1970). But Canelones appears nowhere in it.
The note's "Concejo de Morcin, Asturias" is the bride's birthplace: Josefa
Fernandez Tresguerras, born 1778 in Asturias, of the Operativo Patagonia
convoy - which is why Tresguerras sits in no Uruguayan index, a question
this archive raised and could not answer. Every file here has been welding
a sourced date to an unsourced venue. The venue is still the best
inference going, because the 1812 padron lists all six children as
naturales del Canelon with the eldest aged 21.
And that padron holds what this archive did not: the household in full,
the father-in-law Rodrigo Fernandez, 63, asturiano, living in it, and four
enslaved people. It also gives Juan Agustin as 21 in 1812. This archive
had argued against itself that "Juan Agustin cannot be Sancho's son, who
would be a child in 1812" - bad arithmetic, withdrawn. He and his sister
Agustina, 17, are the two godparents written "Serena" and "Perena" at that
1812 font. The archive talked itself out of a correct reading with an age
it never checked.
The earlier verdict that the 1791 register is "probably not digitised" is
also overstated: it rested on a full-text search, and full text covers a
fraction of what is filmed. Guadalupe de Canelones has marriage books from
1775. Whether its images are browsable has never been checked, and that is
the first job when the block lifts.

commits.subject: A 404 that navigates, a share card, and styles for print
commits.body:
None of the seven had any of the three.
A mistyped address — or one of the URLs these archives have retired and
redirected over the years — fell through to GitHub's own 404, which offers no
way back in. This one says what happened in a line and then hands over the
ways in, because an archive's 404 should not apologise, it should navigate.
The share card is typographic: the archive's name, its own one-line thesis,
its own accent, and no imagery at all — so nothing on it can be mistaken for
a photograph this family does not have. The kit already emitted og:image when
a file existed; six archives simply had no file.
And print. These are documents people take to a registry office, and printing
one dropped its sources. Links now expand to their addresses, because a
printed claim without its source is just an assertion.
Writing the 404 found a latent crash. Base referenced `description` without
declaring it, saved only by `dek ||` short-circuiting before it — so on three
archives ANY page without a dek would have failed the build. There had never
been one until now.

commits.subject: The Granada act, and the son who signed himself Lerena y Aguilar
commits.body:
Geneanet left a fifty-year span and an errand: open the act for an exact
date. The act is FamilySearch 1:1:C9WG-BGW2 - Sancho de Lerena y Armenta,
born Cordoba, son of Sancho de Lerena y Velasco and Maria Antonia de
Armenta y Guebara, married Ana Maria de Aguilar of La Malaha at Santa Ana,
Granada, 17 November 1754. Two generations above the groom, and the image
is marked unavailable.
The full text carried it further than the index could. "Lerena y Armenta"
returns 55 hits: Madrid notarial records 1766-1808, so the groom became a
vecino of Madrid; and a Cordoba testament of 14 June 1751 witnessed by his
brother Antonio. Then the load-bearing one - a Madrid act of 27 March 1790
signed, between the witnesses and the notary, "Juan de Lerena y Aguilar".
One man, that compound. The name the trees give our Sancho is a name real
people bore, in the right family and generation.
Three things this commit refuses to claim.
The Cordoba on that act is the 1754 groom's birthplace, not the Uruguayan
Sancho's. I wrote it into the register as if it settled this row's
Cordoba-versus-Granada question, caught it, and corrected both files: what
closed is a question about the Spanish record, and the Uruguayan
birthplace is exactly as open as it was yesterday.
The one Montevideo hit for "Lerena y Aguilar" would have been the bridge.
Opened, it reads "padrinos Mauricio Lerena y Petrona Aguilar" - two
godparents, "y" meaning "and". The same shape as the Santo Oficio trap: a
phrase search cannot tell a compound from a conjunction.
And the search that would have settled it - the exact phrase "Sancho de
Lerena y Aguilar" - rendered "(0)" with no "No Results Found" line, no
control, and the next request returned "Access Denied - Error 15". That
zero is not recorded as a null. Re-running it with a control is the first
job when the block lifts.
A controlled null did hold: no indexed baptism names that couple as
parents in Spain, against a control of 12. It means no indexed baptism,
not no children - the Madrid signature proves otherwise.
Also bumps the kit pin to d7e3fce, which has the NotFound component an
uncommitted 404 page in the tree was importing; the build could not run
without it.

commits.subject: Repin: the gazetteer no longer plots a town on a shop
commits.body:
Thirty-three places across the estate were sitting on streets, bus stops and
a furniture shop — right country, wrong kind of thing, so nothing caught them.

commits.subject: Geneanet explains "Aguilar", and it points at Granada
commits.body:
David's brief said Geneanet was already blocked once and not worth trying
scripted. It was not blocked today, and it answered a question this archive
spent the whole day calling unattested.
Two Spanish archive indexes - the Index des mariages catholique de Grenade
and Spain, Marriages 1565-1950 - carry a marriage of SANCHO LERENA y
ARMENTA to ANA MARIA DE AGUILAR, Diocese of GRANADA, between 1725 and 1775.
A son of that couple would be styled LERENA y AGUILAR. Which is exactly the
name every tree gives the Sancho born in 1767. So "Aguilar" - absent from
all fourteen Uruguayan records, and marked here this morning as coming from
a tree and from nowhere read - is a real Spanish matronymic pointing at a
grandmother, not a habit somebody invented.
NOT ADOPTED. The index is read and the image is not; the date range is a
fifty-year span; and nothing yet joins that couple to a son born in 1767.
What changed is that an unattested word became a testable claim in a named
diocese - the first thing this archive has ever held that could document
this family in Spain. Logged as an errand with the test.
It also puts GRANADA against the trees' CORDOBA - ckurti says ZUHEROS,
Cordoba - where the Uruguayan census says only ANDALUZIA, which both
satisfy, while the surname's own home town of Llerena is in EXTREMADURA.
That tension is sharpened, not resolved.
And four trees give Sancho a death in 1832, where this archive has none. If
true, his son's 1836 marriage petition names a dead man, which is ordinary.
THE CENTRAL NULL HOLDS ON A THIRD PLATFORM. "Juan Carlos Lerena" returns
exactly one result in all of Geneanet - a "del Campo Lerena", where Lerena
is the second surname. He is absent from FamilySearch, from WikiTree and
from Geneanet alike.
AND verify.sh NOW BUILDS FROM CLEAN. It failed on a stale dist - leftovers
from this afternoon's broken build made astro report a missing chunk. rm
